**Example 1.2**   John undertook a diagnostic test for heart disease. It is known that 1% of the whole population suffers from the disease. Suppose that 95% of patients (having disease) would be diagnosed by the test as positive, i.e., the accuracy of the test is 95%. On the other hand, 95% of healthy individuals would be correctly diagnosed as negative. Unfortunately, John's test result was positive.

Let ![upper A](images/c01-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the event of John having heart disease and ![upper B](images/c01-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be the event of having a positive test result. Then we have:

![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper B vertical-bar upper A right-parenthesis equals 0.95 equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper B overbar vertical-bar upper A overbar right-parenthesis period](images/c01-math-0056.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#256;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> ![FIGURE 1.1 Comparison between MLE (a) and Bayesian inference (b). MLE draws the conclusion ModifyingAbove theta With Ì‚ equals 5, while Bayesian inference deduces that the conditional probability of normal theta equals 5 given the sample is the highest, yet it does not eliminate other possible values as the true parameter value of theta.](images/c01f001.png)

[**FIGURE 1.1**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0001) Comparison between MLE (a) and Bayesian inference (b). MLE draws the conclusion ![ModifyingAbove theta With Ì‚ equals 5](images/c01-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, while Bayesian inference deduces that the conditional probability of ![normal theta equals 5](images/c01-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> given the sample is the highest, yet it does not eliminate other possible values as the true parameter value of ![theta](images/c01-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>.

Prior to the test, we know ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis equals 0.01](images/c01-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math>. Given the positive result, the conditional probability of John having the disease becomes

[(1.11)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0056)![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper A vertical-bar upper B right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 0.95 times 0.01 Over 0.95 times 0.01 plus 0.05 times 0.99 EndFraction almost-equals 0.16 period](images/c01-math-0057.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>0.95</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>0.95</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>0.16</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Therefore, even though this diagnostic test has seemingly high accuracy, the probability that John really suffered from the disease given the positive diagnosis result is fairly low. Actually, as we shall elaborate in [Section 10.6](#c10.xhtml#head-2-139), once diagnosed as positive, John can only be classified as either true positive (TP) or false positive (FP), and the quantity ([1.11](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0056)) is exactly the precision of the diagnosis, defined as:

![Precision colon equals StartFraction TP Over TP plus FP EndFraction equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper A vertical-bar upper B right-parenthesis period](images/c01-math-0058.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Precision</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>TP</mtext><mrow><mtext>TP</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>FP</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

**(I) Normal Distribution with Known Variance**

We here present a special case of Bayesian inference for the mean parameter of a normal distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; in particular, we first assume that the variance ![sigma squared](images/c01-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> is known and only make inference on the unknown mean ![mu](images/c01-i0523.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. The case when ![sigma](images/c01-i0524.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is unknown is discussed at the end of this section.

Let ![bold x equals left-brace normal x Subscript i Baseline right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c01-i0525.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> be a random sample from ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0526.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then given ![mu](images/c01-i0527.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, the density of ![normal x Subscript i](images/c01-i0528.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is:

(1.12)![f Subscript normal x Sub Subscript i Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over StartRoot 2 pi sigma squared EndRoot EndFraction exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline minus mu right-parenthesis squared Over 2 sigma squared EndFraction right-parenthesis comma for x Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R comma](images/c01-math-0059.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

and the conditional joint density of ![bold x](images/c01-i0529.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> given ![mu](images/c01-i0530.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is:

(1.13)![f left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts f Subscript normal x Sub Subscript i Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis period](images/c01-math-0060.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

In the Bayesian framework, the knowledge of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is considered uncertain, and its uncertainty is described by a (subjective) probability distribution. By Bayes' theorem, the conditional density of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> given that the random sample ![bold x equals bold-italic x](images/c01-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></math> is:

(1.14)![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis Over integral Subscript negative infinity Superscript infinity Baseline f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar nu right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis nu right-parenthesis d nu EndFraction comma](images/c01-math-0061.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is known as the *prior* distribution of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, and ![f left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is known as the *posterior* distribution of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> given the sample. Without any prior knowledge, we usually prefer the prior to be uniform over ![double-struck upper R](images/c01-i0538.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> so that ![normal mu](images/c01-i0539.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> takes any possible real value with equal probability before training, while noting that such a distribution is ill-posed as it cannot be integrated to 1. Alternatively, we may assume the prior distribution to be normal with mean ![mu 0](images/c01-i0540.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and variance ![sigma 0 squared](images/c01-i0541.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, i.e., ![normal mu tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0542.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; indeed, it will resemble a uniform distribution over ![double-struck upper R](images/c01-i0543.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> as ![sigma 0 squared right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0544.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, as shown in [Figure 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0002), which justifies this choice of prior.

![FIGURE 1.2 Density of script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis with sigma 0 squared equals 1 (red solid), 5 (orange dashed), 10 (blue dotted) and 20 (green dot-dashed).](images/c01f002.png)

[**FIGURE 1.2**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0002) Density of ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with ![sigma 0 squared equals 1](images/c01-i0546.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (red solid), 5 (orange dashed), 10 (blue dotted) and 20 (green dot-dashed).

We next derive the posterior distribution ![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Let

![upper C colon equals integral Subscript negative infinity Superscript infinity Baseline f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar nu right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis nu right-parenthesis d nu](images/c01-math-0062.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></math> 

be the normalizing constant, then the posterior can be rewritten as:

[(1.15)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0062)![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over upper C EndFraction f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis comma](images/c01-math-0063.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>C</mi></mfrac><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

which integrates to 1. For notational convenience, we further denote ![beta colon equals StartFraction 1 Over sigma squared EndFraction](images/c01-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> and ![beta 0 colon equals StartFraction 1 Over sigma 0 squared EndFraction](images/c01-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></math>; formally, such reciprocals of the variance of a normal distribution are called the *precision*. Since the prior distribution is ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we have:

where the proportionality constant is independent of ![mu](images/c01-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. Then, we expand the exponent in ([1.16](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0063)) as:



where the constants ![k 1](images/c01-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![k 2](images/c01-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are independent of ![mu](images/c01-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. By writing

and substituting ([1.17](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0064)) and ([1.18](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0065)) into ([1.16](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0063)), we see that

Hence, we conclude that the posterior distribution of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is still a normal distribution but with a mean ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> and variance ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1](images/c01-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, i.e., ![normal mu vertical-bar bold x equals bold-italic x tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu Subscript n Baseline comma beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

As mentioned before, to mimic a uniform prior, we simply let ![sigma 0 squared right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>. Then in the limiting case, ![beta 0 equals 0](images/c01-i0561.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![mu Subscript n Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline comma](images/c01-i0562.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> i.e., the sample mean ![x overbar Subscript n](images/c01-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math> of the training data; this result is consistent with the maximum likelihood estimator of ![mu](images/c01-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. On the other hand, as ![beta 0 right-arrow 0](images/c01-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, the variance of the posterior distribution tends to

![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over n beta EndFraction equals StartFraction sigma squared Over n EndFraction comma](images/c01-math-0068.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

which decreases in magnitude with ![n](images/c01-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>; graphically, the bell-shaped curve in [Figure 1.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0003) would degenerate at ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>.

For a small sample size ![n](images/c01-i0568.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, we have a rather low confidence that the true value of ![mu](images/c01-i0569.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is equal to ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0570.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, in the sense that the posterior variance ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1](images/c01-i0571.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is not too small. This confidence increases with ![n](images/c01-i0572.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and eventually becomes certain as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0573.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, by then ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-arrow 0](images/c01-i0574.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> which further implies ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue normal mu minus mu Subscript n Baseline EndAbsoluteValue greater-than epsilon vertical-bar bold x equals bold-italic x right-parenthesis right-arrow 0](images/c01-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for any ![epsilon greater-than 0](images/c01-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> in light of *Chebyshev's inequality*. This is also consistent with the conclusion drawn by using MLE. In this way, we may consider *Bayesian inference* as supplementing MLE.

Secondly, from ([1.18](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0065)), the posterior mean ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is indeed the weighted average of the sample mean ![x overbar Subscript n](images/c01-i0578.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math> and the prior mean ![mu 0](images/c01-i0579.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, with their respective weights proportional to ![n beta](images/c01-i0580.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></math> and ![beta 0](images/c01-i0581.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>: the weight for ![x overbar Subscript n](images/c01-i0582.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math> in ![mu Subscript n Baseline equals StartFraction n beta x overbar Subscript n Baseline plus beta 0 mu 0 Over n beta plus beta 0 EndFraction](images/c01-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>, namely ![StartFraction n beta Over n beta plus beta 0 EndFraction](images/c01-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>, is known as the *credibility factor* in actuarial science. For any fixed value of ![sigma 0 squared](images/c01-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> (or equivalently, ![beta 0](images/c01-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>), ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> always depends increasingly more on ![x overbar Subscript n](images/c01-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math> than ![mu 0](images/c01-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> when ![n](images/c01-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is large, meaning that for a sufficiently large sample, the choice of prior does not significantly affect the posterior estimate of ![mu](images/c01-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>.

![FIGURE 1.3 The posterior distribution f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis.](images/c01f003.png)

[**FIGURE 1.3**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0003) The posterior distribution ![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Let us illustrate this claim using a concrete example. We generate a random sample of size ![n](images/c01-i0592.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> from ![script upper N left-parenthesis 2 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and perform Bayesian inference on the mean ![mu equals 2](images/c01-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> with a prior distribution of ![script upper N left-parenthesis negative 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by pretending that we did not know the mean. [Figure 1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0004) shows the posterior distributions of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, and the posterior mean and variance are denoted by ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0597.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> and ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c01-i0598.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, respectively. We can observe that the posterior distribution of the mean detaches from the prior distribution and gets closer to the true value of 2 as ![n](images/c01-i0599.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> increases.

**(II) Mathematical connection between MLE and Bayesian inference**

We next provide another mathematical perspective to justify the connection between Bayesian inference and MLE in general. Recall the posterior distribution formula ([1.15](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0062)):

![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar normal x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over upper C EndFraction f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis period](images/c01-math-0069.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>C</mi></mfrac><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

For the common choice of the prior distribution ![pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0602.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as a constant function independent of ![mu](images/c01-i0603.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> (which can be made well-posed by restricting it to compact domain), we have ![f left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis proportional-to f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0604.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8733;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and the optimal point ![mu](images/c01-i0605.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> maximizes both the posterior distribution ![f left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0606.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and the likelihood function ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0607.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> simultaneously, which implies agreement between MLE and Bayesian inference. A similar interpretation can be drawn if the likelihood function ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x vertical-bar mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0608.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> “dominates” the prior distribution ![pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0609.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> especially when the domain for ![mu](images/c01-i0610.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is bounded. This observation serves as another justification for considering Bayesian inference to be in some sense an extension of MLE.

![FIGURE 1.4 Posterior distributions of normal mu with different values of n.](images/c01f004.png)

[**FIGURE 1.4**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0004) Posterior distributions of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0600.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> with different values of ![n](images/c01-i0601.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

**(III) Inference on the Sampling Distribution**

Besides the parameters of the distribution of ![bold x](images/c01-i0611.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, sometimes we are also interested in estimating the distribution itself. Following the previous example, with the knowledge of ![mu](images/c01-i0612.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma squared](images/c01-i0613.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, the distribution of ![normal x](images/c01-i0614.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. However, the actual value of ![mu](images/c01-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is unknown, hence we have to make use of the posterior distribution ![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to describe the distribution of ![normal x](images/c01-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, under the assumption that ![sigma squared](images/c01-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> is known.

By virtue of Bayes' theorem, the predictive distribution of ![normal x Subscript n plus 1](images/c01-i0620.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> given the sample ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline](images/c01-i0621.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is simply the conditional distribution of the feature observation ![normal x Subscript n plus 1](images/c01-i0622.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> given the sample, so it is the weighted average of the conditional distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0623.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of ![bold x](images/c01-i0624.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> with weights ![f Subscript normal mu vertical-bar bold x Baseline left-parenthesis mu vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0625.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, i.e.,

Note that the exponent of the first term on the right-hand side can be rewritten as:

where the constant ![c](images/c01-i0630.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is independent of ![x](images/c01-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, while the integrand in the second term is just proportional to a normal density with mean ![StartFraction beta Subscript n Baseline mu Subscript n Baseline plus beta x Over beta Subscript n Baseline plus beta EndFraction](images/c01-i0632.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> and variance ![StartFraction 1 Over beta Subscript n Baseline plus beta EndFraction](images/c01-i0633.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>, hence

Altogether this yields

![ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis proportional-to exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction left-parenthesis x minus mu Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis squared Over 2 left-parenthesis beta Superscript negative 1 Baseline plus beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction right-parenthesis comma](images/c01-math-0076.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8733;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

which implies that the predictive distribution is ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu Subscript n Baseline comma beta Superscript negative 1 Baseline plus beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0634.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>.

We observe that an additional factor ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1](images/c01-i0635.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> appears in the variance of this predictive distribution compared with its original conditional distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0636.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given ![left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0637.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; this reflects the additional uncertainty regarding the convergence of ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0638.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> to ![mu](images/c01-i0639.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. Recall that ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1](images/c01-i0640.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is the posterior variance of ![normal mu](images/c01-i0641.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> given ![bold x equals bold-italic x](images/c01-i0642.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></math>, which decreases to zero with the increase of the sample size ![n](images/c01-i0643.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and so does the variance of this predictive distribution. That means as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0644.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, ![beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-arrow 0](images/c01-i0645.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and the variance of ![normal x](images/c01-i0646.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> reduces to ![beta Superscript negative 1 Baseline equals sigma squared](images/c01-i0647.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, which echoes the convergence of ![mu Subscript n](images/c01-i0648.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> towards the true value of ![mu](images/c01-i0649.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. Altogether this implies that the predictive distribution of ![normal x Subscript n plus 1](images/c01-i0650.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> converges to the true distribution as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0651.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>.

As an illustration, we revisit the example in [Figure 1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0004), where the samples are drawn from ![script upper N left-parenthesis 2 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0652.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and we perform Bayesian inference on the mean with the prior distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis negative 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0653.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In [Figure 1.5](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0005), we plot the predictive distribution of ![normal x Subscript n plus 1](images/c01-i0654.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> for various values of sample size ![n](images/c01-i0655.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, namely ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu Subscript n Baseline comma s Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline colon equals beta Superscript negative 1 Baseline plus beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0656.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (in solid lines), with the true distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis 2 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0657.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (in dashed line), and clearly the former converges to the latter as ![n](images/c01-i0658.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> increases.

**(IV) Normal Distribution with Unknown Variance**

In Bayesian inference, we can choose virtually any arbitrary distribution as the prior ![pi left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0661.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. However, in practice, we usually prefer to choose ![pi left-parenthesis mu right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0662.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that could simplify the expression of the posterior distribution ([1.15](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0062)). One common choice can be warranted by the concept of *conjugate prior* for the likelihood function, so that the prior distribution itself and its corresponding posterior one belong to the same family of distribution. For instance, the prior distribution of ![normal mu tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0663.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> introduced earlier in the section is a conjugate prior for the likelihood function of a normally distributed sample, since the posterior ![normal mu vertical-bar bold x equals bold-italic x tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu Subscript n Baseline comma beta Subscript n Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0664.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is also a normal distribution.

Let us illustrate the technique by studying the extended case when both parameters ![mu](images/c01-i0665.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma squared](images/c01-i0666.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> of the normal distribution are unknown. For notational simplicity, we use the precision ![lamda equals sigma Superscript negative 2](images/c01-i0667.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> instead of variance, then we have ![normal x vertical-bar left-parenthesis normal mu equals mu comma normal lamda equals lamda right-parenthesis tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma lamda Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0668.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. With observations ![bold-italic x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0669.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the likelihood function reads:

We conclude this section with a remark on the practical use of normal-Wishart distributions in actuarial science. In credibility theory, they have been widely adopted in the formulation of hierarchical models, such as models for severity per claim, which helps to determine the pure premium by multiplying the estimated mean annual claim frequency and the estimated mean severity per claim to estimate the mean of the annual aggregate loss. In addition, these models can also facilitate an efficient estimation of the variance of each individual, leading to a justifiable pricing of the risk premium for the policyholders; see [\[12\]](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0012) for example. Meanwhile, in the rise of the trendy *evolutionary credibility theory*, which allows for time-varying mean and variance, the incorporation of temporal structures is inevitable for enhancing the practical value of the normal-Wishart model. A possible resolution has been proposed in a more recent study [\[3\]](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0003) under a semi-parametric evolutionary setting, allowing simultaneous estimation of both mean and variance of the policyholder at each time point based on his/her past claim history; this formulation includes the class of static normal-Wishart models above as an interesting special case, and can hence be regarded as its viable extension with the presence of a temporal dependence structure. We anticipate more research developments to emerge along this direction.

# CHAPTER 2  
Introduction to Python and R

 

## 2.1 WHAT IS PYTHON?

Python is used *very* widely as a scripting language. For instance, *Pixar*

In Python, we can enjoy the following features:

1.  No need to declare the types of variables. For example, we write `x = 1` in Python compared to `int x = 1` in `C++`. You can first write `x = 1` (an integer), then `x = "statistics"` (a string) in the later parts of the same programme;
2.  The environment, in which you work, lets you type bits of code and allows you to see what happens without an intermediate compiling step, making experimentation and testing very simple;
3.  It is very easy to read, and uses English keywords and natural-sounding syntax, for instance,
    
    **Example**
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0001.png)
4.  Instead of using curly braces to delimit code blocks, Python uses (for instance) 4 whitespace indentations (in fact any number of indentations is allowed as long as the practice is consistent throughout the programme). Correctly nesting your code now has a semantic meaning.

Python is similar to Java in the sense that it also handles your memory management: it allocates memory for different uses, and has the capacity to free up that memory once it is no longer needed. In the rest of this book, the Python coding shown is consistent with version 3.9 of Python.

 

## 2.2 WHAT IS R?

**R** is a free and integrated programming language for statistical computing and graphical display. It is widely used among probabilists, statisticians and data scientists. Some elementary statistical tests and functions are already built in **R**, such that no extra libraries have to be called out. The name **R**

 

## 2.3 PACKAGE MANAGEMENT IN PYTHON AND R

Python and **R** are two very popular programming languages for machine learning and deep learning developers, and there are hundreds of packages and libraries available online.

In Python, one cannot install the packages directly in the console. Using *Anaconda* ![FIGURE 2.1 Typing “pip install tensorflow” in Anaconda prompt.](images/c02f001.png)

[**FIGURE 2.1**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0001) Typing “pip install tensorflow” in *Anaconda prompt*.

Here `pip` is used to install the Python related packages. There is another command `conda`, which is used to install packages written in any languages available in *Anaconda*. After the installation, we can import the package in the console by typing:

![](images/c02-gra-0002.png)

Here `tf` is used as a self-defined, short-handed notation for `tensorflow`. The tensorflow package is widely used for deep learning. It has an advanced version that utilises the full power of *Graphics Processing Unit* (GPU), which is called the `tensorflow-gpu`. It significantly reduces the training time of a deep learning model, but it requires a decent GPU and additional installations of software *Compute Unified Device Architecture* (CUDA) and *CUDA Deep Neural Network library* (cuDNN). Moreover, the importation of `tensorflow-gpu` is achieved by the command “`import tensorflow as tf`”; GPU will then automatically be used instead of CPU. We can check our CPU and GPU by:

![](images/c02-gra-0003.png)![](images/c02-gra-0004.png)

Here “`GeForce RTX 2070 SUPER`” is the GPU used and the reference index for this GPU is 0. If there exists another GPU in use, the reference index for the second GPU is 1, and so on. The memory limits for CPU and GPU are shown in bytes, and we see that, for instance, the limit of the present GPU is 30 times more than that of CPU.

Meanwhile, In **R**, the installation and the importation of packages are done directly in the console:

![](images/c02-gra-0005.png)

Here `e1071` is one of the packages for building a *support vector machine* (SVM) model in **R**. This SVM model will be discussed in detail in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#head-2-145).

 

## 2.4 BASIC OPERATIONS IN PYTHON AND R

In this section, some basic operations in Python and **R** which are essential for statistical computing are briefly described. For more comprehensive treatments of these two languages, we refer the reader to \[2, 4, 5, 6\]. The dataset `fin-ratio.csv` (see [Example 1.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-fea-0006)) is used as an illustration for the first and the second items:

1.  **(I)** **Read and Write csv/txt Files**:
    
    `csv` (Comma Separated Values) files or `txt` (TeXT) files are two common file types for data storage. In Python, we need the `pandas` (deriving its name from PANel DAta, *i.e*. observations over multiple time periods for the same object) library:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0006.png)
    
    Note that `data` must be a `pandas.DataFrame` object in order to use the `to_csv()` function. In **R**, there is no need to import any libraries for this action.
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0007.png)
2.  **(II)** **Computations of Sample Mean, Sample Variance, and Sample Covariance Matrix**:
    
    In Python, the `pandas` library have built-in functions for sample means, sample variances, and sample covariances.
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0008.png)![](images/c02-gra-0009.png)
    
    In **R**, there is no need to import any libraries for this action.
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0010.png)
    
    Here the `apply()` function “applies” a function specified by the parameter `FUN` by returning a vector along the dimension as specified by the parameter `MARGIN`, in which the argument `MARGIN=2` indicates the function is applied on the second dimension, *i.e*. along the *column* direction.
    
3.  **(III)** **Building a Mathematical Function**:
    
    In Python, we need to import the `math` library or the `numpy` (stands for NUMerical PYthon) library for the `exp` operation for taking exponents.
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0011.png)
    
    Within the same folder, we can call back our `MyFun()` function in another file with the following command:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0012.png)![](images/c02-gra-0013.png)
    
    In **R**, there is no need to import any libraries for the `exp` operation for taking exponents. Nevertheless, let us build a simple function as follows:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0014.png)
    
    Similarly, within the same folder, we can call back our `MyFun()` function in another file with the following command:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0015.png)
    
    For both Python and **R**, due to the limited space for display, the printed results can only show a few significant figures, while in the calculations themselves, more significant figures are used. Actually, Python uses more digits in various calculations than **R**.
    
4.  **(IV)** **Recursion Operation – For-Loop**:
    
    In Python, any loop iteration starts from zero:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0016.png)![](images/c02-gra-0017.png)
    
    However, in **R**, any loop iteration starts from 1:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0018.png)
    
    Similarly, all indices in Python start at 0 while indices in **R** start at 1 as seen above. Therefore, additional attention has to be taken when translating indexing between Python and **R**.
    
5.  **(V)** **Help Function**:
    
    In Python, you can call `help(function)`. Moreover, in *Spyder*, one of the most popular programming platforms for the Python language, one can just place the cursor over the function to see documentation (See [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002)). In **R**, you can always call `help(function)` or `?function` for helpful documentation about the function. For example, `help(mean)` or `?mean` provides the documentation of the mean function.
    
    ![FIGURE 2.2 Function documentation can be shown when the cursor is placed over that function.](images/c02f002.png)
    
    [**FIGURE 2.2**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0002) Function documentation can be shown when the cursor is placed over that function.
    

1.  **(VI)** **Matrix Computation**:
    
    In Python, we need to import the `numpy` library for matrix operations as shown below:
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0019.png)![](images/c02-gra-0020.png)
    
    In **R**, we do not need to import any libraries to conduct basic matrix manipulation. Some simple illustrations are shown below.
    
    ![](images/c02-gra-0021.png)

 

## 2.5 ONE-WAY ANOVA AND TUKEY'S HSD FOR STOCK MARKET INDICES

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used to compare the means of ![StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue colon equals StartAbsoluteValue StartSet c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript upper K Baseline EndSet EndAbsoluteValue greater-than-or-equal-to 2](images/c02-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> categorical and independent groups of data with only one continuous feature (independent) variable

![upper H 0 colon mu 1 equals mu 2 equals midline-horizontal-ellipsis equals mu Subscript StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue Baseline equals mu comma](images/c02-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where, as always, we reject the null hypothesis by claiming that the population means are not all equal if the ![p](images/c02-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the test statistics is smaller than 0.05. However, if the null hypothesis is rejected, one-way ANOVA cannot provide us with much knowledge on which population mean(s) ![mu Subscript k](images/c02-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>('s) is (are) significantly different from the others. [\[8\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0008) proposed the Tukey's HSD (*Honest Significant Difference*) which considers all possible pairs of population means.

Suppose that for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue](images/c02-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>, we draw an iid sample of size ![upper N Subscript k](images/c02-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> from the ![k](images/c02-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-th group following a normal distribution with the mean ![mu Subscript k](images/c02-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> and the variance ![sigma squared](images/c02-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> that is common across groups, while we also assume mutual independence among groups. The pooled variance of the combined sample is defined as ![upper S Subscript p Superscript 2 Baseline colon equals StartFraction sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue Endscripts left-parenthesis upper N Subscript k Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis upper S Subscript k Superscript 2 Baseline Over sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue Endscripts left-parenthesis upper N Subscript k Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c02-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>, where ![upper S Subscript k Superscript 2](images/c02-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is the sample variance of the group ![k](images/c02-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
