where ![c left-parenthesis x Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the corresponding group index of observation ![x Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, ![n equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c02-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math>. In particular, the numerator is sometimes called the *within-group sum of squared errors* (within-group SSE):

![SSE Subscript within Baseline colon equals sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript StartLayout 1st Row 1 less-than-or-equal-to n less-than-or-equal-to upper N 2nd Row c left-parenthesis x Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals k EndLayout Endscripts left-parenthesis x Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline minus x overbar Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis squared period](images/c02-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>within</mtext></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></munderover><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></math> 

Then Tukey's HSD statistic can also be written as:

[(2.2)](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-disp-0008)![StartLayout 1st Row q Subscript Tukey comma i j Baseline equals StartFraction x overbar Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline minus x overbar Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline Over StartRoot left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper N Subscript i Baseline EndFraction plus StartFraction 1 Over upper N Subscript j Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis StartFraction SSE Subscript within Baseline Over upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction EndRoot EndFraction comma for all i not-equals j period EndLayout](images/c02-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mtext>Tukey</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>within</mtext></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for all</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

The common practice for performing the Tukey HSD test is on one chosen pair of groups at a time, which we shall follow in our discussions below. In contrast, the test can also be conducted for all pairs with a total of ![StartBinomialOrMatrix StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue Choose 2 EndBinomialOrMatrix](images/c02-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math> Tukey's HSD statistics in a simultaneous manner. To this end, we carry out simultaneous pairwise comparisons with the corresponding ![t](images/c02-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distributions to conclude if a difference between any two group means is significantly different from 0. Moreover, recalling that each ![normal t Subscript i j](images/c02-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> has a common ![t](images/c02-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution with ![upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue](images/c02-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> degrees of freedom and they are still dependent on each other as a group, then the upper bound of the ![p](images/c02-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the simultaneous test can be obtained using the celebrated *Bonferroni inequality*:

![p equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis union Underscript i comma j Endscripts left-brace StartAbsoluteValue normal t Subscript i j Baseline EndAbsoluteValue greater-than q Subscript i j Baseline right-brace right-parenthesis less-than sigma-summation Underscript i comma j Endscripts double-struck upper P left-parenthesis StartAbsoluteValue normal t Subscript i j Baseline EndAbsoluteValue greater-than q Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis equals colon sigma-summation Underscript i comma j Endscripts p Subscript i j Baseline comma](images/c02-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><munder><mo>&#8899;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![p Subscript i j](images/c02-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the ![p](images/c02-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the single pairwise comparison of the groups ![i](images/c02-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and ![j](images/c02-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>. Then we reject the null hypothesis of simultaneous equality of pairwise means across groups at a significant level ![alpha](images/c02-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> if ![sigma-summation Underscript i comma j Endscripts p Subscript i j Baseline less-than alpha](images/c02-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></math>.

Next, we shall illustrate the applications of one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD for three stock market indices, namely the S&P500, HSI, and FTSE via both Python and **R**; note that for this particular example, we shall prioritize on elaborating the implementation in **R**, supplemented by their Python counterparts. The data files `SPX.csv`, `HSI.csv`, and `FTSE.csv` are the adjusted closing prices of S&P500, HSI, and FTSE respectively, dating from 4 January 1984 to 26 April 2021. In particular, two time periods of data will be analyzed, namely (i) from 2005 to 2007; and (ii) from 2018 to 2020.

![](images/c02-gra-0022.png)

For [Programme 2.13](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00013) in **R**, `as.Date()` function converts the date character string from the index name of the dataframe into a datetime object, in which the argument `format="%d/%m/%Y"` indicates that the input string has a date format of (two digits) / month (two digits) / year (four digits). After that, `format()` is immediately applied with an argument `"%Y"` indicating that only the year is returned, and this is augmented into the corresponding stock market index dataframe in a new column named as `Year`. The logarithmic return, i.e., the logarithm of the ratio of consecutive prices, is computed by the `log()` function, then taking the difference of consecutive terms via the `diff()` function. Note that the logarithmic return on the first day (4 January 1984) is unavailable because we do not have the adjusted closing price on the previous day. Therefore, we supplement at the beginning of the list of logarithmic return figures with `NA`, and we place it in the new column named `log_return`. We then remove the data on the very first day by using `[-1,]`.

For the `Remove_Outlier()` function (defined in **R** in [Programme 2.13](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00013) or in Python in [Programme 2.14](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00014)), we used the convention that any data points which are lower than the lower quartile minus 1.5 times the inter-quartile range or greater than the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the inter-quartile range are regarded as outliers. If each stock market index follows a standard normal distribution, then the 25% (resp. 75%) quantile represents a quantile value of −0.6745 (resp. 0.6745) under ![script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. With a multiplier of 1.5 times of the interquartile range as the `outlier_factor`, the `lower_bound` (resp. `upper_bound`) represents the quantile value ![negative 0.6745 plus 1.5 dot left-parenthesis 0.6745 minus left-parenthesis negative 0.6745 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals negative 2.6960](images/c02-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.6745</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.6745</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.6745</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2.6960</mn></math> (resp. 2.6960). Therefore, under ![script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we are selecting the middle portion of ![normal upper Phi left-parenthesis 2.6960 right-parenthesis minus normal upper Phi left-parenthesis negative 2.6960 right-parenthesis equals 0.9930](images/c02-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2.6960</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2.6960</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9930</mn></math>, where ![normal upper Phi left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the *cumulative distribution function* (cdf) of a standard normal distribution. Therefore, if the stock market index follows a heavier-tailed distribution than ![script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then the outliers account for roughly more than 1% of the dataset.

The equivalent code in Python is shown below:

![](images/c02-gra-0023.png)

Now, we extract the data from 2005 to 2007 and plot a histogram for the logarithmic returns of each cleansed stock market index. [Programme 2.15](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00015) contains the **R** code; [Programme 2.16](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00016) the Python.

![](images/c02-gra-0024.png)

Through various statistical tests (such as the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) to be introduced in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml), we shall see in general that the logarithmic returns of stock market indices barely follow a normal distribution, except the central portion during fair weather days. Nevertheless, [Figure 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) and [Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005), produced via **R** and Python respectively, show that the histograms of the daily logarithmic returns for all three stock market indices having a bell-shaped distribution. Despite the lack of normality, as long as the underlying distribution is symmetric enough and light-tailed, the celebrated Central Limit Theorem can still warrant that the corresponding sample mean of log-returns of each index closely follows a normal distribution even with a small sample size, thanks to the Berry–Esseen bound [\[1](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0001), [3\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0003). Therefore, the results of one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD tests are still robust enough to cover the present comparative study.

![FIGURE 2.3 Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2005 to 2007 in R.](images/c02f003.png)

[**FIGURE 2.3**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0003) Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2005 to 2007 in **R**.

![FIGURE 2.4 Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2018 to 2020 in R.](images/c02f004.png)

[**FIGURE 2.4**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0004) Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2018 to 2020 in **R**.

[Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) shows the results (from **R**) of replicating [Programme 2.15](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00015), but this time over a different time period, 2018 to 2020, via `start_year <- 2018` and `end_year <- 2020`.

We have the same illustration via Python codes in [Programme 2.16](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00016) with histograms shown in [Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005) for the period 2005 to 2007 and [Figure 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006) for 2018 to 2020, respectively.

![](images/c02-gra-0025.png)![FIGURE 2.5 Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2005 to 2007 in Python.](images/c02f005.png)

[**FIGURE 2.5**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0005) Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2005 to 2007 in Python.

![FIGURE 2.6 Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2018 to 2020 in Python.](images/c02f006.png)

[**FIGURE 2.6**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0006) Histograms of the daily logarithmic returns from 2018 to 2020 in Python.

Next, in [Programme 2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00017), we perform both one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD tests in **R** for the period 2005 to 2007. The `aov()` function is used for performing one-way ANOVA with (i) a group variable `Index` which consists of three categories `SPX`, `HSI`, and `FTSE`; and (ii) a numerical response variable `log_return` for the daily logarithmic returns of the corresponding market index. The relatively large ![p](images/c02-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value (![0.152 greater-than 0.05](images/c02-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.152</mn><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>) of the ANOVA test indicates that we fail to reject the null hypothesis of the equality of all means of ![mu Subscript SPX Baseline comma mu Subscript FTSE Baseline](images/c02-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub></math> and ![mu Subscript HSI](images/c02-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub></math> over the period 2005 to 2007. This claim is further supported by the large ![p](images/c02-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of the Tukey HSD tests on all three possible pairs of stock market indices via the `TukeyHSD()` function in **R**, as there are three stock market indices, and there are ![StartBinomialOrMatrix 3 Choose 2 EndBinomialOrMatrix equals 3](images/c02-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> possible pairs. More graphical illustrations can be seen in [Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0007).

 ![](images/c02-gra-0026.png) ![FIGURE 2.7 Boxplot, meanplot, and Tukey HSD plot for three stock market indices from 2005 to 2007 in R.](images/c02f007.png)

[**FIGURE 2.7**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0007) Boxplot, meanplot, and Tukey HSD plot for three stock market indices from 2005 to 2007 in **R**.

However, over the period 2018 to 2020, using [Programme 2.18](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00018) (written in **R**), the small ![p](images/c02-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value (![0.019 less-than 0.05](images/c02-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.019</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>) from the ANOVA test indicates that we should reject the null hypothesis on the equality of all means, meaning that the corresponding population means ![mu Subscript SPX Baseline comma mu Subscript FTSE Baseline](images/c02-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub></math> and ![mu Subscript HSI](images/c02-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub></math> are not all equal. We further adopt the Tukey HSD tests to the three possible pairs of stock market indices to test which pair(s) of means are unequal. The corresponding small ![p](images/c02-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value (![0.0168939 much-less-than 0.05](images/c02-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.0168939</mn><mo>&#8810;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>) of the Tukey HSD test for `HSI` against `SPX` indicates that the population means for `HSI` and `SPX` are unlikely the same, i.e. ![mu Subscript HSI Baseline not-equals mu Subscript SPX](images/c02-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub></math>. Meanwhile, for the Tukey HSD test for `FTSE` against `HSI`, the large ![p](images/c02-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value (![0.7091423 much-greater-than 0.05](images/c02-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.7091423</mn><mo>&#8811;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>) indicates that we do not reject the equality of the means ![mu Subscript FTSE Baseline equals mu Subscript HSI](images/c02-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub></math>; the analogous conclusion of ![mu Subscript FTSE Baseline equals mu Subscript SPX](images/c02-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub></math> can also be drawn from the Tukey HSD test for `FTSE` against `SPX`, yet based on its relatively small ![p](images/c02-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of 0.1226088 (![greater-than 0.05](images/c02-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>), it is more likely that the two means may be unequal. Indeed, the discrepancy between US and Hong Kong markets may be explained by the economic conflict between US and China throughout that period, which brought along uncertainty and concern on various prospects of the economic growth in Asia-Pacific region, including but not limited to tariff levels and trade negotiations. As a result, Chinese companies with a significant exposure to the US market were most severely affected, and the overall performance of the Hang Seng Index, where these companies played a crucial role, deviated inevitably from that of the S&P500 Index. We can also use the Sharpe ratio to study any possible differences between the performances of financial markets in different countries, for instance, see [\[10](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0010), [11\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0011).

 ![](images/c02-gra-0027.png)

From [Figure 2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0008)b, the mean of the daily logarithmic returns for `SPX` is significantly higher than the corresponding means of `HSI`, which is in agreement with the result obtained from the Tukey HSD tests that ![mu Subscript HSI Baseline not-equals mu Subscript SPX](images/c02-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub></math>. Certainly, there are limitations to our present study. For instance, we assume the stationarity of both the means and variance of log-returns over not too short periods. Since the economic environments over those periods were rather stable, one can argue this assumption is legitimate. Nevertheless, we shall introduce more sophisticated models allowing for more realistic assumptions later in [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml), [7](#c07.xhtml) and [8](#c08.xhtml).

![FIGURE 2.8 Boxplot, meanplot, Tukey HSD plot for three stock market indices from 2018 to 2020 in R.](images/c02f008.png)

[**FIGURE 2.8**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0008) Boxplot, meanplot, Tukey HSD plot for three stock market indices from 2018 to 2020 in **R**.

The resulting plots are illustrated in [Figures 2.9](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0009) and [2.10](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0010), respectively.

Lastly, in Programmes 2.21 and 2.22 via **R** (resp. Programmes 2.23 and 2.24 via Python), we replicate the result of `tukey.test` in **R** (resp. `tukeyhsd` in Python) based on ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0008)). We first compute the individual sample means ![mu Subscript SPX](images/c02-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub></math>, ![mu Subscript FTSE](images/c02-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub></math>, ![mu Subscript HSI](images/c02-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub></math>, the individual sum of squared errors ![SSE Subscript SPX](images/c02-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub></math>, ![SSE Subscript FTSE](images/c02-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub></math>, ![SSE Subscript HSI](images/c02-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub></math>, and the total degrees of freedom (![upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue equals upper N Subscript SPX Baseline plus upper N Subscript FTSE Baseline plus upper N Subscript HSI Baseline minus 3 equals 2 comma 184](images/c02-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>184</mn></math> for the period 2005 to 2007 and ![upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue equals 2 comma 117](images/c02-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>117</mn></math> for the period 2018 to 2020). Then, we compute the within-group mean squared error defined as ![MSE Subscript within Baseline equals SSE Subscript within Baseline slash left-parenthesis upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis SSE Subscript SPX Baseline plus SSE Subscript FTSE Baseline plus SSE Subscript HSI Baseline right-parenthesis slash left-parenthesis upper N minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper C EndAbsoluteValue right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>MSE</mtext><mtext>within</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>within</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>SPX</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>FTSE</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mtext>SSE</mtext><mtext>HSI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In both **R** and Python, ![MSE Subscript within](images/c02-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>MSE</mtext><mtext>within</mtext></msub></math> is recorded in the summary table of the one-way ANOVA; in **R** for [Programme 2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00017) for the period 2005 to 2007 (resp. [Programme 2.18](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00018) for the period 2018 to 2020), it is stated directly in the `Mean Sq` of `Residuals`; in Python for [Programme 2.19](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00019) for the period 2005 to 2007 (resp. [Programme 2.20](#c02.xhtml#c02-gra-00020) for the period 2018 to 2020), it can be computed by dividing the `sum_sq` by `df` of `Residual`. The `ptukey()` function in **R** (resp. the `psturng()` function in Python) computes the probability ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis q Subscript Tukey comma i j Baseline greater-than q right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mtext>Tukey</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of the Tukey HSD test given (i) the quantile value `q`; (ii) the number of groups `nmeans` in **R** (resp. `r` in Python); and the degrees of freedom `df` in **R** (resp. `v` in Python).

![](images/c02-gra-0031.png)![](images/c02-gra-0032.png) ![](images/c02-gra-0033.png)![](images/c02-gra-0034.png) ![](images/c02-gra-0035.png)

Notice that the ![p](images/c02-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of the Tukey HSD tests computed from `tukeyhsd` and `qsturng`, both provided by the `statsmodels` library in Python, are slightly different, no matter which time period (2005–2007 or 2018–2020). The difference in values is due to the inability of the solver `fminbound` used in `psturng` to locate the minimizer accurately. We therefore recommend readers to use the `tukeyhsd` function in Python directly for performing the Tukey HSD tests in practice.

# CHAPTER 3  
Statistical Diagnostics of Financial Data

 

The simple version of *Black–Scholes–Merton* model assumes that the returns of the stock on different days are iid normal, but in reality, with real securities data, we see that the normality assumption is usually invalid because of the nature of the fatter-tailed distribution of the returns. In the latter part of this chapter, we shall replace the normal distribution with other fatter-tailed distributions for the logarithm of the ratio of prices, and then investigate the validity of these new models.

 

## 3.1 NORMALITY ASSUMPTION FOR RELATIVE STOCK PRICE CHANGES

The basic assumption of the Black–Scholes–Merton model [\[1\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0001) is that the percentage change in the stock price over a short period of time of length ![delta t](images/c03-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> is normally distributed; that means, approximately,

(3.1)![delta normal upper S slash normal upper S tilde script í’© left-parenthesis mu delta t comma sigma squared delta t right-parenthesis comma](images/c03-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![delta normal upper S](images/c03-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></math> is the change in the stock price ![normal upper S](images/c03-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></math> over the short time interval ![left-parenthesis t comma t plus delta t right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![mu delta t](images/c03-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> and ![sigma StartRoot delta t EndRoot](images/c03-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> are the mean and standard deviation of the percentage change, respectively. Here, ![mu](images/c03-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is called *drift rate* and ![sigma](images/c03-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> stands for the *volatility*. Usually the stock price is observed over a fixed time interval (let's say the closing price is observed daily, so that ![delta t equals 1 slash 252](images/c03-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>252</mn></math> as there are normally around 252 trading days in a year). For ![n](images/c03-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> consecutive daily stock prices ![normal upper S 1 comma ellipsis comma normal upper S Subscript n Baseline](images/c03-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, we define the daily arithmetic return as:

where ![tau equals 1 slash 252](images/c03-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>252</mn></math>. To see whether this modeling is appropriate in practice, we can use some graphical methods to test for normality. Let us illustrate this by the following example.

 

**Example 3.1**   The file `stock_1999_2002.csv` contains adjusted daily closing prices of the stocks HSBC (0005), CLP (0002) and Cheung Kong (0001) from 1 January 1999 to 31 December 2002. Let us first read in these stock prices and compute the corresponding ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for each stock according to ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)); we also centralize them by subtracting ![ModifyingAbove mu With Ì‚ tau equals colon mu overbar](images/c03-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math>. We then produce a time series plot, a histogram, and a normal quantile-quantile plot (normal Q-Q plot) for ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> through [Programme 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0001) via Python (resp. [Programme 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0002) via **R**). Often, ![ModifyingAbove mu With Ì‚ tau](images/c03-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>&#964;</mi></math> is so small that we may take it as zero whence testing for normality.

![](images/c03-gra-0001.png)![](images/c03-gra-0002.png)

From [Figure 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001) via Python (resp. [Figure 3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0003) via **R**), these time series plots show the sample ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s fluctuating around zero. The volatility is small over certain periods and large over others, appearing in clusters. Obviously, the volatility varies with time. We shall discuss how to model this time-changing volatility in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml), but first let us focus on the plausibility of the normality assumption for ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>.

According to ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)), ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is expected to be normally distributed. To check the normality assumption, the most basic method is through a graphical approach with histograms. However, a histogram only gives us a general idea about the distribution. A more sophisticated graphical method is through the use of the normal Q-Q plot. To this end, we order the sample ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in ascending order of magnitude denoted by ![u Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>, resulting in ![u Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline less-than-or-equal-to u Subscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis Baseline less-than-or-equal-to ellipsis less-than-or-equal-to u Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>. The normal Q-Q plot is the plot of these ordered ![u Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>'s against ![q Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>'s, the ![i](images/c03-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th quantile of the standard normal distribution, where ![q Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> is the value that satisfies ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal z less-than q Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis i minus 0.5 right-parenthesis slash n](images/c03-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></math> (with this 0.5 as a continuity adjustment) with ![normal z](images/c03-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow></math> being the standard normal random variable. Conceptually, the right-hand side should be ![i slash n](images/c03-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, yet the probability of ![left-parenthesis i minus 0.5 right-parenthesis slash n](images/c03-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></math> is used to avoid the difficulty encountered when ![i equals n](images/c03-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math> as there will likely be some other observations larger than this present largest ![u Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>. If the samples ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are normally distributed, this plot should be close to a straight line making, an angle of ![pi slash 4](images/c03-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></math> with the horizontal axis. The sample plots illustrate that the proportional changes are usually heavily tailed in favour of large gains and losses, and a mild positive skewness is also noted from the histograms. In particular, the normal Q-Q plots of the samples ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s show that the distribution of each sequence of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s have a fatter tail than the normal distribution. More seriously, the *Value-at-Risk* (V@R) will be under-estimated if the normal model is adopted; see more discussions in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml).

The normal Q-Q plot is a graphical method for testing univariate normality, and indeed is very effective. That said, there are other formal statistical tests for testing normality; for instance, this Q-Q plot can be officially formalized as a *Shapiro–Wilk* (SW) test [\[15\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0015), which is a formal way of testing whether a sample is normally distributed. And there are other simpler normality tests available.

The *Kolmogorov–Smirnov* (KS) test can be used to test whether a random sample is coming from a specific distribution. The test statistic is ![upper D Subscript n Baseline colon equals sup Underscript x element-of double-struck upper R Endscripts StartAbsoluteValue upper F Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis minus upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue](images/c03-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">sup</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>, where ![upper F Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are respectively the empirical distribution function, based on a random sample of size ![n](images/c03-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and theoretical distribution function. Note that the distribution of ![StartRoot n EndRoot normal upper D Subscript n](images/c03-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> converges to that of the absolute maximum value of a standardized *Brownian bridge* ![](images/c03-gra-0005.png)![](images/c03-gra-0006.png)

Another commonly used normality test is the *Jarque–Bera* (JB) test. It is based on the fact that the ![skewness equals 0](images/c03-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>skewness</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and the ![kurtosis equals 3](images/c03-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>kurtosis</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> for the standard normal distribution. Meanwhile, for the sake of illustration, we also write the following function `JB_test()` in Python in [Programme 3.7](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0007) (resp. the function `JB.test()` in **R** in [Programme 3.8](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0008)) to perform this JB test.

The ![p](images/c03-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values for ![u 1 comma u 2](images/c03-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![u 3](images/c03-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> from both the KS test and the JB test are small, thus we conclude the normality assumptions for them are not valid, which is consistent with the observation from the normal Q-Q plots.

 

## 3.2 STUDENT'S ![equation](images/c03-i0067.png)<MATH XMLNS="HTTP://WWW.W3.ORG/1998/MATH/MATHML" DISPLAY="INLINE" OVERFLOW="SCROLL"><MSUB><MI></MI><MI>&#957;</MI></MSUB></MATH>\-DISTRIBUTION FOR STOCK PRICE CHANGES

To cope with the heavy tails commonly observed among securities, one may use a scaled Student's ![t](images/c03-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution, denoted by ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>, with ![nu](images/c03-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom and a scaling parameter ![sigma](images/c03-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> to model relative price changes ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s. The density of the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution is given by:

![normal upper T tilde f left-parenthesis t semicolon nu right-parenthesis equals StartFraction normal upper Gamma left-parenthesis left-parenthesis nu plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 right-parenthesis Over normal upper Gamma left-parenthesis nu slash 2 right-parenthesis StartRoot nu pi sigma squared EndRoot EndFraction left-parenthesis 1 plus StartFraction t squared Over nu sigma squared EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript minus left-parenthesis nu plus 1 right-parenthesis slash 2 Baseline comma for nu greater-than 2 comma](images/c03-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.4em"/><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></math> 

where its first four moments are: (i) mean: ![mu equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper T right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c03-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; (ii) variance: ![sigma squared equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper T squared right-parenthesis equals sigma squared nu slash left-parenthesis nu minus 2 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#957;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; (iii) standardized skewness: ![zeta 1 equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper T cubed right-parenthesis slash sigma cubed equals 0](images/c03-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#950;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; (iv) standardized excess kurtosis: ![zeta 2 equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper T Superscript 4 Baseline right-parenthesis slash sigma Superscript 4 Baseline minus 3 equals 6 slash left-parenthesis nu minus 4 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#950;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. More details for the ![t](images/c03-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution as well as its common use in statistics can be found in standard textbooks such as [\[2](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0002), [4](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0004), [7](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0007), [16\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0016).

The tail of the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution is heavier than that of any normal distribution. In principle, it becomes normal when ![nu right-arrow infinity](images/c03-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> and ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distributions are commonly used to model security data with fat tails. For common securities, the value of ![nu](images/c03-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> ranges from 3 to 6 as pointed out in [\[11\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0011); specifically, Harry Markowitz noted that a degree of freedom around 4 yields the best estimate and is consistent with the observations from S&P500 stock returns. We can lay down ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> Q-Q plots to see whether the fittings look better. First, we need to estimate the degrees of freedom ![nu](images/c03-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math>. One simple way is to match the sample excess kurtosis ![ModifyingAbove zeta 2 With Ì‚](images/c03-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>&#950;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> computed from the sample ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s to the theoretical value of ![6 slash left-parenthesis nu minus 4 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which gives an estimate of ![nu equals 6 slash ModifyingAbove zeta 2 With Ì‚ plus 4](images/c03-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>&#950;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. The ![p](images/c03-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-th quantile of the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution is obtained by setting ![double-struck upper P left-brace normal upper T less-than-or-equal-to t Subscript nu Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis right-brace equals p](images/c03-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, denoted by ![q Subscript p Baseline colon equals t Subscript nu Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In [Programmes 3.9](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0009) (in Python) and [3.10](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00010) (in **R**), we can respectively use the `t_QQ_plot()` and `t.QQ.plot()` functions to produce the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> Q-Q plots.

![](images/c03-gra-0009.png)

From [Figures 3.5](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0005) and [3.6](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0006), we note that the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution fits the fat tails better than the normal distribution. Again, we can use the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test to test whether ![normal u 1](images/c03-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![normal u 2](images/c03-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![normal u 3](images/c03-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> follow a ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution via [Programmes 3.11](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00011) (in Python) and [3.12](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00012) (in **R**).

![FIGURE 3.5 Student's t Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK via Python, generated by Programme 3.9.](images/c03f005.png)

[**FIGURE 3.5**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0005) Student's ![t](images/c03-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK via Python, generated by [Programme 3.9](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-0009).

 ![FIGURE 3.6 Student's t Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK via R, generated by Programme 3.10.](images/c03f006.png)

[**FIGURE 3.6**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0006) Student's ![t](images/c03-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK via **R**, generated by [Programme 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00010).

 ![](images/c03-gra-0010.png)![](images/c03-gra-0011.png)![](images/c03-gra-0012.png) ![](images/c03-gra-0013.png)

Again the ![p](images/c03-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of HSBC and CLP are small, yet much bigger than those from fitting the normal distribution. We still conclude ![normal u 1](images/c03-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal u 2](images/c03-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> (returns of HSBC and CLP) do not completely follow a ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution. However, since the ![p](images/c03-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of CK is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, and it is viable to claim ![normal u 3](images/c03-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> follows a ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution. Significant deviation from the ![t Subscript nu](images/c03-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>\-distribution occurs at the very extreme negative values of relative price changes, as the extreme return happens more likely during market downturns.

 

## 3.3 TESTING FOR MULTIVARIATE NORMALITY

The normal Q-Q plots in the previous section are only for checking normality in a univariate setting. We may want to test whether the ![p](images/c03-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional daily returns of a portfolio of ![p](images/c03-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> stocks jointly follow a multivariate normal distribution, that is,

We can extend the idea of normal Q-Q plots to test multivariate normality by using the notion of the squared generalized distance (*Mahalanobis distance* [\[12\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0012)):

(3.3)![d Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline equals left-parenthesis bold-italic u Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic u overbar right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper S Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic u Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic u overbar right-parenthesis for i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c03-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="8.5359pt"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="8.5359pt"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold-italic u overbar](images/c03-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> and ![bold-italic upper S](images/c03-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> are the sample unbiased estimates of ![bold-italic mu dot delta t](images/c03-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>&#183;</mi><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> and ![delta t dot bold upper Sigma](images/c03-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></math> respectively. Note that ![d Subscript i](images/c03-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is a number representing the distance from an individual observation ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> to the central tendency indicated by the sample mean, and ![d Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c03-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is sometimes called the *squared generalized distance* of ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. It can be shown that if ![bold u Subscript i](images/c03-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> has a multivariate normal distribution, then for a large ![n](images/c03-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, ![d Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c03-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> will approximately follow a chi-square distribution with ![p](images/c03-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom; also recall Property 6 in [Section 1.4.2](#c01.xhtml#head-3-3). Therefore, we can generate a chi-square Q-Q plot for those Mahalanobis distances as follows:

1.  Order the ![d Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c03-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> in ascending order in magnitude, and denote them by ![d Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Superscript 2](images/c03-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> in order;
2.  Compute ![q Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the ![i](images/c03-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th quantile of the chi-square distribution with ![p](images/c03-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom, that means ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis chi Subscript p Superscript 2 Baseline less-than q Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis i minus 0.5 right-parenthesis slash n](images/c03-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#967;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, after the continuity correction;
3.  Plot ![d Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Superscript 2](images/c03-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> against ![q Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. If the points are close to a straight line at an angle of ![pi slash 4](images/c03-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></math> against the horizontal axis, the original ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are likely to come from a multivariate normal distribution.

Let us illustrate the approach of using a chi-square Q-Q plot for ![bold u equals left-parenthesis normal u 1 comma normal u 2 comma normal u 3 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c03-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> to see whether it has a tri-variate normal distribution; refer to [Programmes 3.13](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00013) via Python and [3.14](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00014) via **R**. First, we compute the sample mean vector and the sample variance-covariance matrix ![bold-italic upper S](images/c03-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> of the daily returns using the most recent 180 days. Then we compute the inverse of ![bold-italic upper S](images/c03-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math>, the squared generalized distances and the quantiles of the chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom 3. Note that Python does not have a built-in function for finding the inverse of a matrix, yet we can use the function `inv()` in `numpy.linalg` to do it. From the Q-Q plots in [Figure 3.7](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0007), the distribution of the return vector in the past 180 days, stored as `u_180`, is not significantly different from a multivariate normal distribution, except for the tail part. We can again use the KS test to test whether ![normal d Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline tilde chi Subscript p Superscript 2](images/c03-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8764;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#967;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>.

![FIGURE 3.7 Chi-square Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK.](images/c03f007.png)

[**FIGURE 3.7**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0007) Chi-square Q-Q plots for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK.

 ![](images/c03-gra-0014.png)![](images/c03-gra-0015.png)

Note that as the ![p](images/c03-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value is larger than 0.05, we may not reject the null hypothesis that the vector of ![d Subscript i](images/c03-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s stored in `md2_180` follows a chi-square distribution, or ![bold u equals left-parenthesis normal u 1 comma normal u 2 comma normal u 3 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c03-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> has an almost tri-variate normal distribution. In [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), we shall illustrate a better fit by using copulae. More advanced methods of testing for normality can be found in [\[18\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0018).

 

## 3.4 SAMPLE CORRELATION MATRIX

When we consider more than one random variable, correlations between any two random variables serve as important parameters. Let us compute the correlation matrix of `u_180` by [Programmes 3.15](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00015) in Python and [3.16](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00016) in **R**.

![](images/c03-gra-0016.png)![](images/c03-gra-0017.png)![](images/c03-gra-0018.png)

For Python, we can generate the scatter plot matrix of these daily returns by using the function `pandas.plotting.scatter_matrix()`. This can be considered as a graphical illustration of the correlation matrix.

From the output of [Programmes 3.15](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00015) and [3.16](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00016), generally speaking we see that the pairs of `u1` and `u2` as well as `u2` and `u3` are mostly uncorrelated; but `u1` and `u3` are positively correlated. The sample correlation matrix can be computed from the sample covariance matrix ![bold-italic upper S](images/c03-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> by using the relations ![r Subscript i j Baseline equals StartFraction s Subscript i j Baseline Over StartRoot s Subscript i i Baseline s Subscript j j Baseline EndRoot EndFraction](images/c03-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math>, for ![i comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c03-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Pictorial illustrations of the pairwise correlations are provided in [Figure 3.8](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0008) and [Figure 3.9](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0009) via [Programme 3.17](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00017) (Python) and [Programme 3.18](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00018) (**R**) respectively.
