## 3.5 EMPIRICAL PROPERTIES OF STOCK PRICES

Without a doubt, modeling the price of a stock is one of the most active research areas in *Quantitative Finance* and *Econometrics*. In the last few sections, we demonstrated some primitive approaches of modeling stock prices. However, in reality stock prices are affected by many factors such as interest rates, and various economic and political factors; see more discussion in [\[3](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0003), [10\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0010) for instance. Despite the complexity, there are some empirical findings and conventions about stock prices that are widely accepted in the industry. Here is a list of the most notable ones; a more comprehensive account can be found in [\[3\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0003).

1.  Instead of modeling a stock price itself, we usually model the (daily) returns of the stock. There are two types of returns:
    
    1.  logarithmic return ![u overtilde Subscript i Baseline equals ln left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis minus ln left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#361;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and
    2.  arithmetic return ![u Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline minus upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis slash upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline equals upper S Subscript i Baseline slash upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline minus 1 period](images/c03-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>
    
    These two returns are close in value if ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is small. This can be easily seen by the fact that ![u overtilde Subscript i Baseline equals ln left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline slash upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis equals ln left-parenthesis 1 plus u Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis almost-equals u Subscript i](images/c03-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#361;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Although the logarithmic return is additive, we usually use arithmetic returns in practice, for simplicity.
    
2.  If the time interval is short, say a day, ![delta t equals 1 slash 252 equals 0.004](images/c03-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>252</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.004</mn></math>, out of 252 trading days per year on average, then we may assume the mean of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> to be zero. This reduces the complexity of the model, although this is less of a concern with high computing performance these days.
3.  There is little autocorrelation in ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, i.e., ![Corr left-parenthesis normal u Subscript i plus k Baseline comma normal u Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis almost-equals 0](images/c03-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Corr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for ![k equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c03-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math> In other words, returns are almost impossible to be “linearly” predicted from their own history.
4.  Although the Black–Scholes–Merton model assumes that the distribution is normal, its distribution is generally believed to have fatter tails than those of the normal in many circumstances. Fatter tails imply a higher probability of large losses (or profit) than that offered by the normal distribution; see [\[5\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0005) for more details on the modelling in this regard. This is particularly important when one calculates Value-at-Risks (V@Rs); more details can be seen in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml).
5.  The standard deviation of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is large compared with the mean of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Empirical findings show that the standard deviation of daily returns usually lies between 0.95% and 3.15% during normal times, but was between 2% and 8% (for the US market) during the first half of 2020 – the pandemic year!
6.  This standard deviation certainly varies with time and depends on many unknown and uncontrollable factors, and so the Black–Scholes–Merton model is not so reliable for long-term modelling; more sophisticated time series models will be introduced in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml).
7.  Since the sample mean of ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is taken to be zero, the variance of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c03-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> can be estimated by the sample mean of the squared returns ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c03-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>'s. For these squared returns, some positive autocorrelation exists, meaning ![Corr left-parenthesis normal u Subscript i plus k Superscript 2 Baseline comma normal u Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c03-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Corr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for small values of ![k](images/c03-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
8.  A generic stochastic model for the return is ![normal u Subscript i Baseline equals mu Subscript i Baseline plus sigma Subscript i Baseline normal z Subscript i](images/c03-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, where ![normal z Subscript i](images/c03-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are iid according to a distribution with a mean 0 and variance 1. A special case of this is ![normal u Subscript i Baseline equals mu delta t plus sigma StartRoot delta t EndRoot normal z Subscript i](images/c03-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, where ![normal z Subscript i](images/c03-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s follow iid ![script í’© left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is the celebrated Black–Scholes–Merton model.

To understand the difference in statistical properties between the original time series ![upper S Subscript i](images/c03-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s of stock prices and the relative returns ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s, we generate the respective histogram and the normal Q-Q plot for ![upper S Subscript i](images/c03-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![upper S Subscript i plus 1](images/c03-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> vs ![upper S Subscript i](images/c03-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![u Subscript i plus 1](images/c03-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> vs ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in [Figures 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0010) in Python and [3.11](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0011) in **R** via [Programmes 3.19](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00019) and [3.20](#c03.xhtml#c03-gra-00020) respectively.

 ![](images/c03-gra-0021.png)![](images/c03-gra-0022.png)

Compared with the plots of ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in [Section 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0002), it is obvious that the distributions of the ![upper S Subscript i](images/c03-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are non-normal. More importantly, strong autocorrelations exist in ![upper S Subscript i](images/c03-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s while there is almost none in ![u Subscript i](images/c03-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s. These plots show that ![left-brace upper S Subscript i Baseline right-brace](images/c03-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> has strong autocorrelation (of lag 1) while ![left-brace u Subscript i Baseline right-brace](images/c03-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> has a small or no autocorrelation, which confirms the claim made in item 3. We can also plot the *autocorrelation function* (*acf*) of lag ![k](images/c03-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> for sample sequence ![StartSet a 1 comma ellipsis comma a Subscript n Baseline EndSet](images/c03-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>:

![r Subscript k Baseline colon equals StartFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n minus k Endscripts left-parenthesis a Subscript i Baseline minus a overbar right-parenthesis left-parenthesis a Subscript i plus k Baseline minus a overbar right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis a Subscript i Baseline minus a overbar right-parenthesis squared EndFraction comma for k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K comma](images/c03-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#257;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#257;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#257;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo></math>  ![FIGURE 3.10 Empirical properties of the prices and returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK via Python, generated by Programme 3.19.](images/c03f010.png)

## 3.A APPENDIX

  

### \*3.A.1 Shapiro–Wilk Statistic

Very often, we test whether the hypothesis that the underlying distribution of a random sample is normal is true or not. To this end, we first rank the sample in ascending order ![normal y 1 less-than-or-equal-to midline-horizontal-ellipsis less-than-or-equal-to normal y Subscript n](images/c03-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>. If the hypothesis of normality is true, we can write ![normal y Subscript i Baseline equals mu plus sigma normal z Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c03-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, where ![normal z Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline](images/c03-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> is an *ordered* random sample of ![n](images/c03-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> iid standard normal random variables. Here, ![mu](images/c03-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma](images/c03-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> are the unknown population mean and standard deviation. We denote by ![bold-italic m equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis bold z right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold-italic upper V equals upper V a r left-parenthesis bold z right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> the mean vector and covariance matrix, respectively, of these ![n](images/c03-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> normal order statistics ![bold z equals left-parenthesis normal z Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c03-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. And ![bold 1 Subscript n](images/c03-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is an ![n](images/c03-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector having all components equal to 1, ![bold-italic upper A colon equals left-parenthesis bold 1 Subscript n Baseline comma bold-italic m right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is an ![n times 2](images/c03-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> matrix, and ![bold-italic theta colon equals left-parenthesis mu comma sigma right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline element-of double-struck upper R squared](images/c03-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. Since ![normal z 1 comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript n Baseline](images/c03-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> follow a symmetric distribution, the two sets of ordered observations ![normal z Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline](images/c03-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> and ![minus normal z Subscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma minus normal z Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline](images/c03-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> have exactly the same joint distribution; The key idea of the Shapiro–Wilk test is that when one is regressing the ordered sample ![normal y 1 comma ellipsis comma normal y Subscript n Baseline](images/c03-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> against the corresponding expected normal order statistics ![bold-italic m](images/c03-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi></mrow></math> under the null hypothesis, a linear fit can be expected if the sample really comes from a normal distribution. The Shapiro–Wilk test statistic ![upper W](images/c03-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>, motivated by the ![upper R squared](images/c03-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>\-statistic in simple linear regression, determines how good this linear fit is. Recall that ![upper R squared](images/c03-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> [\[21\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0021) for a simple linear regression of ![y Subscript i Baseline equals beta 0 plus beta 1 x Subscript i Baseline plus epsilon Subscript i](images/c03-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c03-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, is given by

Under the null hypothesis, if the population distribution is normal, then ![bold-italic y](images/c03-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> has a linear relation with ![bold-italic m](images/c03-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi></mrow></math>, which leads to a stronger alignment between ![bold-italic y](images/c03-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic a](images/c03-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> and so a larger value of ![upper W](images/c03-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>. which tells us the largest possible value for ![upper W](images/c03-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> is one. As a result, if ![upper W](images/c03-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> is much smaller than 1, we are more confident to reject the null hypothesis of the normal nature of the underlying sample. For more discussion on the statistical properties of the test, such as its *consistency*, we refer readers to [\[8](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0008), [13](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0013), [18\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0018). Meanwhile, some variants of the Shapiro–Wilk test are also available in various references including [\[14](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0014), [18\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0018).

 

### 3.A.2 Kolmogorov–Smirnov Test

In fact, we also have the following stronger result of uniform convergence.

 

**Theorem 3.1 *(Glivenko–Cantelli* [\[6](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0006), [19](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0019), [20\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0020)*)***   ![ModifyingAbove normal upper F With Ì‚ Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> converges to ![upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> uniformly in ![x](images/c03-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> on ![double-struck upper R](images/c03-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c03-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>.

The celebrated Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic for a random sample following a distribution ![upper F 0](images/c03-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> is defined as:

# CHAPTER 4  
Financial Forensics

 

Banks and financial corporations are often vulnerable to fraudulent activities due to some misbehaviour of employees or procedures not followed correctly; criminals might take advantage of some basic accounting loopholes to commit illegal financial activities like money laundering. Financial forensics is an important tool for detecting such behaviour. In the era of big data, there is a vast amount of information to be processed, and it becomes nearly impossible for humans, no matter how large the working team is, to look deeply in every case worthy of investigation. As examples, Benford's Law and Zipf's Law can be adopted to quickly locate any potential areas that are prone to fraudulent activity. For real-world naturally arising numbers, Benford's Law tells us the distribution of the first few leading-digits in financial statements, whereas Zipf's Law tells us the rank-frequency distribution in macroeconomic data and social sciences.

 

## 4.1 BENFORD'S LAW

In 1881, American mathematician *Simon Newcomb* (1835–1909) made an offbeat observation about books of logarithms. He noticed that earlier pages of the books are more smudged and worn much more than later pages; those numbers with smaller leading digits were being looked up more often for calculations than those with larger ones, and he formulated the empirical law that the proportion of numbers starting with the digit ![d](images/c04-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is not uniform, instead it is governed by ![log Subscript 10 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 plus 1 slash d right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![d equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma 9](images/c04-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></math>. This phenomenon was mentioned in an article in *American Journal of Mathematics* in 1881 yet at that time he could not provide a rigorous mathematical justification for his own claim.

Later in 1938, physicist *Frank Benford* made the same observation as Newcomb. He compiled a table of ![Number 2 0 comma 2 2 9](images/c04-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>20,&#8201;229</mn></mrow></math> numbers from a wide variety of datasets of areas of rivers, death rates, baseball statistics, numbers in magazine articles and many others. His results were largely consistent with the pattern previously observed by Newcomb. This counterintuitive law of nature, rather than the uniform one, has been named after him.

Undoubtedly, many sets of numbers do not follow Benford's law, such as random numbers and numbers drawn from other statistical distributions. In 1996, *Theodore Hill*, from the Georgia Institute of Technology, showed that if the sampling distributions are selected at random such that samples are drawn from each of these distributions, i.e. drawing samples from an uncertain distribution, the leading-digit frequencies of the combined sample would eventually converge to Benford's law, even though this may not be true for individual samples taken from a fixed distribution.

An alternative way to understand this empirical Benford's law is to see the collection of all numerical figures as base-independent, and the same law is applicable to any other base systems different from base-10. We expect the same law should remain valid even after a change of measurement unit, which is achieved by a multiplication with some scaling number. This property is called *scaling invariance*. For instance, 100 meters can be transformed to 0.1 kilometers or ![Number 1 0 comma 0 0 0](images/c04-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10, 000</mn></mrow></math> centimeters, but the leading digit 1 remains unchanged regardless of the convention of measurement used. In 1961, the mathematician *Roger Pinkham* of Rutgers University proved that scaling invariance does imply Benford's law. As an illustration, consider a set of numbers from the ![upper U left-bracket 1 comma 10 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> distribution so that the expected frequency of each leading digit ![d](images/c04-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is 1/9. We change the unit by multiplying with a factor 2. [Table 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0001) shows the resulting leading digits of the newly obtained numbers and their corresponding expected frequencies (probabilities). It clearly shows that the uniform nature of the distribution is lost after this simple scaling, with an expectation that ![5 slash 9](images/c04-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>9</mn></math> of the resulting numbers have 1 as their leading digit. Hence, the uniform distribution cannot be scale-invariant.

![TABLE 4.1  The expected frequencies of the leading digits of randomly selected numbers after scaling by a factor 2.](images/c04-i0010.png)

[**TABLE 4.1**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0001)  The expected frequencies of the leading digits of randomly selected numbers after scaling by a factor ![2](images/c04-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.

We next assign a scale-invariant ![sigma](images/c04-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>\-finite measure on ![left-bracket 1 comma infinity right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, with the aim of explaining the phenomenon of the distribution of the leading digit. We first rewrite the number ![x greater-than 1](images/c04-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in its scientific notation ![x equals x overbar times 1 0 Superscript k](images/c04-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>k</mi></msup></math>, where ![1 less-than-or-equal-to x overbar less-than 10](images/c04-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>10</mn></math> is called the *mantissa* of ![x](images/c04-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> for some ![k element-of double-struck upper Z Subscript plus](images/c04-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math>. The leading digit, denoted by ![d 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is simply the integral part of ![x overbar](images/c04-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math>, that is, ![d 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals left floor x overbar right floor](images/c04-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8970;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8971;</mo></math>. By the very definition, the leading digit of a number after scaling, with whatever factor ![alpha greater-than 1](images/c04-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, remains in ![left-bracket 1 comma 10 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then what sort of probability distribution does this leading digit ![d 1 left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> follow if ![normal x element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper M right-bracket](images/c04-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> follows ![f Subscript normal x Superscript left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> when ![upper M](images/c04-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is very large? ## 4.3 BENFORD'S LAW IN BUSINESS REPORTS

The use of Benford's law as a method of fraud detection has become prevalent in recent years, motivated by the ever increasing amount of data available for checking by regulators, for which automated methods of fraud detection are needed in order to scan through these data effectively. This is of particular importance since investigations by regulators are often very costly, in terms of both time and money, and it is more favourable to have a computer-based checking to clear the fog so that they only have to focus on the most suspicious transactions. Therefore, Benford's law can serve as a very useful empirical law to screen data for any possible irregularities. If irregularities are detected, it may not be due to fraudulent activities, and a more comprehensive investigation is initiated to ascertain their cause. Among the earliest research, which proposed utilizing the leading digit frequencies and Benford's law to serve as a baseline for fraud detection, was [\[49\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0049), wherein the author indicated that socio-economic or financial data is often drafted with a bias to support critical policy plannings by manual intervention. He further suggested that a common way of creating fictitious data tends to distribute the digits involved uniformly owing to human intuition and prejudice on natural symmetry. In contrast, most realistic socio-economic or financial data will obey scale-invariance with respect to different measurement units, which ultimately leads the digits to follow Benford's law approximately. The scholar *Mark J. Nigrini*, from West Virginia University, has coined the name of using Benford's law for accounting fraud detection as “digit analysis”, which is a special quantitative method in “forensic auditing”. In particular, he describes:

> “*Benford's Law provides auditors with the expected digit frequencies in tabulated data. By examining the digit and the number frequencies, auditors can gain data insights that might be missed using traditional analytical procedures and sampling methods. The digit and number patterns could point to number invention, systematic frauds, data errors, or biases in the data. Research is currently underway on advanced tests to detect anomalies in data subsets*.”

Furthermore, Nigrini [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0031) proposed a “five-digit test” as a formal and systematic framework to quickly screen out any fraudulent numbers present in public filings, so that companies with the most anomalous data are targeted for another deeper level of expert auditing. The “five-digit test” examines the validity of the following digits against Benford's law, with the respective expected frequencies listed aside:

1. where the second inequality is due to a simple application of the mean value theorem. As a truncated tailed sum of the convergent Euler's series ![pi squared slash 6 equals 1 plus 1 slash 2 squared plus 1 slash 3 squared plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis](images/c04-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;&#8201;</mi></math>, we clearly see that the last expression must converge to zero as ![script l](images/c04-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math> goes to infinity. Therefore, for large ![script l](images/c04-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math>, all ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis d Subscript script l Baseline left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals i right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>'s, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 9](images/c04-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, are essentially the same numerically.

Next we describe the five-digit test procedure. Firstly, tests against the first and second leading digits are regarded as the high level ones for screening out whether or not a company's public filing is reasonable. For those companies having financial reports containing the first and second digits whose frequencies deviate significantly from Benford's law, the first two and the first three digits are further tested in order to narrow down the list of companies to be targeted for auditing. Further, if these two tests cannot be passed, we further test for the last two digits so as to detect any fabricated and rounded numbers; readers with interest can also refer to [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0031) for a more extensive discussion and in-depth guidelines on Benford's law in forensic accounting.

In [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0031), there is an empirical analysis about the personal spending of the former president of the United States *Bill Clinton*. Since his presidency in 1993, taxes paid by both Bill and *Hillary Clinton* were repeatedly under investigation. For instance, in [\[40\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0040) and [\[48\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0048) the authors used line-item

Lastly, in [\[10\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0010), two tables ([Tables 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0002) and [4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0003)) are constructed, which summarize when analysis via Benford's law is appropriate or not. For instance, numbers could be easily influenced by human thought as some numbers are considered (un)lucky; ATM withdrawals tend to be biased towards a certain symmetry. Both these cases do not follow Benford's law [\[32\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0032). In particular, machine assigned numbers, like cheque numbers or purchase order numbers, are more likely to follow a uniform distribution on ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma 9 EndSet](images/c04-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Moreover, [\[10\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0010) also indicated that sellers tend to round-down the prices to raise psychological attention, for example the selling price of $2.00 is likely to be rounded down to $1.99 in order to attract more customers, causing an excess of last digit 9s at the expense of having 0s. In contrast, [\[4\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0004) suggested that managers tend to round-up net incomes that were just below the psychological boundaries.

 ![Table 4.2 When Benford analysis is likely useful?](images/c04-i0139.png)

[**Table 4.2**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0002) When Benford analysis is likely useful?

[**Table 4.3**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0003) When Benford analysis is not likely useful?

| Not Likely Useful || Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Collection of assigned numbers || Cheque numbers, invoice numbers, zip codes |
| --- | --- |
| Numbers subject to behavioral influence of human such as firm-specific numbers || Prices that with psychological preferences ($1.99 vs $2.00), ATM withdrawals, typical refunds |
| Set of numerical figures with a notable portion of missed transaction records || Bribes, thefts, kickbacks, contract rigging |

 

### 4.3.1 Benford's Law in US Census Data (2010)

Here we outline an interesting example of Nigrini's testing procedure [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0031) on US census data of the year 2010. This dataset contains population sizes of 3,142 counties in the United States, and the purpose is to investigate the quality of the data via testing whether these altogether conform with Benford's law by using Nigrini's “five-digit test”. To begin, we load the census data in [Programme 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-gra-0001) via Python (resp. [Programme 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-gra-0002) via **R**).

![](images/c04-gra-0001.png)![](images/c04-gra-0002.png) ![](images/c04-gra-0003.png)

Let ![upper K](images/c04-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> denote the total number of possible digits in a chosen test, e.g. ![upper K equals 9](images/c04-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math> and ![upper K equals 10](images/c04-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> for the first digit test and the second digit test, respectively. Other than the test based on *Mean Absolute Deviation* (MAD) proposed in [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0031), we here introduce two common tests for conformity of the dataset with Benford's law by computing the absolute deviation between the actual proportion ![AP Subscript i](images/c04-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>AP</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and the expected (theoretical) proportion ![EP Subscript i](images/c04-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>EP</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c04-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>; also see [Appendix 4.A.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0023) for an introduction to goodness-of-fit tests.

In the chi-square goodness-of-fit test, [Table 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0004) is a list of suggested ![p](images/c04-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value critical levels for the levels of conformity with Benford's law.

 

[**Table 4.4**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0004) Suggested “five-digit test” ![p](images/c04-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value criteria for the chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

| Range || Conformity |
| --- | --- |
| 0.1 to 1 || Close |
| --- | --- |
| 0.05 to 0.1 || Acceptable |
| 0.01 to 0.05 || Marginally acceptable |
| 0 to 0.01 || Not acceptable |

![](images/c04-gra-0004.png) ![](images/c04-gra-0005.png)

In [Programme 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-gra-0003) via Python (resp. [Programme 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-gra-0004) via **R**), the `Benford_Analysis()` function is defined in the same fashion with four input arguments, namely: `Count` as the Python `pandas` dataframe (resp. **R** `table`) of actual frequencies for each digit to be inputted; `EP` for the expected proportion for each digit of the chosen test calculated in accordance with Benford's law; `DIGITS` for the set of the possible leading digits of interest for a test; and `x_label` for the name of the chosen test printed in the ![x](images/c04-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>\-axis of the bar chart. Moreover, this `Benford_Analysis()` function also exports a frequency plot that shows how the actual digit frequencies deviate from those expected ones according to Benford's law (depicted by the blue broken line). In particular, the digits which violate Benford's law (having a small ![p](images/c04-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value (![less-than 0.05](images/c04-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>) value using the folded ![upper Z](images/c04-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>\-statistics) will be colored in red. Lastly, the ![p](images/c04-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test for all digits at once is also returned.

As an illustration for the Nigrini “five-digit test”, we shall perform all five tests without regard to their individual conformity with Benford's law. For each of these five Nigrini's digit tests, we first extract the digit frequencies of interest from our dataset, and then construct a Python `pandas` dataframe (resp. **R** `table`) that contains the corresponding actual frequencies observed in the numerical figures of the dataset along with the expected proportions (EP) as predicted by Benford's law in accordance with ([4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0016)), ([4.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0017)), ([4.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0018)) and ([4.6](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0019)).

In conclusion, [Table 4.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0005) shows a summary of the “five-digit test” for the US census dataset in 2010. For the first (resp. second) digit test, its ![p](images/c04-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of 0.061537 (resp. 0.103993) of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test concludes acceptable (resp. close) conformity of the dataset with Benford's law; indeed, we clearly see an astonishingly high degree of alignment between the actual and expected proportions in [Figure 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0003) (resp. [Figure 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0004)). In particular, for the first digit test, the small ![p](images/c04-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the folded ![upper Z](images/c04-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> test for the first digit of 5 shows rejection of the Benford's law, and this is further highlighted by the bar with a deeper color in red in [Figure 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0003). However, for the second digit test, no digit is rejected by the test using the folded ![upper Z](images/c04-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>\-statistics.

Although the first digit and second digit tests conclude there is at least an acceptable conformity with Benford's law, for the purpose of illustration, we also continue the discussion on the remaining three digit tests. For the first-two digit test (also see [Figure 4.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0005)), its ![p](images/c04-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of 0.028652 of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test indicates a marginally acceptable conformity of the dataset with Benford's law. Interestingly, no digit in the first-two digit test is rejected by the test using folded ![upper Z](images/c04-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>\-statistics. For the tests on first three and last two digits (also see [Figures 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0006) and [4.7](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0007), respectively), their small respective ![p](images/c04-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of 0.007938 and 0.004605 of the corresponding chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests suggest a rejection to Benford's Law: particularly, five numbers listed at the bottom for the last-two test case and 24 numbers listed in the first-three test case are rejected by the test using folded ![upper Z](images/c04-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>\-statistics.

 

## 4.4 BENFORD'S LAW IN GROWTH FIGURES

 

### 4.4.1 For Macroeconomic and Social Science Data

We here discuss how a sequence of temporal data, arisen in finance and econometrics, with an exponential growth (or decay) can naturally conform with Benford's law, at least approximately, and we defer its rigorous mathematical proof until [Subsection \*4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0010). Let ![normal upper X left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denote the nominal gross domestic product (GDP) of a country at time ![t](images/c04-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, and model the evolution of this process in a discrete-time setting as:

[(4.9)](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-disp-0025)![normal upper X left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 plus normal upper G Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis normal upper X left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma for t equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma](images/c04-math-0025.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal upper G Subscript t](images/c04-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s are assumed as iid random variables such that each ![normal upper G Subscript t](images/c04-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> represents the growth rate of the overall economic activity for the period from ![t](images/c04-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> to ![t plus 1](images/c04-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. One criticism of this simple model might be that the growth rate ![normal upper G Subscript t](images/c04-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is not completely independent of the present level of GDP ![normal upper X left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> or the timing of ![t](images/c04-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, since more developed economies and aging populations tend to grow slower; however, so long as the overall time period does not span several decades, the approximation of using iid assumption is still reasonably good and Benford's law likely holds. A formal statement of this claim is based on [Theorem 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0002), together with its proof, and the discussion thereafter in [Subsection \*4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0010). Likewise, the same kind of dynamics modeling can explain the emergence of Benford's law in stock prices, company revenues and profits, units of product sold and so on. More discussions can be found in [\[25\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0025).

Over the years, many research studies have shown that Benford's law can detect economic fraudulent data from government authorities. For instance, [\[36\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0036) found that among eurozone countries, Greek economic data deviated the most from Benford's law, and this deviation persisted across leading digits and first few leading digits combinations. The authors also indicated that this possibility of manipulating data was later confirmed by the European Commission.

Benford's law is also very useful for monitoring the fairness of elections, so as to detect any electoral fraud through screening various official election statistics. That said, this detection is complicated by the respective privacy protection rules. Recent examples include the 2009 Iranian presidential election [\[38\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0038) and the presidential and parliamentary elections in Turkey over 2017–2018 [\[21\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0021). Unfortunately, the efficacy of Benford's law in election monitoring has not yet been rigorously established [\[8\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0008) due to the lack of a prominent and definite explanation for why the phenomenon may emerge in most election data.

 

### 4.4.2 COVID-19 Figures in Healthcare Management

A recent work [\[20\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0020) identified the emergence of Benford's law in the early stages of the epidemic of the contemporary outbreak of COVID-19. whose form is the reason why the Benford's law emerges. As mentioned previously, the formal statement of this claim is made in [Theorem 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0014), and its proof is laid down in [Subsection \*4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0010). In particular, evidence of Benford's law is illustrated by using various case numbers for COVID-19 across many different countries. [Figure 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0008) shows the leading digit frequencies of daily COVID-19 case figures and [Table 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0006) shows the ![p](images/c04-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of the chi-square goodness-of-fit tests in nine countries over a period of ![upper T equals 30 comma 40](images/c04-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>40</mn></math> days:

where ![x Subscript upper T comma d](images/c04-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the actual frequency and ![upper E Subscript upper T comma d Baseline equals upper T dot log Subscript 10 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 plus 1 slash d right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the expected Benford's frequency of the leading digit ![d](images/c04-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> over a period of ![upper T](images/c04-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> days.

Clearly, from [Figure 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0008), with ![upper T equals 30](images/c04-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math>, numbers corresponding to Canada, Germany, and USA do not follow Benford's law. This observation is further supported by the small ![p](images/c04-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values ![left-parenthesis less-than 0.05 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in their chi-square goodness-of-fit tests shown in [Table 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0006). A possible explanation is that the start day of counting is too early for these three countries, in which the cumulative growths of figures appear not too geometric in nature. Finally, China's data over a period of ![upper T equals 40](images/c04-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></math> days also appears to not follow Benford's law. A plausible explanation is that the Chinese central government introduced lockdowns at a very early stage to badly affected cities in Hubei province, and as a result those ![normal xi Subscript t](images/c04-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#958;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s could not evolve freely.

The bolded figures in red are below the 1% significant level.

 

### \*4.4.3 Proof by Fourier Analysis for the Emergence of Benford's Law in Temporal Data

As we have seen, there can be more than one explanation behind the emergence of Benford's law for leading digits. In particular, there is an alternative interpretation as a “central limit” theorem for the mantissas of random variables, but under multiplication [\[3\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003). Following the idea of [\[3\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003), we here introduce how Benford's law can be established via *Fourier analysis* when the random growth rates of the figures over different periods are independent and follow a common distribution. For example, if a city has an initial population ![upper P 0](images/c04-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and grows with a rate of ![normal r Subscript i](images/c04-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in the ![i](images/c04-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th year, then its population in the ![n](images/c04-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-th year is given by

[(4.11)](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-disp-0030)![normal upper P Subscript n Baseline equals upper P 0 left-parenthesis 1 plus normal r 1 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 1 plus normal r 2 right-parenthesis ellipsis left-parenthesis 1 plus normal r Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c04-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is clearly a random variable by its own right.

Given two numerical figures ![x equals x overbar times 1 0 Superscript k Super Subscript x](images/c04-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></msup></math> and ![y equals y overbar times 1 0 Superscript k Super Subscript y](images/c04-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></msup></math> are multiplied, the mantissa ![ModifyingAbove left-parenthesis x dot y right-parenthesis With bar](images/c04-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> of the resulting product ![x y](images/c04-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></math> is:

Equivalently, we must have

As a result, the limiting distribution of the logarithm ![normal z overbar](images/c04-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> of a random variable ![normal z equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts normal x Subscript i](images/c04-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is determined by the limiting distribution of the sum of random variables ![sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts log Subscript 10 Baseline ModifyingAbove normal x With bar Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In the rest of this section, we shall prove the following version of the central limit theorem on a torus by means of Fourier analysis. Its immediate consequence will give the emergence of Benford's law for time series data governed by the dynamics given by ([4.9](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0025)) or ([4.11](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0030)).

 

**[Theorem 4.1](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fea-0002) *(Central Limit Theorem on the torus T¹)***   Let ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript k Baseline](images/c04-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> be independent and identically distributed continuous random variables on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> with a common probability density function ![f element-of upper L squared left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, also denote ![normal w equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript k Endscripts normal x Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Then, as ![k right-arrow infinity](images/c04-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, ![normal w](images/c04-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi></mrow></math> approaches a uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>.

To see [Theorem 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0002) can warrant the emergence of Benford's law, for if ![normal y](images/c04-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is a random variable on ![double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline equals left-bracket 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> such that ![log Subscript 10 Baseline normal y left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;y</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> follows a uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, we can show that ![d 1 left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> must follow a Benford's law. On the other hand, to prove [Theorem 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0002), for the sake of convenience, under 1-modular arithmetics, we assume that the density function ![f left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is periodic with period 1 and so, if defined on ![double-struck upper R Subscript plus](images/c04-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math>,

**[Lemma 4.1](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fea-0004)**   Assume that ![f element-of upper L squared left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is a probability density function. Then,

1.  ![ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c04-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>;

To establish the last claim about the boundedness of the supremum, note that by Parseval's identity, ![StartAbsoluteValue ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue right-arrow 0](images/c04-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> as ![StartAbsoluteValue n EndAbsoluteValue right-arrow infinity](images/c04-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, therefore, all ![StartAbsoluteValue ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue](images/c04-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math>'s except finitely many of them are less than ![1 slash 2](images/c04-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, while for those finitely many ![StartAbsoluteValue ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue](images/c04-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math>'s which are not less than ![1 slash 2](images/c04-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, each of them is still strictly less than 1, and so the claim follows.

Consider ![normal z equals normal x plus normal y left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![normal x](images/c04-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal y](images/c04-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> are continuous random variables on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with respective density functions ![f](images/c04-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> and ![g](images/c04-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>. Then ![normal z](images/c04-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow></math> is also a continuous random variable, and it has a density ![h](images/c04-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> such that

![h left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals integral Subscript 0 Superscript 1 Baseline f left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis g left-parenthesis t minus u right-parenthesis d u equals left-parenthesis f asterisk g right-parenthesis left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis comma](images/c04-math-0044.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is the usual convolution of ![f](images/c04-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> and ![g](images/c04-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> on a bounded range. The Fourier coefficient ![modifying above h with caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![n element-of double-struck upper Z](images/c04-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>, can then be computed as the product of ![ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![modifying above g with caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#285;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>:

 

[**Lemma 4.2**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fea-0008)   Let ![f comma g](images/c04-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></math> and ![h](images/c04-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> be the continuous probability density functions of ![normal x comma y](images/c04-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></math> and ![normal z equals normal x plus normal y left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, respectively, where ![normal x](images/c04-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal y](images/c04-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> are continuous random variables on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. *Proof of Theorem 4.1*: Let ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript k Baseline](images/c04-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> be iid continuous random variables on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a common density ![f element-of upper L squared left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> and consider ![normal w colon equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript k Endscripts normal x Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Then it is clear that ![normal w](images/c04-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi></mrow></math> is also a continuous random variable on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and its density function ![h](images/c04-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>, by [Lemma 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0008), has Fourier coefficients ![modifying above h with caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript k](images/c04-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math> for ![n element-of double-struck upper Z](images/c04-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>. In order to show that ![normal w](images/c04-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi></mrow></math> approaches to a uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, it suffices to show that ![h right-arrow 1](images/c04-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in the ![upper L squared](images/c04-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>\-norm on ![upper L squared left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> as ![k right-arrow infinity](images/c04-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>.
