[**Lemma 4.3**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fea-0012)   Let ![normal x](images/c04-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> be a continuous random variable on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a probability density ![f element-of upper L squared left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, and let ![normal z equals m normal x left-parenthesis mod 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for a fixed ![m element-of double-struck upper Z](images/c04-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>. Thus, these explain the emergence of Benford's law for COVID-19 figures governed by the dynamics of ([4.10](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0027)).

## 4.5 ZIPF'S LAW

Zipf's law is another empirical law that has been observed to naturally occur in datasets from both social and physical sciences. The law is named after the linguist *George Kingsley Zipf* who noticed that the frequency of a given word in a corpus of natural language is inversely proportional to its rank in the corresponding frequency [table \[51](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0051), [52\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0052). Mathematically, given an ordered dataset ![z 1 greater-than z 2 greater-than ellipsis greater-than z Subscript n](images/c04-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, in which each datum ![z Subscript r](images/c04-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> is labeled by its own rank (![r](images/c04-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>), Zipf's law is said to hold if the log-log plot of ![ln left-parenthesis z Subscript r Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![ln left-parenthesis r right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is approximately linear. More precisely, Zipf's law asserts that

[(4.13)](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-disp-0050)![ln left-parenthesis r right-parenthesis equals alpha minus beta ln left-parenthesis z Subscript r Baseline right-parenthesis plus epsilon Subscript r](images/c04-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> 

for ![r equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c04-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, where ![alpha comma beta greater-than 0](images/c04-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and these ![epsilon Subscript r](images/c04-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math>'s are independent error terms. This linear regression relationship is also referred to as the rank-size rule. Some authors, such as [\[14\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0014), use Zipf's law to refer specifically to phenomena following power law distributions, of which this rank-size rule is a direct consequence. This claim can be proved by using the theory of order statistics under the power law distribution. In particular, for a power law distribution ![normal upper Z](images/c04-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi></mrow></math> with the survival function ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal upper Z greater-than z right-parenthesis tilde StartFraction e Superscript alpha overTilde Baseline Over z Superscript beta Baseline EndFraction](images/c04-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></math>, we take the logarithm of both sides to obtain ![ln double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal upper Z greater-than z right-parenthesis almost-equals alpha overTilde minus beta ln z](images/c04-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>z</mi></math>; on the other hand, let ![q Subscript left-parenthesis gamma right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> be the quantile at the upper tail level ![gamma](images/c04-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal upper Z greater-than q Subscript left-parenthesis gamma right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals gamma](images/c04-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi></math>, then we have ![ln gamma almost-equals alpha overTilde minus beta ln q Subscript left-parenthesis gamma right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>. Therefore, for the sample observation, since ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal upper Z greater-than z right-parenthesis vertical-bar Subscript z equals z Sub Subscript r Subscript Baseline almost-equals StartFraction r Over n EndFraction](images/c04-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>, we then have ![ln StartFraction r Over n EndFraction almost-equals alpha overTilde minus beta ln z Subscript r](images/c04-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>&#8776;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> or ![ln r almost-equals left-parenthesis alpha overTilde plus ln n right-parenthesis minus beta ln z Subscript r](images/c04-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math>.

Zipf's law has been observed in different areas ranging from pure sciences to social sciences, for example the ranking of city sizes by population found in [\[14\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0014). In fact, that city rankings have been demonstrated to obey, approximately, Zipf's law is particularly interesting given the uncontrolled nature of city growths. This observation holds in the United States throughout the 20th Century [\[23](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0023), [24\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0024), and for most other countries [\[37\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0037); indeed, a study by Moura and Ribeiro [\[29\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0029) found that Brazilian cities also obey the law over a period of at least 50 years. On the other hand, the emergence of Zipf's law in epidemiological data is of significance as it provides a practical means of flagging data for further analysis in *healthcare management*. To see why Zipf's law emerges naturally in epidemiology, we first present a brief summary of the explanation in the context of city population ranking below.

Let ![normal upper S Subscript t Superscript i](images/c04-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> denote the normalized size of city ![i](images/c04-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> at time ![t](images/c04-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> among a collection of ![n](images/c04-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> cities, and this total number of cities is fixed and finite. Moreover, the normalized city size is simply city's population divided by the total population in all ![n](images/c04-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> cities, and the initial distribution of population to cities is arbitrary. It is assumed that the normalized city sizes, at least over a certain range, evolve randomly over time. More precisely, assume that in the upper tail the evolution of the ![i](images/c04-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th city size is in the form

As discussed above, the rank-size relationship ([4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0050)) is then a consequence of the power law distribution

It is easy to see that if ([4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0050)) holds for normalized ![z Subscript r](images/c04-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math>, it clearly holds for unnormalized ![z Subscript r](images/c04-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> by absorbing the normalizing constant into ![alpha](images/c04-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> of ([4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0050)).

Few empirical phenomena obey power law distributions for all values of ![x](images/c04-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>; instead, power laws typically only hold for values greater than some minimum value ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>, which must be estimated. In that case, Zipf's law remains valid for large enough values of ![z Subscript r](images/c04-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math>. In particular, the rank-size relationship can be seen in the size rankings of naturally occurring cities [\[19\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0019), gross domestic products [\[6\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0006), world cities [\[6\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0006), and English text frequencies [\[28\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0028).

 

## 4.6 ZIPF'S LAW AND COVID-19 FIGURES

The emergence of Zipf's law in epidemiological data is of significance as it provides a practical means of flagging data for further analysis in healthcare management. Investigations are generally costly, and they should be initiated only if there is a good reason to suspect data of being fraudulent. Central governments compile data from many different sources, such as local governments or directly from healthcare faculties, and so there is a clear need to automate and streamline fraud detection procedures. Furthermore, the use of Zipf's law for fraud detection is strengthened by the central government's monopoly on civil information; if the government does not publish the regional breakdown of the data in question, it would be difficult for local authorities to falsify data in accordance with Zipf's law. By monitoring the data over time, and not publishing them in detail, the central government can ascertain the expected Zipfian pattern in the data, upon which an automated fraud detection system can be developed.

After explaining the emergence of Zipf's law in city population rankings in the previous discussion, we now turn to the topic of why it should emerge within the early stages of an epidemic. Consider a country comprised of a collection of regions such as states or provinces If a common disease is simultaneously imported to each region and begins to spread locally, let ![normal upper I Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be the normalized number of infections in the region ![i](images/c04-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c04-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>; in other words, ![normal upper I Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the number of infected individuals in the region ![i](images/c04-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> divided by the total number of infected nationally over ![n](images/c04-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> regions. Considering that the disease is identical across each region, with a given level of infectiousness, and supposing that there is homogeneity among regions in terms of culture, population density, and development, assume that each region shares a common level of infectiousness ![theta greater-than 0](images/c04-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and a common recovery rate ![delta greater-than 0](images/c04-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. We should emphasize that Condition ([4.19](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0058)) does not mean that each number of infections does not increase; since we are considering the normalized numbers of infections, this condition only refers to the number of infections in the region ![i](images/c04-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> relative to the rest of the whole country.

There are three obvious areas where the above construction might fall short, and they must be considered when determining the cause of anomalous data. Firstly, if the regions are very different from one another in terms of culture, population density, demographics, or development, then clearly the assumption of common infectiousness and recovery parameters is questionable, and this likely leads to deviations from Zipf's law. Therefore, if there is a handful of regions that deviate significantly from the nationally predicted rank-size relationship, the first course of action is to check whether these regions differ meaningfully from the rest of the country. This includes whether the policy response of the local authorities differed from that of the central government, or if the response followed a very different timeline. Secondly, the assumption of the iid nature of ![normal gamma Subscript t Superscript i](images/c04-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>'s, which implies the independence of the number of infections, may not be absolutely correct in practice. In particular, centralized and decentralized preventative measures could impose an effect on the dynamics of disease spread, and the likelihood of such measures being implemented clearly increases with disease prevalence in a region. Finally, the assumption that the disease is imported to all regions simultaneously can be susceptible, as in reality, the disease emerges in larger transport hubs long before the rural regions. The timeline of infections should therefore be examined to check whether cases in anomalous regions could emerge much earlier or later than the rest of the country. More discussions on this topic can be traced in our work [\[20\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0020).

For the estimation of ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>, we recall the notion of Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) distance as introduced in [Section 3.1](#c03.xhtml#head-2-19), and then follow the approach proposed in [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005). Consider the truncated KS distance beyond ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> between the empirical and theoretical power law distributions defined by:

(4.20)![upper K left-parenthesis x Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals max Underscript x greater-than-or-equal-to x Subscript min Baseline Endscripts StartAbsoluteValue ModifyingAbove upper F With caret left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis minus upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue comma](images/c04-math-0059.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![ModifyingAbove upper F With caret left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the empirical distribution of the data above ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>, and ![upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the power law distribution of best fit for data above ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>; also see [\[7\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0007). To estimate ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>, [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005) suggests the estimate ![ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> to be the minimizer of ![upper K left-parenthesis x Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which can be numerically obtained via the **R** package `poweRlaw`.

Having obtained an estimate ![ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>, the two most common approaches to estimating the parameter ![beta](images/c04-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> in ([4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0050)) are ordinary least squares (OLS) and Hill's estimator. As noted in [\[16\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0016), while OLS is the most common method employed in the empirical literature, it tends to underestimate the power exponent. An alternative estimator known as Hill's estimator was proposed by [\[17\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0017), and is defined by

(4.21)![ModifyingAbove normal beta With Ì‚ Subscript Hills Baseline colon equals StartFraction n Subscript tail Baseline minus 1 Over sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Subscript tail Baseline minus 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis ln left-parenthesis normal z Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis minus ln left-parenthesis normal z Subscript n Sub Subscript tail Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndFraction period](images/c04-math-0060.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mtext>Hills</mtext></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

A test for whether the underlying distribution of the data above this estimated minimal threshold ![ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> is a power law distribution with the estimated tail index ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚](images/c04-i0418.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> is proposed in [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005); again, this can be implemented using the package `poweRlaw`. This test is motivated by the notion of *bootstrapping* (see alternative discussion in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml)), in the sense that the distribution of the test statistic, namely the truncated KS distance ![normal upper K left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is approximated by the empirical distribution of the truncated KS distances of the bootstrapped samples from the fitted distribution.

Specifically, let ![n Subscript tail](images/c04-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub></math> denote the number of data points greater than ![ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> in the observed dataset of size ![n](images/c04-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, whose truncated distance is denoted by ![upper K Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. We generate a total of ![upper M](images/c04-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> (usually ranging from 1,000 to 10,000) bootstrapped samples, each of size ![n](images/c04-i0425.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, where every sample point is generated independently in the following manner: with a probability of ![StartFraction n Subscript tail Baseline Over n EndFraction](images/c04-i0426.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>, the point is generated from the power law distribution with the scaling parameter ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚](images/c04-i0427.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> and the support ![x greater-than-or-equal-to ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0428.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math>; otherwise, with a probability of ![1 minus StartFraction n Subscript tail Baseline Over n EndFraction](images/c04-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tail</mtext></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>, the point is drawn uniformly from the portion below ![ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min](images/c04-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> in the original observed dataset. We then calculate the truncated KS distance for the ![m](images/c04-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>\-th bootstrapped sample, denoted by ![upper K Subscript m Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![m equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper M](images/c04-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math>, and the ![p](images/c04-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of this test is defined as the empirical survival function of the bootstrapped truncated KS distances at ![upper K Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>:

![p hyphen value colon equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue StartSet m colon upper K Subscript m Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than upper K Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove x With caret Subscript min Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet EndAbsoluteValue Over upper M EndFraction period](images/c04-math-0061.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mtext>-value</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>M</mi></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

Intuitively, a small ![p](images/c04-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value below a pre-specified significance level ![alpha](images/c04-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> indicates that the truncated KS distance of the observed dataset is larger than most of those in the bootstrapped samples, leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis at the significance level ![alpha](images/c04-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> that the upper tail of the dataset follows the fitted power law. Also see [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005) for detailed discussions on the test.

In what follows, we consider an empirical analysis of the regional COVID-19 case figures as of 11 May 2020 for 14 countries

We focus on the column ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> in [Table 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0007), which is the ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> statistic for the regression model ([4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0050)). For all countries except China and Russia, ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> exceeds 0.9, testifying to the presence of Zipf's law for the regional distribution of COVID-19 cases in a country.

Among the only exceptions, the low ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> for China (without Hubei) and Russia can be justified by a change in the power law exponent, as shown in the log-log plots of [Figure 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0009). This is because the estimation procedure for ![x Subscript min](images/c04-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi></msub></math> as outlined in [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005) locates the point where the second power law ends, but not the one where the power law exponent first changes, resulting in inaccurate results. Such change points might be explained if the regions can be separated into two homogeneous subgroups, such as urban and rural regions, so that each of them possesses similar within-group growth trajectories. In particular, further analysis on the Russia data shows that the first power law applies to major developed cities and seaports in the European part of the country, and a similar analysis for China (without Hubei) indicates the presence of the first power law mostly in coastal provinces, which are more developed. As a result, the change points can be justified in relation to the level of development and geographical location of the place, which in turn explains the relatively low ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> values.

![Table 4.7 Regional COVID-19 cases by country extracted from \[20\].](images/c04-i0439.png)

[**Table 4.7**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0007) Regional COVID-19 cases by country extracted from [\[20\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0020).

 ![FIGURE 4.9 Log-log plots of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Russia (black solid), China with Hubei (green dashed), and China without Hubei (blue dotted). Note the change in power law indicated by the change in slope.](images/c04f009.png)

[**FIGURE 4.9**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0009) Log-log plots of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Russia (black solid), China with Hubei (green dashed), and China without Hubei (blue dotted). Note the change in power law indicated by the change in slope.

 

On the other hand, when Hubei is included in the analysis for China, then the low ![upper R squared](images/c04-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> can no longer be explained by a change point; there were far more cases in Hubei relative to the remaining provinces. However, this discrepancy might be explained by the entirely different growth trajectories following Chinese government intervention. The virus spread uncontrollably in Hubei for three weeks in January 2020, before the extraordinary quarantine measures undertaken by the government came into force just before the Chinese New Year, which effectively halted the transmission of the virus to other provinces via the *Chunyun* (a.k.a. *Spring Festival Travel Rush*).

The applicability of Zipf's law can also be assessed visually via log-log plots. [Figures 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0009) and [4.10](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0010) present log-log plots of regional COVID-19 cases for the countries considered. Again, the plots are roughly linear for all countries except China and Russia, which supports Zipf's law in general. The estimates of ![beta](images/c04-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> for the countries using either OLS or Hill estimation are mostly around 1, echoing the theoretical arguments based on the construction by [\[14\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0014) and our discussions in [Section 4.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0019), which predicts a power law exponent of ![beta equals 1](images/c04-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; yet there are still some deviations in which some estimates vary quite substantially and notably different from 1. For instance, Canada has an OLS estimate of ![beta](images/c04-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> as small as 0.34, while that for the United Kingdom is as large as 2.24. This difference is caused by the fact that the Canadian cases are highly concentrated in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, which together account for 84% of COVID-19 cases in Canada. On the other hand, the two largest regions in the United Kingdom accounted for only 30% of all cases.

![FIGURE 4.10 Log-log plots of confirmed COVID-19 cases in each country.](images/c04f010.png)

[**FIGURE 4.10**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0010) Log-log plots of confirmed COVID-19 cases in each country.

Besides the examples illustrated in this chapter, Benford's law and Zipf's law still have various potential applications in a wide range of disciplines. Nevertheless, data collection is always the first and foremost step of such analyses. In the event that the data are heavy-tailed, they may be handled better by utilizing other statistical tools, e.g., *Taylor's law* of fluctuation for heavy-tailed data recently studied in [\[2\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0002). We shall leave these explorations for future research.

Before proceeding to the discussion of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test, we first introduce an important matrix inverse formula:

 

**[Proposition 4.1](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fea-0018) *(Sherman–Morrison formula* [\[18](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0018), [41\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0041)*)***   Suppose that ![bold-italic upper A](images/c04-i0482.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is an ![n times n](images/c04-i0483.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> invertible square matrix, and ![bold-italic u comma bold-italic v](images/c04-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi></math> are ![n](images/c04-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vectors. ## NOTES

1.  [1](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-note-0001)   A ![sigma](images/c04-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>\-finite measure ![mu](images/c04-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> means that for any compact subset ![upper K](images/c04-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> of ![double-struck upper R](images/c04-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> now, ![mu left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is finite; this allows the possibility that the ![mu](images/c04-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>\-measure of the totality can be infinite.
2.  [2](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-note-0002)   Line-item in accounting is an item of revenue or expenditure in a budget or other financial statements or reports.

# CHAPTER 5  
Numerical Finance

 

This chapter mainly introduces the use of simulations for the pricing of financial derivatives. Different basic simulation techniques will be introduced first. Regarding the origins of simulation, the idea started with the building of atomic bombs in the *Manhattan Project* [\[8\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0008) in 1942 during World War II. Scientists, including *Albert Einstein*, *J. Robert Oppenheimer* and *John von Neumann*, were the first to investigate the phenomenon of nuclear fission. When the nucleus of an atom is bombarded by a neutron, it will decompose into two lighter nuclei and release some more neutrons, emitting a huge amount of energy as a byproduct. These newly separated-out neutrons will further collide with other nuclei, and henceforth trigger a chain reaction. Physicists found a good use of statistics to predict and describe the aggregated behavior of the collective atom movements by treating every single atom as a random object whose moving trajectory is independent of those of the others.

 

## 5.1 FUNDAMENTALS OF SIMULATION

One hurdle faced in the implementation of modelling atomic behavior is the generation of genuine random numbers between 0 and 1; indeed, true randomness cannot be achieved by routine calculating machines. A *pseudorandom number generator* is used to mimic the truly random phenomenon of generating seemingly unordered values, and does so through a deterministic mechanism related to *chaotic dynamical systems*.

In *Chaos Theory*, the apparent random and irregular occurrence of states of a dynamical system are actually led by deterministic initial conditions. This kind of dynamical generating mechanism is very sensitive to the initial environment; indeed, even a tiny disturbance in the initial condition, after a short time, can cause the output state of the dynamical system to differ significantly from the original state. Due to this apparent unpredictability, a source of randomness can be obtained.

For pseudorandom number generators, the general idea is to choose an arbitrary initial seed every time, and then use the same dynamical system to generate a long sequence of its future states. We then dispose of the first portion of the numbers generated, and take the tail sequence of numbers as the random sample observations. Mathematically, this procedure of random number generation is justifiable, as discussed below.

One possible dynamical system used is the *linear congruential generator* which is one of the most common pseudorandom number generators. The generating algorithm is simple, and is defined by:

![x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline identical-to left-parenthesis a x Subscript n Baseline plus c right-parenthesis left-parenthesis mod m right-parenthesis comma for n equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma](images/c05-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![x 0](images/c05-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> is a known initial “seed”, the integer ![m](images/c05-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is usually selected to be a large prime number, and ![c](images/c05-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is chosen to be small ![left-parenthesis 0 less-than c less-than m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in comparison with ![m](images/c05-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. However, the value of ![left-parenthesis a x Subscript k Baseline plus c right-parenthesis left-parenthesis mod m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>mod</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is very sensitive to a slight change of ![x Subscript k](images/c05-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>; meanwhile, any tiny difference in the value of ![a x Subscript k plus c](images/c05-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></math> can lead to a substantial deviation in the later sequential values. After a long run, the sequence of numbers ![x Subscript n](images/c05-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>'s will notably be uncorrelated with the original seed ![x 0](images/c05-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> or any other ![x Subscript k](images/c05-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s obtained in the previous iteration steps. We can then take the fraction ![x Subscript k Baseline slash m](images/c05-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>m</mi></math> as a sample observed value of the uniform random variable on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. This procedure is justified in accordance with the following well-known result in *Ergodic Theory* [\[5](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0005), [19\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0019): for any ![0 less-than a less-than b less-than 1](images/c05-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>,

![limit Underscript n right-arrow infinity Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript j equals 0 Overscript n minus 1 Endscripts double-struck 1 Subscript left-bracket a comma b right-bracket Baseline left-parenthesis StartFraction x Subscript j Baseline Over m EndFraction right-parenthesis equals b minus a comma](images/c05-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">1</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mi>m</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

which ensures that for an arbitrary initial seed ![x 0](images/c05-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, the relative frequency of those later values of ![x Subscript k Baseline slash m](images/c05-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>m</mi></math> lying in an interval of ![left-parenthesis a comma b right-parenthesis subset-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8834;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> converges to ![b minus a](images/c05-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi></math> as the number of iterations ![n](images/c05-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> tends to infinity. Programme codes in Python and **R** for the linear congruential generator are shown in [Programmes 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0001) and [5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0002), respectively; its comparisons with the built-in random number generators in Python and **R** are also provided in [Figures 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001)a and [5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001)b, respectively.

![](images/c05-gra-0001.png) ![](images/c05-gra-0002.png)![FIGURE 5.1 Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for the uniform distribution on left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket.](images/c05f001.png)

**FIGURE 5.1** Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for the uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>.

Next, we discuss some common simulation techniques for non-uniform distributions; some standard references of this topic include [\[4](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0004), [15](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0015), [16\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0016).

Let ![f Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be the probability density function and the cumulative distribution function of a random variable ![normal x](images/c05-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> respectively. Suppose that we can generate a sample out from a uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. Then we can simulate ![normal x](images/c05-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> using the knowledge of the explicit expression of the inverse of ![upper F Subscript normal x](images/c05-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></math>; indeed, if ![normal u tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, i.e. ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal u less-than-or-equal-to u right-parenthesis equals u](images/c05-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></math>, for ![u element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then

![normal x overTilde colon equals upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis normal u right-parenthesis equals min left-brace right-brace colon t colon greater-than-or-equal-to greater-than-or-equal-to of FFx left-parenthesis right-parenthesis tu tilde upper F Subscript normal x Baseline period](images/c05-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

To see this, we note that ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis normal u right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to x right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal u less-than-or-equal-to upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Therefore, if one can generate uniform samples, then in principle, if ![upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be explicitly spelt out, we can generate a random sample from ![upper F Subscript normal x](images/c05-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></math>. This simulation approach is said to be via *inverse function transform*. Conversely, we also have ![upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> if ![normal x tilde upper F Subscript normal x](images/c05-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></math> and ![upper F Subscript normal x](images/c05-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></math> is continuous; its proof is simple, and we leave it as an exercise for readers. By applying this inverse transform technique, we can now simulate random variables of other distributions such as the common exponential distribution; see the programme codes for Python in [Programme 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0003) and for **R** in [Programme 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0004). The corresponding histograms are shown in [Figures 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002)a and [5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002)b, respectively.

![](images/c05-gra-0003.png)![](images/c05-gra-0004.png) ![FIGURE 5.2 Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for the exponential distribution.](images/c05f002.png)

**FIGURE 5.2** Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for the exponential distribution.

Although the *inverse function transform* method looks fundamental for general distribution simulations, an immediate limitation to this approach is that very often the inverse ![upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1](images/c05-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> cannot be expressed explicitly, and without this the programme coding cannot be implemented conveniently. This is particularly the case for the normal distribution, as the inverse of a normal cumulative distribution function cannot be written as a sum of finitely many elementary functions. Fortunately, an alternative approach called the *Box–Muller transformation* can be adopted, allowing a pair of standard normal random variables to be easily be generated. Consider the following transformation, where ![normal u 1](images/c05-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal u 2](images/c05-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are independent uniformly distributed random variables on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>:

Since the joint probability density function of ![normal u 1](images/c05-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal u 2](images/c05-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> is simply:

![f left-parenthesis u 1 comma u 2 right-parenthesis equals 1 comma u 1 comma u 2 element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis comma](images/c05-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

it follows that the joint probability density function of ![normal z 1](images/c05-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal z 2](images/c05-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> should be:

![g left-parenthesis z 1 comma z 2 right-parenthesis equals StartAbsoluteValue StartFraction negative 1 Over 2 pi EndFraction exp left-brace minus StartFraction q Over 2 EndFraction right-brace EndAbsoluteValue dot left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 2 pi EndFraction exp left-brace minus StartFraction z 1 squared plus z 2 squared Over 2 EndFraction right-brace comma z 1 comma z 2 element-of double-struck upper R period](images/c05-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Note that there is some difficulty with the well-posedness of the inverse transformation, particularly when ![z 1 equals 0](images/c05-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; fortunately, this singularity only occurs with a zero probability measure, hence this causes no issues in the actual implementation. Again, programme codes in the Python and **R** environments are included in [Programmes 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0005) and [5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0006) respectively; while their respective comparisons with the built-in normal distribution generators are illustrated in [Figures 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)a and [5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)b.

![](images/c05-gra-0005.png)![](images/c05-gra-0006.png) ![FIGURE 5.3 Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for normal distribution.](images/c05f003.png)

**FIGURE 5.3** Histograms of the samples from pseudo generators for normal distribution.

In the more general case beyond normal distribution, the method of *rejection sampling*, also known as the *acceptance-rejection method*, is commonly adopted; this method essentially dates back to the needle experiment by French mathematician *Comte de Buffon* in estimating the circumference-diameter ratio ![pi](images/c05-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math>. We here only elaborate the case of univariate distribution, while the multivariate case is analogous.

To generate samples from a random variable ![normal x](images/c05-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> with a density ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> over its support ![script upper X Subscript f](images/c05-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub></math>, we can propose a candidate density ![g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a support ![script upper X Subscript g](images/c05-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>g</mi></msub></math> such that ![script upper X Subscript f Baseline subset-of script upper X Subscript g](images/c05-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>g</mi></msub></math>, from which it is much easier to draw samples, that “envelopes” ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; more precisely, as long as there exists a finite constant ![upper M greater-than 1](images/c05-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> such that ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to upper M g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for all ![x element-of script upper X Subscript f](images/c05-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub></math>. The following algorithm explains the general procedure of the rejection sampling:

1.  Generate ![normal x Subscript i Baseline tilde g left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>;
2.  Generate ![normal u Subscript i Baseline tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and accept ![normal x Subscript i](images/c05-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> if ![normal u Subscript i Baseline less-than-or-equal-to StartFraction f left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over upper M g left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c05-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>, otherwise reject ![normal x Subscript i](images/c05-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>;
3.  Repeat steps 1) and 2) for ![upper N](images/c05-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> times, and only keep those accepted ![normal x Subscript i](images/c05-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s as the generated sample.

which holds by noting the very definition of the density ![f](images/c05-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, namely ![integral Underscript script upper X Subscript f Baseline Endscripts f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis d x equals 1](images/c05-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c05-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> whenever ![x element-of script upper X Subscript g minus script upper X Subscript f](images/c05-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>&#8726;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub></math>. In other words, the aforementioned sample average converges to the theoretical quantity of ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis h left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and hence the algorithm is indeed valid. As an illustration, for instance, readers may refer to [Subsection \*6.4.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0035) for an application of this sampling method in the context of *stochastic volatility* models.

 

## 5.2 VARIANCE REDUCTION TECHNIQUE

Most often, after knowing how to simulate a sequence of random variables, the next immediate application is to estimate various quantities of interest, or simply some statistics, of a more complicated probability distribution. For instance, we are often interested in estimating the underlying unknown theoretical mean ![mu Subscript normal x Baseline colon equals í”¼ left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and one may think of using the *Monte Carlo* method. As pointed out in [Section 1.4](#c01.xhtml#head-2-8), one direct approach is to use the sample mean

![ModifyingAbove normal mu Subscript normal x Baseline With Ì‚ equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts normal x Subscript i Baseline comma](images/c05-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

as the estimator, where ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript n Baseline](images/c05-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is a random sample simulated from the distribution of ![normal x](images/c05-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>. The accuracy of this estimator can be assessed by examining its variance. As discussed in [Subsection 1.4.2](#c01.xhtml#head-3-3), it is given by:

![upper V a r left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal mu Subscript normal x Baseline With Ì‚ right-parenthesis equals upper V a r left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over n squared EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts upper V a r left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction upper V a r left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis period](images/c05-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

Clearly, from the expression above, one common way to obtain a more accurate estimate is to increase the number of simulations ![n](images/c05-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, as this reduces the variance of the sample mean estimator. Another way is to cleverly find an alternative random variable ![normal z](images/c05-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow></math> with the same theoretical mean as ![normal x](images/c05-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> but a smaller variance, i.e. ![mu Subscript normal z Baseline colon equals í”¼ left-parenthesis normal z right-parenthesis equals í”¼ left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals mu Subscript normal x Baseline](images/c05-i0086.png)<math **[Example 5.1](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0002)**   Suppose that we would like to estimate the integral ![script upper I colon equals integral Subscript 0 Superscript 1 Baseline x cubed left-parenthesis 1 minus x right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5 Baseline d x](images/c05-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">I</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math> with ![n equals 10 comma 000](images/c05-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> generated samples. We observe that ![script upper I](images/c05-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">I</mi></mrow></math> can be expressed as ![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal u cubed left-parenthesis 1 minus normal u right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> where ![normal u tilde normal upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Thus, we can first simulate ![u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript 10 comma 000 Baseline](images/c05-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and then compute the following estimate:

![ModifyingAbove theta With Ì‚ equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts u Subscript i Superscript 3 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus u Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5 Baseline period](images/c05-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></math> 

Indeed, this integral is related to the **beta distribution** with a pdf:

![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over normal upper B left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis EndFraction x Superscript alpha minus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus x right-parenthesis Superscript beta minus 1 Baseline comma for 0 less-than x less-than 1 comma](images/c05-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![alpha comma beta greater-than 0](images/c05-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and

![normal upper B left-parenthesis alpha comma beta right-parenthesis equals StartFraction normal upper Gamma left-parenthesis alpha right-parenthesis normal upper Gamma left-parenthesis beta right-parenthesis Over normal upper Gamma left-parenthesis alpha plus beta right-parenthesis EndFraction period](images/c05-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

It is clear that ![script upper I equals normal upper B left-parenthesis 4 comma 3.5 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">I</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In [Programme 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0007) (resp. [Programme 5.8](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0008)) with Python (resp. **R**) codes, we repeat the above simulation procedure 1,000 times and return the mean and the (sample) variance of the estimates obtained.
