Notice that, as long as one can find a random variable ![normal z](images/c05-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow></math> that is negatively correlated with ![normal x](images/c05-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. ![Cov left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma normal z 1 right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c05-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, we can then have ![upper V a r left-parenthesis normal psi Subscript upper A Baseline right-parenthesis less-than upper V a r left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis slash n equals upper V a r left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal mu Subscript normal x Baseline With Ì‚ right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#968;</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. One easy way to generate the pair ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that satisfies all the above requirements is to take ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis colon equals left-parenthesis upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis normal u right-parenthesis comma upper F Subscript normal x Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus u right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>1</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>u</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![normal u](images/c05-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></math> is a uniform random variable on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. For example, when ![normal x tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we just take ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis normal u comma 1 minus normal u right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![normal u tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; when ![normal x tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we may take ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis normal x comma 2 mu minus normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn mathvariant="normal">2</mn><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. These pairs of variables ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are called *antithetic*. The following theorem shows that antithetic variables are indeed negatively correlated.

 

[**Proposition 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0004)   Given an increasing function ![h left-parenthesis theta comma normal gamma right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in ![theta element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a parameter ![gamma](images/c05-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>, if ![normal u tilde upper U left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![normal gamma 1](images/c05-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal gamma 2](images/c05-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are independent random variables, then

![Cov left-parenthesis h left-parenthesis normal u comma normal gamma 1 right-parenthesis comma h left-parenthesis 1 minus normal u comma normal gamma 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to 0 period](images/c05-math-0018.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Then ![normal x colon equals h left-parenthesis normal u comma normal gamma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![normal z colon equals h left-parenthesis 1 minus normal u comma normal gamma 2 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> form a pair of antithetic variables.

*Proof.*   We first prove a special case: if the deterministic functions ![g 1 left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![g 2 left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are increasing in ![theta element-of double-struck upper R](images/c05-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, then for any random variable ![normal x](images/c05-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, the variables ![g 1 left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![g 2 left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are positively correlated. To this end, let ![normal x overTilde](images/c05-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></math> be another random variable which is independent of ![normal x](images/c05-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> yet has the same distribution as that of ![normal x](images/c05-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>. As both ![g 1](images/c05-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![g 2](images/c05-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are increasing, clearly ![left-parenthesis g 1 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis minus g 1 left-parenthesis x overTilde right-parenthesis right-parenthesis left-parenthesis g 2 left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis minus g 2 left-parenthesis x overTilde right-parenthesis right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c05-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for any ![x comma x overTilde element-of double-struck upper R](images/c05-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, and so

![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis left-parenthesis g 1 left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis minus g 1 left-parenthesis normal x overTilde right-parenthesis right-parenthesis left-parenthesis g 2 left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis minus g 2 left-parenthesis normal x overTilde right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0 period](images/c05-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math>

By the first assertion, we just established that

On the other hand, since ![normal gamma 1](images/c05-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal gamma 2](images/c05-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are independent themselves, and they are also independent of ![normal u](images/c05-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></math>, ![h left-parenthesis normal u comma normal gamma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![h left-parenthesis 1 minus normal u comma normal gamma 2 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are still conditionally independent given ![normal u](images/c05-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></math>, thus the conditional covariance given ![normal u](images/c05-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></math> is

![Cov left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z vertical-bar normal u right-parenthesis equals Cov left-parenthesis h left-parenthesis normal u comma normal gamma 1 right-parenthesis comma h left-parenthesis 1 minus normal u comma normal gamma 2 right-parenthesis vertical-bar normal u right-parenthesis equals 0 period](images/c05-math-0022.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Finally, by the tower property,

![Cov left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z right-parenthesis equals í”¼ left-parenthesis Cov left-parenthesis normal x comma normal z vertical-bar normal u right-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus Cov left-parenthesis í”¼ left-parenthesis normal x vertical-bar normal u right-parenthesis comma í”¼ left-parenthesis normal z vertical-bar normal u right-parenthesis right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to 0 period](images/c05-math-0023.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mtext>Cov</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

For applications of this approach, readers may refer to [\[11](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0011), [15](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0015), [16\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0016) for more discussions. Meanwhile, we shall continue to use the target integral of [Example 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0002) for the sake of consistent presentation and comparison. [Example 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0008) serves as a counter-example that a mis-use of this approach may lead to a worse performance in terms of the accuracy of estimation. While many other textbooks focus on the merits such as the convenient implementation of [Proposition 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0004), [Example 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0008) suggests that extra caution should be exercised in actual practice.

 

**[Example 5.2](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0008) *(Continuation of [Example 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0002))***   We first simulate ![u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript 5 comma 000 Baseline](images/c05-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></msub></math> and then compute the antithetic samples with ![v Subscript i Baseline equals 1 minus u Subscript i](images/c05-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 5 comma 000](images/c05-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math>. The estimate is then given as in ([5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0016)):

where we take ![x Subscript i Baseline colon equals u Subscript i Superscript 3 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus u Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5](images/c05-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup></math> and ![z Subscript i Baseline colon equals v Subscript i Superscript 3 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus v Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5](images/c05-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup></math>. Again, we repeat the simulation procedure for 1,000 times, and in [Programme 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-0009) via Python (resp. [Programme 5.10](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00010) via **R**), we also report the mean and the (sample) variance of the estimates obtained in Python (resp. **R**). Clearly, the function ![f left-parenthesis w right-parenthesis equals w cubed left-parenthesis 1 minus w right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5](images/c05-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup></math> is not monotonic, and the numerical value of the sample (bootstrapped) variance is larger than that in [Example 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0002). Altogether this illustrates that the sufficient condition of [Proposition 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0004) is in some sense also necessary.

### 5.2.2 Control Variates

Let ![normal y](images/c05-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> be a random variable with a known mean ![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis equals mu Subscript normal y](images/c05-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></msub></math>. Instead of conditioning, we can refine the random variable ![normal x](images/c05-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> directly, so as to reduce the variance of the estimator. For any constant ![b element-of double-struck upper R](images/c05-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, the random variable ![normal z colon equals normal x plus b left-parenthesis normal y minus mu Subscript normal y Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is clearly an unbiased estimator of ![mu Subscript normal x](images/c05-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub></math>. For the *control variate technique*, we aim to pick a ![b](images/c05-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> such that ![upper V a r left-parenthesis normal z right-parenthesis less-than upper V a r left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. To this end, note that

As before, we repeat the simulation procedure for 1,000 times, and in [Programme 5.11](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00011) (resp. [Programme 5.12](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00012)), we also report the mean and the (sample) variance of the estimates obtained in Python (resp. **R**). We can clearly see that the sample (bootstrapped) variance is smaller than that obtained in [Example 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0002).

[Programme 5.14](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00014) in **R**). ### 5.2.3 Stratified Sampling

Let ![normal y equals h left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> where ![normal x](images/c05-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is a random variable with the density function ![p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> on the domain ![script upper X](images/c05-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math> of ![normal x](images/c05-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>. [Programme 5.16](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00016) in **R**).

![](images/c05-gra-0019.png)![](images/c05-gra-0020.png)![](images/c05-gra-0021.png)

To summarize, let us compare the sample means and sample (bootstrapped) variances of various estimates obtained by the different methods shown in the previous examples. From [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001) in Python (resp. [Table 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0002) in **R**), stratified sampling provides the smallest sample variance among all estimations; while the antithetic variable gives the largest, even larger than that of the plain Monte Carlo method; as a counter-example, recall that the function of interest ![w cubed left-parenthesis 1 minus w right-parenthesis Superscript 2.5](images/c05-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>w</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2.5</mn></msup></math>, for ![w element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, does not satisfy the monotone condition. When comparing the single control variate technique with the multiple counterpart, the latter results in a smaller variance as expected. However, one should notice that choosing appropriate control variates might be challenging in an actual implementation.

## 5.3 A REVIEW OF FINANCIAL CALCULUS AND DERIVATIVE PRICING

To facilitate a better understanding of the rest of this chapter, a rudimentary knowledge of financial derivatives and basic stochastic calculus cannot be avoided. Excellent accounts of this subject area can be found in standard textbooks [\[3](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003), [7](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0007), [9](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0009), [17](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0017), [18](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0018), [20\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0020) amongst others.

**Definition 5.1**   A stochastic process ![left-brace normal w Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c05-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, for ![t greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c05-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, is the standard one-dimensional *Wiener process* (Brownian motion) *if and only if* the following conditions hold:

1.  ![normal w 0 equals 0](images/c05-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> with a probability 1;
2.  almost all sample paths are continuous with probability 1;
3.  ![left-brace normal w Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c05-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> has stationary and independent increments;
4.  the increment ![normal w Subscript t Baseline minus normal w Subscript s](images/c05-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></math> has the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance ![t minus s](images/c05-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>s</mi></math> for any ![0 less-than-or-equal-to s less-than t](images/c05-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>t</mi></math>.

The very existence of a standard Wiener process is one of the cornerstone results in *Stochastic Analysis*. Next, we list some key properties and provide a proof for the heuristic that ![delta normal w almost-equals StartRoot delta t EndRoot](images/c05-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> and ![d normal w almost-equals StartRoot d t EndRoot](images/c05-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math>.

The left-hand side expression is called the *quadratic variation* of ![normal w Subscript dot](images/c05-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo>&#183;</mo></msub></math> on ![left-bracket 0 comma upper T right-bracket](images/c05-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, and we say it is equal to ![upper T](images/c05-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> in the ![upper L squared](images/c05-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> sense.

Recall from (3.1) that the change in the stock price over a short period of time of length ![delta t](images/c05-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> under the Black–Scholes–Merton model is approximately ![delta normal upper S Subscript t Baseline equals mu normal upper S Subscript t Baseline delta t plus sigma normal upper S Subscript t Baseline delta normal w Subscript t](images/c05-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>&#948;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, where ![delta normal w Subscript t Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma delta t right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In financial mathematics, as a limit, the infinitesimal form of the stock price is often modeled to be governed by a *Geometric Brownian Motion*:

[(5.6)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0053)![d normal upper S Subscript t Baseline equals mu normal upper S Subscript t Baseline d t plus sigma normal upper S Subscript t Baseline d normal w Subscript t Baseline comma t element-of left-bracket 0 comma upper T right-bracket comma](images/c05-math-0053.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is the stock price at time ![t](images/c05-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, ![mu](images/c05-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is the constant drift term, ![sigma](images/c05-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is the constant volatility, and ![left-brace normal w Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c05-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is the standard Brownian motion with ![normal w Subscript t Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma t right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for any ![t greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c05-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. A fundamental theorem of *Stochastic Analysis* states that the sample path ![StartSet normal upper S Subscript t Baseline colon t greater-than-or-equal-to 0 EndSet](images/c05-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> generated by ([5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0053)) is (almost surely) nowhere differentiable, thus we cannot use the usual Riemann integration to interpret the infinitesimal dynamics of the stock price evolution. Indeed ([5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0053)) is a typical example of a class of differential equations called *stochastic differential equations* (SDEs). To solve it, we need a chain rule of differentiation for the calculus of this class of random functions: the famous *Itô's lemma*. This chain rule is different from the ordinary Newton–Leibniz one as we are now dealing with random functions.

The higher-order terms of ![upper O Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis delta Subscript t Superscript 3 slash 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> refer to terms that contain ![delta t](images/c05-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> of power strictly greater than 1. With Itô's lemma in hand, we are now ready to solve the SDE in ([5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0053)). The problem of simulating their stock price dynamics (approximately) over a tiny time interval ![left-bracket t comma t plus delta t right-bracket](images/c05-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> then lies in generating random samples from a ![p](images/c05-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-variate normal distribution with a mean vector ![delta t bold-italic mu](images/c05-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></math> and a covariance matrix ![delta t bold upper Sigma equals delta t left-parenthesis sigma Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis Subscript i comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c05-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math>. To this end, we shall make use of the Cholesky decomposition of ![bold upper Sigma equals upper C Superscript down-tack Baseline upper C](images/c05-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi>C</mi></math> for some upper triangular matrix ![upper C](images/c05-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>; recall [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007) for more details. More precisely, we aim to generate ![p](images/c05-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-variate normal random vectors with a mean vector ![bold 0 Subscript p](images/c05-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mi>p</mi></msub></math> and a covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c05-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> through ![p](images/c05-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> independent standard normal random numbers:

1.  First, we generate ![p](images/c05-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> independent standard normal random numbers, ![bold z Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis normal z Subscript t comma 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript t comma p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c05-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, where ![normal z Subscript t comma i](images/c05-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s are iid ![script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c05-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>;
2.  Compute ![StartRoot delta t EndRoot upper C Superscript down-tack Baseline bold z Subscript t Baseline tilde script upper N Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis bold 0 Subscript p Baseline comma delta t bold upper Sigma right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Then, the following recursive formula computes the approximated simulated joint sample paths of the ![p](images/c05-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> stocks:

[(5.9)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0065)![bold upper S Subscript t plus delta t Baseline equals bold upper S Subscript t Baseline circled-dot left-parenthesis bold 1 Subscript p Baseline plus delta t bold-italic mu plus StartRoot delta t EndRoot upper C Superscript down-tack Baseline bold z Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c05-math-0065.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8857;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

We shall illustrate the use of the recursive relation of ([5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0065)) to simulate the stock prices of HSBC, CLP and CK via Python in [Programme 5.17](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00017) (via **R** in [Programme 5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00018)). Since the time unit for both ![bold-italic mu](images/c05-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold upper Sigma](images/c05-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> is one day, we simply take ![delta t equals 1](images/c05-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. At the start of each programme, leaving room for setting the initial (random) seed in the simulation ensures that the same set of pseudo-random numbers is generated each time. This is useful as it allows us to check and debug our programmes.

 ![](images/c05-gra-0022.png)![](images/c05-gra-0023.png)

In [Programme 5.17](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00017), the command line for the random seed generator is placed outside the “for-loop”, so as to ensure the pseudo-randomly generated numbers are under the same random seed. For the far-end terms of the generated sequence, they can be regarded as iid samples in accordance with the ergodic theory mentioned in [Section 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0002). If we instead put the command inside the “for-loop”, it will generate a new seed every time when the algorithm gets back into the “for-loop”, and the numbers generated will end up not possessing the pseudo-independence structure.

With these simulated stock prices, we can calibrate the price of the portfolio or that of relevant derivative products. Here we simulated only one sample path of these stock prices as shown in [Figures 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0004) and [5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005). In principle, we can simulate as many paths as we want and build up the corresponding (empirical) loss distribution of a portfolio from which the V@R can be calibrated.

For instance, in accordance with no-arbitrage pricing theory [\[3](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003), [20\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0020), the price ![upper V 0](images/c05-i0364.png)<math display="inline" Next, we discuss the pricing of a continuous arithmetic Asian call option whose payoff is equal to ![left-parenthesis upper A left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis minus upper K right-parenthesis Subscript plus](images/c05-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>+</mo></msub></math> with ![upper K](images/c05-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> as the strike price and ![upper A left-parenthesis upper T right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over upper T EndFraction integral Subscript 0 Superscript upper T Baseline upper S left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis d t](images/c05-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, the average price of the underlying stock over the period ![left-bracket 0 comma upper T right-bracket](images/c05-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. By using either of the Euler–Maruyama or Milstein schemes, we can first generate ![n](images/c05-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> sample paths ![left-brace ModifyingAbove normal upper S With Ì‚ Subscript m Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace Subscript m equals 0 Superscript upper M](images/c05-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c05-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. Similar to [Example 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0026), due to the fundamental theorem of asset pricing, the arbitrage-free price of this Asian option is given by the risk-neutral expectation of the discounted terminal payoff. Therefore the time-zero current price of the Asian call can be estimated by:

[(5.12)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0080)![StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts e Superscript minus r upper T Baseline left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over upper M plus 1 EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript m equals 0 Overscript upper M Endscripts ModifyingAbove normal upper S With Ì‚ Subscript m Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline minus upper K right-parenthesis Subscript plus Baseline period](images/c05-math-0080.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

On the other hand, unlike [Example 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0026), there is no elementary closed-form pricing formula for arithmetic Asian call options, even under the Black–Scholes framework, due to the difficulty in determining the distribution of the sum of lognormal random variables. Researchers and practitioners have tried various approaches to tackle this problem, for instance via numerical PDEs or infinite series. In practice, for large enough values of ![upper M](images/c05-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and ![n](images/c05-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, the result of ([5.12](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0080)) calculated via the standard Monte Carlo approach, and utilizing the exact expression of ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, is usually regarded as the theoretical price.

 

**[Example 5.7](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0028)**   Consider an Asian call option with ![upper S 0 equals 10 comma upper K equals 8 comma r equals 0.05 comma sigma equals 0.3](images/c05-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></math>, and ![upper T equals 1](images/c05-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Under the Black–Scholes framework, ![sigma left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal upper S With Ì‚ Subscript m Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis identical-to sigma](images/c05-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8801;</mo><mi>&#963;</mi></math> in ([5.11](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0073)) for ![m equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper M minus 1](images/c05-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n equals 100 comma 000](images/c05-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math>. We use the two discretization schemes discussed above to estimate the current price of this Asian call option by using different values of ![upper M element-of StartSet 10 comma 100 comma 1000 EndSet](images/c05-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. We shall first lay down the code for the simulation of the Asian call option in [Programme 5.19](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00019) via Python and in [Programme 5.20](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00020) via **R**. Note that for the sake of fair comparison between the two schemes in this example, we also compute an “exact” price for every candidate value of ![upper M](images/c05-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> via the standard Monte Carlo approach, as a benchmark of comparison. Readers may verify on their own, by choosing larger values of ![upper M](images/c05-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and ![n](images/c05-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> in the programmes, that the “exact” theoretical price of the continuous arithmetic Asian option in question lies within the range of ![2.19 plus-or-minus 0.01](images/c05-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2.19</mn><mo>&#177;</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math>.

 ![](images/c05-gra-0024.png)![](images/c05-gra-0025.png)

To compare the performance of the two discretization methods, the histograms of ![modifying above upper S with caret Subscript upper M Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline minus upper S Subscript upper M Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#348;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 1 0 Superscript 5](images/c05-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></math>, are considered, in which each ![modifying above upper S with caret Subscript upper M Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#348;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is simulated by the corresponding numerical scheme and each ![upper S Subscript upper M Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is generated as in [Example 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0026). The results are reported in [Programme 5.19](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00019) via Python (resp. [Programme 5.20](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00020) via **R**).

![](images/c05-gra-0026.png)![](images/c05-gra-0027.png)![](images/c05-gra-0028.png)

From [Figures 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006) via Python and [5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007) via **R**, we see that the range of all the histograms of the Milstein scheme for ![upper M equals 10 comma 100 comma 1000](images/c05-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn></math> are much smaller in size than that of the Euler–Maruyama scheme, and the ratio of the two ranges of Euler–Maruyama to Milstein gets larger in value (from around 6.5 to about 105) as ![upper M](images/c05-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> increases from 10 to 1,000. As predicted by the theory, when the number of discretization steps ![upper M](images/c05-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> increases, the Milstein scheme provides a much better approximation of the Asian call price than the Euler–Maruyama scheme. [Table 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0003) summarizes the approximated Asian call prices using Python and **R**, and all approximated values converge to the true value of about 2.19.

As a generalization of the Black–Scholes model, the class of *constant elasticity of variance* (CEV) models is also prevalent in the financial industries, at least before the 2007–2008 Credit Crunch, for various purposes such as the pricing of equities and commodities. First proposed by *John Cox* in [\[6\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0006), these models can capture random volatility and the leverage effect in a more flexible manner. **[Example 5.8](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0030) *(Continuation of [Example 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0002))***   Suppose that the stock price dynamics now follows a CEV model:

For ![theta equals 1](images/c05-i0493.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, from the results in [Programme 5.23](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00023) via Python and [Programme 5.25](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00025) via **R**, as the number of discretization steps ![upper M](images/c05-i0494.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> increases, the corresponding approximated Asian call prices for both schemes get closer to the benchmark. Moreover, with the aid of ![ModifyingAbove normal upper S With Ì‚ Subscript upper M](images/c05-i0495.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub></math> as the control variate, the resulting sample average of the corresponding estimator gets even closer to the benchmark, and the standard deviation of the estimator is reduced by half. To obtain a better estimation, we can replace ![ModifyingAbove normal upper S With Ì‚ Subscript upper M](images/c05-i0496.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub></math> by the Asian call payoff of a continuous geometric Wiener process (corresponding to ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0497.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>). However, it is beyond the scope of this book and we shall leave it as an exercise for readers. Similar results are obtained in [Programme 5.24](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00024) via Python and [Programme 5.26](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00026) via **R** for ![theta equals 1.8](images/c05-i0498.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>. [Tables 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0004) and [5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0005) summarize the estimated option prices and the standard deviations of the corresponding estimator under the CEV model with ![theta equals 1](images/c05-i0499.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and 1.8, respectively, obtained from Python and **R**, and the estimated values attained converge to a value around 2.14 for ![theta equals 1](images/c05-i0500.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and 2.16 for ![theta equals 1.8](images/c05-i0501.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, respectively.

## \*5.4 GREEKS AND THEIR APPROXIMATIONS

Various sensitivities of derivatives (or portfolios) prices ![upper V](images/c05-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>'s with respect to different model parameters, such as time ![t](images/c05-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, risk-free interest rate ![r](images/c05-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, current asset price ![s](images/c05-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> and volatility ![sigma](images/c05-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>, are called *Greek letters* or simply *Greeks* for short: see [Table 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0006) for some common examples.

For example, a fund manager may want to trade a portfolio that is insensitive to the (small) change of the current price of the underlying asset, that is, a portfolio with a value ![upper V](images/c05-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> such that ![normal upper Delta equals StartFraction partial-differential upper V Over partial-differential upper S EndFraction equals 0](images/c05-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. A portfolio with such a property is called a *delta neutral portfolio*. For instance, a *delta-neutral portfolio* can be formed by selling one European option and holding ![normal upper Delta equals StartFraction partial-differential upper V left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript t Baseline comma t right-parenthesis Over partial-differential upper S EndFraction](images/c05-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> amount of stocks, and this hedging portfolio will remain *riskless* throughout the period under consideration.

 ![TABLE 5.6 Commonly used Greeks. Note that vega is not the name of any Greek letter; it gets the name due to its resemblance to the Latin letter V.](images/c05-i0515.png)

[**TABLE 5.6**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0006) Commonly used Greeks. Note that vega is not the name of any Greek letter; it gets the name due to its resemblance to the Latin letter V.

Furthermore, the *delta* of a European call option is expected to be positive as the price of a call option increases with the current price of the underlying asset. When ![upper S Subscript t Baseline much-less-than upper K](images/c05-i0523.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, i.e. when the call option is far out-of-the-money, call options are mostly worthless, and they have deltas close to 0. On the other hand, managers can construct a portfolio with a positive delta so as to bet on the greater increase in the price of the underlying asset. More specifically, to calculate the Greeks of a European call option under the Black–Scholes framework, we first recall their celebrated formula (also see [Example 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0026)): at time ![t](images/c05-i0524.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, its price is

where ![normal upper Phi left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0525.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the cdf of the standard normal distribution, ![d Subscript plus Baseline colon equals StartStartFraction ln StartFraction upper S Subscript t Baseline Over upper K EndFraction plus left-parenthesis r plus StartFraction sigma squared Over 2 EndFraction right-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper T minus t right-parenthesis OverOver sigma StartRoot upper T minus t EndRoot EndEndFraction](images/c05-i0526.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><msqrt><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math> and ![d Subscript minus Baseline colon equals d Subscript plus Baseline minus sigma StartRoot upper T minus t EndRoot](images/c05-i0527.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msqrt><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math>. In general, there are no immediate tractable expressions for Greeks of most generic financial derivatives. In such cases, using a numerical approximation via the Monte Carlo method serves as a resolution. For simplicity, take the current time as 0, and let ![normal y left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0529.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be the discounted payoff of a European-type derivative which will expire at terminal time ![upper T](images/c05-i0530.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, and let ![alpha left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be the current price of the derivative, where the expectation ![double-struck upper E](images/c05-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow></math> is taken with respect to the risk-neutral probability measure, and ![theta](images/c05-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> represents a particular parameter of interest, such as the current value of the underlying asset or its volatility. We aim to calibrate the sensitivity of the derivative price with respect to ![theta](images/c05-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, by estimating the derivative ![alpha prime left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals StartFraction partial-differential alpha Over partial-differential theta EndFraction](images/c05-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> via different simulation methods. We shall introduce three common approaches, namely (i) finite-difference approximation; (ii) pathwise differentiation; and (ii) the likelihood ratio method. We refer to [\[14](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014), [20\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0020) for more discussions.

**(I) Finite-difference approximation**

By differentiability, we clearly have ![alpha prime left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis almost-equals StartFraction alpha left-parenthesis theta plus h right-parenthesis minus alpha left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis Over h EndFraction](images/c05-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></math> for small enough ![h greater-than 0](images/c05-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, or equivalently

**[Example 5.9](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fea-0032) *(Under a CEV model, delta and vega with finite differences)***   Under the CEV framework with ![theta equals 2 comma 1.8](images/c05-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, and 1, consider a European call option with ![upper S 0 equals 10 comma upper K equals 8 comma sigma equals 0.3 comma r equals 0.05](images/c05-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>, and ![upper T equals 1](images/c05-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Its delta and vega are computed using forward and central differencing in [Programme 5.27](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00027) via Python (resp. [Programme 5.28](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00028) via **R**) by using ([5.14](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0083)) and ([5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0087)), respectively, and the numerical scheme used is the Milstein one.

![](images/c05-gra-0034.png)![](images/c05-gra-0035.png)

Next we estimate the delta and vega of the European call, under CEV model with ![theta equals 2 comma 1.8](images/c05-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, and 1, by using the methods of forward and central differences by choosing ![h equals 0.5 comma 0.45 comma ellipsis comma 0.1 comma 0.05](images/c05-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.45</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math> for delta, and ![0.05 comma 0.045 comma ellipsis comma 0.01 comma 0.005](images/c05-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.05</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.045</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.005</mn></math> for vega. We implement the respective executions of [Programmes 5.27](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00027) and [5.28](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00028) in [Programme 5.29](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00029) via Python and [Programme 5.30](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00030) via **R**.

![](images/c05-gra-0036.png)![](images/c05-gra-0037.png) ![](images/c05-gra-0038.png)  

[Programmes 5.29](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00029) via Python and [5.30](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00030) via **R** report the delta and vega estimates of the European call option under a CEV model with different parameter ![theta](images/c05-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> using the forward and central difference methods. When ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, equivalent to the classical Black–Scholes model, the delta and vega estimates of both methods converge to their theoretical values of 0.8555 and 2.2735 respectively when ![h](images/c05-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> gets smaller. One observes that the central difference method provides more accurate estimates compared to the forward difference method; the estimation performance of vega is inferior to that of delta no matter whether Python or **R** is used. Note that ![sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals sigma normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and ![sigma left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals sigma normal upper S Subscript t Superscript 0.9](images/c05-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0.9</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> for ![theta equals 1.8](images/c05-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, the corresponding dynamics of ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0561.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for ![theta less-than 2](images/c05-i0562.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> is less volatile against its current price level in comparison to that for ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, leading ![sigma](images/c05-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> to be relatively less important in the option price, and so we anticipate a relatively smaller value of vega when ![theta](images/c05-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> gets smaller. In contrast, the initial stock price ![upper S 0](images/c05-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, in the absence of larger volatility, becomes more critical to the option price, and so we expect delta to have a greater value as ![theta](images/c05-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> gets smaller. In particular, for ![theta equals 1.8](images/c05-i0568.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, the delta and vega estimates converge to 0.893 and 1.4, respectively; for ![theta equals 1](images/c05-i0569.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, the delta and vega estimates converge to 0.997 and 0.024, respectively.

**(II) Pathwise Differentiation**

The interchangeability assumption states that ![alpha prime left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals StartFraction d Over d theta EndFraction í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals í”¼ left-parenthesis StartFraction d normal y left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis Over d theta EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0570.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>. This can be valid when the following condition holds:

![StartAbsoluteValue normal y left-parenthesis theta 1 right-parenthesis minus normal y left-parenthesis theta 2 right-parenthesis EndAbsoluteValue less-than upper C StartAbsoluteValue theta 1 minus theta 2 EndAbsoluteValue comma for all theta 1 and theta 2 comma almost surely comma for some upper C greater-than 0 period](images/c05-math-0093.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>for all</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mtext>, almost surely, for some</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>C</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Indeed, this condition warrants the interchange of differentiation and the expectations taking in accordance with the *Lebesgue Dominated Convergence Theorem*.

Suppose that the payoff of a derivative is given by ![normal y equals f left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0571.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. To illustrate how the *pathwise differentiation approach* works, we consider the delta of this derivative under the Black–Scholes framework, which is the price sensitivity with respect to the current stock price ![upper S 0](images/c05-i0572.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>. Based on the interchangeability assumption, we consider the derivative of the random payoff with respect to the current price:

[(5.19)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0095)![normal upper Delta equals í”¼ left-parenthesis f prime left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis StartFraction normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline Over upper S 0 EndFraction right-parenthesis comma](images/c05-math-0095.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></math>

In [Example 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0032), under the CEV model setting, we proposed the approximation of delta and vega of a European call through the finite differencing method. Let us now illustrate how to realize the pathwise differentiation method for this non-trivial model. We approximate the Greeks through the Monte Carlo simulation of the corresponding SDE system, which becomes two-dimensional in nature.
