**Example 5.10 *(Continuation of the CEV model in [Example 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0032), now via pathwise differentiation)***   Under the CEV framework with ![theta equals 2 comma 1.8](images/c05-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math>, and 1, consider a European call option with ![normal upper S 0 equals 10 comma upper K equals 8 comma sigma equals 0.3 comma r equals 0.05](images/c05-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>, and ![upper T equals 1](images/c05-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We now use the standard Euler–Maruyama scheme for the SDE systems obtained through the pathwise differentiations for numerical calibrations for delta and vega. The implementation is carried out in [Programme 5.31](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00031) via Python (resp. [Programme 5.32](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00032) via **R**) by using ([5.20](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0102)) and ([5.21](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0103)), respectively.

![](images/c05-gra-0039.png) ![](images/c05-gra-0040.png)

From [Figures 5.8](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0008) by Python and [5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0009) by **R**, the approximations of both delta and vega under the Black–Scholes framework with ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> respectively converge to the true values of delta and vega as the number of iterations ![n](images/c05-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> increases.

Similarly, we can observe similar convergence results for ![theta equals 1.8](images/c05-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></math> in [Figure 5.10](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0010) by Python (resp. [Figure 5.11](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0011) by **R**) and for ![theta equals 1](images/c05-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in [Figure 5.12](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0012) by Python (resp. [Figure 5.13](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0013) by **R**). We leave it as an exercise for readers to write down the Milstein scheme for the SDE system obtained through pathwise differentiation method; as expected, the corresponding convergence is even faster.

Suppose that we are only interested in approximating one Greek ![StartFraction partial-differential f Subscript gamma Baseline left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis Over partial-differential gamma EndFraction](images/c05-i0601.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>&#947;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> of a derivative with the payoff ![f Subscript gamma Baseline left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0602.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>&#947;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. For the finite differencing method, we have to simulate exactly two out of three different SDE dynamics simultaneously, depending on whether forward or central differencing is used, namely: the three dynamics for the stock price ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0603.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> with ![gamma minus h](images/c05-i0604.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></math>, ![gamma](images/c05-i0605.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>, and ![gamma plus h](images/c05-i0606.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></math> for some desired small enough ![h greater-than 0](images/c05-i0607.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. For the pathwise differentiation method, two dynamics still have to be simulated simultaneously, namely the dynamics for ![StartFraction partial-differential normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline Over partial-differential gamma EndFraction](images/c05-i0608.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> and ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c05-i0609.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. In general, pathwise differentiation is generally faster and accurate enough, while it is at least as memory-efficient as the finite differencing method.

**(III) Likelihood Ratio Method**

Let the density function of ![normal upper S Subscript upper T](images/c05-i0610.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math> be ![g Subscript theta](images/c05-i0611.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub></math>, where ![theta](images/c05-i0612.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is the parameter of interest, and for the moment, take it for granted that we know this expression as a function of ![theta](images/c05-i0613.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. Then the expected discounted payoff can be written as:

![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis equals integral Subscript negative infinity Superscript infinity Baseline f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis g Subscript theta Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis d x period](images/c05-math-0104.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Moreover, if the discounted payoff function ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0614.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is continuous almost surely and ![g Subscript theta Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is differentiable in ![theta](images/c05-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, then the sensitivity of the expected discounted payoff with respect to ![theta](images/c05-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> can be computed as

[(5.22)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0105)![StartFraction partial-differential í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis Over partial-differential theta EndFraction equals integral Subscript negative infinity Superscript infinity Baseline f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis StartFraction partial-differential g Subscript theta Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Over partial-differential theta EndFraction d x equals í”¼ left-parenthesis f left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis StartFraction partial-differential ln g Subscript theta Baseline left-parenthesis normal upper S Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis Over partial-differential theta EndFraction right-parenthesis period](images/c05-math-0105.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

Like the method of pathwise differentiation, we express the price sensitivity as an expectation, which can then be estimated by the Monte Carlo method. The *likelihood ratio method* involves the differentiation of the density function of ![normal upper S Subscript upper T](images/c05-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math> with respect to ![theta](images/c05-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, rather than the differentiation of the payoff function as is the case with the method of pathwise differentiation.

**Example 5.11 *(Continuation of [Example 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0032) for the Black–Scholes model, ![theta equals 2](images/c05-i0628.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> only, with pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods)***   With the same setting as in [Example 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c05-fea-0032), we use the likelihood ratio method to estimate the delta and vega of the European call option under the Black–Scholes framework. Additionally, we compare the results with those obtained by the pathwise differentiation method. The estimates obtained from both methods are plotted against the number of simulations implemented in [Programme 5.33](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00033) via Python (resp. [Programme 5.34](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00034) via **R**).

 ![](images/c05-gra-0041.png) ![](images/c05-gra-0042.png)

[Figures 5.14](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0014) (via Python) and [5.15](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0015) (via **R**) illustrate the respective convergences of the estimators by using pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods. We observe that both methods gradually approach the blue dotted line, leveled at the true value, as the number of paths (simulations) increases, which validates the pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods. However, the approximation of both Greeks in the pathwise differentiation method demonstrates a superior convergence performance compared to the likelihood ratio method.

 ![FIGURE 5.14 Comparison of convergence of the pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods via Python, generated by Programme 5.33.](images/c05f014.png)

[**FIGURE 5.14**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0014) Comparison of convergence of the pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods via Python, generated by [Programme 5.33](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00033).

![FIGURE 5.15 Comparison of convergence of the pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods via bold upper R, generated by Programme 5.34.](images/c05f015.png)

[**FIGURE 5.15**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0015) Comparison of convergence of the pathwise differentiation and likelihood ratio methods via ![bold upper R](images/c05-i0629.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></mrow></math>, generated by [Programme 5.34](#c05.xhtml#c05-gra-00034).

In order to apply this likelihood ratio method, one needs the explicit expression of the sensitivity, with respect to the parameter of interest, of the density of the terminal state. Usually, this may not be immediately achievable in practice. Nevertheless, most security prices are modeled by SDEs, and by using *Malliavin Calculus* [\[2](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0002), [13\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0013), one can still write the density as a function of expectation functionals involving the so-called *Malliavin derivatives* of these SDEs. On this basis, the likelihood ratio method can be used on more occasions. That said, from the last illustration, the pathwise differentiation method shows better performance. Interestingly, its philosophy is closely related to the concept of *Jacobian flow* and consequently it intimately connects with Malliavin's differentiability of SDEs.

Last but not least, Malliavin calculus can help on expressing the hedging portfolio weights in various optimal portfolio selection problems via the celebrated *Clark–Ocone formula*, which again involves Malliavin derivatives but of the terminal payoffs this time. Due to our page limit, we cannot cover this wonderful topic of stochastic analysis in this book, and we invite readers to check out the details in [\[1](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0001), [12\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0012) and the references therein.

# CHAPTER 6  
Approximation for Model Inference

 

The process of fitting models is often accomplished by minimizing the sum of squares (as in regression analysis) or minimizing cross-entropy (as in classification method). These are examples of the *maximum likelihood approach* to fitting. This chapter provides a comprehensive explanation of the maximum likelihood approach and introduces several methods of approximation for the purpose of model inference.

The examples provided in this chapter highlight the practical applications and importance of the algorithms to be introduced. For instance, by leveraging the maximum likelihood approach to fitting within numerical algorithms, it becomes possible to implement handwriting number recognition systems that accurately identify handwritten numbers commonly found on cheques and many business form filings. Estimating quantiles using numerical methods is essential for risk assessment and portfolio management, such as *Value-at-Risk* calibration (to be introduced in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml)). After providing a comprehensive and self-contained introduction to *Markov Chain theory*, we also introduce, with an illustrative example, the very useful *Markov Chain Monte Carlo* (MCMC) method for sampling from complex probability distributions.

 

## 6.1 EM ALGORITHM

The *Expectation–Maximization Algorithm* (or *EM Algorithm* for short) is a parametric learning method first introduced in [\[5\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0005) for tackling parametric estimations, especially with unobservable variates. Instead of looking for an explicit analytic solution, the EM algorithm finds a maximum point of a log-likelihood function via an iterative procedure that can easily be carried out by modern computers. An in-depth account of the general theory of the EM algorithm and its various extensions is given by the classical text [\[22\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0022).

More precisely, let ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> be an observable ![p](images/c06-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional random sample of size ![n](images/c06-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> from a population with a common “mixed joint density” function ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x semicolon bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![bold-italic theta](images/c06-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is a ![k](images/c06-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector of parameters. However, in practice the random feature vector ![bold x](images/c06-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> may not be fully observable, say ![bold x colon equals StartBinomialOrMatrix bold y Choose bold z EndBinomialOrMatrix](images/c06-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd class="array"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math>, where ![bold y](images/c06-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> is the observable part, and ![bold z](images/c06-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> is the unobservable part whose components are called *latent variables*. Note that the maximization ([6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0005)) is usually difficult since the marginal likelihood is often inconvenient to obtain. For instance, if the dimension of ![bold z](images/c06-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> grows exponentially in the sample size ![n](images/c06-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, then the exact calculation will be extremely difficult. The EM algorithm is a prevalent approach to tackle this issue.

 

### 6.1.1 General Theory and Algorithm

Without causing much ambiguity, we shall omit the subscripts of the joint density functions in this subsection, as they can be well-identified from the arguments; this means that while ![f Subscript bold y Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic y semicolon bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denoted the marginal mixed joint density of ![bold y](images/c06-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> before, we write it simply as ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic y semicolon bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Similarly, ![f Subscript bold z vertical-bar bold y Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold-italic y semicolon bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the conditional mixed joint density of ![bold z](images/c06-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> given ![bold y equals bold-italic y](images/c06-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></math>, is now written as ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold-italic y semicolon bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, etc.. The EM algorithm consists of repeating the following two steps: (i) an expectation (E) taking step and (ii) a maximization (M) finding step. These are elaborated in [Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0001) below, where ![epsilon](images/c06-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is a pre-specified threshold.

![](images/c06-gra-0001.png)

Here we describe the idea behind the EM algorithm. Note that in most commonly encountered practical circumstances, the log-likelihood ![ln upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic theta semicolon bold-italic y 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic y Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is bounded, and so the monotone nature of the EM algorithm ensures the convergence of ![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. However, it is sensitive to the initial choice of ![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and therefore the EM algorithm only asserts convergence to a local maxima of ([6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0005)), not necessarily to the ultimate maximum likelihood estimate; see [Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001). Therefore, we should try more initial choices of ![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and look for the largest possible ultimate maxima.

### 6.1.2 Application to Handwriting Recognition

In this subsection, we discuss an immediate application of the EM algorithm to the unsupervised learning of recognizing handwritten Arabic numbers. This can help us easily identify handwritten numerical figures found on cheques and business documents. The training dataset is a collection of labeled black-and-white images of handwritten digits from MNIST

For each handwritten digit, we use 1 to represent a black pixel and 0 for white. The array of pixels is rearranged in a linear order from top down to form a feature vector ![bold-italic x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper K Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, where ![upper K](images/c06-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of pixels, i.e. the size of the rectangular image. For ![m equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma 9](images/c06-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, let ![script upper S Subscript m](images/c06-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></math> be the subset of images of the training dataset that contains the images of the digit ![m](images/c06-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. Then the total sample is a disjoint union ![script upper S equals square-cup script upper S Subscript m](images/c06-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mrow><mover class="overset"><mo>&#8852;</mo><mn>9</mn></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></math> with total sample size ![n](images/c06-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. ![n equals sigma-summation Underscript m equals 0 Overscript 9 Endscripts StartAbsoluteValue script upper S Subscript m Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c06-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>. The mean vector ![bold-italic mu overbar Subscript m](images/c06-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></math> for the digit ![m](images/c06-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is defined by

where ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline colon equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i upper K Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> is the feature vector, or pixel vector, of the ![i](images/c06-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th image, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c06-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. Each entry of ![bold-italic mu overbar Subscript m Baseline colon equals left-parenthesis mu overbar Subscript m Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma mu overbar Subscript m upper K Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> lies in the closed interval ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c06-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. In [Figure 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0003), the image on the right is obtained by averaging a sample of 100 handwritten digits labeled as “2”. One can identify the shape of the digit 2 from this artificial image without much difficulty, even though the image is fairly blurred.

Generally speaking, suppose the training dataset with size ![n](images/c06-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> consists of ![upper M](images/c06-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> different types of handwritten “digits”, to allow for the possibility that ![upper M](images/c06-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is not necessarily 10. With the presence of multiple digits in the dataset, we wish to determine the most “representative” image for each digit. At the same time, we will also try to estimate the prior probability that the representative image of a particular digit is shown. To this end, we consider ![upper M](images/c06-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> different parameter vectors ![bold-italic mu Subscript m](images/c06-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>, ![m equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper M](images/c06-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math>; here ![m](images/c06-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> stands as an index instead of the actual value of the particular chosen digit. Denote by ![pi Subscript m](images/c06-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>, ![m equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper M](images/c06-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math>, the prior probability of selecting ![bold-italic mu Subscript m](images/c06-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>. Naturally these should sum to 1. In the following, we shall denote the collection of parameters by ![bold-italic theta colon equals left-parenthesis bold-italic mu 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic mu Subscript upper M Baseline comma pi 1 comma ellipsis comma pi Subscript upper M Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, with the constraint ![sigma-summation Underscript m equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts pi Subscript m Baseline equals 1](images/c06-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The pixel vector ![bold-italic x](images/c06-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> of a particular image is the observable part, and the parameter vector ![bold z](images/c06-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math>, as a hyper-random vector, chosen to generate this image, is unknown. Here, ![bold z](images/c06-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> acts as a hidden/latent vector, and it can only take ![upper M](images/c06-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> (vector) values of ![bold-italic mu 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic mu Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c06-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></math>. We consider components of ![bold-italic mu Subscript m](images/c06-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> as the success probabilities for the respective components of Bernoulli random vector ![bold i Subscript m Baseline equals left-parenthesis normal i Subscript m Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal i Subscript m upper K Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, where ![normal i Subscript m k](images/c06-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> stands for the color (1 for black, 0 for white) of the ![k](images/c06-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-th pixel in the same image if the ![m](images/c06-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>\-th type of digit is drawn. All the pixel vectors are assumed to be iid in the present modelling framework

With this in mind, given that ![bold z equals bold-italic mu Subscript m Baseline equals left-parenthesis mu Subscript m Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma mu Subscript m upper K Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, the conditional probability of generating an image with the observed pixel vector ![bold-italic x](images/c06-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is:

Thus, the marginal probability of generating this image is, by the law of total probability,

This model is an example of a mixture of Bernoulli distributions. However, the presence of both a product and summation in ([6.10](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0015)) renders an even more complicated expression after taking logarithm. Deriving explicit forms of partial derivatives of the resulting log-likelihood function is unfeasible. Therefore, instead of handling the intractable expression ([6.10](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0015)) analytically, we propose to solve for the optimal generator ![bold-italic theta](images/c06-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> by the EM algorithm as follows:

In the rest of this subsection, we illustrate the implementation of the EM algorithm for the hand-written digits from MNIST. For **R**, we first load the MNIST dataset from the `keras` ![](images/c06-gra-0002.png)

Here, the `unique()` function picks out all the distinguishable elements, in this case ![StartSet 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma 9 EndSet](images/c06-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. The dimension of the training dataset is `60000, 28, 28`, where 60,000 is the total number of samples in the training dataset, and the two 28's are the length and width of each image datum respectively. Next, we build a function to compute the expected log-likelihood ![upper Q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> according to ([6.12](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0017)); refer to [Programme 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-0002) for an implementation of this in **R**.

 ![](images/c06-gra-0003.png)

Referring to lines 4 and 5, we adjust the values of `mu` to avoid **R** returning `Inf` when computing ![ln 0](images/c06-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mn>0</mn></math>; instead it will return a very negative value. Then, in Step 1, we initialize ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> using uniform random numbers. Although the information in label ![y](images/c06-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> should not be used in unsupervised learning, we here initialize ![bold-italic mu](images/c06-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> using ([6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0012)) as an illustration; see [Programme 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-0003) for coding this in **R**.

![](images/c06-gra-0004.png)

In [Programme 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-0004) via **R**, the model is trained based on Step 2 using ([6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0025)) and ([6.17](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0026)) with 10 iterations (see [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005)a for the choice of iterations as it is quite stable around this chosen value of 10).

 ![](images/c06-gra-0005.png)

In the testing stage, to give a predicted label of a test datum ![bold-italic x Subscript test](images/c06-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub></math>, we first compute the posterior probabilities

each of which is similar to ([6.11](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0016)) except that the parameter ![bold-italic theta](images/c06-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> used is the MLE obtained in the training stage. See [Programme 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-0005) for an implementation in **R**. Then the predicted label ![m](images/c06-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is the one corresponding to the largest posterior probability.

![](images/c06-gra-0006.png)

Note that we omit the division of the marginal probability after Line 7, since we are just required to obtain the index position ![m](images/c06-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> which maximizes the posterior probability.

Finally, in [Programme 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-0006) via **R**, the *confusion matrix* (*cross tabulation table*) is used to illustrate the overall performance of the model. We also calculate its accuracy and plot the log-likelihoods for all 10 iterations (see [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005)a).

![](images/c06-gra-0007.png)![FIGURE 6.5 MNIST with Bernoulli Mixture Model, generated by Programme 6.6 in R.](images/c06f005.png)

The accuracy of the model is around 68% and from [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005)a, the log-likelihood becomes stable after the eighth iteration, indicating that only a few iterations are enough for the model to learn. Finally, the average handwritten images of each digit are plotted in [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005)b. From the confusion matrix, we observe that the model performs less favourably in classifying numbers between 3 (`y_hat`) and 8 (`y_test`), 3 and 5, 4 and 9, 5 and 0, and 9 and 4. Indeed, sometimes even us humans struggle to recognise the true number, as [Figure 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0006) demonstrates.

## 6.2 MM ALGORITHM

The *MM algorithm* is a general technique to minimize or maximize a function iteratively. When one is performing minimization, “MM” stands for “Majorize-Minimization”; when one is performing maximization, “MM” stands for “Minorize-Maximization”. The main idea of the MM algorithm is to optimize a *surrogate function* that minorizes or majorizes the objective function at each iteration. Suppose that ![f colon double-struck upper R Superscript n Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c06-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> is the objective function we want to minimize. MM algorithm produces a sequence ![left-brace bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> iteratively as follows: at the ![t](images/c06-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-th iteration, a surrogate function ![bold-italic x right-arrow from bar g left-parenthesis bold-italic x bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8614;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that satisfies

We then minimize this surrogate function and label the minimizer ![bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The sequence ![left-brace bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> produced by this algorithm has the desirable descent property that

which follows from the defining properties of the surrogate function ![g left-parenthesis dot bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>:

![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to g left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to g left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c06-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

When one is trying to *maximize* the objective function, a surrogate function that *minorizes* the objective function and touches it at the current iterate has to be constructed; the next iterate is then the *maximum* point of this surrogate function. Without loss of generality, we shall focus mainly on the minimization problem.

It is known that if the objective function ![f](images/c06-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is strictly convex, then under some mild conditions the MM algorithm will converge to the unique minimum point (if it exists) no matter the initial seed ![bold-italic x 0](images/c06-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> chosen. If convexity is lacking, but all stationary points are isolated, then the MM algorithm will converge to one of them, depending on the position of the initial guess. The performance and the rate of convergence of the MM algorithm depend on how well the surrogate function ![g left-parenthesis dot bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> approximates ![f](images/c06-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, and how easy the minimization of the surrogate function is. In what follows, we highlight several commonly used approaches to construct appropriate surrogate functions. More detailed discussions can be found in [\[18](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0018), [19](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0019), [20\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0020) and the references therein.

Firstly, suppose that the objective function ![f colon double-struck upper R Subscript plus Superscript p Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c06-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> has the form ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis colon equals h left-parenthesis bold-italic c Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for some ![bold-italic c element-of double-struck upper R Subscript plus Superscript p](images/c06-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and a convex function ![h colon double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c06-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>. By Jensen's inequality, given the current iterate ![bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Subscript plus Superscript p](images/c06-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>,

This surrogate function has the important property of being simply a weighted sum of one-dimensional convex functions so that the components of ![bold-italic x](images/c06-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> are separated. This makes the minimization step much easier to perform. The surrogate function ![g left-parenthesis bold-italic x bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is quadratic in ![bold-italic x](images/c06-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, hence its minimization is practically easy. Indeed, the next iterate ![bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> is simply the solution of the equation

![nabla Subscript bold-italic x Baseline g left-parenthesis bold-italic x bar bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals nabla Subscript bold-italic x Baseline f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis bold-italic x minus bold-italic x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper B equals bold 0 comma](images/c06-math-0034.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is a system of linear equations that can be solved efficiently by many well-known algorithms. In the one-dimensional case, we have the explicit formula ![x Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline equals x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline minus f prime left-parenthesis x Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis slash upper B](images/c06-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>B</mi></math>, provided ![upper B not-equals 0](images/c06-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

Fourthly, quadratic surrogate functions are used quite often because the coefficients can be obtained by solving the tangency condition rather easily and finding the minimum point of a quadratic function is straightforward. The next example, taken from [\[12\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0012), uses a quadratic surrogate function to estimate quantiles of a distribution. As such, it has direct relevance for calculating Value-at-Risk, an important measure in risk management.

**Example.** Suppose that we are given ![n](images/c06-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> numbers ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, which are realizations of a certain unknown distribution ![upper F](images/c06-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>. Our objective is to estimate ![upper F Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the ![q](images/c06-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>\-quantile of ![upper F](images/c06-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>, by using the empirical ![q](images/c06-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>\-quantile ![mu Subscript q](images/c06-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></math>, which is a number that satisfies the condition

An interesting feature of this algorithm is that it does not require the numbers ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> to be sorted. We refer to [\[12\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0012) for more discussions on this topic, such as its convergence and further applications.

In [Section 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0010), we shall estimate Value-at-Risk by bootstrapping historical losses. Before then, let us implement the MM algorithm for finding this as a quantile in [Programme 6.10](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00010) via Python (resp. [Programme 6.11](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00011) via **R**). Readers may come back to this example after reading the first few sections of [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml).

![](images/c06-gra-0012.png)![](images/c06-gra-0013.png)

Next, in [Programme 6.12](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00012) in Python (resp. [Programme 6.13](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00013) in **R**), we use the `MM_quantile()` function to compute the 1-day 99% Value-at-Risk with the losses obtained from [Programme 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0001) in Python (resp. [Programme 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0002) in **R**).

![](images/c06-gra-0014.png)![](images/c06-gra-0015.png)![](images/c06-gra-0016.png)

We note here that since ![n q equals 983 times 0.99 equals 973.17](images/c06-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>983</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>0.99</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>973.17</mn></math> is not an integer, the 0.99 quantile may be any number in the interval ![left-parenthesis x Subscript left-parenthesis left floor 973.17 right floor right-parenthesis Baseline comma x Subscript left-parenthesis left floor 973.17 right floor plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-bracket equals left-parenthesis x Subscript left-parenthesis 973 right-parenthesis Baseline comma x Subscript left-parenthesis 974 right-parenthesis Baseline right-bracket equals left-parenthesis 3 comma 538.054 comma 3 comma 570.871 right-bracket](images/c06-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8970;</mo><mn>973.17</mn><mo>&#8971;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8970;</mo><mn>973.17</mn><mo>&#8971;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>973</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>974</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>538.054</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>570.871</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. Under MM algorithm, the quantile is chosen to be the right-hand boundary of 3,570.871. Indeed, when ![mu Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> approaches ![3 comma 570.871](images/c06-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>570.871</mn></math>, ![w Subscript left-parenthesis 974 right-parenthesis Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>974</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> becomes extremely large, causing ![mu Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline almost-equals x Subscript left-parenthesis 974 right-parenthesis Baseline equals 3 comma 570.871](images/c06-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8776;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>974</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>570.871</mn></math>. In comparison, as we shall discuss in detail in [Section 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0010) of [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), the bootstrapping method results in an estimated 0.99 quantile of 3,543.961, which is very close to the linear interpolation for ![x Subscript left-parenthesis 973.17 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>973.17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> using ![x Subscript left-parenthesis 973 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>973</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> and ![x Subscript left-parenthesis 974 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>974</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>, i.e. ![x Subscript left-parenthesis 973 right-parenthesis Baseline plus 0.17 left-parenthesis x Subscript left-parenthesis 974 right-parenthesis Baseline minus x Subscript left-parenthesis 973 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals 3 comma 543.633](images/c06-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>973</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>0.17</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>974</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>973</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>543.633</mn></math>.

More detailed discussions on the MM algorithm can be found in [\[18](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0018), [19](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0019), [20\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0020) and the references therein.

 

## \*6.3 A SHORT COURSE ON THE THEORY OF MARKOV CHAINS

In this section, we provide a concise course on the theory of Markov chains based on which some MCMC algorithms can be built. In particular, we shall see how the network structure of the directed graph of a Markov chain determines its possession of a stationary distribution. For a more comprehensive account of the theory of Markov chains, we refer to [\[9](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009), [16](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0016), [21](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0021), [23](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0023), [25\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0025). A *Markov Chain* on a finite or countable state space is a discrete time stochastic process ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace Subscript n element-of double-struck upper N Often in statistical contexts, the state space ![script upper S](images/c06-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow></math> of a Markov chain is uncountable, say ![script upper S equals double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c06-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> for example. It is implicitly assumed that ![script upper S](images/c06-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow></math> is endowed with a suitable topology and an appropriate ![sigma](images/c06-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>\-field, together with a measure on the latter. In the case of ![script upper S equals double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c06-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>, these correspond to the topology of *Borel sets*, the *Borel* ![sigma](images/c06-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>*\-field* on which the *Lebesgue measure* is defined. When the state space is uncountable, the transition probability cannot be expressed in a matrix form. ### \*6.3.1 Regularity, Irreducibility, and Aperiodicity

A Markov chain with a finite state space and a transition probability matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> is said to be *regular* if all entries in ![bold-italic upper P Superscript n](images/c06-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math> are strictly positive for some integer ![n greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c06-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. We aim to show that if the Markov chain ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is regular and has a finite state space ![script upper S equals StartSet bold-italic s 1 comma bold-italic s 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic s Subscript upper K Baseline EndSet](images/c06-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, then the limiting distribution, ![left-parenthesis pi 1 comma ellipsis comma pi Subscript upper K Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> defined by

![pi Subscript j Baseline equals limit Underscript n right-arrow infinity Endscripts double-struck upper P left-parenthesis bold x Subscript n Baseline equals bold-italic s Subscript j Baseline bar bold x 0 equals bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals limit Underscript n right-arrow infinity Endscripts p Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K comma](images/c06-math-0055.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

exists, and these limits do not depend on the choice of the initial state ![i](images/c06-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

State ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> is said to be *accessible* from state ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, denoted by ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, if ![p Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for some integer ![n greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c06-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Two states ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> are said to *communicate* (denoted by ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>) if they are accessible from each other. It is straightforward to establish that *communication* is an *equivalence relation*: (i) ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> (reflexivity); (ii) if ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, then ![bold-italic s Subscript j Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> (symmetry); and (iii) if ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic s Subscript j Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript k](images/c06-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, then ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript k](images/c06-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> (transitivity). As a result, the states of a Markov chain can be partitioned into disjoint classes of communicating states so that two states ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> belong to the same class if and only if ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline left-right-arrow bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. If the whole state space forms one single communicating class, that is, every state communicates with each other, then the Markov chain is said to be *irreducible*. A sufficient (but not necessary) condition for a Markov chain to be regular is that it is irreducible.

Since ![k plus m](images/c06-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi></math> is a multiple of ![d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![l](images/c06-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> is also a multiple of ![d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0334.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This is true for any ![l](images/c06-i0335.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> such that ![p Subscript j comma j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, which means ![d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by the definition of gcd. Finally, by reflexivity, one also has ![d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. We therefore conclude that ![d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis equals d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.
    
2.  If state ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> has a period ![d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then there is an integer ![upper N](images/c06-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> depending on ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> such that for all integer ![n greater-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c06-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>, ![p Subscript j comma j Superscript left-parenthesis n d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. i.e., a return to state ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> can occur at all sufficiently large multiples of ![d left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The proof of this claim is essentially same as that for the following [Lemma 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0002), and so we omit it here.
3.  Further, if ![p Subscript j comma i Superscript left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, then ![p Subscript j comma i Superscript left-parenthesis m plus n d left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for sufficiently large ![n](images/c06-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

A finite state Markov chain is said to be *aperiodic* if every state has period 1. It is easy to see that if a Markov chain is regular so that all entries of ![bold-italic upper P Superscript n](images/c06-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math> are strictly positive for some ![n](images/c06-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, then so do ![bold-italic upper P Superscript n plus 1 Baseline comma bold-italic upper P Superscript n plus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis](images/c06-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>, hence the Markov chain is aperiodic. In what follows, we prove that the converse is also true: an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space is regular. We first present a lemma, whose proof is taken from [\[1\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0001).
