Then there exists an integer ![upper N](images/c06-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> such that ![n element-of script í’œ](images/c06-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi></math> for all ![n greater-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c06-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>.

If the first condition in this lemma is replaced by gcd![left-parenthesis a 1 comma a 2 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis equals d](images/c06-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></math>, then one can show, by considering the set ![ModifyingAbove script í’œ With tilde colon equals StartSet a d Superscript negative 1 Baseline colon a element-of script í’œ EndSet](images/c06-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>:</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, that there exists an integer ![upper N](images/c06-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> such that ![n d element-of script í’œ](images/c06-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi></math> for all ![n greater-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c06-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>.

*Proof.*   For ![bold-italic s Subscript i Baseline element-of script upper S](images/c06-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></math>, let ![script í’œ Subscript i Baseline equals StartSet n greater-than-or-equal-to 1 colon p Subscript i comma i Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0 EndSet](images/c06-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, that is, ![script í’œ Subscript i](images/c06-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54428;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the set of possible return times to state ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> starting from ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Again, the two states are said to *communicate*, denoted by ![bold-italic s 1 left-right-arrow bold-italic s 2](images/c06-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8596;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, if ![bold-italic s 1 right-arrow bold-italic s 2](images/c06-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![bold-italic s 2 right-arrow bold-italic s 1](images/c06-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>. Similar to the case of a finite or countable state space, communication of states forms an equivalence relation, the proof of which can be found in [Appendix \*6.A.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0037). A Markov chain is said to be *irreducible* if every state communicates with each other.

To simplify the overall treatment, we impose the following technical assumptions.

 

#### [Assumption 6.1](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fea-0012)

The term “stationary” comes from the property that if a Markov chain distributes according to a stationary distribution initially, then the chain will follow the same distribution at all future time points.

By definition, when the limiting distribution ![left-parenthesis pi 1 comma ellipsis comma pi Subscript upper K Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0498.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, defined by

A fundamental theorem in Markov chain theory is that every irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution. To establish this result, we need the following lemma.

Any irreducible Markov chains possessing all finite mean hitting times between any two states are said to be *positive recurrent*.

*Proof.*  By [Corollary 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0008), we can find an integer ![upper M](images/c06-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> such that ![p Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for every pair of ![i comma j](images/c06-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></math> whenever ![m greater-than-or-equal-to upper M](images/c06-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>M</mi></math>. **[Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fea-0030) *(Markov Chain Convergence Theorem: Finite State Space)***   Let ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space ![script upper S equals StartSet bold-italic s 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic s Subscript upper K Baseline EndSet](images/c06-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, a transition matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math>, and an arbitrary initial distribution ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. where ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> is the distribution of ![bold x Subscript n](images/c06-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> initialized by ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>.

*Proof.*  When studying the behavior of ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, we may assume that ![left-parenthesis bold x 0 comma bold x 1 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> has been obtained by the simulation method:

![bold x 0 equals psi Subscript bold-italic mu Sub Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis normal u 0 right-parenthesis tilde bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline comma bold x Subscript n Baseline equals phi left-parenthesis bold x Subscript n minus 1 Baseline comma normal u Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis tilde double-struck upper P left-parenthesis bold x Subscript n Baseline equals dot vertical-bar bold x Subscript n minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis comma n equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma](images/c06-math-0081.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo></math>

Since ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> is a stationary distribution, we have that ![bold x prime Subscript n Baseline tilde bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></math> for all ![n](images/c06-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Also, the chains ![left-parenthesis bold x 0 comma bold x 1 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![left-parenthesis bold x prime 0 comma bold x prime 1 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are independent of each other in accordance with the assumption that the sequences of random variables ![left-parenthesis normal u 0 comma normal u 1 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![left-parenthesis normal u prime 0 comma normal u prime 1 comma ellipsis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are independent of each other.

A key step in the proof is to show that, with probability 1, the two chains will meet, meaning that ![bold x Subscript n Baseline equals bold x prime Subscript n](images/c06-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> for some ![n](images/c06-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. To show this, define the first meeting time ![normal upper T equals min left-brace right-brace colon n colon equals equals xnxn prime](images/c06-i0592.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, with the convention that ![normal upper T equals infinity](images/c06-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> if the two chains never meet. Since the Markov chain ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is irreducible and aperiodic, we can find, using [Corollary 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0008), an integer ![upper M](images/c06-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> such that ![p Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis Baseline greater-than 0](images/c06-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for all ![i comma j](images/c06-i0597.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></math> and ![m greater-than-or-equal-to upper M](images/c06-i0598.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>M</mi></math>. In other words, the chain ![left-brace bold x double-prime Subscript n right-brace](images/c06-i0611.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> evolves exactly like the chain ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0612.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> until the time ![upper T](images/c06-i0613.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> when it first meets the chain ![left-brace bold x prime Subscript n right-brace](images/c06-i0614.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. It then switches to evolving like the chain ![left-brace bold x prime Subscript n right-brace](images/c06-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. It is important to realize that the chain ![left-brace bold x double-prime Subscript n right-brace](images/c06-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> has the same transition matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math>, since at each update, the update function is exposed to a new independent uniform random variable, while each ![bold u Subscript n plus 1](images/c06-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold u prime Subscript n plus 1](images/c06-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> by assumption are independent to all previous uniform random variables with the same distribution.

**Theorem 6.5 *(Uniqueness of the Stationary Distribution)***   Any irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space has exactly one stationary distribution.

*Proof.*  Let ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0626.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space. By [Theorem 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0026), there exists at least one stationary distribution, so we only need to show that there is at most one stationary distribution. Let ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0627.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic pi bold-italic prime](images/c06-i0628.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8242;</mo></msup></math> be two stationary distributions for the Markov chain. Suppose that the Markov chain starts with an initial distribution ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold-italic pi prime](images/c06-i0629.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math>. Then, by the stationarity assumption of ![bold-italic pi prime](images/c06-i0630.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math>, ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold-italic pi prime](images/c06-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> for all ![n](images/c06-i0632.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. On the other hand, by [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030),

![0 equals limit Underscript n right-arrow infinity Endscripts d Subscript TV Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Baseline comma bold-italic pi right-parenthesis equals limit Underscript n right-arrow infinity Endscripts d Subscript TV Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic pi prime comma bold-italic pi right-parenthesis equals d Subscript TV Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic pi prime comma bold-italic pi right-parenthesis period](images/c06-math-0092.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>TV</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>TV</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>TV</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

This implies that ![bold-italic pi equals bold-italic pi bold-italic prime](images/c06-i0633.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8242;</mo></msup></math>. ![](images/box.png)

We summarize [Theorems 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0026) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030): if a Markov chain is irreducible and aperiodic with a finite state space, then it has a unique stationary distribution ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0634.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math>, and the distribution ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0635.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> of the chain at time ![n](images/c06-i0636.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> approaches ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0637.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c06-i0638.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, regardless of the initial distribution ![bold-italic mu Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0639.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. By referring to ([6.22](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0086)), ([6.23](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0088)) and ([6.24](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0089)), we see this convergence is mostly exponentially fast in ![n](images/c06-i0640.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>; also see *Doeblin's theorem*.

In the remainder of this subsection, we discuss the case when the state space of the Markov chain is uncountable. In this circumstance, a probability measure ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0641.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> is said to be *stationary* if it is invariant with respect to the transition operator ![script í’«](images/c06-i0642.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi The following [Theorem 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0027) is an analogy of [Theorem 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0026), which asserts that any irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with an uncountable state space admits a stationary distribution. Its proof is relegated to [Appendix \*6.A.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0042).

 

**Theorem 6.6 *(Existence of Stationary Distribution with an Uncountable State Space)***   Under [Assumption 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0012), every irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with an uncountable state space admits a stationary distribution.

Now, let us provide [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040), which serves an analogy of [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030). It states that the stationary distribution of an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with an uncountable state space is unique. We recall that the total variation distance for general state spaces can still be defined as in ([6.21](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0079)) for discrete state space. The proof of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040), which makes use of the idea of “*almost-coupling*” to adapt the proof of [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030) for the uncountable state spaces case, can be found in [Appendix \*6.A.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0043).

## \*6.4 MARKOV CHAIN MONTE CARLO

As explained in [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml), sometimes it is convenient to approximate ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis g left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0680.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by taking the empirical average of ![sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts StartFraction g left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction](images/c06-i0681.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>, where ![bold-italic x 1 comma bold-italic x 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0682.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> are ![n](images/c06-i0683.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> independent realizations of a distribution ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0684.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> of a random variable ![bold x](images/c06-i0685.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. This (vanilla) Monte Carlo method is only applicable if the form of ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0686.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> is known in a rather explicit manner. To remedy this limitation, the *Markov Chain Monte Carlo* (MCMC) algorithm has been proposed. Its idea is to mechanically construct an irreducible and aperiodic (most often time-reversible) Markov chain ![left-brace bold x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0687.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> with ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0688.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> as the only stationary distribution. To this end, given a target distribution ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0689.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> on a discrete state space, we first construct a transition probability matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0690.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> satisfying reversibility condition ([6.25](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0093)) such that the corresponding Markov chain is also irreducible and aperiodic. Then starting from an arbitrary initial state, we run the Markov chain with this transition probability matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0691.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and collect the chain values ![left-brace bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0692.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. The limiting distribution of the chain is then given by ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0693.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> in accordance with [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030). Furthermore, by the *martingale convergence theorem* [\[15](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0015), [31\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0031), we can estimate ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis g left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0694.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> from

![StartFraction 1 Over upper M EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript t equals upper T plus 1 Overscript upper T plus upper M Endscripts g left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c06-math-0096.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>M</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></munderover><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

for a sufficiently large ![upper T](images/c06-i0695.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>. The time duration before ![upper T](images/c06-i0696.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is called the *burn-in period*, and all samples prior to time ![upper T](images/c06-i0697.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> will be discarded. The MCMC algorithm finds great use in statistics, especially in Bayesian inference (to be introduced in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml)). One can also refer to [\[7](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0007), [8](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008), [10](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010), [26\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0026) for more details. In the following subsections, we shall introduce some common systematic algorithms to generate Markov chain samples. We shall discuss these algorithms for stationary distributions on both discrete and continuum state spaces.

 

### \*6.4.1 Metropolis–Hastings Algorithm

A time-reversible Markov chain whose stationary distribution is some desired ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0698.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math>, such as the posterior distribution of parameters given the observations of some feature vectors, can be constructed systematically by the celebrated *Metropolis–Hastings algorithm*. For discrete state spaces, we start by proposing (guessing) transition probabilities ![p Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0699.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which are formally called *proposal transition probabilities*. If the ![p Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0700.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s already satisfy time reversibility condition ([6.25](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0093)), the corresponding Markov chain is the one we want. Otherwise, either ![pi Subscript i Baseline p Subscript i comma j Baseline greater-than pi Subscript j Baseline p Subscript j comma i](images/c06-i0701.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> or ![pi Subscript i Baseline p Subscript i comma j Baseline less-than pi Subscript j Baseline p Subscript j comma i](images/c06-i0702.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> for some pairs of ![i](images/c06-i0703.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and ![j](images/c06-i0704.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>. Without loss of generality, suppose that ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis bold x Subscript n Baseline equals bold-italic s Subscript j Baseline comma bold x Subscript n minus 1 Baseline equals ![alpha Subscript i comma j Baseline equals StartFraction pi Subscript j Baseline p Subscript j comma i Baseline Over pi Subscript i Baseline p Subscript i comma j Baseline EndFraction period](images/c06-math-0097.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

On the other hand, we do not want to reduce the likelihood of moving from state ![bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0714.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> to state ![bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0715.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, hence we set ![alpha Subscript j comma i Baseline equals 1](images/c06-i0716.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. These considerations motivate us to define the *acceptance probability*: for any ![i not-equals j](images/c06-i0717.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></math>,

and the probabilities

The transition probability matrix ![bold-italic upper P prime](images/c06-i0728.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> corresponds to the following transition mechanism: given that ![bold x Subscript n Baseline equals bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0729.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, a proposal state ![s Subscript j](images/c06-i0730.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> for the next move is drawn in accordance with the ![i](images/c06-i0731.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th row of ![bold-italic upper P](images/c06-i0732.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math>, the transition matrix of a conveniently chosen Markov chain, so that ![alpha Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0733.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> can also be easily computed. We then accept this proposal and set ![bold x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline equals bold-italic s Subscript j](images/c06-i0734.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> with the probability of ![alpha Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0735.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>; otherwise, we set ![bold x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline equals bold-italic s Subscript i](images/c06-i0736.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Recall [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030), this Markov chain over a countable state space, with transition probability matrix ![bold-italic upper P prime](images/c06-i0737.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> being irreducible and aperiodic, the limiting distribution of ![bold x Subscript n](images/c06-i0738.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> uniquely exists and is given by the stationary distribution ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0739.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math>, as requested.

In the case of an uncountable state space ![script upper S](images/c06-i0740.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></mrow></math>, even for a non-compact space such as ![double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c06-i0741.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> (with appropriate light tail requirements), the expression of the acceptance probability is analogous to ([6.27](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0098)). Let ![bold-italic pi left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis colon script upper S right-arrow double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline](images/c06-i0742.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math> be the target probability density, and ![q left-parenthesis dot vertical-bar dot right-parenthesis colon script upper S times script upper S right-arrow double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline](images/c06-i0743.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math> be a pre-specified jointly continuous and strictly positive transition density (kernel). Following the ideas in [Theorems 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040) and [6.9](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0046), one can still establish that the Markov chain with a transition density ![bold-italic mu](images/c06-i0746.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, being a mixture of absolutely continuous and singular parts, can still converge to the stationary distribution ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0747.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math>. In particular, the transition density ![bold-italic mu](images/c06-i0748.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> constructed in ([6.30](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0101)) carries a point mass along the diagonal ![StartSet left-parenthesis bold-italic u comma bold-italic v right-parenthesis colon bold-italic u equals bold-italic v EndSet](images/c06-i0749.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> of ![script upper S times script upper S](images/c06-i0750.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi></math> because of the presence of the Dirac delta function in the second summand of ([6.30](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0101)), thereby making ![bold-italic mu](images/c06-i0751.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> discontinuous on the diagonal and hence apparently violating [Assumption 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0012)(ii). Nevertheless, the presence of the first term on the right of ([6.30](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0101)), which is jointly continuous in ![bold-italic u](images/c06-i0752.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic v](images/c06-i0753.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi></mrow></math> (technically called the core part of *Harris recurrence* [\[6](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006), [15](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0015), [27\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0027)), guarantees that the conclusion of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040) remains valid. The proof of this extension essentially involves the same adaptation as the proof of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040), but we do not go into details here due to the many technicalities involved. Interested readers with a thorough understanding of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040) can try to establish the proof of this extension as a mini-project, while we shall also certainly try to provide a definite answer to this issue in our future publications.

Next, we consider an application of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm in Bayesian inference, where it helps to update the posterior distribution of parameters given the data. The procedure can be stated as follows: let ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0754.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> be ![n](images/c06-i0755.png)<math mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> once more data are collected. Our objective is to construct an appropriate Markov chain ![left-brace bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline equals left-parenthesis theta 1 Superscript function of the sample.

[Algorithm 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0002) states the general procedure of applying the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm in this context, in the continuum state space setting. Note that we actually do not need to know the explicit form of the posterior ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic theta vertical-bar bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0763.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. We specify a multidimensional proposal transition density ![q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic theta right-parenthesis colon double-struck upper R Superscript r Baseline times double-struck upper R Superscript r Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline](images/c06-i0764.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#977;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math>. As mentioned above, given a sufficiently large burn-in time ![upper T](images/c06-i0765.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, an extension of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040) for ([6.30](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0101)) (or [Theorem 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0030) when the parameter space is discrete) tells us that the distribution of ![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0766.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> is close to the joint posterior distribution of ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0767.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![t greater-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c06-i0768.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. Thus, we simulate the Markov chain ![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis upper T plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis upper T plus 2 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis](images/c06-i0769.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>, and the empirical distribution of these subsequent chain values will converge to the desired posterior distribution of ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0770.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Let us illustrate the use of this algorithm in the parameter estimation of the coefficient vector ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0771.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> in binary logistic regression, and compare it with the commonly adopted maximum likelihood approach via the *Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares* (IRLS) method which will be discussed in detail in [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#head-2-137). From the Bayesian perspective, we generate a sequence of ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0772.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>'s through its proposal transition density, and the MH estimate can be the mean, median, or mode statistic of the generated empirical distribution. According to [Algorithm 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0002), we have to define two probability density functions, namely the prior ![bold-italic pi](images/c06-i0773.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi></mrow></math> and proposal transition density ![q](images/c06-i0774.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>. In actual practice, we often take the natural logarithm of the densities to avoid numerical underflow. Recall that by Bayes' theorem, the posterior distribution ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic beta vertical-bar bold-italic upper X comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0775.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is proportional to the product of the likelihood function and the prior density, where we denote ![bold-italic upper X equals left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0776.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Thus ![ln pi left-parenthesis bold-italic beta vertical-bar bold-italic upper X comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0777.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> “![equals](images/c06-i0778.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math>” ![ln upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis plus ln pi left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0779.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> up to a constant, where ![ln upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0780.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is given in (10.14), and ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0781.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the prior distribution of ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0782.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. Note that ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0783.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is often chosen to be non-informative so that the MH algorithm is not biased to any specific features of the prior distribution. For logistic regression, for the prior distribution, we consider a multivariate normal distribution, with a mean vector ![bold 0](images/c06-i0784.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></math> and large componentwise variances with independent components, such as ![bold beta tilde script í’© Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis bold 0 comma 10 0 squared bold-italic upper I Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0785.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#946;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The proposal transition density ![q](images/c06-i0786.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is often chosen to be related to (more technically, to be *conjugate* to) the prior distribution, and its parameter should depend on the current iterate ![bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0787.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. In light of this, we adopt another multivariate normal distribution as the proposal transition distribution with mean vector ![bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0788.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and covariance matrix ![nu left-parenthesis bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1](images/c06-i0789.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#957;</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>, where ![nu greater-than 0](images/c06-i0790.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> is a small positive hyperparameter. By the symmetric expressions of normal distributions, we see that ![q left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline vertical-bar bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals q left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline vertical-bar bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0791.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, hence the acceptance probability can be simplified a bit. It becomes:

First we present the implementation in Python, starting with the construction of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm in [Programme 6.14](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00014).

 ![](images/c06-gra-0018.png)

Here, the hyperparameters (i) `num_it` specifies the total number of iterations; (ii) `burn_in` stands for the number of the first batch of Markov chain samples ![bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis monospace burn bar in negative 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0792.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext mathvariant="monospace">burn\_in</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> to be discarded; (iii) `nu` is the value of ![nu](images/c06-i0793.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> in the variance of the proposal transition density; and (iv) `seed` determines the random initial seed for the simulation for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0794.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. Like most functions for machine learning in the `sklearn` library, we have the `fit()` and `predict()` functions for model fitting and predictions, respectively. The latter takes an extra argument `method`, which indicates the choice of estimation statistics for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0795.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. Lastly, the `plot()` function is used to plot the simulation results.

In [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#head-2-137), the 1999–2002 HSI dataset will be used for demonstrations. Let us apply the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm to this dataset now; see [Programme 6.15](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00015) in Python.

![](images/c06-gra-0019.png)![](images/c06-gra-0020.png)

From the outputs obtained in [Programme 6.15](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00015), the acceptance probability is as high as 0.940952, and the parameter ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0796.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> is estimated by the median and mean, respectively. Note that different random seeds often lead to slightly different estimates in MCMC, especially when some of the feature variables are highly correlated. We shall defer its discussion in [Programme 6.17](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00017) via Python. On the other hand, as shown in [Figure 6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0008), the estimated posterior distribution of each parameter component in the simulated Markov chain ![left-brace bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace](images/c06-i0797.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is often skewed, so in practice we often adopt the median as the estimate instead of the mean in order to maintain the robustness of the estimation. Now, let us compute the MLE for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0798.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, and compare the misclassification of the resulting fitted logistic regression models with those obtained from the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm; the Python codes and results are shown in the following [Programme 6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00016).

![](images/c06-gra-0021.png)![](images/c06-gra-0022.png)

The results obtained from [Programme 6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00016) indicate that both methods yield a nearly perfect fit, but they arrive with slightly different estimates for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0800.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>; indeed, the feature vectors are linearly dependent (see their correlation matrix in [Programme 6.18](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00018) in Python), and this results in the instability of the estimation for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0801.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. The accuracy of the MLE of 0.9926 is slightly higher than that of the MH median estimate of 0.9897. In [Programme 6.17](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00017) (via Python), we plot the simulated paths for ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0802.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>.

![](images/c06-gra-0023.png)![](images/c06-gra-0024.png)![](images/c06-gra-0025.png) ![FIGURE 6.8 Simulation paths and histograms for components of bold-italic beta, generated in Programme 6.17 via Python.](images/c06f008.png)

[**FIGURE 6.8**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0008) Simulation paths and histograms for components of ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0799.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, generated in [Programme 6.17](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00017) via Python.

The simulation paths and the corresponding histograms are shown in [Figure 6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0008) for each component of ![bold-italic beta equals left-parenthesis beta 0 comma beta 1 comma ellipsis comma beta 6 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0803.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. In the simulation plots on the left-hand side, the blue vertical dashed lines represent the end of the burn-in period determined by `burn_in`, whereas the red horizontal dashed lines are the estimates of ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c06-i0804.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s via the median statistics. In the histograms on the right-hand side, the red vertical dashed lines represent the ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c06-i0805.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> estimates obtained by the median. From both diagrams, we observe that the simulations for ![beta 0 comma beta 1](images/c06-i0806.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![beta 3](images/c06-i0807.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> give two modes in their respective histograms. Indeed, according to the correlation matrix shown in [Programme 6.18](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00018), relatively large linear correlations were observed between features ![normal x 1](images/c06-i0808.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c06-i0809.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> with a correlation coefficient of 0.35195 and between features ![normal x 2](images/c06-i0810.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 3](images/c06-i0811.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> with a correlation coefficient of 0.24072. In order to obtain a better estimate, one can also (i) vary the size of the hyperparameter ![nu](images/c06-i0812.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math>; (ii) increase the number of iterations; (iii) burn in more samples; or (iv) adopt more random seeds.

Now, let us turn to the corresponding implementation in **R**. Again, we start with the construction of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm; see the following [Programme 6.19](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00019).

![](images/c06-gra-0026.png)

As a remark, in the **R** environment we are unable to save and retrieve the parameters in the same way as Python. Therefore, we modify the main function `MCMC_logistic()` so that it returns a list containing (i) `beta_hist` for the historical estimate values of the coefficient parameter ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0813.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> for the simulation paths; (ii) `n_accept` for the total number of acceptance for the overall simulations; (iii) `num_it` for the total number of iterations; and (iv) `burn_in` for the number of the first batch of Markov chain samples to be discarded. Next, we apply [Programme 6.19](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00019) to the HSI dataset, and compare the corresponding estimation with the MLE obtained from `glmnet()`; see the **R** codes and results in [Programme 6.20](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-00020).

![](images/c06-gra-0027.png)

In the `glmnet()` function in **R**, ![lamda](images/c06-i0814.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is set to 0 so that no penalty term is added to the objective function of the binary logistic regression, just like the argument `penalty=None` for `LogisticRegression()` in [Programme 6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00016) via Python. `glmnet` adopts a gradient descent algorithm to estimate the coefficient ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0815.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, yet under an unsatisfactory choice of initial point, the algorithm is subject to convergence error if ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0816.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> is directly estimated with ![lamda](images/c06-i0817.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> set exactly to 0. To address this issue, we first estimate ![bold-italic beta](images/c06-i0818.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> with ![lamda equals 1 0 Superscript negative 4](images/c06-i0819.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></math>, and the resulting estimate, which should be quite close to the minimizer of the original objective function, is then used as the initial point for estimation, by then ![lamda](images/c06-i0820.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> can be set to 0. Both the MLE method and MH algorithm with median estimates attain the same training accuracy of 0.9926471.

 

Lastly, we plot the simulation paths and histograms from using **R**; see the code in [Programme 6.21](#c06.xhtml#c06-pre-00021) and the resulting plots in [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0009).

![](images/c06-gra-0028.png) ![FIGURE 6.9 Simulation paths and histograms for components of bold-italic beta, generated in Programme 6.21 via R.](images/c06f009.png)

### \*6.4.2 Variants of the Metropolis–Hastings Algorithm

For sampling in Bayesian inference, for the ease of calculating the acceptance probability and simulating the Markov chain, we may sometimes generate the parameters one by one, rather than independently from those generated previously. The resulting joint transition density can still possess a dependence structure because of the use of the acceptance probability in the construction of the corresponding reversible Markov chain. To this point, for the parameter ![bold-italic theta element-of double-struck upper R Superscript r](images/c06-i0822.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>r</mi></msup></math>, firstly the proposal transition density takes the simple form of a product of ![r](images/c06-i0823.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> univariate conditional densities, i.e., ![q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic theta right-parenthesis equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript r Endscripts q Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis theta Subscript i Baseline bar bold-italic theta Subscript negative i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0824.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#977;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#977;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![bold-italic theta Subscript negative i](images/c06-i0825.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#977;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> stands for the vector with all components in the same order as in ![bold-italic theta](images/c06-i0826.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#977;</mi></mrow></math> except the ![i](images/c06-i0827.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th component is removed. The collection of ![q Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis dot bar dot right-parenthesis colon double-struck upper R times double-struck upper R Superscript r minus 1 Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R Subscript plus Baseline](images/c06-i0828.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma r](images/c06-i0829.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></math>, are all pre-specified marginal conditional densities. In addition, we often simply take the ![q Subscript i](images/c06-i0830.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s to be the same. The resulting special algorithm is commonly called the *Single Component Adaptive Metropolis–Hastings algorithm* for Bayesian inference; see [Algorithm 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0003).

![](images/c06-gra-0029.png)

As shown in [Algorithm 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0002), a vanilla Metropolis–Hastings algorithm generates the candidate sample values of all parameters in one go, which might not be convenient in practice. On the other hand, the single component variant in [Algorithm 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0003) generates one parameter value at a time, making calculations much simpler, yet without identifying any inherent dependence relations among the parameters in advance.

Another natural variant is to decide the update of each single parameter individually, and to utilize the updated parameter values immediately to infer the update of the next parameter component. This alternative approach is the well-known *Gibbs Sampling*; see [\[3](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0003), [26\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0026) for more detailed discussions. As before, we let ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c06-i0831.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> be ![n](images/c06-i0832.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> independent realizations from the same distribution with ![r](images/c06-i0833.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> unknown parameters, ![bold theta equals left-parenthesis normal theta 1 comma ellipsis comma normal theta Subscript r Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c06-i0834.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. For each parameter ![theta Subscript i](images/c06-i0835.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, we specify a one-dimensional conjugate prior ![pi Despite the apparent absence of the acceptance probability and the seemingly different parameter updating mechanism in Gibbs sampling (compared with the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm or its single component variant), there is a close connection between them as each updating substep ![i](images/c06-i0847.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> in a cycle in the former is actually a step in the latter with the corresponding acceptance probability ![alpha Subscript i Baseline identical-to 1](images/c06-i0848.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We have elaborated on the MCMC approach for estimating the posterior distribution in Bayesian inference. In [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml), we shall provide more discussion on Bayesian learning in which more tailor-made tools for different *FinTech* and *InsurTech* problems will be discussed.

Another practical and relevant application of Gibbs sampling in finance is the parameter estimation of stochastic volatility (SV) models [\[13](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0013), [14](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0014), [17](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017), [29](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0029), [30\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0030). In financial time series analysis, volatility is a key ingredient, yet it is not directly observable. As an alternative to the ARCH/GARCH framework (to be introduced in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml) ), SV models treat volatility as a latent (hidden) variable, evolving over time in a stochastic manner. This leads to an immediate problem of parameter estimation in light of the intractable form of the likelihood, to which traditional MLE method may fail to apply.

Denote ![normal y Subscript t](images/c06-i0868.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> as the logarithmic return of the stock price and ![normal h Subscript t](images/c06-i0869.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> as the latent variable for volatility at time ![t](images/c06-i0870.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>.
