The hidden (one-half) log-volatility ![normal h Subscript t](images/c06-i0894.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is assumed to follow a stationary AR(1) process with the persistence parameter ![StartAbsoluteValue phi EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c06-i0895.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; also refer to [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml) for more discussions on AR processes as a special case of ARMA processes.

Given observations ![left-brace y Subscript t Baseline right-brace Subscript t equals 1 Superscript upper T](images/c06-i0896.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, our goal is to provide a Bayesian framework to model the conditional joint density of ![bold h](images/c06-i0897.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold theta](images/c06-i0898.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></math>:

[(6.32)](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-disp-0110)![p left-parenthesis bold-italic h comma bold-italic theta vertical-bar bold-italic y right-parenthesis proportional-to p left-parenthesis bold-italic y vertical-bar bold-italic h comma bold-italic theta right-parenthesis p left-parenthesis bold-italic h vertical-bar bold-italic theta right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis comma](images/c06-math-0110.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8733;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![pi](images/c06-i0899.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math> is a prior distribution of ![bold theta](images/c06-i0900.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> and different ![p left-parenthesis dot vertical-bar dot right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0901.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>'s are the corresponding conditional densities or parametrized densities. However, due to the high-dimensional integration resulting from a long time series of observations, jointly sampling ![bold h](images/c06-i0902.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold theta](images/c06-i0903.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> directly from ([6.32](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0110)) is highly inconvenient. Bayesian researchers [\[13](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0013), [14](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0014), [17\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017) decomposed this sampling problem into two steps: (i) sampling ![normal h Subscript t](images/c06-i0904.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> from ![p left-parenthesis h Subscript t Baseline vertical-bar bold-italic y comma bold-italic h Subscript negative t Baseline comma bold-italic theta](images/c06-i0905.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></math>), for ![t equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper T](images/c06-i0906.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></math>; and (ii) sampling ![normal theta Subscript i](images/c06-i0907.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> from ![p left-parenthesis theta Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold-italic y comma bold-italic h comma bold-italic theta Subscript negative i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0908.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma 3](images/c06-i0909.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>; the corresponding procedure is depicted in [Algorithm 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0005).

![](images/c06-gra-0031.png)

For setting prior distributions for the unknown parameters ![normal mu](images/c06-i0910.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, ![normal phi](images/c06-i0911.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#966;</mi></mrow></math>, and ![normal nu Subscript eta](images/c06-i0912.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#957;</mi><mi>&#951;</mi></msub></math>, since the likelihood is a product of normal densities, we consider Gibbs sampling with the following conjugate priors: (I) ![normal mu tilde script í’© left-parenthesis alpha Subscript mu Baseline comma beta Subscript mu Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0913.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>&#956;</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, a normal distribution; and (III) ![normal nu Subscript eta Baseline tilde script upper I script í’¢ left-parenthesis alpha Subscript nu Baseline comma beta Subscript nu Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0915.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#957;</mi><mi>&#951;</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#8464;</mi><mi mathvariant="script">&#54434;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, an inverse gamma distribution (see [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) ).

Let us establish the conditional distributions in [Algorithm 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-gra-0005) one by one as follows. ## \*6.A APPENDIX

 

This appendix collects proofs of statements concerning Markov chains with uncountable state spaces as formulated in [Section \*6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0006).

### \*6.A.5 Proof of Theorem 6.7

This proof is based on generalizing the coupling argument from the discrete state setting. Again, we construct two independent Markov chains as follows. **Remark 6.2**   The proof of [Theorem 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0040) provides an exponential rate of convergence to the stationary distribution up to a truncation error (![script upper M left-parenthesis script upper S right-parenthesis normal upper Delta Subscript epsilon](images/c06-i1246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#8499;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#119982;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>&#949;</mi></msub></math>), which can be arbitrary small. We refer interested readers to [\[24](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0024), [27\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0027) for more refined convergence rates.

## NOTES

1.  [1](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0001)   The *Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology* database, MNIST database for short, is revised (modified) from the original *National Institute of Standards and Technology* (NIST) database ([https://www.nist.gov/srd/nist-special-database-19](https://www.nist.gov/srd/nist-special-database-19)) by *Yann LeCun*. MNIST consists of 60,000 training images and 10,000 testing images of handwritten digits by high school students and employees of the *United States Census Bureau*, and is commonly used in training image processing systems. The database can be retrieved at [http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/](http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/).
2.  [2](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0002)   Recall the aphorism added by *George Box* (see [\[2\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0002)): “*All models are wrong, but some of them are useful*.”
3.  [3](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0003)   According to the *Keras* website [https://keras.io/about/](https://keras.io/about/), the name *Keras* comes from the Greek word “horn”. It is a reference to a literary image from ancient Greek and Latin literature. In Python, *Keras* is a deep learning (e.g. ANN, CNN, LSTM) API (Application Programming Interface) running on top of the machine learning platform *TensorFlow*.
4.  [4](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0004)   Each pixel of a grayscale image has a value ranging from 0 to 255, whose value represents the amount of light intensity.
5.  [5](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0005)   This is actually the inverse distribution function introduced in [Section 5.1](#c05.xhtml#head-2-45) of [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml), in which various simulation techniques are discussed.
6.  [6](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-note-0006)   According to the celebrated *Hammersley–Clifford Theorem* [\[11\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0011), the *positivity condition*, namely that for all ![theta Subscript i](images/c06-i0863.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma r](images/c06-i0864.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></math>, ![pi Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis theta Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c06-i0865.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, altogether implies that ![pi left-parenthesis bold-italic theta bar bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c06-i0866.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and this ensures the Markov chain to be irreducible and aperiodic.

# CHAPTER 7  
Time-Varying Volatility Matrix and Kelly Fraction

 

Volatilities and correlations are fundamental concepts in quantitative finance, financial statistics and risk management. They serve as parameters in forecasting the trend of riskiness of stock prices, in pricing options and derivatives, in calculating the Value-at-Risk (V@R) of portfolios, in determining the beta factors in CAPM, and so on. In this chapter, first we explain how historical security price data can be used to estimate volatilities and correlations. In particular, we consider some common models like *exponentially weighted moving average* (EWMA), *autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity* (ARCH) [\[11\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0010), and *generalized ARCH* (GARCH) [\[3\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0002). The effectiveness of these models will be illustrated by real financial data. An important characteristic of these models is that volatilities and correlations are not constant, rather they change rapidly with time. A model that allows for this is closer to reality than one that assumes volatility is constant, like the celebrated Black–Scholes–Merton model [\[2\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001). In the second part of this chapter, we present some original research results of the authors, which are about the possible use of the *Kelly fraction* for selling (resp. buying) a stock at a favourable time over a planning horizon. Its implications for apparent calendar effects will also be discussed. Before we begin this journey, let us introduce some notations and definitions of some relevant technical concepts.

 

## 7.1 FLUCTUATION OF VOLATILITIES

Under the classical Black–Scholes–Merton model for a security price, the percentage change in the stock price over a short period of time is assumed to be normally distributed, namely

can serve as an unbiased estimate of ![sigma squared tau](images/c07-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#964;</mi></math>, and so we can estimate ![sigma](images/c07-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> by ![ModifyingAbove sigma With Ì‚ equals s slash StartRoot tau EndRoot](images/c07-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msqrt><mi>&#964;</mi></msqrt></math>. However, choosing an appropriate value for ![n](images/c07-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is not easy. Generally speaking, the estimate is more accurate when ![n](images/c07-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is large. Unfortunately, in reality ![sigma](images/c07-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> does change in time. Including too many past observations may be useless or even harmful for the prediction of the spontaneous volatility. As a rule of thumb, the choice of ![n](images/c07-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> should reflect the length of time the volatility is used. For instance, if we want to estimate the value of a one-year option, the daily stock price for the last year should be taken. More sophisticated methods for estimating volatility will be discussed in later sections of this chapter. For the moment, we first illustrate some simple models with the stocks in [Example 1.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-fea-0006) of [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) . The file `stock_1999_2002.csv` contains adjusted daily closing prices for the stocks HSBC (0005) ![](images/c07-gra-0001.png)![FIGURE 7.1 Reproduced from Figures 3.1 and 3.3: Plots of returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK.](images/c07f001.png)

[**FIGURE 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0001) Reproduced from [Figures 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001) and [3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0003): Plots of returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK.

![](images/c07-gra-0002.png)

Based on the time series plots of the returns of these three stocks in [Figure 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0001), we see that the ![u Subscript i](images/c07-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are roughly fluctuating around zero, while the volatility amplitude is small in certain periods but large in others. Obviously the volatility varies with time rather than staying constant. Let us focus on computing the evolution in time of the standard deviation of ![u Subscript i](images/c07-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s based on a moving window of width ![w](images/c07-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>. First, we compute the standard deviation of the first ![w](images/c07-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> observations ![u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript w Baseline](images/c07-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></math>, and then that of ![u 2 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript w plus 1 Baseline](images/c07-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and so forth. This gives rise to a series of estimated standard deviations.

![](images/c07-gra-0003.png)![](images/c07-gra-0004.png) 

Through [Programme 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0003) in Python (resp. Programme 7.4 in **R**), we illustrate the time-varying nature of volatility estimates in [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0002) (resp. [Figure 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003)), and we also notice that different window widths have a very different effect on the estimates. For the 90-day version, the minimum and maximum values of HSBC's `s_90` for 1999–2002 are respectively 0.00984 and 0.02439, so the minimum and maximum annual volatilities are respectively ![left-parenthesis StartRoot 252 EndRoot right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 0.00984 right-parenthesis equals 15.62 percent-sign](images/c07-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mn>252</mn></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.00984</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>15.62</mn><mi>%</mi></math> and ![left-parenthesis StartRoot 252 EndRoot right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 0.02439 right-parenthesis equals 38.72 percent-sign](images/c07-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mn>252</mn></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.02439</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>38.72</mn><mi>%</mi></math>. Similarly, with a window of 180 days, the minimum and maximum values of HSBC's `s_180` are 0.01172 and 0.02072 and the annual volatilities are ![18.60 percent-sign](images/c07-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>18.60</mn><mi>%</mi></math> and ![32.89 percent-sign](images/c07-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>32.89</mn><mi>%</mi></math>, respectively. Empirical studies often show that the annual volatility of a stock usually lies within the range from ![10 percent-sign](images/c07-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>10</mn><mi>%</mi></math> to ![50 percent-sign](images/c07-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mi>%</mi></math>.

## 7.2 EXPONENTIALLY WEIGHTED MOVING AVERAGE

In the previous section, the “moving” variance at time ![t](images/c07-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> was computed as

![s Subscript t Superscript 2 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over w minus 1 EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals t minus w plus 1 Overscript t Endscripts left-parenthesis u Subscript i Baseline minus u overbar right-parenthesis squared comma](images/c07-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#363;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is an average of the most recent ![w](images/c07-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> terms of ![left-parenthesis u Subscript i Baseline minus u overbar right-parenthesis squared](images/c07-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#363;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> and ![u overbar](images/c07-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#363;</mi></mrow></math> is the moving average of ![u Subscript t minus w plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma u Subscript t Baseline](images/c07-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This estimate assigns equal weights to these ![w](images/c07-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> terms, even though the more recent terms are expected to have a greater relevance for the instantaneous volatility. On the other hand, an influential daily return from the distant past may still have an effect on the volatility today, but this distant past value is now completely excluded from the estimate as it lies outside the moving window. To address these two issues, we introduce the *Exponentially Weighted Moving Average* (EWMA) model that gives the highest weight to the most recent term and gradually down-weights as we move back in time. Before presenting the precise definition of this model, we state the following:

1.  In estimating the volatility, instead of using ![u Subscript i Baseline equals ln left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline slash upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we usually use the percentage change ![u Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline minus upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis slash upper S Subscript i minus 1](images/c07-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. In fact, the values obtained from these two definitions are close if the quotient is small, which is normally the case in practice. This is especially the case when the time segment ![left-bracket t comma t plus delta t right-bracket](images/c07-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is short.
2.  The mean ![u overbar](images/c07-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#363;</mi></mrow></math> of ![u Subscript i](images/c07-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s can be assumed to be zero for simplicity in the course of volatility estimation. In practice, the daily percentage change is small and fluctuates around zero. Assuming a zero mean of the random variables ![normal u Subscript i](images/c07-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s greatly simplifies the model as well.
3.  By replacing ![w minus 1](images/c07-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in the denominator of the definition of ![s Subscript t Superscript 2](images/c07-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> by ![w](images/c07-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>, we obtain the maximum likelihood estimate instead of an unbiased estimate.

To this end, we adopt the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach from now on, by taking

(7.3)![s Subscript t Superscript 2 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over w EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals t minus w plus 1 Overscript t Endscripts u Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline period](images/c07-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>w</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>.</mo></math> 

The standard EWMA model for estimating the variance rate, ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> at the time ![n delta t](images/c07-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, is defined recursively by

[(7.4)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0006)![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals lamda sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus left-parenthesis 1 minus lamda right-parenthesis u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![0 less-than lamda less-than 1](images/c07-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is a parameter to be estimated in this model. To see why this model is called EWMA, let us substitute ![sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> in ([7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0006)) to obtain

Letting ![m](images/c07-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> go to infinity, the last term of ([7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0008)) vanishes under the assumption of uniform boundedness of ![sigma 0 squared comma sigma Subscript negative 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma sigma Subscript negative 2 Superscript 2 Baseline comma ellipsis](images/c07-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>, and the coefficient of the ![u Subscript n minus i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> term is ![left-parenthesis 1 minus lamda right-parenthesis lamda Superscript i minus 1](images/c07-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. These weights decrease exponentially as we run backward in time, and they all sum up to 1. The *Riskmetrics* database developed by *JP Morgan & Chase* (1996) [\[18\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0017) uses this EWMA model with ![lamda equals 0.94](images/c07-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.94</mn></math> for updating the daily volatility estimate. Empirical studies found that this value of ![lamda](images/c07-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> gives a reasonable volatility estimate for most common stocks [\[18\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0017).

Of course, we can also estimate ![lamda](images/c07-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> from historical data by the MLE method. We defer the details of estimating ![lamda](images/c07-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> this way to later in this chapter. In the next section, we shall introduce the celebrated ARIMA time series model, and then more importantly the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model which includes the EWMA model as a special case. We shall then describe the MLE of the parameters in the GARCH model, which can also be applied to estimating ![lamda](images/c07-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> for the EWMA model.

 

## 7.3 ARIMA TIME SERIES MODEL

ARIMA stands for “*Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average*”, a model for time series data. *Autoregressive* refers to the dependence of the present observation on some predefined number of time-lagged observations. “*Integrated*” indicates that the model employs differencing to the raw observations, i.e. the subtraction of an observation from the one at previous time step, or even higher order of differencing, so as to make the time series stationary. *Moving Average* means that the model expresses the relationship between the residual errors incurred over the last few time lags of the observations and the model. An ARIMA model is characterized by three parameters: ![p](images/c07-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, ![d](images/c07-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c07-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, where ![p](images/c07-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c07-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are the respective orders of AR and MA components, and ![d](images/c07-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the number of finite differencing required to ensure the stationary of the time series; if the time series is itself stationary, ![d](images/c07-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is then taken to be 0. The ARIMA model for a time series ![left-brace normal y Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> can be written in the following general form:

(7.6)![normal x Subscript t Baseline equals beta 1 normal x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline plus beta 2 normal x Subscript t minus 2 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus beta Subscript p Baseline normal x Subscript t minus p Baseline plus normal epsilon Subscript t Baseline plus phi 1 normal epsilon Subscript t minus 1 Baseline plus phi 2 normal epsilon Subscript t minus 2 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus phi Subscript q Baseline normal epsilon Subscript t minus q Baseline semicolon](images/c07-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo></math> 

here, ![normal x Subscript t Baseline colon equals left-parenthesis 1 minus upper B right-parenthesis Superscript d Baseline normal y Subscript t Baseline](images/c07-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> where ![upper B](images/c07-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the backward operator so that ![upper B normal y Subscript t Baseline colon equals normal y Subscript t minus 1 Baseline](images/c07-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>B</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> for every ![t](images/c07-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Note the intercept vanishes as ![normal x Subscript t](images/c07-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is now simplified to an ARMA(![p comma q](images/c07-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) model with a constant mean of zero due to the finite differencing.

A commonly used approach in determining the values of ![p](images/c07-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c07-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> of the resulting time series ![left-brace normal x Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is via the use of the plots of sample *autocorrelation function* (ACF) and sample *partial autocorrelation functions* (PACF). These are simply the respective bar plots of the sample ACF values ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> and sample PACF values ![ModifyingAbove phi With Ì‚ Subscript k k](images/c07-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math>, defined as follows, against time lag ![k](images/c07-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. Recall that the ACF at lag ![k](images/c07-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> of a stationary time series ![left-brace normal x Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is ![rho Subscript k Baseline colon equals Corr left-parenthesis normal x Subscript t Baseline comma normal x Subscript t minus k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>Corr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is independent of ![t](images/c07-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> due to the stationarity of ![normal x Subscript t](images/c07-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. The sample PACF at lag ![k](images/c07-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, ![ModifyingAbove phi With Ì‚ Subscript k k](images/c07-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math>, is calculated by solving the sample version of ([7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0012)), with ![rho Subscript k](images/c07-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s replaced by ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s.

In particular, for an AR(![p](images/c07-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>) (resp. MA(![q](images/c07-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>)) model, its ACF (resp. PACF) tails off / decays exponentially (can be sinusoidally) with the lag ![k](images/c07-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, while its PACF (resp. ACF) cuts off / vanishes after lag ![k greater-than p](images/c07-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>p</mi></math> (resp. ![k greater-than q](images/c07-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>q</mi></math>); this latter result is called the *cut-off property*. Their sample counterparts also demonstrate similar trends, see [Figure 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0004) for a numerical illustration. In particular, for the AR(2) model, the sample PACF value does not deviate significantly from 0 for ![k greater-than 2](images/c07-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, which justifies the cut-off property of its PACF at lag 2, and the same argument applies to the ACF of the MA(2) model. The mathematical details of these properties have been thoroughly discussed in various classical textbooks on time series, including [\[15](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0014), [39\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0037) to name a couple. While the properties mentioned above are for pure AR and MA models, they can also be applied to the determination of the values of ![p](images/c07-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c07-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> in the general ARMA model, namely by observing the cut-off point of the sample PACF and ACF plots, respectively. See [Table 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0001) for a summary of the properties of ACF and PACF for ARMA models.

ARIMA models are a useful tool commonly used in a wide range of disciplines, including but not limited to financial forecasting, economic analysis, operations research, and climate modelling. Here, let us illustrate their application to finance under the context of a recent trendy topic, namely the price prediction of *Bitcoin*. Bitcoin is a digital crypto-currency that enables individuals to transfer monetary value to one another without the requirement of the presence of a trusted third party like a bank or payment processor. It is the first decentralized peer-to-peer payment network solely powered by its own users without a central authority. The Bitcoin network monitors the movement of the cryptocurrency among digital wallets to prevent fraud and double spending. Bitcoin represents an innovative new form of digital money that is censorship-proof and accessible to anyone with internet access. New Bitcoins are issued through a process called “mining” in which computers solve complex math problems to discover a new block in the blockchain. Miners are then rewarded with new Bitcoins for verifying transactions and securing the network.

![Table 7.1 Properties of ACF and PACF for ARMA models.](images/c07-i0113.png)

[**Table 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-tbl-0001) Properties of ACF and PACF for ARMA models.

 ![FIGURE 7.4 Respective sample ACF and PACF plots of AR(2) and MA(2) models.](images/c07f004.png)

[**FIGURE 7.4**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0004) Respective sample ACF and PACF plots of AR(2) and MA(2) models.

From the late 2010s onwards in particular, Bitcoin has been fiercely volatile and risky as an investment, yet it has gained popularity among those seeking decentralized digital currencies. The value of Bitcoin has increased significantly since it was first introduced in 2009, making many early investors wealthy. However, the high volatility and unregulated nature of Bitcoin make it too risky as a way to save money.

The `Bitstamp_BTCUSD_2018_minute.csv` dataset contains intraday minute data for Bitcoin in 2018. Let us train an ARIMA model using the observations of `Close` in the fourth quarter of 2018, save for the last day, 31 December. Indeed, we want to use our ARIMA model to predict the closing prices every minute that day. Note that in 2018, unlike the rapid rise in the previous years, the value of a Bitcoin dropped drastically from USD 13,841 to USD 3,689. The upper plot in [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005) via Python (resp. [7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0006) via **R**) illustrates the movement of Bitcoin minute closing prices in the fourth quarter of 2018, and we note that there are many fierce jumps in the closing prices. These are likely to be regime-switching signals for parameters, and it would be reasonable to assume that the prices before and after the jumps should have different moving dynamics, and different statistical mean and volatility. Therefore, with this in mind, we choose only the time period after the most recent significant spike of standard deviation as the training period for our ARIMA model, that is after 00:21:00 on 30 Dec 2018 as indicated by the orange dashed line on the bottom plot in [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005) via Python (resp. [7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0006) via **R**).

![](images/c07-gra-0005.png)![](images/c07-gra-0006.png) ![FIGURE 7.5 Plots of Bitcoin minute prices and standard deviations over 30-minute moving windows via Python, generated by Programme 7.5.](images/c07f005.png)

[**FIGURE 7.5**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0005) Plots of Bitcoin minute prices and standard deviations over 30-minute moving windows via Python, generated by [Programme 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0005).

![](images/c07-gra-0007.png)

We then select an appropriate ARIMA model by determining the values of the model parameters ![p comma d comma q](images/c07-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>; see the respective Python codes in [Programme 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0007) and **R** codes in [Programme 7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0008), and the corresponding sample ACF and PACF plots are shown in [Figures 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0007) and [7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0008), respectively. We observe that the sample ACF plot of the time series does not have a cut-off point, nor does it decay exponentially, indicating the non-stationarity of the time series and the need for differencing. After applying 1-lag differencing to the Bitcoin prices, i.e., ![d equals 1](images/c07-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, both sample ACF and PACF plots of the resulting time series roughly exhibit the cut-off property at ![k equals 2](images/c07-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. We therefore consider ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 0](images/c07-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></math>), ARIMA(![0 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>), and ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) as the candidate models.

![FIGURE 7.6 Plots of Bitcoin minute prices and standard deviations over 30-minute moving windows via R, generated by Programme 7.6.](images/c07f006.png)

[**FIGURE 7.6**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0006) Plots of Bitcoin minute prices and standard deviations over 30-minute moving windows via **R**, generated by [Programme 7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0006).

For the selection between these three candidates, the arguably most prevalent thresholds are various *information criteria*, which depend on both the likelihood ![ModifyingAbove upper L With caret](images/c07-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> of the fitted model and the number ![m](images/c07-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> of model parameters. Here we adopt the *Akaike Information Criterion* ![AIC colon equals minus 2 ln ModifyingAbove upper L With caret plus 2 m](images/c07-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>AIC</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></math> as the decision criterion of model selection; a smaller value of AIC indicates a better model; also see [Section 10.6](#c10.xhtml#head-2-139) in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) for more discussions on AIC and BIC. We can simply fit the candidate models above and prompt for their respective AIC values, as shown in [Programme 7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0009) via Python and 7.10 via **R**. The AIC values of the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 0](images/c07-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) and ARIMA(![0 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) are 8,319.95 and 8,316.41, respectively; both are higher than that of the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) model (less than 8,300), therefore ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) is our preferred model for this example.

![](images/c07-gra-0008.png)![](images/c07-gra-0009.png)![FIGURE 7.7 Sample ACF and PACF plots of Bitcoin prices in Python, generated in Programme 7.7.](images/c07f007.png)

[**FIGURE 7.7**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0007) Sample ACF and PACF plots of Bitcoin prices in Python, generated in [Programme 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0007).

![FIGURE 7.8 Sample ACF and PACF plots of Bitcoin prices in R, generated in Programme 7.8.](images/c07f008.png)

[**FIGURE 7.8**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0008) Sample ACF and PACF plots of Bitcoin prices in **R**, generated in [Programme 7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0008).

 ![](images/c07-gra-0010.png)

In fact, both Python and **R** already have various built-in functions that carry out the entire procedure of model fitting (as introduced above) in one go, such as the `auto_arima()` function in the `pmdarima` library for Python and the `auto.arima()` function in the `forecast` library for **R**. Specifically, given the user inputs of ![p Subscript max Baseline comma d Subscript max Baseline comma q Subscript max Baseline](images/c07-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></math> and the information criterion selected, these functions fit all the ARIMA(![p comma d comma q](images/c07-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) models for ![p equals 0 comma ellipsis comma p Subscript max Baseline](images/c07-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></math>, ![d equals 0 comma ellipsis comma d Subscript max Baseline](images/c07-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></math>, ![q equals 0 comma ellipsis comma q Subscript max Baseline](images/c07-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></math>, and return the best-fitted model in terms of the specified information criterion. Interestingly, with ![p Subscript max Baseline equals q Subscript max Baseline equals 5](images/c07-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> and ![d Subscript max Baseline equals 2](images/c07-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, the output from [Programme 7.10](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00010) via **R** indicates that the ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) model is the best in terms of AIC, which agrees with our earlier conclusion. However, [Programme 7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0009) via Python determines that the best model in terms of AIC is ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c07-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) with an AIC value of 8,295.22, lower than that of 8,299.16 for ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) in [Programme 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-0007). In view of this, we shall conduct further analysis on both of these models as follows:

![](images/c07-gra-0011.png) ![](images/c07-gra-0012.png)![](images/c07-gra-0013.png)

We evaluate the goodness-of-fit of the fitted models, namely ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c07-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) via Python and ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) via **R**, by using the Ljung–Box test, a kind of portmanteau test. Specifically, given an observed times series ![left-brace x Subscript t Baseline right-brace Subscript t equals 1 Superscript n](images/c07-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, the null hypothesis ![upper H 0](images/c07-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> of this test states that the data are independently distributed, while the alternative hypothesis ![upper H 1](images/c07-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> states that the data exhibits serial correlation. The test statistic is

![chi Subscript upper K Superscript 2 Baseline colon equals n left-parenthesis n plus 2 right-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript upper K Endscripts StartFraction r Subscript k Superscript 2 Baseline Over n minus k EndFraction comma](images/c07-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#967;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is the sample ACF of ![left-brace x Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> of lag ![k](images/c07-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. In general, as a means of hypothesis testing, the test statistic has an approximate chi-square distribution of ![upper K](images/c07-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom; see [Appendix \*7.A.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0024) for more detailed discussions. In contrast, in our current context of diagnostics for fitted ARIMA models, the ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s computed based on fitted residuals are not linearly independent; it can be shown that ![p plus q](images/c07-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></math> extra linear constraints are imposed accordingly in relation to the ARMA parameters ![beta Subscript i](images/c07-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s and ![phi Subscript j](images/c07-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s, see equation (2.9) in [\[6\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005). To establish the asymptotic distribution of the corresponding test statistic under this scenario, we can work in parallel with the arguments in [Appendix \*7.A.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0024), which relies on the quadratic form expression, yet the sandwiched square matrix, originally with full rank, will have its rank reduced by the number of parameters estimated, namely ![p plus q](images/c07-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></math>, hence showing that the asymptotic distribution of the corresponding test statistic in this case is still a chi-square distribution, yet with ![upper K minus left-parenthesis p plus q right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> degrees of freedom ![](images/c07-gra-0014.png)![FIGURE 7.9 Plot of the residuals of the fitted ARIMA(2 comma 1 comma 3) model in Python, generated by Programme 7.11.](images/c07f009.png)

[**FIGURE 7.9**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0009) Plot of the residuals of the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c07-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) model in Python, generated by [Programme 7.11](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00011).

 ![](images/c07-gra-0015.png)![](images/c07-gra-0016.png)

Finally, we apply the fitted ARIMA models to the test dataset and predict the Bitcoin prices on a minute basis on 31 Dec 2018. We also include a naïve prediction strategy for comparison, namely setting the closing price of the previous minute as the predicted closing price of the current minute; see [Programmes 7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00013) and [7.14](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00014) for the codes in Python and **R**, respectively. The testing mean squared error (MSE) of the naïve approach is 19.726, while the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c07-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) model in Python performs better with a lower testing MSE of 19.249; the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) model in **R** results in a slightly higher testing MSE (19.261), yet it still outperforms the naïve approach; see [Figure 7.11](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0011) in Python and [Figure 7.12](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0012) in **R** for the illustration of price predictions. In [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml), we shall introduce a more sophisticated model, namely the *Long-Short Term Memory* (LSTM), to strive for a slightly better prediction of the Bitcoin price.

![FIGURE 7.10 Plot of the residuals of the fitted ARIMA(2 comma 1 comma 2) model in R, generated by Programme 7.12.](images/c07f010.png)

[**FIGURE 7.10**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0010) Plot of the residuals of the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c07-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) model in **R**, generated by [Programme 7.12](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00012).

![](images/c07-gra-0017.png)![](images/c07-gra-0018.png) ![FIGURE 7.11 Bitcoin price prediction with the fitted ARIMA(2 comma 1 comma 3) model on 31 December 2018 in Python, generated by Programme 7.13.](images/c07f011.png)

[**FIGURE 7.11**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0011) Bitcoin price prediction with the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c07-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) model on 31 December 2018 in Python, generated by [Programme 7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00013).

![](images/c07-gra-0019.png) ![FIGURE 7.12 Bitcoin price prediction with the fitted ARIMA(2 comma 1 comma 2) model on 31 December 2018 in R, generated by Programme 7.14.](images/c07f012.png)

## 7.4 ARCH AND GARCH MODELS

While ARIMA models do take possible non-stationarity of the time series itself into consideration, they still require stationary behaviour for the time series' variance process. This is not always satisfied in reality, as we saw in the Bitcoin price modelling. Therefore, we have to proceed to the next level of sophistication that can decently explain those inhomogeneous volatility phenomena. In this regard, we first consider the *autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity* model ARCH(![m](images/c07-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>) for variance proposed by the Nobel-winning economist Robert F. Engle in 1982 [\[11\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0010). This model assumes that the current variance rate ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> depends on the ![m](images/c07-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> most recent values of ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> as well as a long-run level average variance rate ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math>, so that

[(7.10)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0014)![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma upper V Subscript upper L Baseline plus alpha 1 normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus alpha Subscript m Baseline normal u Subscript n minus m Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the coefficients ![gamma greater-than 0 comma alpha 1 comma ellipsis comma alpha Subscript m Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c07-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> satisfy ![gamma plus alpha 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus alpha Subscript m Baseline equals 1](images/c07-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We further assume the following conditional independence of ![normal u Subscript i](images/c07-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s given the latest volatility:

[(7.11)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0015)![StartFraction normal u Subscript i Baseline Over normal sigma Subscript i Baseline EndFraction vertical-bar left-parenthesis normal sigma Subscript i Baseline comma normal u Subscript i minus 1 Baseline comma normal u Subscript i minus 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal u 1 right-parenthesis equals Overscript d Endscripts StartFraction normal u Subscript i Baseline Over normal sigma Subscript i Baseline EndFraction vertical-bar normal sigma Subscript i Baseline equals sigma Subscript i Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis period](images/c07-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover class="overset"><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></mover><mfenced open="" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

One advantage of this ARCH(![m](images/c07-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>) model is that it introduces a long-run variance rate around which the variance rates fluctuate over time. The disadvantages are that there are too many parameters to be estimated especially if ![m](images/c07-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is large, and that this model lacks a simple autoregressive recursive relationship as found in the EWMA model. However, by combining the ideas in the EWMA model ([7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0006)) and the ARCH model ([7.10](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0014)), one arrives at the following celebrated GARCH model.

The *generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity* model GARCH(![p comma q](images/c07-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) was first proposed in the doctoral thesis of the economist *Tim Bollerslev* in 1986 [\[3\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0002), under the supervision of Robert Engle. Recall that in the EWMA model ([7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0006)), ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is defined recursively in terms of both ![sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>; while in the ARCH(![m](images/c07-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>) model ([7.10](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0014)), ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is defined in terms of ![m](images/c07-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> most recent values of ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> with a long-run variance rate ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math>. As a hybrid, a GARCH(![p comma q](images/c07-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) model takes the following general form:

![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma upper V Subscript upper L Baseline plus alpha 1 normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus alpha Subscript p Baseline normal u Subscript n minus p Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta 1 normal sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus beta Subscript q Baseline normal sigma Subscript n minus q Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0016.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![gamma greater-than 0 comma alpha 1 comma ellipsis comma alpha Subscript p Baseline comma beta 1 comma ellipsis comma beta Subscript q Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c07-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> satisfy ![gamma plus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript p Endscripts alpha Subscript i Baseline plus sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript q Endscripts beta Subscript j Baseline equals 1](images/c07-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> is the long-run average variance rate. We shall explain later why we call ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> the long-run average variance rate. In particular, the simplest case of ![p equals q equals 1](images/c07-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> corresponds to the following GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model:

[(7.12)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0017)![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma upper V Subscript upper L Baseline plus alpha normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta normal sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0017.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

which clearly reduces to the simpler EWMA model when ![gamma equals 0](images/c07-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. In financial practice, we use the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model much more often than other models for time-varying volatility estimation.

 

### 7.4.1 MLE for GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) Model

We now turn to the estimation of the parameters of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model ([7.12](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0017)). There are four unknown positive parameters ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math>, ![gamma](images/c07-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> to be estimated, subject to one linear constraint: ![gamma plus alpha plus beta equals 1](images/c07-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We rewrite the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model as

[(7.13)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0018)![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals omega plus alpha normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta normal sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0018.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![omega colon equals gamma upper V Subscript upper L Baseline equals left-parenthesis 1 minus alpha minus beta right-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline](images/c07-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math>. By recalling the conditional distribution of ![normal u Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar normal sigma Subscript i Baseline equals sigma Subscript i Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma sigma Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and abbreviating ![nu Subscript i Baseline colon equals sigma Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, the likelihood function for ![bold-italic u colon equals left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is

(7.14)![upper L left-parenthesis omega comma alpha comma beta semicolon bold-italic u right-parenthesis equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over StartRoot 2 pi nu Subscript i Baseline EndRoot EndFraction exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction u Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline Over 2 nu Subscript i Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis comma](images/c07-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

hence the log-likelihood function is

We aim to find the parameters ![omega](images/c07-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> such that the function
