is maximized. Note that the parameters are entered implicitly into function ([7.16](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0021)) through ![nu Subscript i](images/c07-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> which satisfies the recursive relation of ([7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0018)), so it is a rather complicated maximization problem. Let us illustrate numerically with the HSBC stock data, using ![u Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis upper S Subscript i Baseline minus upper S Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis slash upper S Subscript i minus 1](images/c07-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, the percentage change in stock price, to fit a GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model and obtain the corresponding MLEs for ![omega](images/c07-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>; see [Programmes 7.15](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00015) and [7.16](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00016) for Python and **R** codes, respectively.

![](images/c07-gra-0020.png)![](images/c07-gra-0021.png)![](images/c07-gra-0022.png)

From the Python output of [Programme 7.15](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00015), and the summary of results in [Programme 7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00018) by using the command `res_HSBC.summary()`, the MLEs of ![omega](images/c07-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> for HSBC over the period of 1999–2002 are respectively ![6.172 times 1 0 Superscript negative 6](images/c07-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>6.172</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></math>, ![4.997 times 1 0 Superscript negative 2](images/c07-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>4.997</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> and ![9.293 times 1 0 Superscript negative 1](images/c07-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>9.293</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. The maximum log-likelihood value in ([7.15](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0020)) is ![2 comma 659.993](images/c07-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>659.993</mn></math> and the estimated long-run variance rate is ![upper V Subscript upper L Baseline equals omega slash left-parenthesis 1 minus alpha minus beta right-parenthesis equals 0.0002977](images/c07-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0002977</mn></math>. However, from the **R** output in [Programme 7.16](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00016) and the summary in [Programme 7.18](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00018), the MLEs of ![omega](images/c07-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> for the same set of 1999–2002 HSBC data are respectively ![1.491 times 1 0 Superscript negative 5](images/c07-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1.491</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></math>, ![6.279 times 1 0 Superscript negative 2](images/c07-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>6.279</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>, and ![8.820 times 1 0 Superscript negative 1](images/c07-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>8.820</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>, the corresponding maximum log-likelihood value of ([7.15](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0020)) is ![2 comma 660.307](images/c07-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>660.307</mn></math>, and the estimated long-run variance rate is 0.0002652.

![](images/c07-gra-0023.png)![](images/c07-gra-0024.png)

The discrepancy between the outputs obtained from Python and **R** could be explained as follows. From the Python output of [Programme 7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00018), the parameter estimates for ![omega](images/c07-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math> and ![beta](images/c07-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> have small ![p](images/c07-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values below 0.05, thus these two coefficients are significantly different from zero. However, the ![p](images/c07-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value for ![alpha](images/c07-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> exceeds the threshold of 0.05, meaning that we cannot reject the null hypothesis that ![alpha](images/c07-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is equal to zero. Therefore, based on the Python output, we suspect that the (arithmetic) return of HSBC does not follow a GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model; another possibility is that the MLEs obtained in the `arch` library of Python are not accurate enough.

In fact, we can change the optimization method used in Python to a two-step scheme, first using an extension of the *limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno* (L-BFGS) algorithm, called L-BFGS-B for short, followed by the *sequential least squares programming* (SLSQP). The first stage of using L-BFGS-B is often adopted in practice to solve an optimization problem. However, L-BFGS-B only supports bounded constraints for each parameter such as ![omega comma alpha comma beta greater-than 0](images/c07-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![alpha comma beta less-than 1](images/c07-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> as required by the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, while other constraints that involve multiple parameters at once, such as ![alpha plus beta less-than 1](images/c07-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, are not supported. We therefore require a second stage of optimization, namely by SLSQP. By the implementation as shown in [Programme 7.19](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00019), the resulting MLEs are close to those obtained by **R** in [Programme 7.16](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00016). This also justifies the accuracy of the results obtained by **R**; to this end, in the later development of the various GARCH models, while we still present results via both Python and **R**, we may primarily use the outputs from **R** for demonstration if the results from the two environments do not match.

![](images/c07-gra-0025.png)![](images/c07-gra-0026.png)

To further justify the results from **R**, we also demonstrate the MLE seeking procedure in **R** without the use of the `fGARCH` package. In particular, in [Programme 7.20](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00020) via **R**, we use the `constrOptim()` function to perform minimization subject to inequality constraints. The first argument is the decision variable; the second argument is the function to be minimized; `grad=NULL` means that no gradient function is provided; `u=u1` is the extra argument inserted in the `GARCH_11()` function; `method=c("Nelder-Mead")` indicates that the *Nelder–Mead* optimization algorithm proposed in [\[24\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0022) is adopted

### 7.4.2 Model Diagnostics for GARCH

In [Programme 7.21](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00021) via Python, we can plot the fitted volatility, the sample ACF of HSBC's squared returns ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, as well as the sample ACF of the squared standardized residuals ![left-parenthesis u Subscript i Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared](images/c07-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> and the normal Q-Q plot of the standardized residuals.

Recall that ![normal u Subscript i Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma sigma Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given ![normal sigma Subscript i Baseline equals sigma Subscript i](images/c07-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. If GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) is the true model, then each standardized residual ![normal u Subscript i Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> holds true for every ![i](images/c07-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. The bottom right plot in [Figure 7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0013) is the normal Q-Q plot of the standardized residuals ![u Subscript i Baseline slash sigma Subscript i](images/c07-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s, which indicates that the residuals are approximately normally distributed except at both extreme tails. More importantly, the sample ACF plot of the returns on the top right corner in [Figure 7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0013) clearly indicates that serial correlations exist in ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, which can be removed by fitting a GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, as demonstrated in the bottom left sample ACF plot of squared standardized residuals ![left-parenthesis u Subscript i Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared](images/c07-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.

Similar to [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0004), we perform the Ljung–Box test to determine whether the observed time series ![left-brace x Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> exhibits autocorrelations. See the summary output in [Programmes 7.21](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00021) for Python and [7.22](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00022) for **R**, where we compute the Ljung–Box test statistics with ![upper K equals 15](images/c07-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math> for both ![u Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> and the squared residuals ![u Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, respectively ![](images/c07-gra-0028.png)![](images/c07-gra-0029.png) ![FIGURE 7.13 Plots of model diagnostics for a GARCH(1 comma 1) model fitted to HSBC returns in Python, generated by Programme 7.21.](images/c07f013.png)

### 7.4.3 Forecasting Future Volatilities

With the estimates of ![omega](images/c07-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, we can use the fitted GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model to forecast future volatilities. Recall that in ([7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0018)),

so ![sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline minus upper V Subscript upper L Baseline equals alpha left-parenthesis u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline minus upper V Subscript upper L Baseline right-parenthesis plus beta left-parenthesis sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline minus upper V Subscript upper L Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></math>. We remark the following about ([7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0026)):

1.  Note that when ![k](images/c07-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is large and ![0 less-than alpha plus beta less-than 1](images/c07-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> is a convergent series in ![n](images/c07-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and so ![sup Underscript n Endscripts double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">sup</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is bounded. Therefore, the expected variance rate tends to ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> as ![k](images/c07-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> goes to infinity. This is the reason why ![upper V Subscript upper L](images/c07-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> is called the long-run variance rate. 
2.  The EWMA model can be considered a special case of GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) with ![omega equals 0](images/c07-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![lamda equals beta](images/c07-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></math> so that ![alpha plus beta equals 1](images/c07-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. In this case, from ([7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0026)), the expected variance rate is constant over time. This is possibly an undesirable property of the EWMA model. 
3.  As shown in [Appendix \*7.A.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0025), the rescaled GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, as the step size between two consecutive time instances approaches 0, tends to a continuous variance model ![normal upper V Subscript t Baseline colon equals normal sigma Subscript t Superscript 2](images/c07-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> satisfying the following stochastic differential equation (SDE): ![d normal upper V Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis 1 minus alpha minus beta right-parenthesis left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus normal upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis d t plus StartRoot 2 EndRoot alpha normal upper V Subscript t Baseline d normal z Subscript t Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0027.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mi>&#945;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 
    
    where ![left-brace normal z Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is the standard Brownian motion, (see [Section 5.3](#c05.xhtml#head-2-53) of [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml) for a quick review). This is also called the *diffusion limit* of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, see [\[25\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0023). Note that it has a similar form as the celebrated *Cox–Ingersoll–Ross* (CIR) interest rate model

### 7.4.4 Correlation and GARCH

GARCH models are commonly used to model the dynamical movement of the volatility of one single asset. What about the volatility of a basket of securities? In addition to the evolution of an individual volatility, knowing the correlations among securities is also essential. In fact, correlation plays an important role in assessing the risk of a portfolio, being an important parameter for calculating Value-at-Risk (See [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml) ), and in the active portfolio management. As variance varies over time, it is not surprising that correlation also varies over time. We can extend the EWMA model and GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model to estimate the inherent pairwise correlations among several securities.

Here, we illustrate the detailed procedure for a pair of stocks. Let

![normal x Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction normal upper S Subscript 1 comma i Baseline minus normal upper S Subscript 1 comma i minus 1 Baseline Over normal upper S Subscript 1 comma i minus 1 Baseline EndFraction and normal y Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction normal upper S Subscript 2 comma i Baseline minus normal upper S Subscript 2 comma i minus 1 Baseline Over normal upper S Subscript 2 comma i minus 1 Baseline EndFraction](images/c07-math-0031.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> 

be the daily percentage changes of stocks ![normal upper S 1](images/c07-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal upper S 2](images/c07-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, respectively. The estimated covariance between ![normal upper S 1](images/c07-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal upper S 2](images/c07-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> based on the most recent ![m](images/c07-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> observations on day ![n plus t](images/c07-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi></math>, where ![n](images/c07-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> stands for the current day, is as follows:

However, this naïve approach faces the same inaccuracy issues as described for the estimation of variance rates in [Sections 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0002) and [7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0003). Following the discussion there, we shall first take the current estimates of ![cov Subscript n plus 1](images/c07-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>cov</mtext><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![normal rho Subscript n plus 1](images/c07-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> on day ![n](images/c07-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> from ([7.18](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0032)) and ([7.19](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0033)) with a reasonable choice of ![m](images/c07-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> (neither too short nor too long). Then the estimates of ![cov Subscript n plus t](images/c07-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>cov</mtext><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![normal rho Subscript n plus t](images/c07-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> can be updated daily, for ![t equals 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c07-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>, by using an EWMA or a GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model as follows. For an EWMA model,

where ![normal sigma Subscript normal x comma n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![normal sigma Subscript normal y comma n Superscript 2](images/c07-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> are updated according to the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model by using ([7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0018)) with the same parameter values of ![omega](images/c07-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> and ![beta](images/c07-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> throughout.

In the general case of ![p](images/c07-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> securities, a similar GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model can be built. In finance, a standardized version of the corresponding dynamical correlation movement analysis is considered, called the *Dynamic Conditional Correlation GARCH* (DCC-GARCH) model in the literature [\[13\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0012). The implementation of DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) will be deferred to [Subsection 7.4.6.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0014).

![](images/c07-gra-0033.png)![](images/c07-gra-0034.png)![](images/c07-gra-0035.png)

It is important to note that the estimated values of the parameters in ([7.20](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0035)) and ([7.21](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0036)) used in updating the variance rate and the covariance should be the same for the sake of convenience and tractability of the models. Let us illustrate this by the following example. First, we compute the correlation matrix of the daily percentage returns of HSBC, CLP and CK for 1999–2002; see [Programmes 7.25](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00025) and [7.26](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00026) for implementation in Python and **R**, respectively.

From the outputs, we note that HSBC and CK are relatively more strongly correlated while CLP has relatively weaker correlations with HSBC and CK. Next, we consider the DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model without standardization. To this end, the current values of ![u italic 1](images/c07-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>1</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![u italic 2](images/c07-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>2</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![u italic 3](images/c07-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>3</mi></mrow></msub></math>, i.e., ![u Subscript i comma 0](images/c07-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>'s, and the entries in the covariance matrix will be used as the initial condition for the recursive relations ([7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0018)) and ([7.21](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0036)). However, computing the common values of ![omega comma alpha](images/c07-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></math> and ![beta](images/c07-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> could be cumbersome. Instead, we may adopt the following convenient numerical scheme, which is still accurate enough for most practical situations. We first fit the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) models to `u1`, `u2` and `u3` separately, which returns three different sets of estimated parameters for ![omega](images/c07-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> and ![beta](images/c07-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, and then use the average of these three sets of estimated parameters as the combined estimates for ![omega](images/c07-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> and ![beta](images/c07-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. Then we update the variance rates and the correlations accordingly. This ensures that the correlation matrix obtained is positive definite; see [Programme 7.27](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00027) via Python and [Programme 7.28](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00028) via **R**.

![](images/c07-gra-0036.png)![](images/c07-gra-0037.png)

Now we have all the numbers required to update the variance rates and the correlations according to ([7.13](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0018)) and ([7.21](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0036)), using the corresponding values for ![u Subscript i comma 0](images/c07-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>'s, ![sigma Subscript i comma 0 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>'s and ![sigma Subscript i j comma 0](images/c07-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>'s in [Programme 7.27](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00027) via Python. They are:

![omega equals 0.0000106034 comma alpha equals 0.0771472 comma beta equals 0.890035 period](images/c07-math-0037.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0000106034</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0771472</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.890035</mn><mo>.</mo></math>

### 7.4.5 Combining GARCH with Linear Models

One obvious application of the GARCH model is to address the constant volatility assumption of the Black–Scholes model (as introduced in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml) ). Recall that, for the Black–Scholes model,

Given ![omega](images/c07-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, ![alpha](images/c07-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, ![beta](images/c07-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma Subscript t Superscript 2](images/c07-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, we can simulate ![p](images/c07-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> sample paths for ![p](images/c07-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> different stocks with ![normal u Subscript i comma t plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal u Subscript i comma t plus upper K Baseline](images/c07-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c07-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math> according to the following scheme:

1.  Generate ![p](images/c07-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> iid standard normal random numbers ![normal z 1 comma ellipsis comma normal z Subscript p Baseline](images/c07-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>;
2.  For ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c07-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, compute ![normal u Subscript i comma t plus 1 Baseline equals normal sigma Subscript i comma t plus 1 Baseline normal z Subscript i](images/c07-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![normal sigma Subscript i comma t plus 2 Superscript 2 Baseline equals omega plus alpha normal u Subscript i comma t plus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta normal sigma Subscript i comma t plus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>;
3.  Repeat Steps 1 and 2 from ![t equals t plus 1](images/c07-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> to ![t equals t plus upper K](images/c07-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></math>.

Note that we have to generate a new set of ![p](images/c07-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> normal random numbers in Step 1 for every new value of ![t](images/c07-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Once we have ![p](images/c07-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> simulated sample paths of ![normal u Subscript i comma t plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal u Subscript i comma t plus upper K Baseline](images/c07-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></math>, we can evaluate the prices of different derivatives from these sample paths by taking an appropriate average of the corresponding payoffs, each of which is evaluated along one simulated sample path.

Other models can be simulated similarly. For example, we can combine the standardized ![t Subscript nu](images/c07-i0418.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> distribution with the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model: ![normal u Subscript i Baseline slash normal sigma Subscript i Baseline tilde t Subscript nu](images/c07-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> and ![normal sigma Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline equals omega plus alpha normal u Subscript i minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta normal sigma Subscript i minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>. This is known as the ![t](images/c07-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) stock price model. Alternatively, one can also use the ![EWMA left-parenthesis lamda right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>EWMA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> model, instead of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0425.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, to assimilate the evolutional dynamics of volatilities.

When using regression models for financial time series data, the errors are usually autocorrelated. We can handle this problem by fitting an AR(![m](images/c07-i0426.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>) model to several consecutive error terms in the regression model of the time series. For example,

This model is sometimes called the AR(![m](images/c07-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>)-GARCH(![p comma q](images/c07-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) model. In SAS, there is an AUTOREG procedure to fit this model, and the `rugarch` package in **R** can also serve this purpose. However, there is no well-established library in Python with the same function, hence we need to perform the fitting in the sequential manner described above. This procedure allows us to fit a GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model to the percentage change of stock price.

 

### 7.4.6 Extensions of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) Model

In this subsection, we introduce two commonly used extensions of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model. We shall analyze the results obtained in **R**, while for Python, only the calibration procedure is provided.

 

**7.4.6.1 Leverage GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) (L-GARCH)**   The *Leverage GARCH* (L-GARCH) model is also known as the *Threshold GARCH* (T-GARCH) model, or the *Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle GARCH* (GJR-GARCH) model [\[14\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0013). To account for the asymmetric effect of negative movement of the stock price on the volatility, we extend the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model to the following GJR-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model:

[(7.24)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0043)![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals omega plus beta normal sigma Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus alpha normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus theta normal upper I Subscript n minus 1 Baseline normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0043.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal upper I Subscript n minus 1 Baseline equals 1](images/c07-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> if ![normal u Subscript n minus 1 Baseline less-than 0](images/c07-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> or ![normal upper I Subscript n minus 1 Baseline equals 0](images/c07-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> otherwise. The stationarity condition for the threshold GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model is ![alpha plus beta plus gamma theta less-than 1](images/c07-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, where ![gamma](images/c07-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is the proportion of the number of negative returns to the total number of returns; this is set at 0.5 in practice under the assumption of a zero-mean and symmetrically distributed returns. Note that if ![theta greater-than 0](images/c07-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, a piece of bad news (![normal u Subscript n minus 1 Baseline less-than 0](images/c07-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) has an effect of ![left-parenthesis alpha plus theta right-parenthesis normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> on the variance rate, while a piece of good news (![normal u Subscript n minus 1 Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c07-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) has the relatively lower effect of ![alpha normal u Subscript n minus 1 Superscript 2](images/c07-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>.

![](images/c07-gra-0039.png)

We try to fit this GJR-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model for HSBC, CLP and CK stocks in [Programme 7.29](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00029) via **R**. We then analyze the fitted standardized residuals for the GJR-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model in [Programme 7.30](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00030) via **R**.

![](images/c07-gra-0040.png)

The bottom right plot in [Figure 7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0017) is the normal Q-Q plot of the (standardized) residuals ![u Subscript 1 comma i Baseline slash sigma Subscript 1 comma i](images/c07-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> of HSBC returns. The residuals are approximately normally distributed except at the two tails. More importantly, the sample ACF plots on the bottom left of [Figure 7.17](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0017) clearly indicate that the autocorrelation of squared HSBC returns ![u Subscript 1 comma i Superscript 2](images/c07-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> are successfully removed by fitting an L-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model. In particular, the large ![p](images/c07-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of the Ljung–Box tests, with ![upper K equals 15](images/c07-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>, ![FIGURE 7.17 Plots of model diagnostics for L-GARCH(1 comma 1) fitted with HSBC returns in R, generated by Programme 7.30. 4 parameters](images/c07f017.png)

Similarly, we implement the same estimation in [Programme 7.31](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00031) via Python, by first finding the MLEs of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0475.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) models using the same two-stage optimization scheme in [Programme 7.19](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00019), with ![theta equals 0.005](images/c07-i0476.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.005</mn></math> as the initial condition for the GJR-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0477.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model.

**7.4.6.2 Dynamic Conditional Correlation GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0478.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>)**   The *Dynamic Conditional Correlation GARCH* (DCC-GARCH) model, proposed by Robert Engle [\[12\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0011), is a widely used multivariate volatility model that allows for time-varying conditional correlations among financial assets. This DCC-GARCH model combines the flexibility of the GARCH model for modelling the marginal evolution of each asset with the ability to capture dynamic correlations. In this model, the volatility of each asset is captured using a GARCH process, while the conditional correlation matrix, representing the interdependencies between assets, is modeled separately and updated dynamically. Also refer to [\[32\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0030) for more discussions on the model.

The DCC-GARCH model proposes to estimate the dynamic covariance matrix ![bold upper H Subscript t](images/c07-i0479.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> by

where ![bold upper D Subscript t Baseline colon equals diag left-parenthesis normal sigma Subscript 1 t Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal sigma Subscript p t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0480.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>diag</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold upper R Subscript t](images/c07-i0481.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is the conditional time-varying correlation matrix given ![normal sigma Subscript i t](images/c07-i0482.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s. The variance ![normal sigma Subscript i t Superscript 2](images/c07-i0483.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> in ![bold upper D Subscript t](images/c07-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for each security ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c07-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math> can be modelled by an independent GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) process. Denote the marginally standardized innovation vector by ![bold eta Subscript t Baseline equals bold upper D Subscript t Superscript negative 1 Baseline bold r Subscript t](images/c07-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#951;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, where ![normal r Subscript i t](images/c07-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the return of security ![i](images/c07-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> at time ![t](images/c07-i0490.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. The DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0491.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model incorporates time-varying conditional correlations through the evolutionary covariance matrix, denoted by ![bold upper Q Subscript t](images/c07-i0492.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This covariance matrix is recursively modeled as:

mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

Clearly, ![bold-italic upper D Subscript t](images/c07-i0504.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is known, since the variance ![sigma Subscript i t Superscript 2](images/c07-i0505.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> for each security ![i](images/c07-i0506.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is modelled by an independent GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) process before the determination of ![theta 1](images/c07-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![theta 2](images/c07-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. The MLEs for ![theta 1](images/c07-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![theta 2](images/c07-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are the minimizers of the function below:

(7.28)![script l left-parenthesis theta 1 comma theta 2 semicolon bold-italic eta 0 right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript t equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis ln StartAbsoluteValue bold-italic upper R Subscript t Baseline EndAbsoluteValue plus bold-italic eta Subscript t Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper R Subscript t Superscript negative 1 Baseline bold-italic eta Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c07-math-0048.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

Next, we shall fit the DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model to the HSBC, CLP, and CK stock returns with the `rmgarch` library, where `m` stands for multivariate. Indeed, the standardized residuals ![bold-italic eta Subscript t](images/c07-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for HSBC, CLP, and CK can be obtained by fitting the corresponding returns into independent GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) models using the `rugarch` library, where `u` stands for univariate. After fitting the DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model in [Programme 7.32](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00032) via **R**, the evolutionary covariance matrix ![bold-italic upper Q Subscript t](images/c07-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and the evolutionary correlation matrix ![bold-italic upper R Subscript t](images/c07-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for all time ![t](images/c07-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> can be retrieved through the codes `dcc_GARCH@mfit$Q` in [Programme 7.34](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00034) and `dcc_GARCH@mfit$R` in [Programme 7.35](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00035) via **R**, respectively.

![](images/c07-gra-0043.png)

In Python in [Programme 7.33](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00033), with the MLEs obtained in [Programme 7.27](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00027), the MLEs for ![theta 1](images/c07-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![theta 2](images/c07-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> of the DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model can be obtained as follows: note that each `eta[i,:]`, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c07-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, is a one-dimensional `numpy` array, `eta[i,:] @ inv(R) @ eta[i,:]` will return a numerical value equivalent to ![bold-italic eta Subscript t Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper R Subscript t Baseline bold-italic eta Subscript t](images/c07-i0523.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>.

![](images/c07-gra-0044.png) ![](images/c07-gra-0045.png)![](images/c07-gra-0046.png)

Finally, we shall adopt the Mahalanobis distance and use the last 180 days of returns in 2002 to check whether the residuals obtained in the DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0524.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model follow a tri-variate normal distribution.

 ![](images/c07-gra-0047.png) ![FIGURE 7.18 Plots obtained in a DCC-GARCH(1 comma 1) model in R, generated by Programme 7.35.](images/c07f018.png)

[**FIGURE 7.18**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0018) Plots obtained in a DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0525.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model in **R**, generated by [Programme 7.35](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00035).

From [Figure 7.18](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0018), the residuals obtained from a DCC-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0526.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model present a much better fit as a tri-variate normal distribution than the residuals computed from the sample mean and sample covariance of the last 180 days of returns of the three stocks.

 

## \*7.5 KELLY FRACTION

All stock trading strategies strive for a sole ultimate goal: buy at the lowest possible price and sell at the highest viable one so as to maximize the trading profit. However, without a crystal ball, the highest and the lowest stock prices over a fixed investment horizon can never be anticipated with certainty until the terminal time of the planning horizon is reached. To this end, a more reasonable and achievable objective is to find a trading price which, under some notion of difference, is as close as possible to the non-previsible target price. This problem formulation is classified as an optimal prediction problem [\[27](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0025), [28\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0026), a branch of *optimal stopping theory* in *Stochastic Analysis*. To facilitate our discussion, we assume that the underlying stock price process ![left-brace normal upper S Subscript t Baseline right-brace Subscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c07-i0527.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></math> follows a Black–Scholes model with a constant rate of return ![mu](images/c07-i0528.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and a constant volatility ![sigma](images/c07-i0529.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>:

[(7.29)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0049)![StartFraction d normal upper S Subscript t Baseline Over normal upper S Subscript t Baseline EndFraction equals mu d t plus sigma d normal w Subscript t Baseline comma normal upper S 0 equals x 0 comma](images/c07-math-0049.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![left-brace normal w Subscript t Baseline right-brace Subscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c07-i0530.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></math> is a standard Brownian motion. A reasonable objective proposed in [\[29\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0027) is the minimization of the expected relative error between the selling price ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c07-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> of a stock and its ultimate maximum price ![normal upper M Subscript upper T Baseline colon equals sup Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to upper T Endscripts normal upper S Subscript t Baseline](images/c07-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">sup</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> over the investment horizon ![left-bracket 0 comma upper T right-bracket](images/c07-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, or equivalently maximizing the expected relative ratio of ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c07-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> to ![normal upper M Subscript upper T](images/c07-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>. More formally, the problem can be formulated as follows:

[(7.30)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0050)![sup Underscript 0 less-than-or-equal-to normal tau less-than-or-equal-to upper T Endscripts double-struck upper E left-parenthesis StartFraction normal upper S Subscript normal tau Baseline Over normal upper M Subscript upper T Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis comma](images/c07-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">sup</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the supremum is taken over all stopping times ![normal tau less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c07-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>

![normal tau Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 0 comma 2nd Column if alpha less-than one half semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column upper T comma 2nd Column if alpha greater-than-or-equal-to one half period EndLayout](images/c07-math-0051.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

This ![alpha](images/c07-i0544.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is actually the well-known *Kelly fraction* ([\[30](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0028), [31\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0029)):

[(7.31)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0052)![kappa equals StartFraction mu minus r Over sigma squared EndFraction comma](images/c07-math-0052.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

with the risk-free interest rate ![r](images/c07-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> set to 0. This Kelly fraction also plays a major role in portfolio selection. Under the Black–Scholes model, ![kappa](images/c07-i0546.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi></mrow></math> and ![1 minus kappa](images/c07-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi></math> are the respective optimal constant proportions of a wealth to be invested in the stock and bond so as to maximize the expected logarithmic return of the portfolio. To see this, recall that the dynamics of the bond value is described by the following simple differential equation:

[(7.32)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0053)![StartFraction d upper B Subscript t Baseline Over upper B Subscript t Baseline EndFraction equals r d t period](images/c07-math-0053.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Consider a portfolio in which a constant portion of wealth ![omega](images/c07-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math> is invested in the stock and the remaining portion ![1 minus omega](images/c07-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></math> is invested in the bond. Let ![left-brace normal upper X Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> be the wealth process at time ![t](images/c07-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Then the number of stocks bought at time ![t](images/c07-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is ![omega normal upper X Subscript t slash normal upper S Subscript t](images/c07-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, while the units of bond bought is ![left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis normal upper X Subscript t slash upper B Subscript t](images/c07-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. By ([7.29](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0049)) and ([7.32](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0053)), the wealth process ![left-brace normal upper X Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> then satisfies the dynamics ![d normal upper X Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis StartFraction omega normal upper X Subscript t Baseline Over normal upper S Subscript t Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis d normal upper S Subscript t Baseline plus left-parenthesis StartFraction left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis normal upper X Subscript t Baseline Over upper B Subscript t Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis d upper B Subscript t](images/c07-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. Thus ![left-brace normal upper X Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> satisfies the SDE:

![StartFraction d normal upper X Subscript t Baseline Over normal upper X Subscript t Baseline EndFraction equals omega StartFraction d normal upper S Subscript t Baseline Over normal upper S Subscript t Baseline EndFraction plus left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis StartFraction d upper B Subscript t Baseline Over upper B Subscript t Baseline EndFraction equals left-parenthesis omega mu plus left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis r right-parenthesis d t plus omega sigma d normal w Subscript t Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0054.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

whose solution, given an initial wealth ![upper X 0](images/c07-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, is simply:

![normal upper X Subscript normal t Baseline equals upper X 0 exp left-parenthesis left-parenthesis omega mu plus left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis r minus StartFraction omega squared sigma squared Over 2 EndFraction right-parenthesis t plus omega sigma normal w Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c07-math-0055.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>&#963;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

Therefore, the (one period) expected logarithmic return of the portfolio wealth is equal to:

![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis ln normal upper X Subscript t Baseline minus ln upper X 0 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis omega mu plus left-parenthesis 1 minus omega right-parenthesis r minus StartFraction omega squared sigma squared Over 2 EndFraction right-parenthesis t comma](images/c07-math-0056.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

and the Kelly fraction is the value of ![omega](images/c07-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math> that maximizes this latest quantity. In particular, the first order condition ![StartFraction d Over d omega EndFraction double-struck upper E left-parenthesis ln normal upper X Subscript t Baseline bar normal upper X 0 equals upper X 0 right-parenthesis equals mu minus r minus sigma squared omega Superscript asterisk Baseline equals 0](images/c07-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> gives ![omega Superscript asterisk Baseline equals StartFraction mu minus r Over sigma squared EndFraction](images/c07-i0561.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math>, which is exactly the ![kappa](images/c07-i0562.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi></mrow></math> in ([7.31](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0052)).

Turning back to the optional selling problem ([7.30](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0050)), we can interpret the mathematical result as saying one should buy a stock and hold it until the end of the investment horizon at ![upper T](images/c07-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> when ![alpha greater-than-or-equal-to 1 slash 2](images/c07-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>; otherwise, one should sell it at once when ![alpha less-than 1 slash 2](images/c07-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Detailed proofs and variants of the problem can be found in \[[9, 10, 17, 29, 36–38](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0036)\]. Nonetheless, for this buy-and-hold or sell-at-once strategy, as it is dependent on a single index, the ultimate benefit can only be achieved on the average. Instead, in the following trading strategy, we focus on the optimal stopping time in a *probabilistic* manner (more along *pathwise sense*), which is more realistic and likely leads to a more profitable strategy. To this end, we first formally state both the corresponding optimal selling and buying problems as follows:

It was found that their optimal solutions are determined by: the *goodness index* ![lamda](images/c07-i0574.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> of the stock (a modified version of Kelly fraction with ![r equals 0](images/c07-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>); the selling threshold ![epsilon Subscript upper S](images/c07-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></math>; and the buying threshold ![epsilon Subscript upper B](images/c07-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></math>; we define these as:
