The following two propositions delineate the possible optimal times for selling and buying, that is, the solutions to Problems ([7.33](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0057)) and ([7.34](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0058)).

 

**[Proposition 7.1](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fea-0004)**   (Refer to [\[26\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0024)) The optimal selling time ![normal tau Subscript upper S Superscript asterisk](images/c07-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> of the stock for Problem ([7.33](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0057)) is given in a specific form in exactly one of the following four cases:

*   Case 1: if ![phi left-parenthesis t semicolon lamda comma epsilon Subscript upper S Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> admits no root, then ![normal tau Subscript upper S Superscript asterisk Baseline colon equals inf left-brace right-brace colon less-than-or-equal-to less-than-or-equal-to tT colon equals equals St times times pMt logical-and upper T](images/c07-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">inf</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>&#8743;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. If ![lamda](images/c07-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is very negative in value, the stock simply drops without rising much throughout the planning horizon, so its initial value is likely the largest, and so it is almost optimal to sell-at-once. See the blue solid line in [Figure 7.19](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0019);
*   Case 2: if ![phi left-parenthesis t semicolon lamda comma epsilon Subscript upper S Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> admits a unique (double) root ![s Superscript asterisk](images/c07-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> with ![phi left-parenthesis s semicolon lamda comma epsilon Subscript upper S Baseline right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c07-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for any ![s not-equals s Superscript asterisk](images/c07-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math>, then ![normal tau Subscript upper S Superscript asterisk Baseline colon equals inf left-brace right-brace colon less-than-or-equal-to less-than-or-equal-to tT colon equals equals St times times pMt logical-and upper T](images/c07-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">inf</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>&#8743;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. See the red dashed line in [Figure 7.19](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0019);

### \*7.5.1 Trading Strategies Using the Goodness Index

Suppose that in a given calendar year, we would like to trade one or multiple stocks without any of their derivatives, so as to maximize our profit. This problem is time-inconsistent in nature, as our objective may change day-by-day. In the following, we shall introduce a class of trading strategies with different odds that utilize consecutive optimal selling and buying times, as introduced in [Propositions 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0004) and [7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0006).

Generally, while stock returns are expected to be non-stationary, their changes are usually mild within a shorter time frame. For the sake of illustration, here we set ![upper T](images/c07-i0645.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> to 4 so that each trading horizon contains ![upper T plus 1 equals 5](images/c07-i0646.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> trading days, or one week. This motivates us to assume that ![mu](images/c07-i0647.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma](images/c07-i0648.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> are constant throughout the trading horizon, and we denote their estimates of the ![k](images/c07-i0649.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-th trading horizon spanning from day ![t Subscript k comma 0](images/c07-i0650.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math> to day ![t Subscript k comma upper T Baseline colon equals t Subscript k comma 0 Baseline plus upper T](images/c07-i0651.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>T</mi></math> by ![mu Subscript t Sub Subscript k comma 0](images/c07-i0652.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> and ![sigma Subscript t Sub Subscript k comma 0](images/c07-i0653.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, respectively. We defer the discussion of parameter estimation to the subsequent subsections, while here we focus on discussing our proposed trading mechanism which is quite counterintuitive and not so immediately straightforward. However, it is inspired by and works consistently with our proposed theory.

The design of trading horizons can greatly influence trading strategies. Take a pre-commitment strategy as an example: a calendar year can be split into a number of relatively short trading horizons that are fixed in advance in a non-overlapping manner, namely the stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in [Proposition 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0006) for buying. Note that we may hold the stock until the end of one of the trading horizons, and at that point we refresh our decision whether to sell or hold it for the next period.

However, by adopting the aforementioned strategy, at most one buying transaction or one selling transaction will take place within a trading horizon, and no action will be considered for the remaining portion of the horizon. As such, we may miss out the possible profit over this remaining period; indeed, this strategy's performance is probably not as good as simply holding the S&P500. This hints that pre-commitment strategies may not perform extremely well for any time-inconsistent problem. For example, consider a pre-commitment strategy of buy-and-holding the stock throughout a 10-day trading horizon. Say the stock keeps decreasing for the next five days due to randomness, then on day 5, we may undo our investment decision (made at time 0) by selling the stock immediately to avoid greater losses, and this can fail our initial goal of profit maximization at time 0. As an alternative, we can devise another trading strategy to cope with this time-inconsistent problem by defining a number of more frequent trading horizons as follows: once we perform a transaction on day ![s](images/c07-i0660.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> within the ![k](images/c07-i0661.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-th trading horizon, we set the subsequent trading day as ![t Subscript k plus 1 comma 0 Baseline equals s plus 1](images/c07-i0662.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, the start of the subsequent ![left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0663.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th trading horizon; otherwise, if no transaction is made in this trading horizon, then the subsequent trading day of its end day ![t Subscript k comma upper T](images/c07-i0664.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></math> is set as the start of the ![left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0665.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th trading horizon, meaning that ![t Subscript k plus 1 comma 0 Baseline equals t Subscript k comma upper T Baseline plus 1](images/c07-i0666.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

We construct an artificial “trading horizon” of length of ![upper T plus 1](images/c07-i0667.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> days starting from every trading day, and from now on, we call this artificial “trading horizon” an *examination window* to avoid ambiguity. Clearly, for a chosen trading day ![s](images/c07-i0668.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, it is enclosed in a total of ![upper T plus 1](images/c07-i0669.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> different examination windows, such that the ![left-parenthesis j plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0670.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th examination window spans from day ![s minus upper T plus j](images/c07-i0671.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></math> to day ![s plus j](images/c07-i0672.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></math>, for ![j equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper T](images/c07-i0673.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. Below, with an initial capital of USD ![100 comma 000](images/c07-i0716.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math>, we propose the following three Kelly fraction-based candidate strategies with different odds for each transaction:

### \*7.5.2 Backtesting

Recall that in determining whether the current day ![s](images/c07-i0769.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is in the action period ([7.39](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0063)) within the ![left-parenthesis j plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0770.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th examination window from day ![s minus upper T plus j](images/c07-i0771.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></math> to day ![s plus j](images/c07-i0772.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![epsilon Subscript upper S comma s minus upper T plus j](images/c07-i0774.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![epsilon plus j](images/c07-i0776.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![sigma Subscript s minus upper T plus j](images/c07-i0777.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> on day ![s minus upper T plus j](images/c07-i0778.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></math>, and the performance of this newly proposed trading strategy is certainly linked to the accuracy of these estimations. In this subsection, we assess its performance from the viewpoint of *backtesting*.

Regarding the estimation of ![mu](images/c07-i0779.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, let's say for a given trading day ![t](images/c07-i0780.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, being the beginning of some ![left-parenthesis j plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0781.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th examination window, we can obtain a better estimate by also using future returns as well as historical ones. To this end, the following *two-stage approach* is introduced: we obtain a preliminary estimate ![mu overTilde Subscript t](images/c07-i0782.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> in the first step, by calculating the weighted geometric return over 3 consecutive trading days starting from the previous day ![t minus 1](images/c07-i0783.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>:

(7.41)![mu overTilde Subscript t Baseline equals product Underscript i equals negative 1 Overscript 1 Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 plus u Subscript t plus i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript omega Super Subscript i Superscript Baseline minus 1 comma](images/c07-math-0065.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![sigma-summation Underscript i equals negative 1 Overscript 1 Endscripts omega Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c07-i0784.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; for the current backtesting, we rely more on the return of the following day, by taking ![omega Subscript negative 1 Baseline equals 0.1](images/c07-i0785.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math>, ![omega 0 equals 0.3](images/c07-i0786.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></math>, and ![omega 1 equals 0.6](images/c07-i0787.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></math>.

In the second step, ![mu overTilde Subscript t](images/c07-i0788.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is adjusted further based on whether the stock has been in a superior, neutral or inferior state, with reference to a designated period of 11 trading days, namely from day ![t minus 9](images/c07-i0789.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>9</mn></math> to day ![t plus 1](images/c07-i0790.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Specifically, we compute the standard deviation using only the positive (resp. negative) returns among ![u Subscript i](images/c07-i0791.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s within the period, denoted by ![sigma overTilde Subscript plus comma t](images/c07-i0792.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> (resp. ![sigma overTilde Subscript minus comma t](images/c07-i0793.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math>), with the convention that ![sigma overTilde Subscript plus comma t Baseline equals 0](images/c07-i0794.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> (resp. ![sigma overTilde Subscript minus comma t Baseline equals 0](images/c07-i0795.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) whenever none of the trading days within the period has a positive (resp. negative) return. Using these, we obtain three candidate estimates, namely ![mu overTilde Subscript t Baseline plus sigma overTilde Subscript plus comma t slash 2](images/c07-i0796.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, ![mu overTilde Subscript t](images/c07-i0797.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, and ![mu overTilde Subscript t Baseline minus sigma overTilde Subscript minus comma t slash 2](images/c07-i0798.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, corresponding to superior, neutral and inferior states for the stock, respectively. Finally, we set ![mu Subscript t](images/c07-i0799.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> to the candidate estimate that is closest to the return ![u Subscript t](images/c07-i0800.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> on day ![t](images/c07-i0801.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. As a remark, the hyperparameters ![p element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0802.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![q greater-than 1](images/c07-i0803.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> should be chosen with care, usually based on some preliminary analysis on the historical performance of the stock, say via the goodness index ![lamda Subscript t](images/c07-i0804.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. The actual tuning of these hyperparameters based on this fundamental principle is left as a project for readers. We also note that the aforementioned estimation procedure is different from knowing and using the exact price from the future, which requires much more information, as it even includes the noisy observations. Instead, for our proposed approach, it suffices for us to know the trend only, which we can also guess by analyzing the historical information contained in different sources, including volume trading as well as social medias and news, using tools such as text mining beyond the numerical approaches.

Regarding the estimation of ![sigma](images/c07-i0805.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> mentioned above, say for an arbitrary trading day ![t](images/c07-i0806.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, being the beginning of some ![left-parenthesis j plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0807.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th examination window, we use 61 days of historical returns ![u Subscript t minus 60 Baseline comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma u Subscript t Baseline](images/c07-i0808.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> to fit an L-GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0809.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model as specified in ([7.24](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0043))

Furthermore, based on our observations, the stock prices also exhibit a one-day lagging effect, which can be justified since investors may need some time to digest and react to the information emerging in the market. Therefore, a possible approach to further improve the performances of our proposed investment strategy is to consider the following back-shifted rolling maximum and minimum, particularly for the ![left-parenthesis j plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0815.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th examination window, ![j equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper T](images/c07-i0816.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></math>:

### \*7.5.3 Kelly Fraction in Practice

A key contributing factor for the high profitability of strategies ![normal upper K Subscript IC](images/c07-i0831.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mtext>IC</mtext></msub></math>, ![normal upper K Subscript AC](images/c07-i0832.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mtext>AC</mtext></msub></math>, and ![normal upper K Subscript normal upper L](images/c07-i0833.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></math> is the unrealistically high accuracy of the estimate of ![mu Subscript t](images/c07-i0834.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> on day ![t](images/c07-i0835.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> due to the use of the return on day ![t plus 1](images/c07-i0836.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in the calibration of the trend. In reality, these strategies can hardly be expected to perform as well with only past returns available. The accuracy of estimates of ![mu Subscript t](images/c07-i0837.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s based on past returns is relatively lower when compared to those of ![sigma Subscript t](images/c07-i0838.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s. For example, consider the weighted geometric returns of the past 3 consecutive trading days:

Therefore, we usually prefer the more moderate and conservative Strategy ![normal upper K Subscript AC](images/c07-i0855.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mtext>AC</mtext></msub></math> in practice.

As a remedy, we can mitigate the limitation of relatively insecure estimations of ![mu Subscript t](images/c07-i0856.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s by utilizing some common technical indicators, which are normally used by traders to predict future price trends and then make trading decisions. One of the commonly used technical indicators is the *Bollinger Bands*, first proposed by *John Bollinger* in the early 1980s; see [\[19](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0018), [22](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0020), [23\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0021) for details. For an arbitrary trading day ![t](images/c07-i0857.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> as discussed above, Bollinger Bands are computed from the simple moving average and simple moving standard deviation of the stock prices over the past ![d](images/c07-i0858.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> trading days. The bands are in the form of a stock price interval with the upper and lower endpoints given by

Naturally, a stock price ![normal upper S Subscript t](images/c07-i0862.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> above the upper band ![BOLU Subscript t](images/c07-i0863.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>BOLU</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub></math> (resp. below the lower band ![BOLL Subscript t](images/c07-i0864.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>BOLL</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub></math>) indicates a selling (resp. buying) signal. Therefore, we can also take this into consideration when determining whether or not to trade on the current day ![s](images/c07-i0865.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, so as to make up for our lack of firm grasp of the conditions (S1) and (S2) for selling (resp. (B1) and (B2) for buying) based on ([7.36](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0060)). To this end, we perform the selling action on day ![s](images/c07-i0866.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> if at least one of the following holds:

1.  Both conditions (S1) and (S2) are satisfied;
2.  ![normal upper S Subscript s Baseline greater-than BOLU Subscript s](images/c07-i0867.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mtext>BOLU</mtext><mi>s</mi></msub></math>;

while we perform the buying action on day ![s](images/c07-i0868.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> if at least one of the following holds:

1.  Both conditions (B1) and (B2) are satisfied;
2.  ![normal upper S Subscript s Baseline less-than BOLL Subscript s](images/c07-i0869.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mtext>BOLL</mtext><mi>s</mi></msub></math>.

Recall that prior to the selling (resp. buying) action, we shall first close the existing long (resp. short-selling) position in the same manner as mentioned in [Subsection \*7.5.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0018). With this modified strategy, ![normal upper K Subscript AC](images/c07-i0870.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mtext>AC</mtext></msub></math> can yield an annual return of 10.4% on average from 2003 to 2022, still outperforming the buy-and-hold strategy of the S&P500 index which only yields an average annual return of 6.8% throughout the period.

As a closing remark, better trading strategies are not impossible, while they may require the use of different combinations of technical indicators, they ultimately relate to the Kelly fraction. We encourage readers to explore their own profitable trading strategies.

 

## 7.6 CALENDAR EFFECTS

Just as we commonly observe various business cycles in economies, seasonal effects are believed to be prevalent in stock price movements. These effects are also called *calendar effects* when they appear to be related to the calendar. It is undoubtedly crucial for profit-seeking investors to take full advantage of these effects by purchasing stocks at the start of periods of upward trends within cycles, and selling them just before periods of downward trends begin. For example, the well-known maxim of “*sell in May and go away*”

Despite the lack of consensus on the cause of such calendar effects, we can still examine their empirical validity using the data from stock markets. In particular, we adopt the *goodness index* ![lamda Subscript t](images/c07-i0871.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> in ([7.35](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0059)) to measure the performance of the market on any given day ![t](images/c07-i0872.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>:

where ![r Subscript t](images/c07-i0876.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is the (logarithmic) return on day ![t](images/c07-i0877.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, and ![m](images/c07-i0878.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is some positive integer (hyperparameter) so that ![2 m plus 1](images/c07-i0879.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is the width of the moving window. Note that in the current context of experiential study instead of real-life trading, we adopt moving windows including both historical and future returns for the sake of better estimation, so as to study the regular pattern of the markets concerned.

Following the procedure above, for the three selected stock indices, namely S&P500 Index in the US, *FTSE 100* Index in the UK and Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong, we compute the value of the goodness index ![lamda Subscript t](images/c07-i0880.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for each stock index on every trading day between 2000 and 2015 ![FIGURE 7.21 Bar chart of three stock indices based on the goodness index from 2000 to 2015.](images/c07f021.png)

[**FIGURE 7.21**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0021) Bar chart of three stock indices based on the goodness index from 2000 to 2015.

 ![](images/c07-gra-0049.png) ![](images/c07-gra-0050.png) 

Last but not least, we provide statistical justifications for our fitted models via the Ljung–Box test, so as to demonstrate the statistical reliability of the results obtained above. The output of [Programme 7.36](#c07.xhtml#c07-gra-00036) via Python is a `dataframe` that records the ![p](images/c07-i0885.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values from the Ljung–Box test with lag

In summary, we have ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal r Subscript k comma n Baseline dot normal r Subscript l comma n Baseline right-parenthesis right-arrow 0](images/c07-i0971.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and so ![Cov left-parenthesis normal r Subscript k comma n Baseline comma normal r Subscript l comma n Baseline right-parenthesis right-arrow 0](images/c07-i0972.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c07-i0973.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>. Consequently, ![normal r Subscript k comma n](images/c07-i0974.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![normal r Subscript l comma n](images/c07-i0975.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> are asymptotically uncorrelated for ![k not-equals l](images/c07-i0976.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>l</mi></math>. Furthermore, if ![normal r Subscript k comma n](images/c07-i0977.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![normal r Subscript l comma n](images/c07-i0978.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math>, after rescaling, are asymptotically normal, then they will also be independent asymptotically.

Next, we investigate the asymptotic distribution of the following term for an arbitrary ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c07-i0979.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>:

![StartFraction n left-parenthesis n plus 2 right-parenthesis Over n minus k EndFraction normal r Subscript k comma n Superscript 2 Baseline equals left-parenthesis 1 plus StartFraction 2 Over n EndFraction right-parenthesis StartStartFraction StartFraction normal x squared left-parenthesis k comma n right-parenthesis Over n minus k EndFraction OverOver left-parenthesis StartFraction normal y left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis Over n EndFraction right-parenthesis squared EndEndFraction period](images/c07-math-0090.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mfrac><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

Recall that ![StartFraction normal y Subscript n Baseline Over n EndFraction](images/c07-i0980.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math> converges to ![sigma squared](images/c07-i0981.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> in probability. As for the numerator, we note that ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal a Subscript i Baseline normal a Subscript i plus k Baseline bar script upper F Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c07-i0982.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> by a simple application of the tower property, hence the ![normal a Subscript i Baseline normal a Subscript i plus k](images/c07-i0983.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s form another time series of martingale differences. Then, by recalling that ![normal x left-parenthesis k comma n right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n minus k Endscripts normal a Subscript i Baseline normal a Subscript i plus k](images/c07-i0984.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> with mean 0 and variance ![left-parenthesis n minus k right-parenthesis sigma Superscript 4](images/c07-i0985.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>, an application of the martingale central limit theorem

 

### \*7.A.2 Differential Equation Analogue of GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0997.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>)

Recall that the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i0998.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) process is

![normal sigma Subscript n plus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma upper V Subscript upper L Baseline plus alpha normal u Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0091.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math>

Hence, at the ![n](images/c07-i1000.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-th time unit given ![normal sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i1001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>,

![normal sigma Subscript n plus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline minus sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis plus alpha left-parenthesis normal u Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline minus sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c07-math-0092.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Using the iid random variables ![normal z Subscript i Baseline equals normal u Subscript i Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Baseline tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-i1002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for all ![i](images/c07-i1003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, we have

[(7.52)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0094)![normal sigma Subscript n plus 1 Superscript 2 Baseline minus sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline equals gamma left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis plus alpha sigma Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline left-parenthesis normal z Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis period](images/c07-math-0093.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Note that ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal z Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c07-i1004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper V a r left-parenthesis normal z Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis equals 2](images/c07-i1005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

Now, we let ![delta t](images/c07-i1006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> be the uniform step size between two time instances. Define ![upper V Subscript t Baseline colon equals sigma Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c07-i1007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, such that ![t equals n dot delta t](images/c07-i1008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> is the present time at the ![n](images/c07-i1009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-th instance. Then ([7.52](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0094)) can be rewritten by taking care of the wait time being ![delta t](images/c07-i1010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> now,

![normal upper V Subscript t plus delta t Baseline minus upper V Subscript t Baseline equals gamma left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis delta t plus alpha upper V Subscript t Baseline StartRoot 2 EndRoot normal w Subscript t Baseline StartRoot delta t EndRoot comma](images/c07-math-0094.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal w Subscript t](images/c07-i1011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>'s are iid random variables with common mean 0 and common variance 1. As a result, the term ![normal w Subscript t Baseline StartRoot delta t EndRoot](images/c07-i1012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> has mean 0 and variance ![delta t](images/c07-i1013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math>. As we pass ![delta t](images/c07-i1014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></math> to ![d t](images/c07-i1015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, ![normal w Subscript t Baseline StartRoot delta t EndRoot](images/c07-i1016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> tends to a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance ![d t](images/c07-i1017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></math> by invoking the central limit theorem. Thus in the limit, ![normal w Subscript t Baseline StartRoot delta t EndRoot](images/c07-i1018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> becomes an infinitesimal increment ![d normal z Subscript t](images/c07-i1019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> where ![left-brace normal z Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c07-i1020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is a standard Brownian motion. To this end, we arrive at the following SDE:

[(7.53)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0096)![d normal upper V Subscript t Baseline equals gamma left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus normal upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis d t plus alpha normal upper V Subscript t Baseline StartRoot 2 EndRoot d normal z Subscript t Baseline period](images/c07-math-0095.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

Indeed, one can verify that this is the diffusion limit of the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c07-i1021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) model, also see [\[25\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0023).

Taking the expectation on both sides of ([7.53](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0096)), we obtain the following ordinary differential equation:

![d double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis equals gamma left-parenthesis upper V Subscript upper L Baseline minus double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis d t comma](images/c07-math-0096.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

whose solution is

![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper V Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper V Subscript upper L Baseline plus left-parenthesis upper V 0 minus upper V Subscript upper L Baseline right-parenthesis e Superscript minus gamma t Baseline period](images/c07-math-0097.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math> 

Finally, by noting that ![ln left-parenthesis 1 plus x right-parenthesis almost-equals x](images/c07-i1022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi>x</mi></math> for small ![x](images/c07-i1023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>,

![ln left-parenthesis alpha plus beta right-parenthesis equals ln left-parenthesis 1 minus gamma right-parenthesis almost-equals negative gamma](images/c07-math-0098.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi></math> 

for small enough ![gamma](images/c07-i1024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>, we arrive at the following approximation:

5.  [5](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-note-0005)   We adopt the Nelder–Mead method since it is the only option in `constrOptim()` which does not require the specification of gradient function `grad`.
6.  [6](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-note-0006)   Different from ARIMA model diagnostics, the sample ACF ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s of fitted residuals here are subject to a set of possibly non-linear constraints, say ![psi Subscript j Baseline left-parenthesis r 1 comma ellipsis comma r Subscript upper T Baseline right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c07-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper J](images/c07-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi></math>, where ![upper J equals p plus q plus 1](images/c07-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is the number of estimated parameters in a GARCH(![p comma q](images/c07-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></math>) model. Nevertheless, ![r Subscript k](images/c07-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s are close to their respective true population values when the sample size ![n](images/c07-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is large, then by Taylor expansion (a perturbation analytical approach, see [\[4](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0003), [33](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0031), [34\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0032)), these ![psi Subscript j](images/c07-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s are dominated by their respective zeroth- and first-order terms, and hence we arrive at ![upper J](images/c07-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> approximate linear constraints similar to the ARIMA case. That is why the asymptotic distribution of the corresponding test statistic, when applied to fitted residuals, is again a chi-square distribution with ![upper K minus upper J](images/c07-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>J</mi></math> degrees of freedom; readers may refer to \[[1](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-1001), [5](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0004), [20](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0019), [21](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-1019)\] for more discussions on this issue.
7.  [7](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-note-0007)   The CIR model is popular for modelling term structures of interest rates. The dynamics of the model admits the form: ![d normal r Subscript t Baseline equals theta left-parenthesis mu minus normal r Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis d t plus sigma StartRoot normal r Subscript t Baseline EndRoot d normal z Subscript t](images/c07-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt><mi>d</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, where ![theta](images/c07-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, ![mu](images/c07-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![sigma](images/c07-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> are constants; ![mu](images/c07-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is also called the *retention level* about which the interest rate fluctuates.
8.  [8](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-note-0008)   The general argument remains valid, similar to the standard GARCH model, the test statistic for fitted residuals should follow a chi-square distribution with ![upper K minus 4 equals 11](images/c07-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math> degrees of freedom, as there are 4 parameters estimated.
9.
