# CHAPTER 8  
Risk Measures, Extreme Values, and Copulae

 

Financial institutions usually manage hundreds, or even thousands, of portfolios of securities and derivatives every day. It is important to have a single number that summarizes the total risk in a portfolio of financial assets, so as to measure the overall potential contingencies to which the financial institution is exposed. *Value-at-Risk* (V@R) is an attempt to provide such an index (measurement). It was pioneered by J.P. Morgan [\[32\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0032) and has been adopted by the *Basel Committee* [\[7\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0007) in setting capital requirements for banks throughout the world. Closely related to V@R is *Expected Shortfall* (ES) which is utilized in accordance with *Basel III*

 

## 8.1 VALUE-AT-RISK AND EXPECTED SHORTFALL

Consider a portfolio and let ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math> be the loss in its value over a 1-day horizon. We say that the 1-day value-at-risk of such portfolio at the confidence level ![p element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, denoted by ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, equals ![upper V](images/c08-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> if we are ![100 p](images/c08-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>100</mn><mi>p</mi></math>% certain that we shall not lose more than ![upper V](images/c08-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> dollars on the next day. Usually, the confidence level ![p](images/c08-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is taken to be close to 1, such as ![p equals 0.99](images/c08-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.99</mn></math>. If we denote by ![upper F Subscript normal upper L](images/c08-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></math> the cdf of the loss variable ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math>, then ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is just the ![p](images/c08-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-quantile of the loss distribution:

![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals upper F Subscript normal upper L Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals min left-brace right-brace colon element-of element-of lR colon greater-than-or-equal-to greater-than-or-equal-to of FFL left-parenthesis right-parenthesis lp period](images/c08-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#125;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

In particular, if ![upper F Subscript normal upper L](images/c08-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></math> is continuous and strictly increasing, then ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is simply the unique solution to the equation ![upper F Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis equals p](images/c08-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, also see [Figure 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0001).

 ![FIGURE 8.1 Illustration of upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis.](images/c08f001.png)

[**FIGURE 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0001) Illustration of ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Note that the ![upper N](images/c08-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-day ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, denoted by ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis upper N comma x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, equals ![StartRoot upper N EndRoot dot upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mi>N</mi></msqrt><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> assuming the daily changes are iid normal over the ![upper N](images/c08-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-day period; this calculation also implicitly assumes that ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper L right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c08-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

 

**Example 8.1**   Suppose that ![normal upper L tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. By solving the equation ![p equals upper F Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis equals normal upper Phi left-parenthesis StartFraction l minus mu Over sigma EndFraction right-parenthesis equals p](images/c08-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math> for ![l](images/c08-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>, we obtain ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals mu plus sigma normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

**Example 8.2**   Assume that the daily loss distribution ![upper F Subscript normal upper L](images/c08-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></math> of a portfolio is normally distributed with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of ![dollar-sign 20 normal upper M](images/c08-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>20</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. Then the 1-day ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis 0.95 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis dollar-sign 20 normal upper M right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 1.645 right-parenthesis equals 32.9 normal upper M](images/c08-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.95</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>20</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.645</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>32.9</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> and the 1-day ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis 0.99 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis dollar-sign 20 normal upper M right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 2.326 right-parenthesis equals dollar-sign 46.52 normal upper M](images/c08-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.99</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>20</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2.326</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>46.52</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. If we further assume that daily losses are independent, then the loss over an ![upper N](images/c08-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-day period is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation ![dollar-sign 20 StartRoot upper N EndRoot normal upper M](images/c08-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>20</mn><msqrt><mi>N</mi></msqrt><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. Therefore, the 10-day ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis 0.95 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.95</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is ![left-parenthesis StartRoot 10 EndRoot right-parenthesis left-parenthesis dollar-sign 32.9 normal upper M right-parenthesis equals dollar-sign 104.04 normal upper M](images/c08-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mn>10</mn></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>32.9</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>104.04</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> and the 252-day ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis 0.99 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.99</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is ![left-parenthesis StartRoot 252 EndRoot right-parenthesis left-parenthesis dollar-sign 46.52 normal upper M right-parenthesis equals dollar-sign 738.48 normal upper M](images/c08-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mn>252</mn></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>46.52</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>738.48</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>.

The V@R risk measure asks how bad the loss will be, while *Expected Shortfall* (ES) asks: if things do get bad, what is the expected loss? Mathematically speaking, the expected shortfall ![ES Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> at confidence level ![p](images/c08-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> of the loss variable ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math> is defined as

![ES Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction 1 Over 1 minus p EndFraction integral Subscript p Superscript 1 Baseline upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis d x comma](images/c08-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is finite when ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math> is integrable; see [Figure 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0002) for an illustration. ES is also known as *conditional tail expectation* (CTE) for the following reason: if the loss variable ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math> is continuous, then ![ES Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> equals ![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal upper L bar normal upper L greater-than upper V commercial-at upper R left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mtext>V@R</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; see also Section 2.3.4 of [\[33\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0033).

![FIGURE 8.2 Illustration of ES Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis, which equals the area of the blue region.](images/c08f002.png)

[**FIGURE 8.2**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0002) Illustration of ![ES Subscript normal upper L Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which equals the area of the blue region.

 

**Example 8.3**   Consider a $10 million 1-year loan which has a ![1.25 percent-sign](images/c08-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1.25</mn><mi>%</mi></math> chance of defaulting. If the loan defaults, the recovery of the loan principal is equally likely from ![0 percent-sign](images/c08-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mi>%</mi></math> to ![100 percent-sign](images/c08-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>100</mn><mi>%</mi></math>. Find the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>V@R</mtext></mrow></math> and the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> ES, respectively.

![](images/c08uf001.png)

If the loan defaults (with the probability of 0.0125), let ![x](images/c08-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> be the percentage of loan principal recovered. Then ![left-parenthesis 0.0125 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals 0.01](images/c08-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.0125</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math>, or ![x equals 0.8](images/c08-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.8</mn></math>, implies that ![80 percent-sign](images/c08-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>80</mn><mi>%</mi></math> of ![dollar-sign 10 normal upper M equals dollar-sign 8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>10</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> will be recovered with a probability of 0.01; or ![upper V commercial-at upper R left-parenthesis 0.99 right-parenthesis equals dollar-sign 10 normal upper M minus dollar-sign 8 normal upper M equals dollar-sign 2 normal upper M](images/c08-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>V@R</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.99</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>10</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. In other words, the probability of loss greater than ![dollar-sign 2 normal upper M](images/c08-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> is ![80 percent-sign](images/c08-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>80</mn><mi>%</mi></math> of ![1.25 percent-sign equals 1 percent-sign](images/c08-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1.25</mn><mi>%</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>%</mi></math>.

Besides, the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> ES is the expected loss given that the loss is greater than ![dollar-sign 2 normal upper M](images/c08-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. Since the loss is uniformly distributed between ![dollar-sign 2 normal upper M](images/c08-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> to ![dollar-sign 10 normal upper M](images/c08-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>10</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>, the mean is ![dollar-sign 6 normal upper M](images/c08-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>6</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. Note that a uniform random variable ![normal x](images/c08-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> conditional on the event that ![normal x greater-than x](images/c08-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>x</mi></math> still has a uniform distribution.

 

**Example 8.4**   Consider a portfolio consisting of two $10 million 1-year loans as in [Example 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0005). For simplicity, we further assume that if one loan defaults then it is certain that the other loan will not default. If a loan does not default, a profit of $0.2 million is made. Find the 1-year 99% V@R and 1-year 99% ES of this portfolio.

![](images/c08uf002.png)

Each loan defaults with a probability of ![1.25 percent-sign](images/c08-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1.25</mn><mi>%</mi></math> and they never default together. Therefore a default occurs with a probability of ![2.5 percent-sign](images/c08-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2.5</mn><mi>%</mi></math>. Let ![x](images/c08-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> be the percentage of loan principal recovered. Then ![left-parenthesis 0.025 right-parenthesis left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals 0.01](images/c08-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.025</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math>, or ![x equals 0.4](images/c08-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></math>, implies that ![40 percent-sign](images/c08-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>40</mn><mi>%</mi></math> of ![dollar-sign 10 normal upper M equals dollar-sign 4 normal upper M](images/c08-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>10</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> will be recovered with a probability of 0.01. However, a profit of ![dollar-sign 0.2 normal upper M](images/c08-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>0.2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> is made on the other loan, hence the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>V@R</mtext></mrow></math> is ![dollar-sign 10 normal upper M minus dollar-sign 4 normal upper M minus dollar-sign 0.2 normal upper M equals dollar-sign 5.8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>10</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>0.2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>5.8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>.

Moreover, the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> ES of this portfolio is the expected loss given that the loss is greater than ![dollar-sign 5.8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>5.8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>. Since the loss is uniformly distributed between ![dollar-sign 5.8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>5.8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> and ![dollar-sign 9.8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>9.8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>, the mean is ![dollar-sign 7.8 normal upper M](images/c08-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>7.8</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math>.

 

## 8.2 BASEL ACCORDS AND RISK MEASURES

Risk measures is used for specifying capital requirements that must be added to a bank or a financial institution to provide a buffer for the underlying risk in order to satisfy regulators. In 1980, with the aim of monitoring and maintaining a healthy investment environment, supervisory authorities of Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, UK and US formed a committee for banking supervision, known as the *Bank for International Settlements* (BIS). The authorities of several other countries and territories have joined since. They meet regularly in the city of Basel in Switzerland (see the map in [Figure 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003)), and in 1996 the Basel Committee issued an amendment to the 1988 Accord, which was then referred to as “BIS 88” [\[6\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0006) or “Basel I”

Mathematically, there are some desirable properties that a risk measure ![rho left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis colon script upper L squared left-parenthesis normal upper Omega semicolon double-struck upper P right-parenthesis right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, defined on the space of random variables with finite second moments, should preferably have. In what follows, ![normal upper L Subscript normal upper A](images/c08-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub></math> and ![normal upper L Subscript normal upper B](images/c08-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub></math> are loss variables of portfolios A and B, respectively.

![FIGURE 8.3 The location of Basel, Switzerland. Canton of Basel-Stadt map with cities and towns. Photo retrieved from https://ontheworldmap.com/switzerland/canton/basel-stadt/canton-of-basel-stadt-map-with-cities-and-towns.html.](images/c08f003.png)

[**FIGURE 8.3**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0003) The location of Basel, Switzerland. Canton of Basel-Stadt map with cities and towns. Photo retrieved from [https://ontheworldmap.com/switzerland/canton/basel-stadt/canton-of-basel-stadt-map-with-cities-and-towns.html](https://ontheworldmap.com/switzerland/canton/basel-stadt/canton-of-basel-stadt-map-with-cities-and-towns.html).

1.  *Monotonicity:* If the loss amount of a portfolio is less than that of another portfolio for every possible outcome from the sample space, its risk measure should be smaller than that of the second. \[![normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline less-than-or-equal-to normal upper L Subscript normal upper B Baseline right double arrow rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper B Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo>&#8658;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\]
2.  *Translational invariance:* If a deterministic cash amount of ![upper K](images/c08-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is added to a loss, its risk measure should go up by ![upper K](images/c08-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. \[![rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline plus upper K right-parenthesis equals rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline right-parenthesis plus upper K](images/c08-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi></math>\]
3.  *Homogeneity:* Changing the size of a portfolio by a factor ![k](images/c08-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> should result in the risk measure being multiplied by ![k](images/c08-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. \[![rho left-parenthesis k normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline right-parenthesis equals k rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\]
4.  *Subadditivity:* The risk measure of two portfolios after being merged should not be greater than the sum of the individual risk measures of the respective portfolio components. \[![rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline plus normal upper L Subscript normal upper B Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper A Baseline right-parenthesis plus rho left-parenthesis normal upper L Subscript normal upper B Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\]

The first three conditions are natural enough while the fourth condition means that the diversification helps to reduce the inherent risks. Risk measures satisfying all four conditions are said to be *coherent*, see [\[3\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0003).

Recall that in [Examples 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0005) and [8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0006), the 1-year ![99 percent-sign](images/c08-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>99</mn><mi>%</mi></math> V@R of the two loans separately is ![dollar-sign 2 normal upper M plus dollar-sign 2 normal upper M equals dollar-sign 4 normal upper M](images/c08-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> which is less than $5.8M, the V@R of the portfolio. This implies that V@R does not always satisfy the subadditivity condition, yet it remains subadditive among *elliptical distributions*

 

**Proposition 8.1 *(Subadditivity of ES)***   Let ![normal x](images/c08-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal y](images/c08-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> be two random variables, and let ![ES Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (resp. ![ES Subscript normal y Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>) denote the expected shortfall of ![normal x](images/c08-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> (resp. ![normal y](images/c08-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>) at confidence level ![p element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Although V@R is not coherent, it is easier to understand and backtest than ES. Therefore, V@R has become the most popular risk measure among regulators and risk managers, as suggested by Basel II. In fact, although coherent risk measures are a rather commonly used concept within academia, they were not as important in actual practice before Basel III. Now, in accordance with Basel III, the ES of the portfolio at a base liquidity horizon of 10 days has to be provided [\[8\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0008).

 

## 8.3 HISTORICAL SIMULATION (BOOTSTRAPPING)

In the previous (simplified) examples, we calculated V@R by assuming that the return of the portfolio follows a uniform or normal distribution for simplicity. Similar calculations can be performed for other distributions as long as the inverse of the distribution function can be computed analytically; but this is generally not viable in practice. There is another approach to calculating V@R based on historical data. Suppose that today is day ![n](images/c08-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and we define ![v Subscript i](images/c08-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> to be the value of a market variable (stock price or index) on day ![i](images/c08-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, for ![i equals 0 comma 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c08-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. The daily returns of the past ![n](images/c08-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> days provide us with ![n](images/c08-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> possible scenarios of the return on the day ![n](images/c08-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. The predicted value ![ModifyingAbove v With caret Subscript n plus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of the value tomorrow ![normal v Subscript n plus 1](images/c08-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, based on the ![i](images/c08-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th scenario, is given by ![v Subscript n Baseline times v Subscript i slash v Subscript i minus 1](images/c08-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c08-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. From these ![n](images/c08-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> estimates of ![normal v Subscript n plus 1](images/c08-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, we can then estimate its 1-day V@R as the empirical quantile of the set ![StartSet ModifyingAbove v With caret Subscript n plus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma ModifyingAbove v With caret Subscript n plus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c08-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#125;</mo></math>. Let us illustrate this by the data in `stock_1999_2002.csv`. Suppose that we spend $40,000 for the purchase of stocks of HSBC, $30,000 on stocks of CLP and $30,000 on those of CK on 31 December 2002. The following programs compute the 1-day V@R of this portfolio using historical simulation, see [Programmes 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0001) and [8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0002) for Python and **R**, respectively.

![](images/c08-gra-0001.png) ![](images/c08-gra-0002.png)![](images/c08-gra-0003.png)

Note that the cost of the portfolio is $100,000 based on the closing price on 31 December 2002. Then we compute the estimated stock prices under these ![n](images/c08-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> scenarios and save them in `h_sim`. Further, we compute the estimated portfolio value of `p_n` and the losses of these ![n](images/c08-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> scenarios, and finally the estimated 1-day 99% V@R is taken as the 99-th percentile, `VaR_sim = $3,543.961`.

The historical simulation (bootstrapping) method above puts equal weight to each historical observation. This method can be modified by putting different weights depending on the ratio of the ![left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>\-th and ![i](images/c08-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th volatilities. To this end, we assume that the normalized daily returns ![StartFraction 1 Over sigma Subscript i Baseline EndFraction StartFraction normal v Subscript i Baseline minus normal v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline Over normal v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline EndFraction](images/c08-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> follow a common distribution such as ![script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> or ![t Subscript nu](images/c08-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>. An estimate of the value of ![normal v Subscript n plus 1](images/c08-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> can be obtained from the ![i](images/c08-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th scenario by matching ![StartFraction 1 Over sigma Subscript n plus 1 Baseline EndFraction StartFraction ModifyingAbove v With caret Subscript n plus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis minus v Subscript n Baseline Over v Subscript n Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over sigma Subscript i Baseline EndFraction StartFraction v Subscript i Baseline minus v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline Over v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline EndFraction](images/c08-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>. This produces the following ![n](images/c08-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> estimates of ![normal v Subscript n plus 1](images/c08-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>:

(8.1)![ModifyingAbove v With caret Subscript n plus 1 Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis equals v Subscript n Baseline times StartFraction v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus left-parenthesis v Subscript i Baseline minus v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis sigma Subscript n plus 1 Baseline slash sigma Subscript i Baseline Over v Subscript i minus 1 Baseline EndFraction with i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c08-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>with</mtext><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math>  

where ![sigma Subscript i](images/c08-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the estimated volatility using the EWMA or ![GARCH left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>GARCH</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> model introduced in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml) ; see [Programmes 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0003) and [8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0004) for the corresponding calibrations in Python and **R**, respectively. Note that the estimated 1-day V@R under this approach, `VaR_GARCH = $2,538.037` (in Python), is much lower than `VaR_sim`; indeed, for these three major stocks in the Hong Kong market, their prices exhibited a similar downward trend to the Hang Seng Index near the end of 2002, while being less volatile compared with the earlier years, altogether this leads to a lower V@R estimate by the GARCH model compared with the bootstrapping approach. While the estimate can yield a better prediction, the underlying model may change completely within a short period, and by then the V@R calculated by the current model may become too low.

Note that ![StartRoot bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper S bold-italic omega EndRoot](images/c08-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> can also be obtained by directly computing the sample standard deviation of ![normal upper Delta normal p](images/c08-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi></math>. Let us illustrate this using the `stock_1999_2002.csv` example again with the Python and **R** codes in [Programmes 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0005) and [8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0006), respectively.

![](images/c08-gra-0006.png)![](images/c08-gra-0007.png)

The 1-day 99% V@R using the normal model is `VaR_N = $3,143.753` which is less than the historically simulated `VaR_sim = $3,543.961`. The normality assumption may not be valid since most returns have heavier tails than those specified by the normal distribution. Hence, the ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>V@R</mtext></mrow></math> under the normality assumption mostly falls small. Recall, from [Section 3.2](#c03.xhtml#head-2-21), that we can model the return by a Student's ![t](images/c08-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution ![t Subscript nu](images/c08-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> with ![nu](images/c08-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom. Notice that for ![normal t tilde t Subscript nu](images/c08-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math> where ![nu greater-than 2](images/c08-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, ![upper V a r left-parenthesis normal t right-parenthesis equals StartFraction nu Over nu minus 2 EndFraction](images/c08-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>. Therefore, we may assume ![normal t colon equals StartFraction normal upper L minus 0 Over StartRoot bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper S bold-italic omega EndRoot EndFraction times StartRoot StartFraction nu Over nu minus 2 EndFraction EndRoot tilde t Subscript nu Baseline](images/c08-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#215;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></math>, and the 1-day 99%-V@R, denoted as ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal t](images/c08-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></msub></math>, satisfies the equation:

where ![upper T Subscript nu Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the inverse cdf of the standard Student's ![t](images/c08-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution with ![nu](images/c08-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom.

Let us compute the sample excess kurtosis ![ModifyingAbove zeta With Ì‚ Subscript 2](images/c08-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#950;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> of ![normal upper Delta normal p](images/c08-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi></math>, as then we estimate the degrees of freedom by ![StartFraction 6 Over ModifyingAbove zeta With Ì‚ Subscript 2 Baseline plus 4 EndFraction](images/c08-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#950;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>, rounded to the nearest integer; see [Programmes 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0007) in Python and [8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0008) in **R**.

![](images/c08-gra-0008.png)![](images/c08-gra-0009.png)

The 1-day 99% V@R using Student's ![t](images/c08-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-model is `VaR_t = $3,424.005`, which is larger than the one obtained by using the normal model (`VaR_N = $3,143.753`), but smaller than the historically simulated value `VaR_sim = $3,543.961`.

 

## 8.5 USE OF EXTREME VALUE THEORY

In modelling empirical data, one useful law is the *Power Law*, first properly proposed by *Vilfredo Pareto* in 1897 [\[37\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0037). This law is said to hold if the survival function of a random variable ![normal y](images/c08-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is proportional to a power function: ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal y greater-than x right-parenthesis proportional-to x Superscript negative alpha](images/c08-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8733;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></msup></math> for some ![alpha greater-than 0](images/c08-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; it also provides a good model for estimating the tail probability of rare events. Let ![upper F](images/c08-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> be the cdf of a random variable ![normal x](images/c08-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x less-than-or-equal-to u right-parenthesis equals upper F left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then given ![normal x greater-than u](images/c08-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>u</mi></math>, the conditional probability of ![u less-than normal x less-than-or-equal-to u plus y](images/c08-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></math> is

![upper F Subscript u Baseline left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis colon equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x minus u less-than-or-equal-to y bar normal x greater-than u right-parenthesis equals StartFraction upper F left-parenthesis u plus y right-parenthesis minus upper F left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis Over 1 minus upper F left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis EndFraction period](images/c08-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

It has been shown ([\[4](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0004), [23](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0023), [38\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0038)) that for a large class of distributions ![upper F](images/c08-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>, ![upper F Subscript u Baseline left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis right-arrow upper G Subscript xi comma beta Baseline left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> uniformly in ![y greater-than 0](images/c08-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> as ![u right-arrow infinity](images/c08-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, where

![upper G Subscript xi comma beta Baseline left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 1 minus left-parenthesis 1 plus xi StartFraction y Over beta EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 slash xi Baseline comma 2nd Column xi not-equals 0 comma 2nd Row 1st Column 1 minus exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction y Over beta EndFraction right-parenthesis comma 2nd Column xi equals 0 comma EndLayout](images/c08-math-0016.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>&#958;</mi><mfrac><mi>y</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>y</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and is called the *generalized Pareto distribution* with a shape parameter ![xi](images/c08-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></math> and a scale parameter ![beta greater-than 0](images/c08-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, in which ![y greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c08-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> when ![xi greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c08-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, or ![0 less-than-or-equal-to y less-than-or-equal-to minus StartFraction beta Over xi EndFraction](images/c08-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>&#958;</mi></mfrac></math> when ![xi less-than 0](images/c08-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. For common financial data, ![xi greater-than 0](images/c08-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and it falls in the range from 0.1 to 0.4, see [\[27\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0027) for details. For more introduction to extreme value theory (EVT), we refer to [\[25](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0025), [40\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0040).

Suppose that we sort ![n](images/c08-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> financial observations ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline](images/c08-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> in descending order, and there are ![n Subscript u](images/c08-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></math> observations greater than ![u](images/c08-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>. Assume that the previous theorem of *Gnedenko–Pickands–Balkema–de Haan* (“*Gnedenko's theorem*” in short hereafter) is applicable to the underlying distribution of this sample, then for a large enough ![u](images/c08-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, we can estimate ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x greater-than u plus y bar normal x greater-than u right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by ![1 minus upper G Subscript xi comma beta Baseline left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and ![1 minus upper F left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by ![StartFraction n Subscript u Baseline Over n EndFraction](images/c08-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>. As a result, the unconditional probability is approximately given by

and then obtain an estimate of the 1-day V@R of ![normal x](images/c08-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> at the confidence level ![p](images/c08-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> given by

(8.3)![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals u plus StartFraction ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Over ModifyingAbove xi With Ì‚ EndFraction left-bracket left-parenthesis StartFraction n left-parenthesis 1 minus p right-parenthesis Over n Subscript u Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript minus ModifyingAbove xi With Ì‚ Baseline minus 1 right-bracket period](images/c08-math-0025.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></mfrac><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

The only remaining question is the choice of the threshold value ![u](images/c08-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>. In practice, we should first apply the standardized transformation ![z Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction x Subscript i Baseline minus x overbar Over s EndFraction](images/c08-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>s</mi></mfrac></math>, set ![u](images/c08-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> to be close to the 0.95-quantile of the empirical distribution of the standardized sample ![z 1 greater-than ellipsis greater-than z Subscript n](images/c08-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>

Let us illustrate this by continuing the previous example. Note that we use the `minimize()` function in the `scipy` library in Python in [Programme 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-0009) or the **R** built-in function `optim()` in **R** in [Programme 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00010) to minimize the negative of the log-likelihood function; also see `help(optim)` in **R** for details.

![](images/c08-gra-0010.png)![](images/c08-gra-0011.png)

Recall that the 1-day 99% V@R using the normal-model is `VaR_N = $3,143.753`; using the ![t](images/c08-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-model it is `VaR_t = $3,424.005`; and using extreme value theory it is `VaR_EVT = $4,045.817` (in Python). A natural question is: which V@R is more appropriate? In general, EVT is theoretically the most rigorous, and should be preferred if there are abundant data, as EVT uses only data at the tail of the loss distribution. For small datasets, the ![t](images/c08-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-model is preferred against the normal-model as loss distributions are more likely to have heavy tails. We can actually test these V@Rs using historical data to see which one is more reasonable; this procedure is called *backtesting*.

 

## 8.6 BACKTESTING

Calculation of V@R is based on the knowledge of the loss distribution. It is important to test how accurate the V@R estimate really is. An important reality check is backtesting. Let the 1-day V@R at the confidence level ![p](images/c08-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> be ![dollar-sign upper V](images/c08-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mi>V</mi></math>. We say that an exception occurs if the loss in the portfolio value is greater than ![dollar-sign upper V](images/c08-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mi>V</mi></math> on a given day. If the V@R model is accurate, the probability of the loss in the portfolio value greater than ![dollar-sign upper V](images/c08-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mi>V</mi></math> on any given day is ![q equals 1 minus p](images/c08-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Suppose that over an ![n](images/c08-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-day horizon we observe that ![m](images/c08-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> exceptions occur in these ![n](images/c08-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> days, where the proportion ![StartFraction m Over n EndFraction greater-than q](images/c08-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>q</mi></math>. Should we reject the model as it produces an underestimate of the V@R? This can be tested formally by using the following binomial test [\[34\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0034):

![upper H 0](images/c08-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> (null hypothesis): Probability of an exception on any given day is ![q](images/c08-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>;

![upper H 1](images/c08-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> (alternative hypothesis): Probability of an exception on any given day is greater than ![q](images/c08-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.

Note that this is a one-sided test as we now observe that ![StartFraction m Over n EndFraction greater-than q](images/c08-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>q</mi></math>, and we place greater attention on the underestimation of V@R and are less concerned about any overestimation. Under ![upper H 0](images/c08-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, the probability of having at least ![m](images/c08-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> exceptions out of ![n](images/c08-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> days is

(8.4)![upper P 0 equals sigma-summation Underscript k equals m Overscript n Endscripts StartBinomialOrMatrix n Choose k EndBinomialOrMatrix q Superscript k Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus q right-parenthesis Superscript n minus k Baseline period](images/c08-math-0026.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac></mfenced><msup><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math> 

We reject ![upper H 0](images/c08-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> at the significance level of ![alpha](images/c08-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> if ![upper P 0 less-than alpha](images/c08-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></math>, as a smaller ![q](images/c08-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> tends to give a smaller ![upper P 0](images/c08-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>; typically, we take ![alpha equals 0.05](images/c08-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>. Let us set ![n equals 250](images/c08-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn></math> days, ![p equals 0.99](images/c08-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.99</mn></math> so that ![q equals 0.01](images/c08-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math>. We compute ![upper P 0](images/c08-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> for ![m equals 0 comma ellipsis comma 10](images/c08-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, in Python in [Programme 8.11](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00011) and in **R** in [Programme 8.12](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00012).

![](images/c08-gra-0012.png)![](images/c08-gra-0013.png)

From the outputs, it is clear that ![upper P 0 greater-than 0.05](images/c08-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math> if ![m less-than 5](images/c08-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. In practice, the 1986 BIS Amendment requires V@R models to be backtested. Banks should look at the number of exceptions ![m](images/c08-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> during the previous 250 days. If ![m less-than 5](images/c08-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, then the riskiness of the portfolio is considered in the green zone. The capital requirement is then computed by multiplying the V@R with the regulatory multiplier ![k equals 3](images/c08-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. If ![m](images/c08-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, the riskiness of the portfolio is considered in the yellow zone, and ![k](images/c08-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is set at ![3.4 comma 3.5 comma 3.65 comma 3.75](images/c08-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3.4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.65</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.75</mn></math> and 3.85, respectively. Finally, if ![m greater-than-or-equal-to 10](images/c08-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, ![k](images/c08-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> will be set to 4, and the riskiness of the portfolio is considered in the red zone; also see [\[5\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0005) for further discussions, and a summary is provided in [Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001). [Figure 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0004) shows that ![k](images/c08-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> possesses a linear relationship with ![m](images/c08-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> in the yellow zone, and the other values of ![k](images/c08-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> in this zone can be calculated by linear interpolation from the values of ![k](images/c08-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> for ![m](images/c08-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> in the range of 4 to 10.

Now let us continue with the data in `stock_1999_2002.csv` and backtest the 1-day 99% V@R using all the aforementioned V@R models. From the outputs in [Programmes 8.13](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00013) (in Python) and [8.14](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00014) (in **R**), the numbers of exceptions in the past 250 days for all approaches are all less than 5, and as such, the regulatory multiplier should be set to 3 for each approach. In [Figure 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0005) for Python and in [Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0006) for **R**, we depict the histogram of profit and loss over the previous 250-day period, and also the calibrated V@Rs under normal, ![t](images/c08-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-, and bootstrapping with equal or unequal weighting models.

Therefore, the expected shortfall on ![normal upper L](images/c08-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></math> is:

3.  On the other hand, if there are enough data, the expected shortfall can be more accurately estimated by the generalized Pareto distribution under EVT. Recall that for any large value of ![u greater-than 0](images/c08-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, the generalized Pareto distribution function ![upper G Subscript xi comma beta](images/c08-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></msub></math> serves as an approximation of the conditional probability ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x less-than-or-equal-to u plus x bar normal x greater-than u right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> by Gnedenko's theorem.     for ![0 less-than xi less-than 1](images/c08-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, ![limit Underscript y right-arrow infinity Endscripts left-parenthesis 1 plus xi StartFraction y Over beta EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript 1 minus 1 slash xi Baseline equals 0](images/c08-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>&#958;</mi><mfrac><mi>y</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, hence

    Thus, we have the following:
    
    1.  If the conditional distribution of ![normal x minus upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given that ![normal x greater-than upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is approximated by the generalized Pareto distribution ![upper G Subscript xi comma beta](images/c08-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></msub></math> with ![0 less-than xi less-than 1](images/c08-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#958;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, then the expected shortfall of ![normal x](images/c08-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> at level ![p](images/c08-i0334.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> can be approximated by:
        
        ![ES Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal x bar normal x greater-than upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis plus StartFraction beta Over 1 minus xi EndFraction period](images/c08-math-0035.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>ES</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 
        
        Given plenty of data of losses greater than ![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0335.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>V@R</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the parameters ![xi](images/c08-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></math> and ![beta](images/c08-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> can then be accurately estimated.
