Lastly, we shall compute the empirical expected shortfall for the portfolio consisting of HSBC, CLP, and CK under all the aforementioned V@R calibration methods.

![](images/c08-gra-0017.png)![](images/c08-gra-0018.png)

From [Programmes 8.15](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00015) via Python and [8.16](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00016) via **R**, the expected shortfalls computed from the GARCH(![1 comma 1](images/c08-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) non-parametric bootstrapping approach (![dollar-sign 3 comma 599.886](images/c08-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>599.886</mn></math>) and the normal parametric model (![dollar-sign 3 comma 561.068](images/c08-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>561.068</mn></math>) are the smallest; while the expected shortfalls computed from the Student's ![t](images/c08-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-model (![dollar-sign 4 comma 265.071](images/c08-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>265.071</mn></math>), the EVT approach in Python (![dollar-sign 4 comma 981.691](images/c08-i0366.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>981.691</mn></math>) (resp. ![dollar-sign 4 comma 998.013](images/c08-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>998.013</mn></math> in **R**) and the distribution-free approach ([8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0040)) (![dollar-sign 4 comma 611.053](images/c08-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>611.053</mn></math>) are larger. Since we know that the Student's ![t](images/c08-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> and the EVT are better at capturing the tail behaviour of the loss distribution, we tend to adopt the ES coming from either one of these two models.

 

## 8.8 DEPENDENCE MODELLING VIA COPULAE

In this section, we shall use ![d](images/c08-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> for the dimension of the underlying multivariate risks, and ![p](images/c08-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> for the critical level of the probability in context. Copulae are used to model and extract the dependence structure among marginal random variables in multivariate distribution functions. Mathematically speaking, a ![d](images/c08-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional copula is simply a ![d](images/c08-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional distribution function on the hyper-cube ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript d](images/c08-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></math> whose ![d](images/c08-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> marginal distributions follow a uniform distribution on ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c08-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. The main reason why copulae are relevant is due to the celebrated *Sklar's theorem* [\[41\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0041), which asserts that for any ![d](images/c08-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional joint distribution function ![upper F](images/c08-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> with marginal distributions ![upper F 1 comma ellipsis comma upper F Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, there always exists a ![d](images/c08-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional copula ![upper C colon left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript d Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> such that for any ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript d Baseline element-of double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>,

[(8.10)](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-disp-0041)![upper F left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper C left-parenthesis upper F 1 left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma upper F Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0041.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Such a copula is unique if all the marginal distributions are continuous; in this case, this unique copula in ([8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0041)) can be expressed explicitly as

(8.11)![upper C left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper F left-parenthesis upper F 1 Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma upper F Subscript d Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma for u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket period](images/c08-math-0042.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Equation ([8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0041)) demonstrates that the joint distribution function can always be decomposed into the underlying marginal distributions linked by a copula function. Hence the copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> captures all the information about how the marginal random variables depend on one another. This fact, that the copula fully reflects the dependence structure, is manifested by its invariance property: the copula remains the same upon any strictly increasing transformations of the marginal distributions. Conversely, for any copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> with ![d](images/c08-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> arguments and marginal distributions ![upper F 1 comma ellipsis comma upper F Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, the function on the right of ([8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0041)) defines a joint distribution function whose marginal distributions are ![upper F 1 comma ellipsis comma upper F Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, respectively. This fact gives us a useful way to construct multivariate distribution functions from given marginal distributions through various choices of copulae. Refer to [\[28](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0028), [31](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0031), [33](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0033), [35\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0035) for further discussions on the theoretical and practical aspects of copulae.

Apart from ([8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0041)) which relates the joint lower tail probability to a copula, one may also consider the upper tail counterpart, which can be formulated as follows. For any random vector ![bold x](images/c08-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>,

![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x 1 greater-than x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline greater-than x Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis equals ModifyingAbove upper C With caret left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove upper F With bar Subscript 1 Baseline left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma ModifyingAbove upper F With bar Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript d Baseline comma](images/c08-math-0043.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret](images/c08-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> is called the *survival copula* of ![bold x](images/c08-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, and ![upper F overbar Subscript i](images/c08-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the survival distribution of the random variable ![normal x Subscript i](images/c08-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d](images/c08-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></math>.

In finance, copulae have proven useful in various fields of finance, including but not limited to quantitative risk management, portfolio management and optimization, and pricing of financial derivatives. A typical example of its application is tests on the stress or robustness of companies, which played a particularly crucial role during the extreme downtime of economies in 2007–2008, when the global financial crisis struck. Besides, the estimation for loss distributions of various financial products, such as bonds and loans, also involve copulae as an important tool.

Many investors would exhibit the behavior known as *flight-to-quality* during bear markets, namely making a switch from the riskier equities or real estates to the “safer” cash or bonds for a refuge; as a result, they tend to get rid of most of the riskier assets within a short time, and that explains why dependencies across equities are stronger during a bear market than in a bull market, which could have disastrous effects on the overall economy; indeed, news on gigantic losses in millions in one day appears on financial headlines far more often than that on huge profits at the same level during a similar time span.

Next, we shall introduce several commonly used copulae.

**(I) Independence Copula**

The *independence copula* is arguably the simplest copula. As the name suggests, it corresponds to the situation where the marginal variables are independent of each other. This copula can be written as follows:

(8.12)![normal upper Pi left-parenthesis bold-italic u right-parenthesis equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript d Endscripts u Subscript i Baseline period](images/c08-math-0044.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

It is an elementary fact that random variables are independent if and only if their copula is the independence copula. Later in this section, we shall see that independence copula is also an Archimedean copula with the generator function ![psi left-parenthesis x comma theta right-parenthesis equals minus ln x](images/c08-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>x</mi></math>.

**(II) Gaussian Copula**

Suppose that ![upper F](images/c08-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> is a ![d](images/c08-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-variate normal distribution function with a mean vector ![bold-italic mu](images/c08-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and a covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c08-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math>. By the invariance property, its copula remains unchanged upon standardization, and so we may simply take ![bold-italic mu equals bold 0](images/c08-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math> and ![bold upper Sigma](images/c08-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> as its own corresponding correlation matrix ![bold-italic upper P Subscript rho](images/c08-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></math>. The *Gaussian copula* is defined as the copula of such a ![d](images/c08-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-variate normal distribution:

![upper C Subscript bold-italic upper P Sub Subscript rho Subscript Superscript Gauss Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic u right-parenthesis equals normal upper Phi Subscript bold-italic upper P Sub Subscript rho Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma for u Subscript i Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d comma](images/c08-math-0045.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext>Gauss</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal upper Phi Subscript bold-italic upper P Sub Subscript rho](images/c08-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> is the joint cdf of the ![d](images/c08-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-variate normal distribution with ![bold-italic mu equals bold 0](images/c08-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math> and the covariance matrix ![bold-italic upper P Subscript rho](images/c08-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></math>, and ![normal upper Phi](images/c08-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow></math> is the cdf of the standard normal distribution. The copula density can be found as follows:

where ![bold-italic z colon equals left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c08-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold-italic upper I Subscript d](images/c08-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> is the ![d times d](images/c08-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>d</mi></math> identity matrix.

The Gaussian copula was widely used in performing stress tests or credit risk analyses before 2008, but as the normal distribution would typically understate the probability of extreme losses, it has been argued that it contributed to the 2007–2008 Credit Crunch. Let us apply the Gaussian copula with empirical marginals to our stock data from `stock_1999_2002.csv` as an illustration.

![](images/c08-gra-0019.png)

In [Programme 8.17](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00017) using Python, we state that the library `copulae` will transform the data into *pseudo observations*, defined as ![nu Subscript i comma j Baseline colon equals rank left-parenthesis x Subscript i comma j Baseline right-parenthesis slash left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>rank</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c08-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> and ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma d](images/c08-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></math>, before fitting the model. In this programme we demonstrate this transformation via the `rankdata()` function from the `scipy` library. After we sample observations ![left-parenthesis nu Subscript i comma 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma nu Subscript i comma d Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> from the fitted Gaussian copula in `copulae`, we compute the empirical inverse of each marginal cdf with `pseudo_quantile()` to obtain component-wise simulated returns of ![ModifyingAbove upper F With caret Subscript j Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis nu Subscript i comma j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d](images/c08-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></math>.

From [Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0007), the plots are fitted by the sample generated by pseudo observations. All three Q-Q plots should be a perfect fit against the theoretical quantiles except for ties, such as in the middle portion of the plots where the return is zero. The same implementation is carried out in **R** through [Programme 8.18](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00018), with an illustration in [Figure 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0008).

Next, in [Programmes 8.19](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00019) via Python and 8.20 via **R**, we aim to fit a Gaussian copula for the dependence structure for three security stocks from `stock_1999_2002.csv`, while keeping the marginal distributions as the individual empirical distribution of each stock's relative price changes. Technically, we fit a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a zero mean vector and covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma equals bold-italic upper P Subscript rho](images/c08-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></math> by using a sample of ![left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis nu Subscript i comma 1 Baseline right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma normal upper Phi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis nu Subscript i comma d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0418.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c08-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> and ![d equals 3](images/c08-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. We also depict the random samples ![bold-italic nu](images/c08-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#957;</mi></mrow></math>'s in ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket cubed](images/c08-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math> and the simulated returns ![bold-italic u](images/c08-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math>'s generated by this fitted Gaussian copula dependence structure in [Figures 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0009) via Python and [8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010) via **R**.

![FIGURE 8.9 Plots from the fitted Gaussian copula in Python, generated by Programme 8.19.](images/c08f009.png)

 ![FIGURE 8.10 Plots from the fitted Gaussian copula in R, generated by Programme 8.20.](images/c08f010.png)

Finally, we consider a Q-Q plot of the empirical returns against the theoretical (actually, simulated) returns from the joint distribution with the fitted Gaussian copula for each stock. In [Programme 8.21](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00021) via Python, we lay down a function for drawing the Q-Q plot.

![](images/c08-gra-0024.png)

Furthermore, we build an auxiliary function `Mahalanobis2()` for computing the squared Mahalanobis distance introduced in (3.3). The main plotting function `QQ_Plot()` aims to plot a Q-Q plot between the parametrically bootstrapped theoretical quantiles from `sim_data` and the actual observations from `raw_data`. Using [Programme 8.22](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00022), we compare this Q-Q plot with the chi-square Q-Q plot depicted in [Section 3.3](#c03.xhtml#head-2-22), under the hypothesis that the returns follow a multivariate normal distribution.

![](images/c08-gra-0025.png)![](images/c08-gra-0026.png)![FIGURE 8.11 Q-Q plots generated in Programme 8.22.](images/c08f011.png)

[**FIGURE 8.11**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0011) Q-Q plots generated in [Programme 8.22](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00022).

 

From [Figure 8.11](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0011), we can see how the Gaussian copula, which fits the dependence structure but does not force the marginals to be normal, performs much better. Indeed, except for a dozen or so outliers, the joint distribution fitted with a Gaussian copula and empirical marginals can explain the joint changing behavior of the three stocks well on most of the fair weather days. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test does allow us to accept the goodness-of-fit of the Gaussian copula model but not the simple multivariate normality fitting. On the other hand, these outliers can be coped with by using the methods we have mentioned in the earlier sections of this chapter.

Similarly, we can carry out the whole procedure in **R** environment: firstly, the special function needed for drawing the Q-Q plot is built in [Programme 8.23](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00023). Finally, the Q-Q plots of the squared Mahalanobis distances are illustrated in [Figure 8.12](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0012). Note that the ![p](images/c08-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the KS test in the **R** output of [Programme 8.24](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00024) is actually the same as that in the Python output of [Programme 8.22](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00022), yet they display differently due to the mechanism in **R** that the minimum displayable positive number is `2.2e-16` (![2.2 times 1 0 Superscript negative 16](images/c08-i0425.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2.2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msup></math>).

![](images/c08-gra-0027.png)![](images/c08-gra-0028.png)

**(III)** ![bold-italic t](images/c08-i0426.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi></mrow></math>**\-copula**

A number of contemporary articles such as [\[9](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0009), [43\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0043) have shown that *Student's* ![t](images/c08-i0427.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>*\-copulae* can in general provide a better empirical fit for financial data than Gaussian copulae, mainly due to the domino effect when the underlying runs to extremes. Generally speaking, ![t](images/c08-i0428.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copulae can better capture the phenomenon of dependent extreme values which are often present in financial data such as returns. Recalling that the notation ![t Subscript nu Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the ![p](images/c08-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-quantile of Student's ![t](images/c08-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution with ![nu](images/c08-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom, the ![t](images/c08-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula with ![nu](images/c08-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> degrees of freedom is defined as: for ![u Subscript i Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma d](images/c08-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></math>,

Sigma](images/c08-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math>. The copula density can be shown to be:

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column c Subscript nu comma bold upper Sigma Superscript t Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic u right-parenthesis equals StartFraction f Subscript nu comma bold upper Sigma Superscript t Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis Over normal upper Pi Subscript i equals 1 Superscript d Baseline f Subscript nu Superscript t Baseline left-parenthesis t Subscript nu Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndFraction comma 2nd Column Blank EndLayout](images/c08-math-0048.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>&#957;</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where ![bold-italic z colon equals left-parenthesis t Subscript nu Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma t Subscript nu Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c08-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>&#957;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, and ![f Subscript nu Superscript t](images/c08-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> is the density function of the standard univariate Student's ![t](images/c08-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution with the same degrees of freedom ![nu](images/c08-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math>.

Let us fit a ![t](images/c08-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula to the financial data in `stock_1999_2002.csv` through [Programme 8.25](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00025) via Python with the `copulae` library. The procedure of finding the parameters of the best-fit ![t](images/c08-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula is essentially the same as that for the Gaussian copula, and so we leave it as an exercise for readers. Again we depict the random samples ![bold-italic nu](images/c08-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#957;</mi></mrow></math>'s in ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket cubed](images/c08-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math> and the simulated returns ![bold-italic u](images/c08-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math>'s, generated by the joint distribution with this fitted ![t](images/c08-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula, in [Figure 8.13](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0013).

![](images/c08-gra-0029.png)![](images/c08-gra-0030.png) ![FIGURE 8.13 Plots from the fitted t-copula in Python, generated by Programme 8.25.](images/c08f013.png)

[**FIGURE 8.13**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0013) Plots from the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula in Python, generated by [Programme 8.25](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00025).

![FIGURE 8.14 Plots from the fitted t-copula via R, generated in Programme 8.26.](images/c08f014.png)

[**FIGURE 8.14**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0014) Plots from the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula via **R**, generated in [Programme 8.26](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00026).

 

Similarly, we implement the same procedure in [Programme 8.26](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00026) via **R** with an illustration in [Figure 8.14](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0014).

![](images/c08-gra-0031.png) ![FIGURE 8.15 Q-Q plots of the empirical squared Mahalanobis distances against those bootstrapped estimates from the fitted t-copula of HSBC, CLP, and CK in Python.](images/c08f015.png)

[**FIGURE 8.15**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0015) Q-Q plots of the empirical squared Mahalanobis distances against those bootstrapped estimates from the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula of HSBC, CLP, and CK in Python.

Next, we shall plot the Q-Q plot for the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula, first by using Python in [Programme 8.27](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00027) and then by using **R** in [Programme 8.28](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00028). In [Figure 8.15](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0015), we also depict the Q-Q plots of the empirical squared Mahalanobis distances against the corresponding bootstrapped quantile estimates from the joint distribution with the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula. From the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, we can see the goodness-of-fit of the ![t](images/c08-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula model, noting it has a larger ![p](images/c08-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value than the Gaussian copula.

![](images/c08-gra-0032.png)![](images/c08-gra-0033.png)![](images/c08-gra-0034.png)

Lastly, we inspect the goodness-of-fit of the Gaussian and ![t](images/c08-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula models by using a Q-Q plot of the empirical squared Mahalanobis distances, and the plot of squared differences of the squared Mahalanobis distances off from the 45-degree reference line. For ease of comparison, we consider quantiles larger than 15 separately in the Q-Q plot and plot the largest 50 squared residuals, excluding the one with the largest value. We implement this comparison in [Programmes 8.29](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00029) via Python and [8.30](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00030) via **R**.

![](images/c08-gra-0035.png)![](images/c08-gra-0036.png)![](images/c08-gra-0037.png)

From [Figures 8.16](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0016) via Python and [8.17](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0017) via **R**, the line of best fit for the ![t](images/c08-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula model is closer to the 45-degree reference line than that for the Gaussian copula model, which indicates that the ![t](images/c08-i0462.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula fits better with the dataset. On the other hand, the squared differences under the fitted ![t](images/c08-i0463.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula model are mostly very slightly smaller than those obtained from the fitted Gaussian copula model. In particular, from both the Q-Q plots and the plots of squared differences, the largest quantile has the largest deviation from the 45-degree reference line; for the Gaussian copula this entry deviates more heavily than for the ![t](images/c08-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula. This observation indicates that ![t](images/c08-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula is indeed more capable of capturing extremal events than Gaussian copula, especially useful for periods like the 2007–2008 Credit Crunch.

 ![FIGURE 8.16 Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and t-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 1999 to 2002 using Python, generated by Programme 8.29.](images/c08f016.png)

[**FIGURE 8.16**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0016) Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and ![t](images/c08-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 1999 to 2002 using Python, generated by [Programme 8.29](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00029).

 ![FIGURE 8.17 Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and t-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 1999 to 2002 using R, generated by Programme 8.30.](images/c08f017.png)

[**FIGURE 8.17**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0017) Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and ![t](images/c08-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 1999 to 2002 using **R**, generated by [Programme 8.30](#c08.xhtml#c08-gra-00030).

Indeed, let us examine the goodness-of-fit of the Gaussian copula and the ![t](images/c08-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula models during the 2007–2008 Credit Crunch period via the dataset `stock_2006_2009.csv`, which records the adjusted closing prices of HSBC, CLP, and CK from 2006 to 2009. From [Figures 8.18](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0018) via Python and [8.19](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0019) via **R**, the largest 50 squared differences under the Gaussian copula model are generally slightly smaller than those under the ![t](images/c08-i0467.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copula model; however they also have much heavier tail sample values. In particular, as expected, on fair weather days, Gaussian copulae perform well for fitting financial return data, while ![t](images/c08-i0468.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-copulae handle extreme values better. During the 2007–2008 Credit Crunch, the volatilities of the stock prices increased sharply and these prices plummeted drastically, leading to more extreme returns compared to those during normal periods.

 ![FIGURE 8.18 Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and t-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 2006 to 2009 using Python, generated by Programme 8.29.](images/c08f018.png)

 ![FIGURE 8.19 Q-Q plot and the plot of squared differences for the fitted Gaussian copula and t-copula models for the returns of HSBC, CLP, and CK over the period of 2006 to 2009 using R, generated by Programme 8.30.](images/c08f019.png)

**(IV) Comonotonic Copula**

The *comonotonic copula* is given by

(8.14)![upper M left-parenthesis bold-italic u right-parenthesis colon equals min left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis comma for u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket period](images/c08-math-0049.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

It corresponds to the case of extremal positive dependence (sometimes called *complete dependence*). The random variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0471.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> have the comonotonic copula if and only if they are increasing transformations of a common source of randomness in the sense that ![x Subscript i Baseline equals f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis normal w right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0472.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>x</mtext><mtext>i</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for every ![i](images/c08-i0473.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, there is an increasing function ![f Subscript i Baseline colon double-struck upper R right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0474.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, and ![normal w](images/c08-i0475.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">w</mi></mrow></math> is a common random variable.

**(V) Upper Tail Comonotonic Copula⁵**

Despite its simplicity and nice analytical tractability, global comonotonicity over the whole domain of definition is too restrictive and has limited scope of application in quantitative finance and risk management. Nevertheless, comonotonicity happening only at the extreme upper tail is a far more realistic modelling choice and this leads us to consider the prevalent notion of *upper tail comonotonicity*, in which the survival copula ![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret](images/c08-i0476.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> satisfies:

![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove upper F With bar Subscript 1 Baseline left-parenthesis x 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma ModifyingAbove upper F With bar Subscript d Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals min left-brace right-brace comma comma of FF bar 1 left-parenthesis right-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma of FF bar d left-parenthesis right-parenthesis xd](images/c08-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#125;</mo></math> 

only for all sufficiently large values of ![x Subscript i](images/c08-i0477.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s. Copulae having this property regardless of the marginal distributions should behave in such a way that

![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis almost-equals min left-brace right-brace comma comma u 1 comma ellipsis comma ud comma](images/c08-math-0051.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

for all sufficiently small values of ![u Subscript i](images/c08-i0478.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s. In addition, to ensure mathematical tractability and facilitate its practical implementation, it is appealing to impose further regularity conditions on ![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret](images/c08-i0479.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math>. One reasonable requirement is scaling invariance, in the sense of a comparable rate of convergence with respect to ![u Subscript i](images/c08-i0480.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s, namely:

![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret left-parenthesis u w 1 comma ellipsis comma u w Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis tilde min left-brace right-brace comma comma times times uw 1 comma ellipsis comma times times uwd comma u down-arrow 0 comma for any w 1 comma ellipsis comma w Subscript d Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0052.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>u</mi><mi>&#8595;</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for any</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

These considerations lead us to define upper tail comonotonicity (cf. [\[26\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0026)) as follows. A random vector ![bold x](images/c08-i0481.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> with a copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0482.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and a survival copula ![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret](images/c08-i0483.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> is said to be *upper tail comonotonic* if for any ![w 1 comma ellipsis comma w Subscript d Baseline element-of left-bracket 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>,

![limit Underscript u down-arrow 0 Endscripts StartFraction ModifyingAbove upper C With caret left-parenthesis u w 1 comma ellipsis comma u w Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis Over u EndFraction equals min left-brace right-brace comma comma w 1 comma ellipsis comma wd period](images/c08-math-0053.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>&#8595;</mi><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>u</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#125;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Such a copula ![ModifyingAbove upper C With caret](images/c08-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> is then said to be an *upper tail comonotonic copula*.

Upper tail comonotonicity is closely connected to the asymptotic additivity of Value-at-Risk. Consider a portfolio of ![d](images/c08-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> loss variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>. We aim to examine the Value-at-Risk of the aggregate loss ![normal s equals normal x 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus normal x Subscript d](images/c08-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>. Suppose that for some ![1 less-than-or-equal-to m less-than-or-equal-to d](images/c08-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi></math>, ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript m Baseline element-of MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Subscript alpha Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0490.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>

1.  ![normal x Subscript j Baseline element-of MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Subscript alpha prime Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0494.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>⁶ with ![alpha prime greater-than alpha](images/c08-i0495.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></math>;
2.  ![normal x Subscript j Baseline element-of MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Lamda right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0496.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>⁶;
3.  ![normal x Subscript j](images/c08-i0497.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> has a finite endpoint.

Under the above setting, our recent work [\[11\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0011) establishes that Value-at-Risk is asymptotically additive for such portfolios:

(8.15)![upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal s right-parenthesis tilde sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript d Endscripts upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis p up-arrow 1 period](images/c08-math-0054.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>p</mi><mi>&#8593;</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Moreover, there are two other scenarios where such asymptotic additivity of Value-at-Risk remains true:

1.  The non-negative random variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript m Baseline](images/c08-i0498.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> are in ![MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Lamda right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0499.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>⁶ with infinite endpoints and they are upper tail comonotonic, while other non-negative ![normal x Subscript m plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0500.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> have finite endpoints.
2.  All the non-negative random variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0501.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> have finite endpoints and they are upper tail comonotonic.

**(VI) Archimedean Copulae**

Archimedean copulae form an associative class of copulae. Explicit formulae are readily available for most commonly used Archimedean copulae, while this is not the case for other classes of copulae such as the commonly used Gaussian copula. Besides, Archimedean copulae can be easily used to model dependent risks in an arbitrarily high dimension, which is another reason of their popularity in practice.

A copula ![upper C Subscript upper A r c h i m e d e a n](images/c08-i0502.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> is called *Archimedean* if it admits the following representation:

[(8.16)](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-disp-0055)![upper C Subscript upper A r c h i m e d e a n Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic u semicolon theta right-parenthesis equals psi Superscript left-bracket negative 1 right-bracket Baseline left-parenthesis psi left-parenthesis u 1 semicolon theta right-parenthesis plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus psi left-parenthesis u Subscript d Baseline semicolon theta right-parenthesis semicolon theta right-parenthesis comma](images/c08-math-0055.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket times normal upper Theta contains-as-member left-parenthesis u comma theta right-parenthesis right-arrow from bar psi left-parenthesis u comma theta right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0503.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mi>&#8715;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8614;</mo><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a continuous, strictly decreasing and convex function in ![u](images/c08-i0504.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> such that ![psi left-parenthesis 1 semicolon theta right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c08-i0505.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, ![theta](images/c08-i0506.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is a parameter within some parameter space ![normal upper Theta](images/c08-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math> governing the underlying dependence of multivariate risks; ![psi](images/c08-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#968;</mi></mrow></math> is often called the *generator function* and ![psi Superscript left-bracket negative 1 right-bracket](images/c08-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></math> is its *pseudo-inverse* defined by

![psi Superscript left-bracket negative 1 right-bracket Baseline left-parenthesis t semicolon theta right-parenthesis colon equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column psi Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis t semicolon theta right-parenthesis comma 2nd Column if 0 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to psi left-parenthesis 0 semicolon theta right-parenthesis semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column 0 comma 2nd Column if psi left-parenthesis 0 semicolon theta right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to infinity period EndLayout](images/c08-math-0056.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>if&#160;&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>if&#160;&#160;</mtext><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Moreover, the above formula ([8.16](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0055)) for ![upper C Subscript upper A r c h i m e d e a n](images/c08-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> yields a copula for ![psi Superscript left-bracket negative 1 right-bracket](images/c08-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></math> if and only if ![psi Superscript left-bracket negative 1 right-bracket Baseline equals psi Superscript negative 1](images/c08-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> is ![d](images/c08-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-monotone on ![left-bracket 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, meaning that if it is ![d minus 2](images/c08-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> times differentiable and its derivatives satisfy the following inequalities (closely related to the notion of completely monotone functions):

![left-parenthesis negative 1 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline left-parenthesis psi Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis t semicolon theta right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0 comma](images/c08-math-0057.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

for all ![t greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c08-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![k equals 0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma d minus 2](images/c08-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, while ![left-parenthesis negative 1 right-parenthesis Superscript d minus 2 Baseline left-parenthesis psi Superscript negative 1 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript left-parenthesis d minus 2 right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis t semicolon infinity right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is also non-increasing and convex.

The class of Archimedean copulae is broad and covers many commonly used copulae as special cases. Below is a partial list; more examples can be found in [Table 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0001) of [\[35\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0035).

1.  *Ali–Mikhail–Haq* family: introduced in [\[2\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0002), the generator of this family is given by ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals ln left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 minus theta Over t EndFraction plus theta right-parenthesis comma theta element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0058.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 
2.  *Clayton* family: introduced in [\[13\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0013), the generator of this family is given by
    
    ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over theta EndFraction left-parenthesis t Superscript negative theta Baseline minus 1 right-parenthesis comma theta element-of left-bracket negative 1 comma infinity right-parenthesis minus StartSet 0 EndSet period](images/c08-math-0059.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#952;</mi></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8726;</mo><mo>&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#125;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 
    
    The function inverse of this generator function is the Laplace transform of a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter ![1 slash theta](images/c08-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></math> and a scale parameter ![theta](images/c08-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, thus the Clayton copula model has a *Gamma-distributed frailty representation* [\[42\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0042).
    
3.  *Frank* family: first appeared in [\[20\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0020), the generator of this family is given by
    
    ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals minus ln left-parenthesis StartFraction e Superscript minus theta t Baseline minus 1 Over e Superscript negative theta Baseline minus 1 EndFraction right-parenthesis comma theta element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma infinity right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0060.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 
    
    In the bivariate case, it is the only Archimedean family which is *radially symmetric*, meaning that its copula and survival copula are the same.
    
4.  *Gumbel* family: introduced in [\[24\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024), the generator of this family is given by ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis minus ln left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript theta Baseline comma theta element-of left-bracket 1 comma infinity right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0061.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 
5.  *Joe* family: discussed in [\[29](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0029), [30\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0030), the generator of this family is given by ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals minus ln left-parenthesis 1 minus left-parenthesis 1 minus t right-parenthesis Superscript theta Baseline right-parenthesis comma theta element-of left-bracket 1 comma infinity right-parenthesis period](images/c08-math-0062.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Note that for all five families, a larger value of the parameter ![theta](images/c08-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> indicates a stronger dependence; all (except the Frank copula) reduce to the independence copula when ![theta](images/c08-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> takes the minimum value in the respective ranges, while for the Frank copula, the limiting case with ![theta](images/c08-i0523.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> approaching 0 corresponds to the independence copula. The scatter plots for the bivariate case of these five copula families, each based on 2,000 simulated points, are depicted in [Figures 8.20](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0020) and [8.21](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0021).

Knowing all of the above, we examine the asymptotic behaviour of the Value-at-Risk, as the probability level approaches 1, of the aggregate loss of a portfolio of risks ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0524.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> whose dependence is given by an Archimedean copula. More precisely, we assume that
