Let us present several numerical examples to illustrate these claims. We consider a Clayton copula with the parameter ![theta equals 1](images/c08-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, whose generator is given by ![psi left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis equals t Superscript negative 1 Baseline minus 1](images/c08-i0561.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We use the **R** package `copula` to simulate the Clayton copula with some given marginals. By generating ![1 0 Superscript 7](images/c08-i0562.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>7</mn></msup></math> data points from the corresponding joint distributions, we plot the V@R ratios of ![StartFraction upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal s right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript d Endscripts upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c08-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> in the ![y](images/c08-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>\-axis against the probability level ![p](images/c08-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> in the ![x](images/c08-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>\-axis, with ![d equals 2 comma 5](images/c08-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. Illustrations for various scenarios are depicted in [Figures 8.22](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0022) to [8.24](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0024).

**(VII) Extreme-value Copulae**

Finally, we introduce the family of extreme-value copulae, whose first construction dates back to [\[15](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0015), [22\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0022). A copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is called an *extreme-value copula* if there exists a copula ![upper C Subscript upper F](images/c08-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></math> such that

![left-parenthesis upper C Subscript upper F Baseline left-parenthesis u 1 Superscript 1 slash n Baseline comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Superscript 1 slash n Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript n Baseline right-arrow upper C left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis as n right-arrow infinity comma](images/c08-math-0068.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>as</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

for all ![left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript d](images/c08-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></math>. The copula ![upper C Subscript upper F](images/c08-i0578.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></math> is said to be in the *domain of attraction* of the copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0579.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. A closely related concept is *max-stability:* a ![d](images/c08-i0580.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional copula ![upper C](images/c08-i0581.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is *max-stable* if it satisfies

![upper C left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis upper C left-parenthesis u 1 Superscript 1 slash m Baseline comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Superscript 1 slash m Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis Superscript m Baseline comma](images/c08-math-0069.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>C</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

for all integers ![m greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c08-i0582.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and all ![left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript d](images/c08-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></math>. A max-stable copula is clearly in its own domain of attraction, and hence it is an extreme-value copula itself. Indeed, these two notions are equivalent: a copula is an extreme-value copula if and only if it is max-stable. To see that extreme-value copulae are also max-stable, let ![upper C](images/c08-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> be an extreme-value copula, and consider a fixed integer ![m greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c08-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and take ![n equals m k](images/c08-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></math>. On the one hand, there is another copula ![upper C Subscript upper F](images/c08-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></math> such that when ![k right-arrow infinity](images/c08-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> and so ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c08-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>,

on the other hand,

as ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c08-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>. Therefore, ![upper C](images/c08-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is max-stable.

We next introduce some common examples of extreme-value copulae.

1.  *Gumbel–Hougaard* copula (Logistic Model): This copula is both an Archimedean copula, with a generator of ![psi left-parenthesis t comma theta right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis minus ln t right-parenthesis Superscript theta](images/c08-i0592.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></msup></math>, and an extreme-value copula. In general, it is defined as ![upper C left-parenthesis u 1 comma ellipsis comma u Subscript d Baseline semicolon alpha right-parenthesis equals exp left-bracket minus left-parenthesis left-parenthesis minus ln u 1 right-parenthesis Superscript alpha Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus left-parenthesis minus ln u Subscript d Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript alpha Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 1 slash alpha Baseline right-bracket comma](images/c08-math-0072.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> where ![alpha greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c08-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The parameter ![alpha](images/c08-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> measures the degree of dependence, ranging from independence with ![alpha equals 1](images/c08-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> to complete dependence (corresponding to the comonotonic compula) when ![alpha equals infinity](images/c08-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>.

When ![alpha right-arrow infinity](images/c08-i0598.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, it refers to complete dependence, corresponding to the comonotonic copula; while when ![alpha right-arrow 0](images/c08-i0599.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, it refers to independence. This multivariate extreme value copula was obtained by [\[21\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0021) as an extreme value limit, just as in ([8.17](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0078)) but for the multivariate case of the multivariate Pareto distribution; also see [\[31\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0031) for more discussions. In the extreme value literature, such as [\[14\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0014), this copula is sometimes called the *negative logistic model*.

 ![FIGURE 8.25 Scatter plots of some extreme-value copulae in R.](images/c08f025.png)

[**FIGURE 8.25**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0025) Scatter plots of some extreme-value copulae in **R**.

The scatter plots of 1,000 observation samples generated by these five copulae for selected parameter values are illustrated in [Figures 8.25](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0025) and [8.26](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0026).

Finally, we have a similar asymptotic result for V@R under extreme-value copulae as that under Archimedean copulae. When the loss variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript d Baseline](images/c08-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> have an *identical distribution* and their dependence is given by an extreme-value copula, [\[10\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0010) established the following results concerning the Value-at-Risk of the aggregate loss ![normal s equals normal x 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus normal x Subscript d](images/c08-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> when the probability level approaches 1:

1.  If ![normal x 1 element-of MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Subscript beta Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>&#946;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi></mrow></math> is (i) asymptotically subadditive when ![beta greater-than 1](images/c08-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; (ii) asymptotically superadditive when ![beta less-than 1](images/c08-i0620.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; and (iii) asymptotically additive when ![beta equals 1](images/c08-i0621.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.
2.  If ![normal x 1 element-of MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Lamda right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0622.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with an infinite right endpoint, then ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0623.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi></mrow></math> is asymptotically subadditive.
3.  If ![normal x 1](images/c08-i0624.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> has a finite endpoint, then ![upper V commercial-at upper R](images/c08-i0625.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi></mrow></math> is asymptotically additive.

 ![FIGURE 8.26 Scatter plots of some extreme-value copulae in R (continued).](images/c08f026.png)

[**FIGURE 8.26**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0026) Scatter plots of some extreme-value copulae in **R** (continued).

We use the **R** package `evd` to simulate the extreme-value copula with some given marginals. As an example, we generate ![1 0 Superscript 7](images/c08-i0626.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>7</mn></msup></math> data points from the corresponding distributions, and plot the V@R ratios of ![StartFraction upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal s right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript d Endscripts upper V commercial-at upper R Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c08-i0627.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">V@R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> with given marginals under the Gumbel–Hougaard copula. In our simulation study, we simply set ![alpha equals 1.5](images/c08-i0628.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.5</mn></math>. See [Figures 8.27](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0027)–[8.29](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0029) for the illustrations.

It is believed that the above claims, 1) to 3), remain valid by and large, even for heterogeneous distributions and when the dependence structures among the variables are modelled by general copulae exhibiting certain kinds of positive dependence, and this would be an interesting future research project.

Last but not least, we give a brief introduction to the trendy *vine copula*, which has found extensive use in finance, such as for the effective modelling of tail risk in portfolio optimization applications (see [\[1\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0001) for detailed discussions). A *vine* is a graphical tool used to label constraints in high-dimensional probability distributions. It is a nested set of connected trees, where the edges in one tree become the nodes of the next tree to be built. As a special case in which all constraints are two-dimensional or conditional two-dimensional, regular vines (a.k.a. R-vines) get more popular since the computation of joint probabilities is carried out in a sequential pairwise manner. Indeed, when the constraints are associated with conditional bivariate copulae, we impose the vine copula, such that any multivariate density can be represented as a product of marginal densities and conditional copula densities on an R-vine. One can interpret vine copulae as copulae that characterize the dependence structures among clusters of random variables. To this end, the *Comonotone-Independence Bayes classifier* (CIBer), which we shall introduce in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml), can be regarded as a special case of vine copula, in that the dependence structures there are handled in an all-or-nothing manner, namely either comonotonicity or independence. Due to space limitations, we shall not present its formulation and applications in detail.

## \*8.A APPENDIX

  

### \*8.A.1 A Quick Review of Extreme Value Theory

In [Section 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0012), we introduced a basic fact in Extreme Value Theory (EVT) that the generalized Pareto distribution is the limit of the tail conditional distributions of a large class of distributions. In this appendix, we present a more comprehensive overview of some other related results in EVT. They are relevant to the discussion on the asymptotic behaviour of Value-at-Risk in [Section 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0015). For a thorough discussion of EVT, one can also refer to [\[25](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0025), [40\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0040).

Let ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript n Baseline](images/c08-i0629.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> be iid non-degenerate random variables and denote their maximum by ![normal upper M Subscript n Baseline colon equals max left-brace right-brace comma comma x 1 comma ellipsis comma xn](images/c08-i0630.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#125;</mo></math>. Two distribution functions ![upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper G left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0632.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are said to be of the *same type* if there exist ![a greater-than 0](images/c08-i0633.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![b element-of double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0634.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> such that ![upper F left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals upper G left-parenthesis a x plus b right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0635.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for all ![x element-of double-struck upper R](images/c08-i0636.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>. These three distribution functions are called *extreme value distributions*. These three MDAs cover most of the distributions that are of interest in finance, insurance, and quantitative risk management. For instance, the distributions in ![MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Phi Subscript alpha Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0650.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> include Cauchy, Pareto, Burr, Stable with index ![alpha less-than 2](images/c08-i0651.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and log-gamma distributions; the distributions in ![MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Lamda right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0652.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> include exponential-like, Weibull-like, gamma, normal, lognormal, exponential behaviour at a finite point ![x Subscript upper F Baseline less-than infinity](images/c08-i0653.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, *Benktander-type I* and *Benktander-type II* distributions; the distributions in ![MDA left-parenthesis normal upper Psi Subscript alpha Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0654.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>MDA</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> include uniform, power law behaviour at a finite point ![x Subscript upper F Baseline less-than infinity](images/c08-i0655.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> and beta distributions. # PART Two  
Linear Models

# CHAPTER 9  
Principal Component Analysis and Recommender Systems

 

*Principal Component Analysis* (PCA) is a classical multivariate statistical technique for a dimension reduction of an underlying set of random variables. It is used to find linear combinations of original variables such that the information in the original data is “essentially” preserved even after the reduction. As a generalization, the collaborative filtering approach in recommender systems is used to preserve the essential information contained in a two‐dimensional array of random numbers. Before we go into its details, we first look at an interesting application of PCA to identify the important factors explaining the term structure of interest rates extracted from the USA bonds market.

 

## 9.1 US ZERO‐COUPON RATES

The file `us‐rate.csv`, of sample size ![n equals 588](images/c09-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>588</mn></math>, contains US zero‐coupon rates

First note that these ![p equals 13](images/c09-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math> variables are highly correlated. This suggests that it is very likely we can use only a few variables (say two or three) to represent the whole dataset without losing a significant amount of information, which is exactly the goal of dimension reduction. A natural question to ask is which variables should we use such that they can contain as much information in the dataset as possible? An immediate answer is not from any of these original variables but linear combinations of them; indeed, let the original variables be ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline](images/c09-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>, we first look for a new variable

mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. The latter condition means that ![bold-italic h 1](images/c09-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold-italic h 2](images/c09-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are *orthogonal* to each other (or equivalently, ![normal y 1](images/c09-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal y 2](images/c09-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are statistically uncorrelated

The third PC can be found similarly, and the process can continue up to the last ![p](images/c09-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐th PC. This gives the basic idea of PCA and the optimization procedure has a nice solution via linear algebra. In particular, it turns out that these loadings are the *normalized eigenvectors*, denoted by ![bold-italic h Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis h Subscript 1 j Baseline comma ellipsis comma h Subscript p j Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, for ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c09-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, for the ![j](images/c09-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th PC, of the correlation matrix or the variance‐covariance matrix of ![bold x](images/c09-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and the variance of ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, the ![j](images/c09-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th PC, is the corresponding *eigenvalue* ![lamda Subscript j Baseline equals upper V a r left-parenthesis normal y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals bold-italic h Subscript j Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper S bold-italic h Subscript j](images/c09-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. This claim is discussed in detail in [Appendix \*9.A.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0017), while readers may refer back to [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007) of [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) for the basic theory of spectral decomposition.

The reason for maximizing the variance of the transformed variable ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> is that we want to preserve as much information in these ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline](images/c09-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> as possible. Conceptually, variation represents information, and so we want the variances of the linearly transformed variables to be as large as possible, also “as soon as possible”, so that the original information in ![bold x](images/c09-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is preserved. The ![j](images/c09-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th eigenvalue ![lamda Subscript j Baseline equals upper V a r left-parenthesis normal y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> indicates the amount of information retained in the ![j](images/c09-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th PC.

 

## 9.2 PCA ALGORITHM

PCA is implemented in Python through the `PCA()` function in the `sklearn` library; while in **R** it is implemented by the built‐in function `princomp()`. First let us continue the US zero‐coupon rates example in [Programmes 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3003) and [9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3004) for Python and **R**, respectively. Throughout this section and the next, for the sake of illustration, we shall treat the standardized random variables ![normal x overTilde Subscript i Baseline colon equals StartFraction normal x Subscript i Baseline minus double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over StartRoot upper V a r left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndRoot EndFraction](images/c09-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math>, ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 13](images/c09-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn></math> as the original variables, and denote ![bold x overTilde colon equals left-parenthesis normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. Note that this standardization may not be necessary when observations of the variables share a similar order of magnitude.

From the output, the first and second PCs are

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column normal y 1 2nd Column equals 0.2732 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus 0.2729 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline equals bold-italic h 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column normal y 2 2nd Column equals 0.4043 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis minus 0.4438 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline equals bold-italic h 2 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde comma EndLayout](images/c09-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2732</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.2729</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8868;</mo></msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4043</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.4438</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8868;</mo></msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

respectively. However, for the third PC, we observe the loadings generated in Python are exactly the negative of those given in **R**. Notice that the unit norm eigenvectors ![bold-italic h Subscript i](images/c09-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are only confined by the conditions that ![bold-italic h Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c09-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (of unit length) and ![bold-italic h Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h Subscript j Baseline equals 0](images/c09-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> (being orthogonal) for ![i not-equals j](images/c09-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></math>. Therefore, these loadings can be presented by their negative counterpart. It is easy to illustrate that ![bold-italic h 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h 1 equals bold-italic h 2 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h 2 equals 1](images/c09-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![bold-italic h 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h 2 equals 0](images/c09-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; also see [Programmes 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3005) for Python and [9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3006) for **R**.

PCA aims at dimension reduction in variables, i.e. we want to represent this `us‐rate.csv` dataset with only a few variables. How many PCs should we use? Before answering this question, let us first look at the variance of these PCs.

From the output in [Programme 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3008) via **R**, we know that the variance of the first PC is 12.7239, and so on; while in [Programme 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3007) via Python, it computes the variance of the sample instead of sample variance, hence these variances are slightly different from those obtained in **R** by a factor of ![left-parenthesis n minus 1 right-parenthesis slash n equals 587 slash 588](images/c09-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>587</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>588</mn></math>. By Property 25 in [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007), we see that the total variance is equal to ![trace left-parenthesis bold-italic upper S right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the trace of ![bold-italic upper S](images/c09-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math>. Note that in our example, all the diagonal elements of ![bold-italic upper S](images/c09-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> are equal to 1 after standardization, hence their sum, the total variance, is simply equal to ![p equals 13](images/c09-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>.

Based on the **R** output, the first PC explained 12.7239/13 = 97.88% of the total variance of 13. The second PC explained 1.83%, the third PC explained 0.19%, and so on. The first PC already captured almost all (![almost-equals](images/c09-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8776;</mo></mrow></math> 97.88%) the information (of the total variance). Even if we only include the first three PCs, 99.90% of all the information is already captured! A plot of variance values (called a *Scree Plot*, “scree” meaning large loose broken “gems”) can help us determine the suitable number of PCs to be used. This plot graphically represents the information retained in each PC graphically; see [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001) generated by [Programmes 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3009) in Python and [9.10](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3010) in **R**.

![FIGURE 9.1 Scree plots of the US rates example.](images/c09f001.png)

[**FIGURE 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0001) Scree plots of the US rates example.

For most applications, we can look at the scree plot to determine the number of PCs to be used. In this US rate example, we can just use the first PC to represent all the 13 variables. However, the first three PCs altogether have more interesting interpretations so that we may want to use these to represent the term structure of the 13 US zero‐coupon rates.

To further elucidate how much information we lose by only using the first few PCs, based on the general theory for PCA given in [Appendix \*9.A.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0017) we note that all ![normal y Subscript i](images/c09-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are orthogonal to each other. Indeed, by spectral decomposition, ![bold-italic upper S equals bold-italic upper H bold-italic upper D bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> and ![bold y equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde](images/c09-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></math>,

![Cov left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis equals Cov left-parenthesis bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde right-parenthesis equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline Cov left-parenthesis bold x overTilde right-parenthesis bold-italic upper H equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper H bold-italic upper D bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper H equals bold-italic upper D comma](images/c09-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, and so all off‐diagonal elements vanished, i.e. ![Cov left-parenthesis normal y Subscript i Baseline comma normal y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c09-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Cov</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, for ![i not-equals j](images/c09-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></math>. Note that in [Section 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0002), we defined ![bold-italic h Subscript j Baseline equals left-parenthesis h Subscript 1 j Baseline comma ellipsis comma h Subscript p j Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> such that ![bold-italic upper H equals left-parenthesis h Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold y equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde](images/c09-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></math>; Clearly, ![bold-italic upper H](images/c09-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow></math> is orthogonal such that ![bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper H equals bold-italic upper H bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline equals bold-italic upper I Subscript p](images/c09-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>, hence ![sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript p Endscripts h Subscript i j Superscript 2 Baseline equals 1](images/c09-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> with ![h Subscript i j Superscript 2 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c09-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. This provides an interesting and useful application of PCA to approximate the Value‐at‐Risk of a portfolio and immunizes the portfolio from various risk factors arising in markets; see [Sections 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0006), [9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0007), and [9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0008).

 

## 9.3 FINANCIAL INTERPRETATION OF PCS FOR US ZERO‐COUPON RATES

Let us plot the first three PCs in Python with [Programme 9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3015) and in **R** with [Programme 9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3016).

Identifying these principal components is important for understanding the term structure of interest rates. Many investment instruments are very sensitive to the movement of interest rates, including stocks, bonds, forward contracts and currency swaps. Knowledge of these principal components is very useful in valuating these instruments.

Recall that the first PC is

![normal y 1 equals 0.2732 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus 0.2729 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2732</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.2729</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math> ![FIGURE 9.2 Loadings of h Subscript i j's for the first three principal components of the US rates example.](images/c09f002.png)

[**FIGURE 9.2**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0002) Loadings of ![h Subscript i j](images/c09-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s for the first three principal components of the US rates example.

whose loadings are almost constant at the level of 0.27 for bond rates of all maturity times. In fact, these loadings are not unique. They are unique only up to a positive or negative sign. That is, we can define a new first PC as ![normal y 1 equals minus left-parenthesis 0.2732 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus 0.2729 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.2732</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.2729</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> whose variance is the same at that of the old one. This PC is interpreted as a *parallel shift* (caused by a “level” shock for example) of the yield curve, and explains the majority of the variances of all bonds. To explain this parallel shift, we refer to a shift in the economic environment caused by some major macroeconomic event, so that the rates of returns for all zero‐coupon bonds with different maturities contribute equally to this principal component representing an average effect. On the other hand, ![normal x overTilde Subscript i Baseline almost-equals h Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline normal y 1](images/c09-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8776;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, so each bond rate is equally affected by the first PC.

The second PC is

![normal y 2 equals 0.4043 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis minus 0.4438 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4043</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.4438</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the loadings are decreasing with maturity. Again, the loadings are not unique. In particular, the alternative second PC could be ![normal y 2 equals minus 0.4043 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline minus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus 0.4438 normal x overTilde Subscript 13](images/c09-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.4043</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.4438</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub></math>, which seems more reasonable since it agrees with *liquidity preference theory*. This theory states that investors prefer to preserve their liquidity and invest in investment vehicles that last for a shorter period of time, and so additional premiums are paid for holding securities with longer time of maturity. This second component is therefore termed as the *tilt* component of the yield curve.

The third PC is

![normal y 3 equals 0.5976 normal x overTilde Subscript 1 Baseline plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus 0.4082 normal x overTilde Subscript 13 Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5976</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.4082</mn><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

whose loadings decrease with maturity up to a certain point and then start increasing again with maturity. This can be interpreted as the *curvature* of the yield curve, which is caused by the higher demand on the relatively short‐term and relatively long‐term bonds. Indeed, the market for short‐term bonds is popular with frequent traders in securities, derivatives and insurance markets, while bonds of longer terms are welcomed by long‐term market participants including insurance and reinsurance companies. Short‐term and long‐term bonds can be used for immunization of interest rate risk for investment vehicles and liabilities of intermediate lifespans, contributing to the convexity in the loadings of this third PC. That said, its eigenvalue (and also variance) is much smaller than those of the first and second PCs, because of the relatively small proportion that insurance markets take up in the entire financial industry; we refer to [Appendix \*9.A.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0020) for a rationale behind this observation.

The original data can be expressed approximately in terms of ![normal y 1](images/c09-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![normal y 2](images/c09-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![normal y 3](images/c09-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> by using the loadings of PC1, PC2 and PC3 in light of the fact that ![bold y equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x overTilde](images/c09-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></math>. These ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s are also called the principal component scores with respect to PC1, PC2 and PC3, respectively. The geometric interpretation of PCA is illustrated by the scatter plot matrix of these scores, see [Figures 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003) via Python and [9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0004) via **R**.

![FIGURE 9.3 Scatter plot for the first three principal components from the US rates example. Generated in Programme 9.13 via Python, we expect to see that these components are uncorrelated.](images/c09f003.png)

[**FIGURE 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0003) Scatter plot for the first three principal components from the US rates example. Generated in [Programme 9.13](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3033) via Python, we expect to see that these components are uncorrelated.

![FIGURE 9.4 Scatter plot for the first three principal components from the US rates example. Generated in Programme 9.14 via R, we expect to see that these components are uncorrelated.](images/c09f004.png)

[**FIGURE 9.4**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0004) Scatter plot for the first three principal components from the US rates example. Generated in [Programme 9.14](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3014) via **R**, we expect to see that these components are uncorrelated.

 

## 9.4 PCA AS AN EIGENVALUE PROBLEM

In general, let ![bold-italic upper X equals left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 comma bold-italic x 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times n](images/c09-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math> be a data matrix of ![n](images/c09-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> sample points (assuming mean zero for simplicity) such that each ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c09-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. The main goal of PCA is to compress the information in ![bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> so that each sample point is effectively projected onto ![double-struck upper R Superscript k](images/c09-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> with ![k less-than p](images/c09-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, while the loss of information is minimized.

Let ![bold-italic upper W equals left-parenthesis bold-italic omega 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic omega Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times k](images/c09-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> be a projection matrix which satisfies

![parallel-to bold-italic omega Subscript i Baseline parallel-to equals 1 comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma k comma and bold-italic omega Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega Subscript j Baseline equals 0 for i not-equals j period](images/c09-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="2em"/><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Then, the compressed data matrix ![bold-italic upper Z](images/c09-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi></mrow></math> takes the form ![bold-italic upper Z equals bold-italic upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math>. From this compressed data matrix, we can retrieve the original data matrix approximately by using ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper X With Ì‚ equals bold-italic upper W bold-italic upper Z equals bold-italic upper W bold-italic upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math>. The question now is how to determine ![bold-italic upper W](images/c09-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></mrow></math> so that the induced approximation error can be minimized. In other words, we aim to solve the following optimization problem:

[(9.1)](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-disp-0012)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column min Underscript bold-italic upper W Endscripts parallel-to bold-italic upper X minus ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper X With Ì‚ parallel-to equals min Underscript bold-italic upper W Endscripts parallel-to bold-italic upper X minus bold-italic upper W bold-italic upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X parallel-to comma 2nd Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column subject to bold-italic upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper W equals bold-italic upper I Subscript k Baseline comma EndLayout](images/c09-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mspace width="-.2em"/><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mspace width="-.2em"/><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math>

## 9.5 FACTOR MODELS VIA PCA

In finance, a reasonable model should provide effective and interpretable predictions with a tractable performance. Factor models are among those most commonly used in practice. Indeed, factor models play an important role in finance: for instance, they provide a decomposition to assist with portfolio hedging; see [Section 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0008). A ![p](images/c09-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional random vector ![bold x Subscript t](images/c09-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is said to follow an ![m](images/c09-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>*‐linear factor model* if

and these first ![m](images/c09-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> PCs maintain a large portion of the variation information (variance) contained in ![bold x](images/c09-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>.

To illustrate this, let us continue with our example of US zero‐coupon yield; their respective individual standard deviations are computed in [Programme 9.15](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3015) via Python and [Programme 9.16](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3016) via **R**. Suppose that we have a bond portfolio with the money exposure ![bold-italic omega](images/c09-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></math> shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), and we are interested in the 10‐day 99% V@R of this bond portfolio. As a benchmark from further calculations in [Programmes 9.15](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3015) via Python and [9.16](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3016) via **R**, the actual standard deviation of ![normal upper Delta normal upper Pi](images/c09-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi></math> is ![StartRoot bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma bold-italic omega EndRoot slash 100 almost-equals 0.07786 normal upper M equals 77 comma 860](images/c09-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>0.07786</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>77</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>860</mn></math>, by using the sample one to estimate the population covariance matrix, and the corresponding 10‐day 99% V@R is ![StartRoot 10 slash 365 EndRoot z 0.99 left-parenthesis 77 comma 860 right-parenthesis equals 29 comma 980](images/c09-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>365</mn></mrow></msqrt><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0.99</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>77</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>860</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>29</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>980</mn></math>. Note that all computations hereafter are based on actual values from the programme outputs, and may be subject to rounding issues.

In this example, it is clear that the first PC alone could only explain around 53% of the total variance, hence using only the first PC will severely underestimate the V@R, as the component change for each bond is quite different from that of another.

As a final remark, note that choosing a suitable number of PCs could be a quite subtle decision in practice. For an extreme scenario, consider a portfolio with weights ![omega Subscript i Baseline equals c StartFraction h Subscript i p Baseline Over sigma Subscript i Baseline EndFraction](images/c09-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> for all ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c09-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math> with a common constant ![c](images/c09-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>. Since the last PC takes the form ![normal y Subscript p Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i Endscripts h Subscript i p Baseline normal x overTilde Subscript i](images/c09-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, due to its lack of correlation with ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s, we can see that ![delta Subscript j Baseline equals c sigma-summation Underscript i Endscripts h Subscript i p Baseline h Subscript i j Baseline equals c bold-italic h Subscript p Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic h Subscript j Baseline equals 0](images/c09-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for all ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p minus 1](images/c09-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; and so ![normal upper Delta normal upper Pi almost-equals zeta](images/c09-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi>&#950;</mi></math> whenever the number ![m](images/c09-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> of PCs is less than ![p](images/c09-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Since the last PC is highly unlikely to appear in any truncated PC procedure, the change in the portfolio value by using any common PCA procedure will never be accurately estimated. However, in most financial applications, investors are only interested in securities, governed by and related to the major risk factors ![normal y 1 comma ellipsis comma normal y Subscript m Baseline](images/c09-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> with ![m much-less-than p](images/c09-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, that contribute to the majority of impacts on the market. Those securities related to ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> for ![j greater-than-or-equal-to m plus 1](images/c09-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> are barely considered since their effects are negligible, and therefore play a very limited role in the investment plans of common investors. Consequently, the corresponding ![StartAbsoluteValue delta Subscript j Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c09-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>'s would be quite small. Unfortunately, concentrating only on a few major financial risk factors, hence a few investment vehicles, may result in increased systemic risk, which mainly consists of risk factors ![normal y Subscript j](images/c09-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> for ![j greater-than-or-equal-to m plus 1](images/c09-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

 

## 9.7 PORTFOLIO IMMUNIZATION

This section only provides a schematic outline on how to hedge a portfolio using principal components against major risk factors. Consider a portfolio that depends on ![upper N](images/c09-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> fundamental assets, which are even non‐tradable or highly illiquid, such as future investment projects, real estates and tangible properties, insurance contracts, or intangible assets such as brand names. Let ![normal r Subscript t Superscript k](images/c09-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> be the value

![normal upper Delta normal r Subscript t Superscript k Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript m Endscripts omega Subscript j Superscript k Baseline normal y Subscript t Superscript j Baseline plus normal epsilon Subscript t Superscript k Baseline comma k equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper N comma](images/c09-math-0032.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal y Subscript t Superscript j](images/c09-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> is the value of the ![j](images/c09-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th principal component or risk factor of these ![upper N](images/c09-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> fundamental assets at time ![t](images/c09-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> for ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></math>; ![omega Subscript j Superscript k](images/c09-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> is the sensitivity in the value of the ![k](images/c09-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th fundamental asset with respect to the ![j](images/c09-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th risk factor; and ![normal epsilon Subscript t Superscript k](images/c09-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> is the residual, or miscellaneous, risk factor.

On one hand, it is common for companies to run several lines of business which plausibly depend on many non‐tradable assets; on the other hand, they often like to hedge out their risky positions, especially after acquiring some notable profit during an up‐and‐down period, as by then they prefer to have a more stable income until the expiry of these projects. Mathematically, to achieve this goal, let ![normal upper Pi Subscript t](images/c09-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> be the value of the portfolio at time ![t](images/c09-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, which depends on those ![upper N](images/c09-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> fundamental assets. By assumption, the change in value of ![normal upper Pi](images/c09-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi></mrow></math> can be mostly explained by using the ![m](images/c09-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> risk factors of ![normal y Subscript t Superscript j](images/c09-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>'s. We expect to use (at least) ![m](images/c09-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> other tradable securities, also depending on these ![upper N](images/c09-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> fundamental assets, to hedge out most of the risks in ![normal upper Pi](images/c09-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi></mrow></math>. Let ![normal upper S Subscript t Superscript l Baseline comma l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m comma](images/c09-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo></math> be the respective prices of those other ![m](images/c09-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> tradable securities at time ![t](images/c09-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>; we also hedge the portfolio by holding ![phi Subscript t Superscript l](images/c09-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> units of the ![l](images/c09-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>‐th tradable security, ![l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></math>. Hence, the value of the combined portfolio at time ![t](images/c09-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is given by
