When solving the system ([9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0038)), companies need the performance data on their own lines of business against all these ![upper N](images/c09-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> fundamental assets, as well as the corresponding sensitivities of other securities publicly traded in the market. In principle, for the former, companies can determine these coefficients using their internal business information extracted from their own financial report figures. As a result, it is relatively easy to acquire all the information for ![bold upper P Subscript t](images/c09-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, which is specifically the sensitivity of our portfolio ![normal upper Pi Subscript t](images/c09-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> to the value of each individual fundamental asset ![normal r Subscript t Superscript k](images/c09-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c09-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math>. For instance, as a simple case from a cash flow perspective, let ![normal r Subscript tau Superscript k](images/c09-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> be the average annual rate of return for the investment made at time ![tau](images/c09-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> on the ![k](images/c09-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th asset, with a cash flow of ![c Subscript tau Superscript k](images/c09-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, and assume that the asset cannot be traded until an expiry date ![upper T](images/c09-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>. Then the time‐![t](images/c09-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> present value of the portfolio of all ![upper N](images/c09-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> assets is given by ![normal upper Pi Subscript t Baseline equals left-parenthesis 1 plus r Subscript f Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript minus left-parenthesis upper T minus t right-parenthesis Baseline sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript tau equals t Overscript upper T Endscripts c Subscript tau Superscript k Baseline left-parenthesis 1 plus normal r Subscript tau Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper T minus tau](images/c09-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></msup></math>, where ![r Subscript f](images/c09-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math> is the deterministic risk‐free rate. Indeed, this scenario is not uncommon in reality; consider the purchase of government bonds for example. Another example is the construction of public infrastructure, where capital injections are required every year in the construction stage, while the profit will not be realized in few years' time until the facilities are put in service and start to generate revenues. In this case, one can easily evaluate the sensitivity as ![StartFraction partial-differential normal upper Pi Subscript t Baseline Over partial-differential normal r Subscript t Superscript k Baseline EndFraction equals left-parenthesis 1 plus r Subscript f Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript minus left-parenthesis upper T minus t right-parenthesis Baseline c Subscript t Superscript k Baseline left-parenthesis upper T minus t right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 1 plus normal r Subscript t Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper T minus t minus 1](images/c09-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c09-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math>. In real practice, despite a possibly more complicated form of ![normal upper Pi Subscript t](images/c09-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, investors should have a rather thorough understanding of their own projects, leading to a reasonable knowledge of the functional form of how the portfolio depends on the fundamental assets, such as the one above. By then they can readily estimate the sensitivity with respect to any argument variables.

for some small change ![normal upper Delta r Subscript t Baseline 0 Superscript k](images/c09-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> in the value of the ![k](images/c09-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th fundamental asset in portfolio ![normal upper Pi Subscript t](images/c09-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#928;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, whereas other ![r Subscript t Baseline 0 Superscript j](images/c09-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>'s, ![j not-equals k](images/c09-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>, are held fixed.

However, the sensitivities of the hedging tradable securities ![normal upper S Subscript t Superscript l](images/c09-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>'s to the value ![normal r Subscript t Superscript k](images/c09-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> of each individual fundamental asset, for ![l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></math> and ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c09-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math>, require much effort as the information of these tradable securities is neither under the control nor a regular entry of the company. One simple approach is to construct a regression model on each historical security price ![normal upper S Subscript t Superscript l](images/c09-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> against the historical values ![normal r Subscript t Superscript k](images/c09-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>'s. The required sensitivity is just the tangent of the corresponding regression model, possibly extrapolated at ![r Subscript t Baseline 0 Superscript k](images/c09-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. For more details on regression models, see [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml). If there are only one or two major risk factors, the immunization strategy would be achievable in reality, just like CAPM; however, if there are quite a number of factors, we would have to rely on big data in order to implement this immunization strategy in reality. In particular, extensions of deep learning methods (to be discussed in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml)) can be useful for future research endeavours on this topic.

 

## 9.8 FACIAL RECOGNITION VIA PCA

In general, PCA is also useful in identifying major factors behind a collection of very high‐dimensional random variables. The same principle can be utilized for image recognition by selecting key features from a class of photos; see [\[2](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002), [8](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008), [10](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010), [18](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018), [21](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021), [22\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0022) for more discussions. Certainly, image recognition plays vital roles in business such as providing more tailor‐made customer services that facilitate the development of online private banking. For instance, facial recognition, as illustrated in [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005), can be used to verify a customer's identity, and henceforth his/her policy and background information can be retrieved and reviewed instantly. This enriches the potential use of online banking with the minimum possible manpower yet can still achieve high precision in the absence of human intervention. Facial recognition is generally much safer to use than the simple log‐in via usernames and passwords. With this technology, future customers can simply capture photos of the relevant documents, and then submit them for services online. The image recognition engine converts the uploaded images to the desired information for further process, and then successful applications can be realized in seconds. In a nutshell, financial corporations and customers can attain a win‐win situation: the management cost for the customers can be much reduced, while the companies can obtain more accurate information.

![FIGURE 9.5 Facial recognition for the actress IU.](images/c09f005.png)

[**FIGURE 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0005) Facial recognition for the actress *IU*.

Let us explain the actual implementation of facial recognition via PCA. The dataset ![bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is an ![left-parenthesis h dot w right-parenthesis times n](images/c09-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrix, where each observation ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c09-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is a face image of a shape of height ![h](images/c09-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> ![times](images/c09-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> width ![w](images/c09-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> being flattened into a one‐dimensional vector of a length ![h dot w](images/c09-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>w</mi></math>. The feature variables, the various pixels of the face image, are highly correlated locally, because the neighborhoods of a pixel often take similar values because they share similar color. Therefore, PCA can be adopted for dimension reduction. In the context of facial recognition, for classification, we compute the Euclidean distance of a query face image ![bold-italic x Subscript asterisk](images/c09-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msub></math> against the database ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c09-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> with respective labels ![y 1 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript n Baseline](images/c09-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>. This methodology actually shares the same philosophy as the ![upper K](images/c09-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐Nearest Neighbour* technique to be discussed in [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml). The *AT&T Database of Faces*

In **R**, the `pixmap` (PIXel MAPs) library is used to process bitmapped images. In particular, the `read.pnm()` (Portable Any Map) function is adopted to read images; see the corresponding implementation in [Programme 9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3018) in the **R** environment.

Notice that the training set ![bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is a ![left-parenthesis 112 dot 92 right-parenthesis times left-parenthesis 9 dot 40 right-parenthesis equals 10 comma 304 times 360](images/c09-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>92</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>40</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>304</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>360</mn></math> matrix, leading to a singular ![10 comma 304 times 10 comma 304](images/c09-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>304</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>304</mn></math> matrix ![bold-italic upper X bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. From [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007) of [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml), we know that the largest 360 (non‐zero) eigenvalues of ![bold-italic upper X bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> and ![bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math> are the same. For ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 360](images/c09-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>360</mn></math>, denote by ![bold-italic u Subscript i](images/c09-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> the ![i](images/c09-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th eigenvector of ![bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math>, then the ![i](images/c09-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th eigenvector of ![bold-italic upper X bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> is given by ![bold-italic h Subscript i Baseline equals bold-italic upper X bold-italic u Subscript i](images/c09-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>; meanwhile, the remaining eigenvalues ![lamda 361 comma ellipsis comma lamda Subscript 10 comma 304 Baseline](images/c09-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>361</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>304</mn></mrow></msub></math> of the singular ![bold-italic upper X bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> are simply zero. Taking advantage of this, we need only consider the spectral decomposition of ![bold-italic upper X Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c09-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math> instead. We implement this in [Programme 9.19](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3019) via Python.

From the outputs of [Programme 9.19](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3019) in Python, 107 PCs suffice to preserve 90% of all information contained in the total variance. Notice that the training set is standardized, so the total variance is then equal to ![p equals h dot w equals 10 comma 304](images/c09-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>304</mn></math>. A similar implementation via **R** can be found in [Programme 9.20](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3020).

In Python, the `PCA` in `sklearn` can also be used directly with the argument `n_components=0.9` to preserve 90% of information; also see [Programmes 9.21](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3021) in Python and [9.22](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3022) in **R**. For **R**, since the training dataset has already been normalized, we call the `prcomp()` function with the two arguments `center=FALSE` and `scale=FALSE`.

Both the training and test datasets are transformed by projecting onto these 107 PCs. We then compare the Euclidean distances between each test observation against all in the training dataset. The observation from the training dataset that yields the shortest distance with the query face image is said to be a match with that test observation.

![FIGURE 9.6 Testing results of matching faces, generated by Programme 9.23 in Python.](images/c09f006.png)

[**FIGURE 9.6**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0006) Testing results of matching faces, generated by [Programme 9.23](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3023) in Python.

![FIGURE 9.7 Bar chart of the Euclidean distances of the projected PCs between the training and test datasets, generated by Programme 9.23 in Python.](images/c09f007.png)

[**FIGURE 9.7**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0007) Bar chart of the Euclidean distances of the projected PCs between the training and test datasets, generated by [Programme 9.23](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3023) in Python.

From [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006), only the rightmost pair of images in the second last row returns a mismatch, as seen in the red box. The test image was of a lady but the programme returns a male with a distance of 78.546, which is the largest among all pairs in [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006). From [Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007), there are three bars whose values are greater than 65, which are query faces No. 1, 16 and 35, indicating that we have a lower confidence on the matching of these query faces with the correct person. Therefore, in practice, if the distance is larger than some threshold ![tau greater-than 0](images/c09-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, for example 65 as mentioned above, and as indicated in the horizontal dashed line in [Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007), we regard the matching process of that query face image with the database as a failure. We also implement the same analysis in [Programme 9.24](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3024) via **R**; see the corresponding testing results and the bar chart in [Figures 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0008) and [9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0009), which agree with the outcomes obtained via Python. Recently, a higher accuracy can be attained by using *Convolutional Neural Networks* (ConvNets or CNNs); more discussions can be found in our upcoming book [\[5\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005).

## 9.9 NON‐LIFE INSURANCE VIA PCA

Casualty insurance can also benefit from image recognition. With the plenty of images available on the Internet, one can identify key information that is crucial for a financial property to be insurable. For example, photos of a house roof can be captured by drones to better understand the condition of the house and to determine any collapse risk, as in [Figure 9.10](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0010). In the old days, insurance companies could only obtain partial information from written historical records. With these pictures, the underwriting process can be implemented in a more comprehensive manner.

![FIGURE 9.10 Property risk analysis through image processing.](images/c09f010.png)

[**FIGURE 9.10**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0010) Property risk analysis through image processing.

Health insurance is another field in which image recognition can help uncover any hidden risk of insureds, which could not be easily detected in the past. In modern medicine applications, image recognition is of great use in diagnosis and prognosis, especially in identifying cancer cells or tumors at a very early stage. Besides taking doctors' viewpoints into account, *Computed Tomography* (CT) images of cancer patients (see [Figure 9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0011)) can also be utilized as another factor for insurance pricing, during steps of underwriting and determination of risk loading. These medical images may provide richer information than the record of diagnosis provided by a medical doctor, which often take a much longer time, and they can therefore help improve the precision of the pricing model and timely action to be taken. Nevertheless, biomedical images are usually corrupted by noisy signals which should be de‐noised, as from these one can extract features and classify images to facilitate better diagnosis. PCA can be used as a digital image compression algorithm without causing too much loss in information. Indeed, PCA can be incorporated into image processing; for example, see [Figure 9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0012), which enhances data texture segmentation (depicting the outlines via PCs), compression, helps removal of redundant information (removing PCs with smaller eigenvalues), and enables noise removal and feature extraction.

![FIGURE 9.11 Biomedical image recognition is commonly used to determine whether a patient has a tumor and how severe it is. Source: \[19\].](images/c09f011.png)

[**FIGURE 9.11**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0011) Biomedical image recognition is commonly used to determine whether a patient has a tumor and how severe it is. Source: [\[19\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0019).

![FIGURE 9.12 Enhancing visibility for biomedical images. Source: \[4\].](images/c09f012.png)

[**FIGURE 9.12**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0012) Enhancing visibility for biomedical images. Source: [\[4\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004).

![FIGURE 9.13 Housing insurance analysis through satellite geographical images. Source: \[19\].](images/c09f013.png)

[**FIGURE 9.13**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0013) Housing insurance analysis through satellite geographical images. Source: [\[19\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0019).

Besides, image recognition techniques also prove helpful in monitoring natural catastrophes, such as typhoons, floods and forest fires, in a real‐time manner; it can also assist in handling the aftermath of the incidents. For instance, upon detection of the trace of a typhoon or a flooded area from the satellite image, the severity of damage of the affected regions can be determined with the aid of image recognition. This gives light to the development of automatic systems for loss prediction, so as to facilitate a better management of foreseeable claims for insurers. Take the analysis on property insurance in [\[19\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0019) for example, where the grey cloud of tornado in the satellite photo ([Figure 9.13](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0013)) is captured to run from west to northeast, whereas the insured properties are denoted by black dots. By applying some image recognition algorithm to this photo, the identification of the tornado path leads to further judgements on the post‐tornado status of the insured homes, namely whether and how severely are they damaged. It is also possible to feed latest photos to the algorithm, such that the estimation procedure can be carried out in a progressive manner, which leads to timely updates of the status of the buildings concerned.

 

## 9.10 INVESTMENT STRATEGIES USING PCA

Apart from image recognition, we can also use PCA to formulate investment strategies. During the first half of 2020, there was a global stock decline, largely attributed to the outbreak of COVID‐19. Let us try to apply PCA to the US stock prices and see if this method can identify whether the key factors behind the decline really coincide with the virus outbreak. Once these key factors are unveiled, we can find those securities that align most favorably with these factors. This information can then be used to formulate a profitable investment strategy; indeed, we can simply pick up well‐performing stocks from the national stock index to build a portfolio that outperforms the underlying market.

On 15 March 2020, the *Federal Reserve* in the US began to conduct its fourth round of *quantitative easing* (QE); the money flow figures are readily available in the public domain, and one naturally expected the stock market to respond positively. To this end, we shall use PCA to select some representative stocks to invest. Suppose that the current time is the end of March 2020, and we have observed the response from the market in the form of a rapid upward trend. Assume that we have an initial investment of USD 100,000 and we would like to invest evenly in 10 US stocks. In [Programme 9.25](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3025) via Python (resp. [Programme 9.26](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3026) via **R**), PCA is applied to the centered logarithmic returns computed from the opening prices from 2 January 2020 to 31 March 2020. The top 10 stocks with the largest loadings (likely positive in value) and the bottom 10 stocks with the smallest loadings (likely negative in value) with respect to the first PC ![normal y 1](images/c09-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> are then selected as candidates

## \*9.11 RECOMMENDER SYSTEM

A recommender system, commonly encountered in *Meta*, *Amazon*, and *Netflix*, helps predict the “rating” or “preference” that a subscriber would give to an item. It has become increasingly popular in recent years, and is utilized in a variety of areas including movies, music, news, books, research articles, search queries, social tags, and even groceries. Recommender systems can be used in marketing science research and business informatics to formulate a better business solution to maximize companies' profit. There are also recommender systems for entertainment enterprises, restaurants, garments, financial services, insurance products, romantic partner finding (online dating), and *X* (formerly *Twitter*) pages.

In the rest of this section, we shall provide the basic connection between the theory behind one of the commonly used recommender systems and PCA. To motivate this, imagine that we found a startup which provides online movie viewing. The company has attracted ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma m](images/c09-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></math> subscribers, and has also acquired ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> movies. Each subscriber is invited to rate a movie after viewing with ![r equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma 5](images/c09-i0366.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></math> (a continuum rating is certainly allowed) such that ![r equals 1](images/c09-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> means the worst and ![r equals 5](images/c09-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> means the best. These ratings are stored in an ![m times n](images/c09-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> sparse ![FIGURE 9.15 Netflix Prize, October 2006. The rating matrix bold-italic upper R is large and sparse with m equals 480 comma 189 and n equals 17 comma 770. Source: Getty Images North America.](images/c09f015.png)

[**FIGURE 9.15**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0015) *Netflix Prize*, October 2006. The rating matrix ![bold-italic upper R](images/c09-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> is large and sparse with ![m equals 480 comma 189](images/c09-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>480</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>189</mn></math> and ![n equals 17 comma 770](images/c09-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>770</mn></math>. Source: Getty Images North America.

Note that the ratings remain at ![r equals 0](images/c09-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for movies that the subscriber has not yet watched or rated. Based on the data, we want to build a recommender system to learn about the taste of each subscriber, so that we can make predictions on a particular subscriber's ratings of those movies that he/she has not watched, and also make recommendations of any future movies.

Here we describe a popular approach called the *latent‐factor method* (matrix factorization) in *collaborative filtering*

On the other hand, these hidden features can also be used to describe the subscribers' preferences for different movies. For the subscriber ![i](images/c09-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, we want to evaluate a sequence of scores ![p Subscript i comma k](images/c09-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> against all hidden features ![k equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c09-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math> that best describe the ![i](images/c09-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th subscriber's taste on movies. These scores are to be collectively stored in another ![m times p](images/c09-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></math> matrix ![bold-italic upper P equals left-parenthesis p Subscript i comma k Baseline right-parenthesis Subscript m times p](images/c09-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which is also to be estimated.

For a fixed ![p](images/c09-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, our task is to approximate the matrices ![bold-italic upper P](images/c09-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic upper Q](images/c09-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math>, which contain a total of ![left-parenthesis m plus n right-parenthesis times p](images/c09-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></math> unknown parameters. The product matrix, ![bold-italic upper P bold-italic upper Q Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> of size ![m times n](images/c09-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> can be compared to the subscriber's ratings stored in ![bold-italic upper R](images/c09-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math>. While ![bold-italic upper R](images/c09-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> is sparse (since each subscriber has only viewed or rated a small portion of the entire movie database), our algorithm aims to minimize the deviation of the average between the known ratings of ![r Subscript i comma j](images/c09-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s and the corresponding ratings predicted by using ![sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript p Endscripts p Subscript i comma k Baseline q Subscript j comma k](images/c09-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math>. In other words, the objective is to minimize the following mean squared error (MSE):

Note the similarity of the format of ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0041)) with that of eigenvalue problem associated with PCA in [Section 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0005). We shall adopt the technique of *Singular Value Decomposition* (SVD) for general rectangular matrices, which can be considered as the generalization of spectral decomposition for positive definite square symmetric matrices.

![FIGURE 9.16 Singular Value Decomposition of the rating matrix bold-italic upper R.](images/c09f016.png)

An optimization scheme is used to find the minimizer by treating ![bold-italic upper P](images/c09-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic upper Q](images/c09-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math> as decision variables. mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>,

This guessed solution can indeed be shown correct by identifying the optimal solution to Problem ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0041)) in accordance with the celebrated *Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem* in the context of *Low‐rank Approximation*, which has different versions in terms of either the *Frobenius norm* or the *spectral norm*. However, their respective proofs are not simple analogies to each other, and here we only present the Frobenius norm version of the theorem, which echoes the setting of Problem ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0041)). Interested readers can refer to [Appendix \*9.A.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0021) for the spectral norm version.

Therefore, our respective guesses of ![bold-italic upper P](images/c09-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic upper Q](images/c09-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math> above are correct; indeed, the resulting ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper R With Ì‚ equals bold-italic upper P bold-italic upper Q Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> is precisely the minimizer of ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0041)).

Note that the optimal solution of Problem ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0041)) suffers from *overfitting*; that is, it fits the known data in the training set so well that it loses the flexibility to adapt to a new dataset, e.g. the test dataset, thereby losing predictive power. To avoid overfitting, we employ common technique of *regularization*, by adding the sum of the squared matrix entries in ![bold-italic upper P](images/c09-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic upper Q](images/c09-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math> together with some penalty parameters. That is, we add ![trace left-parenthesis bold upper Lamda 1 bold-italic upper P bold-italic upper P Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis plus trace left-parenthesis bold upper Lamda 2 bold-italic upper Q bold-italic upper Q Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0490.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to the original objective function ([9.10](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0043)) for some diagonal matrices ![bold upper Lamda 1 element-of double-struck upper R Superscript m times m](images/c09-i0491.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold upper Lamda 2 element-of double-struck upper R Superscript n times n](images/c09-i0492.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math>, which serve as Lagrange multipliers

In general, to optimize ![upper J](images/c09-i0500.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> (equivalently, to solve ([9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0045)), regularized or not), rather than make a guess through SVD as described before, we can instead hold ![bold-italic upper P](images/c09-i0501.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> constant and then vary over ![bold-italic upper Q](images/c09-i0502.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math>, or vice versa. This reduces each iteration problem to the standard least squares problem, which is repeated until convergence is achieved. This approach is commonly called *alternating projections* in the literature based on the usual fixed point argument.

In addition to the latent‐factor method as described above, there is another approach called the *neighborhood model* which is perhaps intuitively simpler. A similarity score for each pair of subscribers is computed, based on the cosine coefficient between the two vectors of ratings of each. The larger the score, the closer these two subscribers are in their taste of movies. We then aim to look for a group of subscribers who are close to a particular user of interest. In order to predict the rating of a movie by a subscriber of interest, we can use a weighted sum of the ratings of a reasonably large number of similar subscribers who have shared their views on that movie. More details on this method can be found in [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011).

Going back to the latent‐factor method, upon completion of the optimization procedure that minimizes the MSE ![upper J](images/c09-i0503.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math>, both the subscribers' tastes on movies ![ModifyingAbove p With caret Subscript i comma k](images/c09-i0504.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> and the nature of movies ![ModifyingAbove q With caret Subscript j comma k](images/c09-i0505.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> can be estimated. The ![m times n](images/c09-i0506.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrix ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper R With Ì‚ equals ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper P With Ì‚ ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper Q With Ì‚ Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> then stores the predicted ratings of all movies by all subscribers. For instance, the ![i](images/c09-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th rows of ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper R With Ì‚](images/c09-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> are row vectors that list the predicted ratings on all movies ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> by the ![i](images/c09-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th subscriber. Notably, these predicted ratings of ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper R With Ì‚](images/c09-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> should be non‐zero for those unknown ratings ![r Subscript i comma j Baseline equals 0](images/c09-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; while for any ![r Subscript i comma j Baseline not-equals 0](images/c09-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, the corresponding estimate ![ModifyingAbove r With caret Subscript i comma j](images/c09-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> should be roughly equal to that known rating ![r Subscript i comma j](images/c09-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>. Afterwards, the procedure described above could then be implemented.

Next we discuss and illustrate, by using the **R** package `recommenderlab`, how recommender systems can serve as an important marketing analytic tool. For example, movie websites want to analyze the collective data (such as watching history and movie ratings) obtained from visitors, and then recommend new movies for them to watch based on the preference predictions acquired from the whole group. Generally, this **R** package provides an infrastructure for testing and developing recommender algorithms, and supports the rating (e.g. 1 to 5 stars) and unary (0 or 1) datasets. We first briefly describe the mathematics behind for training a recommender system using the package via the *SVD with column‐mean imputation* method. This method is toggled by the argument `method="SVD"` in `recommenderlab`, where the rating matrix ![bold-italic upper R](images/c09-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> is first normalized per subscriber (i.e., subtracting the mean and then rescaling by the standard deviation for each row) and the missing entries of the resulting normalized matrix are imputed by their corresponding column means, i.e., the movie‐wise average of existing ratings. The programme then applies SVD to look for the ![p](images/c09-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> largest singular values ![sigma 1 comma ellipsis comma sigma Subscript p Baseline](images/c09-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> and their corresponding singular vectors ![bold-italic upper U Subscript p](images/c09-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic upper V Subscript p](images/c09-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>. In the prediction stage, given a testing rating matrix ![bold-italic upper R Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup></math>, with the same number of columns (movies) as ![bold-italic upper R](images/c09-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> but possibly different number of rows (subscribers), and recalling that ![bold-italic upper R Subscript p Baseline equals bold-italic upper U Subscript p Baseline bold upper Sigma Subscript p Baseline bold-italic upper V Subscript p Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0538.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, we first expect ![bold-italic upper R Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0539.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup></math> to be close to ![bold-italic upper U Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline bold upper Sigma Subscript p Baseline bold-italic upper V Subscript p Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0540.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>. Hence we simply take ![bold-italic upper U Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold-italic upper R Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline Finally, we denormalize ![bold-italic upper R Subscript p Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0543.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>(test)</mtext></mrow></msubsup></math> to give the predictions.

In the meantime, since the actual implementation of SVD in `recommenderlab` adopts the *Lanczos bidiagonalization* algorithm (IRLBA) [\[1\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0001) to approximate the largest few singular values and the corresponding singular vectors of a matrix, where the initial random seed plays a crucial role, it is therefore necessary in practice to build multiple recommender systems and select the one with the best model performance metric, e.g., the lowest MSE, under the validation set; see the **R** codes in [Programme 9.29](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3029). In particular, the function `evaluationScheme` in the `recommenderlab` package splits a dataset into training and validation, two separate datasets, at the ratio of 9:1 as indicated by the argument `train=0.9`, and the validation dataset is further partitioned into two subgroups called `known` and `unknown`. More specifically, given a validation dataset ![bold-italic upper X element-of double-struck upper R Superscript n times p](images/c09-i0544.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>, we generate a Bernoulli random matrix ![bold upper B equals left-parenthesis normal b Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript n times p](images/c09-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> where each entry ![normal b Subscript i j Baseline tilde Overscript i i d Endscripts Ber left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0546.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mover class="overset"><mo>&#8764;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mover><mtext>Ber</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> and ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c09-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, with the success probability ![q](images/c09-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>. The `known` (resp. `unknown`) subgroup is then given by ![bold-italic upper X circled-dot bold upper B](images/c09-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8857;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></math> (resp. ![bold-italic upper X circled-dot left-parenthesis bold 1 minus bold upper B right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8857;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>), where ![circled-dot](images/c09-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8857;</mo></mrow></math> denotes the Hadamard product. Next, all resulting entries of `known` and `unknown` with a value of 0 are regarded as missing. After building a recommender system based on the training dataset, we make predictions on the `known` subgroup of the validation dataset, including those that are not rated by a specific user at all and those that have been rated but whose ratings are assigned to the `unknown` subgroup since their corresponding ![b Subscript i j](images/c09-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s take a value of 0. Then, for the sake of model evaluation, we only compare the non‐missing actual ratings in the `unknown` subgroup of the validation dataset with their predicted counterparts in the `known` subgroup from the previous step.

We are now ready to demonstrate the use of this package by training a recommender system on the `MovieLense` dataset. The dataset collected 99,392 ratings (1 (worst), 2, ![ellipsis](images/c09-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow></math>, 5 (best)) from 943 users on 1,664 movies through the *MovieLens* website ([movielens.umn.edu](https://movielens.umn.edu)) during the seven‐month period from 19 September 1997 to 22 April 1998. In this example, we only consider those data satisfying the following two conditions: (i) users that have rated over 100 movies, so as to ensure sufficient data for the sake of mean centering; and (ii) movies that have at least 30 ratings, so as to ensure sufficient data for the sake of column‐mean imputation. Based on the reduced dataset with the ratings from 358 users on 792 movies, we choose the rating data of the first 300 users as the joint dataset for training and validation `train_valid`, which serves as the input of the `best_rec()` function in [Programme 9.29](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3029), and the best recommender system is then the one that yields the lowest MSE among all `trial=5` trials. Meanwhile, the remaining ![358 minus 300 equals 58](images/c09-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>358</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>58</mn></math> users form the test dataset `test`.

The output in [Programme 9.30](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3030) via **R** illustrates the use of the trained recommender system by selecting the top 10 recommended movies tailor‐made for two users, namely Users 798 and 804. Note that the `predict()` function in `recommenderlab` only makes predictions on the missing entries, and therefore only the movies that are not rated by the user will be recommended by the model. As an interesting observation, while the recommendations for the two users are fairly personalized, let say perhaps User 804 prefers older movies while User 798 prefers more recent ones, they also share several recommended items in common, including *Titanic* in particular. This record‐breaking movie was released in December 1997, which was around the middle of the seven‐month period of ratings collected, so these two users had not watched it at the time of data collection, although they might already have done so shortly afterwards. Anyhow, the high profile of this movie is already strongly evident from its appearance in the top 10 recommendations of both two users, whose preferences are actually quite different. What do you think? Which user do you find closer to your preference on movies?

 

## \*9.A APPENDIX

  

### \*9.A.1 Spectral Decompositions of Square Matrices

The basic idea in PCA, as the first step, is to find a linear combination of the original variables ![normal x Subscript i](images/c09-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s,

![normal y 1 equals h 11 normal x 1 plus ellipsis plus h Subscript p Baseline 1 Baseline normal x Subscript p Baseline equals bold-italic h 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x comma](images/c09-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo></math>

The solution of this optimization problem is related to a well‐known and very useful result in matrix algebra called the *spectral decomposition* of symmetric matrices. For a better understanding of this technique, readers may revisit [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007) of [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) for the relevant concepts of eigenvalues (a.k.a. latent roots), eigenvectors and normalized eigenvectors, as well as some of their important properties.

Next, the second PC is the linear combination

### \*9.A.2 Immunization against Interest Rate Risks

Here we provide a quick review of immunization; more details on this topic can be found in [\[7](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007), [9](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009), [14](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014), [15\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0015). For the sake of simplicity, we only consider deterministic cash flows here.

*Redington Immunization* [\[15\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0015) is a well‐known technique for reducing or even eliminating the influence of interest rate fluctuations on values of portfolios of cash flows. A typical portfolio consists of assets and liabilities. We first define some notations to be used below. The force of interest is denoted by ![delta equals ln left-parenthesis 1 plus iota right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0600.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>&#953;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![iota](images/c09-i0601.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#953;</mi></mrow></math> is the annualized interest rate. The present value at time 0 of the assets evaluated at rate ![delta](images/c09-i0602.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math> is

![upper P Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis colon equals sigma-summation Underscript i Endscripts c Subscript i Superscript upper A Baseline e Superscript minus delta t Super Subscript i Superscript Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0054.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msubsup><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></math>

which is the average payment time of cash flows weighted by the corresponding discounted cash flows. Alternatively, this concept can also be interpreted as the effective lifespan of a project, i.e., the effective number of years before the initial cost for a project is recovered by the future cash flows it generates. where the notations are defined in the same way as those for the assets, except that the amount of the ![i](images/c09-i0608.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th cash flow is replaced by ![c Subscript i Superscript upper L](images/c09-i0609.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. At the force of interest ![delta](images/c09-i0611.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math>, a fund is immunized against a small change ![epsilon](images/c09-i0612.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> in the force of interest if (i) ![upper P Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis equals upper P Subscript upper L Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0613.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and (ii) ![upper P Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta plus epsilon semicolon 0 right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to upper P Subscript upper L Baseline left-parenthesis delta plus epsilon semicolon 0 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0614.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![epsilon](images/c09-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> sufficiently close to 0. Using the Taylor series expansion, these conditions translate to ![upper P prime Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis equals upper P prime Subscript upper L Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper P double-prime Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to upper P double-prime Subscript upper L Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, i.e., the Macaulay duration (resp. convexity) of the assets should be equal to (resp. greater than) that of the liabilities. If we denote the difference of their time values at time ![t](images/c09-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> by ![upper P left-parenthesis delta semicolon t right-parenthesis colon equals upper P Subscript upper A Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon t right-parenthesis minus upper P Subscript upper L Baseline left-parenthesis delta semicolon t right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the conditions above can be rewritten as ![upper P prime left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c09-i0620.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![upper P double-prime left-parenthesis delta semicolon 0 right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c09-i0621.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

Let us provide an example of achieving the *full immunization* against changes of any magnitude in the interest rate. Consider a single liability cash outflow of ![upper L Subscript upper T](images/c09-i0622.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math> at the time ![upper T](images/c09-i0623.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>. Full immunization can be achieved by holding two assets providing cash inflows of ![upper A](images/c09-i0624.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> at time ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper T minus a](images/c09-i0625.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi></math> and ![upper B](images/c09-i0626.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> at time ![upper T plus b](images/c09-i0627.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> respectively, for some ![a comma b greater-than 0](images/c09-i0628.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![a less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c09-i0629.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. Given any two out of the four constants ![upper A comma upper B comma a comma b](images/c09-i0630.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></math> are known, we can obtain the full immunization strategy by solving the remaining two unknowns from the following two equations, using ![upper T](images/c09-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> rather than 0 as the comparison date:

Therefore, ![f](images/c09-i0654.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> takes its global minimum at ![epsilon equals 0](images/c09-i0655.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> with ![f left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c09-i0656.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, hence ![f left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c09-i0657.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for all ![epsilon not-equals 0](images/c09-i0658.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, from which we conclude that ![upper P left-parenthesis delta plus epsilon semicolon upper T right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to upper P left-parenthesis delta semicolon upper T right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0659.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for any ![epsilon element-of double-struck upper R](images/c09-i0660.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, no matter positive or negative or how large it is, hence the full immunization is reached. This result may explain the high demand for short‐term and long‐term bonds in the markets: many insurance products involve random claim times which are usually between 1 and 10 years, and so short‐term and long‐term bonds are needed in order to immunize the interest rate risks. This phenomenon also justifies the convexity in the loadings of the third PC. While the insurance market is a notable component of the financial market, its proportion is still relatively small, which may in turn explain the significantly smaller eigenvalue of the third PC, compared with those of the first two.

 

### \*9.A.3 Singular Value Decomposition

Mathematically, *Singular Value Decomposition* (SVD) is a generalization of eigenvalue decompositions for square symmetric matrices, but now applied to general rectangular ![m times n](images/c09-i0661.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrices. It finds wide applications in machine learning, for instance, in recommender systems as commonly encountered in marketing sciences. SVD claims the following (see [\[6\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)): given an ![m times n](images/c09-i0662.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrix ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0663.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, there exist matrices ![bold-italic upper U comma bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0664.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></math> and ![bold-italic upper V](images/c09-i0665.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow></math> such that

Since we also have

Also note that the right singular vectors ![bold-italic v 1 comma bold-italic v 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic v Subscript r Baseline](images/c09-i0724.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> are in the row space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0725.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by ([9.16](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0065)); while the left singular vectors ![bold-italic u 1 comma bold-italic u 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic u Subscript r Baseline](images/c09-i0726.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> are in the column space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0727.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by ([9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0068)).

To conclude the claim that ![bold-italic upper A bold-italic upper V equals bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0728.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></math>, we only have to pick ![n minus r](images/c09-i0729.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></math> more ![bold-italic v Subscript i](images/c09-i0730.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s and ![m minus r](images/c09-i0731.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></math> more ![bold-italic u Subscript j](images/c09-i0732.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s from the null spaces ![script upper N left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0733.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![script upper N left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0734.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, respectively. Each set of these can be chosen to be the respective orthonormal bases for those two null spaces. Note that by then, they would be orthogonal to the first ![r](images/c09-i0735.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ![bold-italic v Subscript i](images/c09-i0736.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s (being in the row space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0737.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>) and ![bold-italic u Subscript j](images/c09-i0738.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s (being in the column space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0739.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>) respectively. For instance, for ![bold-italic v Subscript r plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic v Subscript n Baseline](images/c09-i0740.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> from ![script upper N left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0741.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![i equals r plus 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0742.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, and ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma r](images/c09-i0743.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></math>, we have

![left pointing angle bold-italic v Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic v Subscript j Baseline right pointing angle equals bold-italic v Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic u Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A bold-italic v Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic u Subscript j Baseline equals 0 comma](images/c09-math-0069.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

by definition. Similarly,

stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold-italic upper U equals left-parenthesis bold-italic upper U Subscript r Baseline semicolon bold-italic u Subscript r plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma
