Also form the ![m times n](images/c09-i0752.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0753.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> by adding to ![bold upper Sigma Subscript r](images/c09-i0754.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>r</mi></msub></math> with ![m minus r](images/c09-i0755.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></math> new zero rows and ![n minus r](images/c09-i0756.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi></math> new zero columns. These definitions lead to ![bold-italic upper A bold-italic v Subscript i Baseline equals bold 0](images/c09-i0757.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math> for ![i equals r plus 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c09-i0758.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, and together with ([9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0068)), we conclude that ![bold-italic upper A bold-italic upper V equals bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0759.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></math>. Finally, since ![bold-italic upper V](images/c09-i0760.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow></math> is orthogonal by construction, we also have ![bold-italic upper A equals bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0761.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>.

To summarize, ![bold-italic u](images/c09-i0762.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math>'s and ![bold-italic v](images/c09-i0763.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi></mrow></math>'s form the bases for the following four fundamental spaces:

*   ![bold-italic u 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic u Subscript r Baseline](images/c09-i0764.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> form an orthonormal basis for the column space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0765.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>;
*   ![bold-italic u Subscript r plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic u Subscript m Baseline](images/c09-i0766.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> form an orthonormal basis for the null space ![script upper N left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0767.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>;
*   ![bold-italic v 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic v Subscript r Baseline](images/c09-i0768.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> form an orthonormal basis for the row space of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0769.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>;
*   ![bold-italic v Subscript r plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic v Subscript n Baseline](images/c09-i0770.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> form an orthonormal basis for the null space ![script upper N left-parenthesis bold-italic upper A right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0771.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

To specify those singular values ![sigma Subscript i](images/c09-i0772.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s, we consider

![bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper A equals left-parenthesis bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis equals bold-italic upper V bold upper Sigma Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper U Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack Baseline equals bold-italic upper V bold upper Sigma Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0071.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

hence ![bold upper Sigma Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0773.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></math> is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of ![bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0774.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></math>, which means that ![sigma Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c09-i0775.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> are non‐zero eigenvalues of ![bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0776.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></math> (and also ![bold-italic upper A bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0777.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> by the discussion above). Also recall that ![bold-italic v Subscript i](images/c09-i0778.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are the eigenvectors of ![bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0779.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></math>, while ![bold-italic u Subscript i](images/c09-i0780.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are the eigenvectors of ![bold-italic upper A bold-italic upper A Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0781.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. Finally, we can also write ([9.14](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0061)) in a “reduced SVD” form as:

![bold-italic upper A equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript r Endscripts sigma Subscript i Baseline bold-italic u Subscript i Baseline bold-italic v Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline equals bold-italic upper U Subscript r Baseline bold upper Sigma Subscript r Baseline bold-italic upper V Subscript r Superscript down-tack Baseline period](images/c09-math-0072.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>r</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>.</mo></math> 

For most applications in practice, we do not always need the exact SVD of the data matrix ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0782.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. It often suffices to have a factorization which well approximates ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0783.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> so as to save storage space and to reduce future computational complexity. In matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0784.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math>, the singular values can be arranged in descending order. Quite often the singular values decrease at a relatively fast rate, and the sum of the first 10% or even 1% of the singular values (say ![p](images/c09-i0785.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> out of ![r](images/c09-i0786.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, with ![p much-less-than r](images/c09-i0787.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>r</mi></math>) already amounts to 99% of the total sum of all the singular values. We also note that both ![bold-italic u Subscript i](images/c09-i0788.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s and ![bold-italic v Subscript j](images/c09-i0789.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s have unit norm. Therefore, it is plausible to describe matrix ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0790.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by using only the first ![p](images/c09-i0791.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> singular values via the decomposition:

![bold-italic upper A almost-equals bold-italic upper U Subscript p Baseline bold upper Sigma Subscript p Baseline bold-italic upper V Subscript p Superscript down-tack Baseline comma](images/c09-math-0073.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8776;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold-italic upper U Subscript p Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript m times p Baseline comma bold upper Sigma Subscript p Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times p](images/c09-i0792.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold-italic upper V Subscript p Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript n times p](images/c09-i0793.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>. Here, ![bold-italic upper U Subscript p](images/c09-i0794.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic upper V Subscript p](images/c09-i0795.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> contain the corresponding first ![p](images/c09-i0796.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> left and right singular vectors, and ![bold upper Sigma Subscript p Baseline equals diag left-parenthesis sigma 1 comma ellipsis comma sigma Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0797.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>diag</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Usually, we require ![p much-less-than r equals min left-brace right-brace comma m comma n](images/c09-i0798.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Hence, ![m times p plus p times p plus p times n equals left-parenthesis m plus n plus p right-parenthesis times p much-less-than m times n](images/c09-i0799.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>,

We conclude this section of the appendix with an alternative version of the *Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem* introduced earlier in [Section \*9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0012) formulated in terms of the spectral norm instead of the Frobenius norm. Recall that the spectral norm of a matrix ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0806.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is defined as ![parallel-to bold-italic upper A parallel-to colon equals max Underscript parallel-to bold-italic x parallel-to equals 1 Endscripts parallel-to bold-italic upper A bold-italic x parallel-to](images/c09-i0807.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.25em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.25em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, where ![parallel-to bold-italic x parallel-to equals StartRoot bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x EndRoot](images/c09-i0808.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-.25em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8741;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></msqrt></math> is the usual Euclidean norm; indeed, it is clearly equal to the largest singular value of ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0809.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by the *spectral decomposition theorem*.

\*9.A.4 Comparison between R functions of SVD and SD 

For a given matrix ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0843.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, the singular value decomposition (SVD) ![bold-italic upper A equals bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack](images/c09-i0844.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> always exists, regardless of whether ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0845.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is square or rectangle, whereas the spectral decomposition (SD) ![bold-italic upper A equals bold-italic upper P bold-italic upper D bold-italic upper P Superscript negative 1](images/c09-i0846.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> can only be valid when ![bold-italic upper A](images/c09-i0847.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is square and symmetric. Even among square matrices, the SD might not always exist. Notice that in [Programme 9.31](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3031), the two **R** functions `prcomp()` and `princomp()` seem to yield the same results.

In fact, when the dataset contains more rows than columns, computing PCA via SVD using the `prcomp()` function provides the same result as that via SD using the `princomp()` function. For example, see the illustration in [Programme 9.32](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3032) and the caption referred therein when the row number is less than the column number. In SVD, the entries returned in the diagonal matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c09-i0848.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> are always real and nonnegative by construction, while in general the entries of ![bold-italic upper D](images/c09-i0849.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi></mrow></math> in SD could be a complex number. Nevertheless, in data analytics, PCA is implemented for the variance‐covariance/correlation matrix of a dataset, and since those matrices are always in squared form, running PCA through both SVD and SD should provide the same result.

# CHAPTER 10  
Regression Learning

 

*Regression Learning* (a.k.a. *Regression Analysis*) is undoubtedly one of the most widely used statistical tools, and its predictive power is mostly determined by appropriate choices of independent variables or covariates, perhaps after transformations. Its name of “regression” was first coined by British statistician *Francis Galton* in 1885 [\[7\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0007), and its context was further consolidated by his disciple *Karl Pearson* in 1903 [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018). Generally speaking, regression analysis estimates the relationship between the response (dependent) and independent variables, which is not completely known but subject to some random error caused by noisy data. To name its immediate application in finance, the celebrated Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) by Markowitz in 1952 [\[16\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0016) is indeed a representative example. In this chapter, starting from this conventional model, we shall revisit the simple and multiple linear regression models, including the special case of polynomial regression, then we discuss several commonly used generalized linear models, namely *logistic regression* and *Poisson regression*, together with their applications in finance as well as the practical considerations for issues such as model selection and evaluation. In addition, echoing the PCA discussion in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml), we shall also introduce the closely related *principal component regression* and illustrate its use in practice.

 

## 10.1 SIMPLE AND MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION MODELS AND BEYOND

CAPM, as mentioned above, is in fact a simple linear regression of an individual asset's return against the market rate of return, namely:

(10.1)![normal r Subscript i Baseline equals r Subscript f Baseline plus beta Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis normal r Subscript m Baseline minus r Subscript f Baseline right-parenthesis plus normal epsilon Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c10-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

so that

[(10.2)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0002)![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal r Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals r Subscript f Baseline plus beta Subscript i Baseline left-bracket double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal r Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis minus r Subscript f Baseline right-bracket comma](images/c10-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal r Subscript i](images/c10-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the relative return of the ![i](images/c10-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th asset, ![normal r Subscript m](images/c10-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> is the relative return of the market of interest, ![r Subscript f](images/c10-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math> is the risk‐free interest rate which is assumed to be the only one in the market; ![beta Subscript i](images/c10-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the ![beta](images/c10-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>‐factor or the sensitivity of the expected excess return of the ![i](images/c10-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th security to the expected excess market return. Also, ![n](images/c10-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of different securities in this market sector. Finally, ![normal epsilon Subscript i](images/c10-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the idiosyncratic noise component with the mean zero and a finite variance ![sigma squared](images/c10-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. We further assume that

CAPM is widely applied in modern finance. For instance, the linear relationship ([10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0002)) between the ![beta](images/c10-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>‐factor and the expected return of the security in the CAPM, a.k.a. the *Security Market Line* (SML), is often used to determine whether an asset is properly valued. Usually, ![beta Subscript i](images/c10-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> stays roughly constant at the equilibrium level for almost every industrial sector, and if the sample mean of ![normal r Subscript i](images/c10-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> over the latest period becomes too high (resp. low) for a stock, it then receives an overall downward (resp. upward) pressure that pushes its price back to the corresponding equilibrium level on the SML. In the real market, these kinds of adjustments often take place in a relatively short time. Moreover, *Jensen's index* [\[11\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011) ![upper J colon equals ModifyingAbove mu With Ì‚ minus left-parenthesis r Subscript f Baseline plus ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ The *Sharpe ratio*, the empirical realization of ![beta Subscript i](images/c10-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction ModifyingAbove mu With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline minus r Subscript f Baseline Over ModifyingAbove sigma With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline EndFraction](images/c10-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>, measures the leverage effect of the ![i](images/c10-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th stock, i.e. its sensitivity to changes of the underlying market risk. If ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c10-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> of a stock is equal to (resp. less than) the market beta ![beta Subscript m](images/c10-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> (or its empirical counterpart ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript m Baseline equals StartFraction ModifyingAbove mu With Ì‚ Subscript m Baseline minus r Subscript f Baseline Over ModifyingAbove sigma With Ì‚ Subscript m Baseline EndFraction](images/c10-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>), then the stock is said to be *efficient* (resp. *inefficient*); likewise if ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline greater-than ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚ Subscript m](images/c10-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></math>, then the stock is considered more efficient than the market portfolio. Last but not least, the certainty equivalent pricing formula is frequently adopted in evaluating (single‐period) future projects for companies, and it is derived from CAPM as follows. To calculate the present value ![upper P](images/c10-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> of a project with a random terminal payoff ![normal upper Q](images/c10-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></math>, we apply CAPM to the expectation of its rate of return ![normal r equals StartFraction normal upper Q minus upper P Over upper P EndFraction](images/c10-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mi>P</mi></mfrac></math>:

That said, it is common practice to enhance the prediction power of the model by including more covariates. Simple linear regression models can then be extended to *multiple linear regression* models, resulting in the well‐known multi‐factor model in finance, a special, celebrated case of which was constructed by Fama and French in 1993 [\[5\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0005). The general form of this model is

The Fama–French three‐factor model uses three feature variables (instead of only one, the market portfolio, in CAPM) to describe the return of a stock. These correspond to: the factor of market risk; the outperformance index of small companies against big ones; and the outperformance indicator of companies with a high book‐to‐market ratio. More precisely, this three‐factor model for the ![i](images/c10-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th security is written as:

![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal r Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis minus r Subscript f Baseline equals alpha Subscript i Baseline plus beta Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline left-parenthesis í”¼ left-parenthesis normal r Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis minus r Subscript f Baseline right-parenthesis plus beta Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline dot SMB plus beta Subscript i Baseline 3 Baseline dot HML comma](images/c10-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><mtext>SMB</mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><mtext>HML</mtext><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the two new factors ![SMB](images/c10-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>SMB</mtext></mrow></math> and ![HML](images/c10-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>HML</mtext></mrow></math> respectively stand for “Small Minus Big”, the historical excess return of companies with smaller market capitalization over those with larger market capitalization, and “High Minus Low”, the historical excess return of stocks with a higher book‐to‐market ratio over those with a lower one. Let us give a brief summary of the calculations of these two factors

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column SMB 2nd Column equals one third left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove SV With bar plus ModifyingAbove SN With bar plus ModifyingAbove SG With bar right-parenthesis minus one third left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove BV With bar plus ModifyingAbove BN With bar plus ModifyingAbove BG With bar right-parenthesis comma 2nd Row 1st Column HML 2nd Column equals one half left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove SV With bar plus ModifyingAbove BV With bar right-parenthesis minus one half left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove SG With bar plus ModifyingAbove BG With bar right-parenthesis period EndLayout](images/c10-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtext>SMB</mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>SV</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>SN</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>SG</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>BV</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>BN</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>BG</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtext>HML</mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>SV</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>BV</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>SG</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mtext>BG</mtext><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

According to [\[4\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0004), the Fama–French three‐factor model explains over 90% of the diversified portfolios returns at their time of study, while the figure is only 70% on the average for CAPM.

In general, given a random variable ![bold x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c10-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> and another response variable of interest ![normal y element-of double-struck upper R](images/c10-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, regression analysis aims to learn the functional dependence of ![normal y](images/c10-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> on ![bold x](images/c10-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. That is, to find a reasonably simple function ![f colon double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c10-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> so that ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can well approximate ![normal y](images/c10-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> by minimizing a certain loss function, for instance, the mean squared error:

![upper L left-parenthesis f right-parenthesis colon equals í”¼ left-parenthesis left-parenthesis normal y minus f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis period](images/c10-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

We can easily deduce that the conditional expectation ![m left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis colon equals í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x equals bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the optimal answer, called the *regression function*; indeed, for any ![f colon double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c10-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>,

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column upper L left-parenthesis f right-parenthesis equals í”¼ left-parenthesis left-parenthesis normal y minus m left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis plus í”¼ left-parenthesis left-parenthesis m left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis minus f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to í”¼ left-parenthesis left-parenthesis normal y minus m left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis comma 2nd Column Blank EndLayout](images/c10-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

hence ![m left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals arg min Underscript f Endscripts upper L left-parenthesis f right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min</mtext><mi>f</mi></munder><mspace width=".2em"/><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as claimed. In practice, we often demand more regularities from ![f](images/c10-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, such as being a polynomial; a smooth enough function; or a linear combination of some regular enough base functions. Therefore, the general rationale behind regression analysis is to estimate the best regression functions (also called *regressors*) of this possibly highly nonlinear conditional expectation under different settings.

Practically, regression analysis consists of two common approaches: *parametric* and *non‐parametric* regressions. A parametric model assumes a prior knowledge of the class of the functions upon certain parameters to be determined. All simple and multiple regressions, together with the non‐linear regressions shown as follows, are typical examples. For non‐linear regression, the regressor ![f](images/c10-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> takes the general form:

![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals f left-parenthesis bold x semicolon beta 0 comma beta 1 comma ellipsis beta Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis and normal y equals f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis plus normal epsilon comma](images/c10-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="2em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the random variable ![normal epsilon](images/c10-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is the random error that varies independently of the pair ![left-parenthesis bold x comma normal y right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Each of the error terms corresponding to different samples therefore follows a common distribution; and these error terms are mostly assumed to be independent of each other.

In contrast, a non‐parametric model does not assume any specific form for the regressor. To name two common methods, they are *Kernel Regression* (to be introduced in Section \*14.3) and Principal Component Regression (to be introduced in [Section \*10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0015)). As a mixture of parametric and non‐parametric models, for a *semi‐parametric model*, the regressor takes the following separable form:

![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals f 1 left-parenthesis bold x semicolon beta 0 comma beta 1 comma ellipsis comma beta Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis plus f 2 left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis and normal y equals f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis plus normal epsilon comma](images/c10-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="2em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![f 1 left-parenthesis bold x semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the parametric functional part involving several parameters ![bold-italic beta equals left-parenthesis beta 0 comma beta 1 comma ellipsis comma beta Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c10-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> with a known functional form of ![f 1](images/c10-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, and the unknown function ![f 2 left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the non‐parametric functional part.

In regard to finding estimates of the optimal parameters ![beta Subscript j](images/c10-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s in the parametric functional part, here we introduce a generic iterative numerical scheme. Consider a dataset ![script upper S equals left-brace left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c10-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, with which we empirically estimate the theoretical mean squared error, and the least square method corresponding to the former is to minimize the empirical mean squared error between the actual observation (label) ![y Subscript i](images/c10-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and the approximant ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c10-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>:

(10.4)![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis colon equals í”¼ left-bracket left-parenthesis normal y minus f left-parenthesis bold x semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-bracket equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared comma](images/c10-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the best estimate ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic beta With Ì‚ equals arg min Underscript bold-italic beta Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p plus 1](images/c10-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min</mtext><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> should satisfy the first‐order condition which is a system of nonlinear equations:

[(10.5)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0015)![nabla Subscript bold-italic beta Baseline upper S vertical-bar Subscript bold-italic beta equals ModifyingAbove bold-italic beta With Ì‚ Baseline equals bold 0 period](images/c10-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mfenced open="" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></msub><mi>S</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Generally speaking, it is often difficult to obtain an analytic solution to the system ([10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0015)). Instead, it is more relevant to solve it numerically. To this point, the *Gauss–Newton method* is one of the commonly used numerical algorithms, and we introduce a modified version here. Readers may refer to [Appendix \*10.A.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0018) for a formal derivation of the Gauss–Newton method.

Define ![n](images/c10-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> functions called residuals; ![r Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis colon equals left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline semicolon bold-italic beta right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared](images/c10-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma n](images/c10-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. The minimization of ![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is equivalent to minimizing the following sum of squares:

Denote by

the Jacobian (rectangular) matrix of (partial derivatives of) ![left-parenthesis r 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma r Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with respect to ![bold-italic beta](images/c10-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. The procedure of the *modified Gauss–Newton algorithm* is the following:

Note that the error ![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> may not be decreasing for every iteration in the Gauss–Newton algorithm but could be oscillating instead. Yet for any sufficiently small ![lamda greater-than 0](images/c10-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, it always holds that ![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline plus lamda bold upper Delta right-parenthesis less-than upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in the neighbourhood of a minimum point of ![upper S](images/c10-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, for ![ModifyingAbove bold upper Delta With Ì‚ equals bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline minus bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Thus the modified version of the Gauss–Newton algorithm incorporates a small enough factor ![lamda](images/c10-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> (learning rate) in each consecutive update. For each iteration, to choose a suitable ![lamda element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> which minimizes the error ![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline plus lamda ModifyingAbove bold upper Delta With Ì‚ right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we can simply apply some popular search algorithms such as the *golden‐section search method*

where the ![i](images/c10-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th summand solely depends on the ![i](images/c10-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th row of ![bold-italic upper J Subscript bold-italic r Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">J</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> which is the gradient of the ![i](images/c10-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th residual ![r Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that in turn is just the residual with respect to the ![i](images/c10-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th datum only; so each of these ![script upper J Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">J</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>'s contributes to ![upper S left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> independently of the others. As an aside, we note the independence among the summands in the representation ([10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0018)) makes parallel computing feasible.

In addition to ordinary linear regression models, there are many other useful variants to be introduced in the following sections; readers can also refer to [\[15\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0015) and references therein for more discussions.

 

## 10.2 POLYNOMIAL REGRESSION

Polynomial regression models a regressor by a polynomial function. Given a dataset ![script upper S equals left-brace left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c10-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, a quadratic regression model takes the form:

![y Subscript i Baseline equals beta 0 plus beta 1 x Subscript i Baseline plus beta 2 x Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline plus epsilon Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c10-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

while a cubic model is:

![y Subscript i Baseline equals beta 0 plus beta 1 x Subscript i Baseline plus beta 2 x Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta 3 x Subscript i Superscript 3 Baseline plus epsilon Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c10-math-0020.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![normal open e Subscript i](images/c10-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#603;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are independent idiosyncratic noises as before. In practice, the degree of the polynomial regressor barely exceeds 5, otherwise the parameters are hard to interpret. Even worse, a high degree polynomial regressor becomes unstable, drastically affecting its performance as it leans towards to overfitting.

For more effective applications, we can include more explanatory variables in regression. For instance, a two‐variable quadratic regression model is given by:

![y Subscript i Baseline equals beta 0 plus beta 1 x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline plus beta 2 x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline plus beta 11 x Subscript i Baseline 1 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta 22 x Subscript i Baseline 2 Superscript 2 Baseline plus beta 12 x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline plus epsilon Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma](images/c10-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>22</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline x Subscript i Baseline 2](images/c10-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> stands for the *interaction term* for the datum ![i](images/c10-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

In principle, a polynomial regression is essentially no different from ordinary linear regressions, except that the regressor is now in terms of powers of the same data input. This means that the same formula for the least squared estimate of ![ModifyingAbove beta With Ì‚](images/c10-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> applies, but the data matrix, say for a regressor with a degree ![p](images/c10-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, takes the form:

![bold-italic upper X equals Start 3 By 5 Matrix 1st Row 1st Column 1 2nd Column x 1 3rd Column x 1 squared 4th Column ellipsis 5th Column x 1 Superscript p Baseline 2nd Row 1st Column vertical-ellipsis 2nd Column vertical-ellipsis 3rd Column vertical-ellipsis 4th Column down-right-diagonal-ellipsis 5th Column vertical-ellipsis 3rd Row 1st Column 1 2nd Column x Subscript n Baseline 3rd Column x Subscript n Superscript 2 Baseline 4th Column ellipsis 5th Column x Subscript n Superscript p Baseline EndMatrix comma](images/c10-math-0022.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd class="array"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd class="array"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd><mtd class="array"><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8230;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8942;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8942;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8942;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8945;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8942;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd class="array"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mtd><mtd class="array"><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8230;</mo></mtd><mtd class="array"><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is a *Vandermonde* matrix (see [\[10\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0010)). Also, the statistical diagnostics is essentially the same as that for multiple linear regressions (via MANOVA).

We next present a real estate price example by using polynomial regression models in an **R** environment. The dataset used is the *Boston Housing Dataset* ![FIGURE 10.1 Neighborhoods of Boston (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/35/Boston\_ONS\_Neighborhoods.svg).](images/c10f001.png)

## 10.3 GENERALIZED LINEAR MODELS

In traditional linear regression models, the response variable ![normal y](images/c10-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is assumed to be normally distributed, while the functional relationship between the predictors ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline](images/c10-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> and ![normal y](images/c10-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is linear. However, many real‐world applications require models to accommodate different types of response variables and nonlinear relationships. Enriching the potential applications of regression analysis, the vast class of *Generalized Linear Models* (GLMs) is prevalent in these scenarios. In these models, the response variables follow a distribution from the so‐called *exponential dispersion family* (EDF), whose mean is connected, via the *link function*, with the *linear predictor* or *systematic component* ![eta equals bold-italic x overTilde Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic beta](images/c10-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></math>, which is a linear combination of the standard versions of the feature (explanatory) variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline](images/c10-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>.

Let us go into more detail of the GLM. For simplicity, we consider a one‐dimensional setting only. We first briefly introduce some fundamental properties of the EDF. The pdf (or pmf in the discrete case) of a distribution in the EDF takes the following general form:

[(10.8)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0023)![StartLayout 1st Row f left-parenthesis y semicolon theta comma phi right-parenthesis equals exp left-parenthesis StartFraction y theta minus b left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis Over phi EndFraction plus upper S left-parenthesis y comma phi right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma EndLayout](images/c10-math-0023.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where ![theta](images/c10-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is called the *natural parameter*, and ![b left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis element-of upper C squared](images/c10-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> and ![upper S left-parenthesis y comma phi right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are known functions. From ([10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0023)), we can see that EDF is a sub‐class of the exponential family where the sufficient statistic of ![theta](images/c10-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> equals ![normal y](images/c10-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> divided by the scale parameter ![phi](images/c10-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math>. Many commonly used distributions in financial and insurance analytics belong to the EDF, including but not limited to the normal, gamma, Poisson and binomial distributions. From ([10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0023)), we can readily derive the mgf of ![normal y](images/c10-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>:
