implying that ![normal y overbar](images/c10-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> is still in the EDF with the same natural parameter ![theta](images/c10-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> and function ![b left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, but the scale parameter changes from ![phi](images/c10-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math> to ![StartFraction phi Over omega EndFraction](images/c10-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>&#969;</mi></mfrac></math>.

On the other hand, the link function ![g left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a one‐to‐one function which maps ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x overTilde equals bold-italic x overTilde right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to ![eta equals bold-italic x overTilde Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic beta](images/c10-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></math>, i.e. ![g left-parenthesis í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x overTilde equals bold-italic x overTilde right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals eta](images/c10-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#951;</mi></math>, or equivalently,

![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x overTilde equals bold-italic x overTilde right-parenthesis equals g Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis eta right-parenthesis equals g Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x overTilde Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic beta right-parenthesis period](images/c10-math-0028.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Note that the selection of the link function may be restricted by the model of the response variable ![normal y](images/c10-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>, as it affects the range of ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x overTilde equals bold-italic x overTilde right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. For example, to model a Bernoulli distributed response variable as a GLM, its link function should be a mapping of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c10-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>. Moreover, we also want the link function to be able to explain the effect of the explanatory variables on the response.

One common choice of the link function is the *canonical link* function that satisfies

[(10.10)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0029)![g ring b prime left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals theta period](images/c10-math-0029.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Using ([10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0025)), where ![b prime left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> stands for the conditional mean ![í”¼ left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar bold x overTilde equals bold-italic x overTilde right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we see that the canonical link function equates the linear predictor ![eta](images/c10-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> with the natural parameter ![theta](images/c10-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. The canonical link function not only possesses appropriate domain and range, but also usually provides a direct interpretation. Unless otherwise specified, all link functions used in this book refer to the canonical link functions.

As a side note in terms of model assessment for GLMs, a commonly adopted measure is *deviance*, defined as twice the difference of the loglikelihood of the *saturated model* (whose number of parameters equals the sample size, but not necessarily the empirical distribution) subtracted by that of the fitted model. In particular, for candidate models under the same distributional family, their corresponding saturated model is the same, and comparing deviances of the candidate models reduces to comparing their likelihoods.

We next introduce a financial example with an inappropriate use of ordinary regression, and then explain how to rescue the situation by using GLMs. To this end, we consider the dataset `fin‐ratio.csv` that contains financial ratios of 680 securities listed in the main board of Hong Kong Stock Exchange in 2002, in which there are six financial variables, namely: *Earning Yield* (`EY`); *Cash Flow to Price* (`CFTP`); *logarithm of Market Value* (`ln_MV`); *Dividend Yield* (`DY`); *Book to Market Equity* (`BTME`); *Debt to Equity Ratio* (`DTE`). The information of these financial variables are publicly available, via *Yahoo Finance* ([https://finance.yahoo.com/](https://finance.yahoo.com/)) for instance. Among these companies, there were 32 Blue Chips which used to be the Hang Seng Index (HSI) Constituent Stocks. The last column `HSI` is a binary variable indicating whether a stock is a Blue Chip or not. We want to find any possible relationship between `HSI` and these six financial variables. In [Programme 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3003), using the built‐in function `lm()` in **R**, we fit an ordinary regression model for `HSI` against these six financial variables. From the output, the ![p](images/c10-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐value of `d$DTE` is the largest, so the coefficient of `DTE` is not significantly different from 0. We then exclude it, and fit the remaining five independent financial variables in another regression as in [Programme 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3004).

We then see that the ![p](images/c10-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐value of `d$BTME` remains large, and we can exclude this `d$BTME` to fit rest for another regression. We keep on excluding variables with the largest ![p](images/c10-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐values step by step until all the listed ![p](images/c10-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐values left behind are small (say, less than 0.1). This overall procedure is known as *backward elimination* for model selection. Finally, we arrive at the “ultimate” model in [Programme 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3005).

The least square regression model reads:

![monospace HSI equals negative 0.454781 minus 0.01026 dot monospace CFTP plus 0.07963 dot monospace ln bar MV period](images/c10-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.454781</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.01026</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mtext mathvariant="monospace">CFTP</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>0.07963</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>.</mo></math> 

There are some serious concerns with this. Firstly, the predicted labels distribute continuously over a large range of values other than 0 or 1. Secondly, if the assumption of the normality of residuals were correct, the normal Q‐Q plot should be close to a straight line, while all other residual plots should show a random pattern.

![FIGURE 10.4 The output of the linear regression model for HSI generated by Programme 10.6.](images/c10f004.png)

[**FIGURE 10.4**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0004) The output of the linear regression model for `HSI` generated by [Programme 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3006).

From [Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0004), for the rightmost bottom plot, the residuals are mainly distributed around 0 and have another, secondary peak at larger positive values; the top left plot of residuals against fitted values indicates the secondary peak of large positive residual values is likely associated with those data with ![monospace HSI equals 1](images/c10-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. In addition, the middle right Q‐Q plot in [Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0004) also shows the heavy‐tail nature of the fitted model. As a whole, the linear regression assumption is seriously violated as the low adjusted ![upper R squared](images/c10-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> of 0.3648, as seen in the output in [Programme 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3005), also implies.

 

## 10.4 LOGISTIC REGRESSION

The last example highlights the shortcoming of ordinary linear regression in the face of binary responses. A better approach is a commonly used special case of GLMs: *logistic regression*. Generally, the root(s) of ![nabla Subscript bold-italic beta Baseline ln upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis equals bold 0](images/c10-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math> cannot be solved explicitly due to the nonlinearity of the logit transform of ![bold-italic x overTilde Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic beta](images/c10-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></math>. Instead, we can efficiently find them numerically via the Gauss–Newton algorithm, see [Appendix \*10.A.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0018). Its detailed adaptation for logistic regression is put in [Appendix \*10.A.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0019). The derived method is called the *Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares* (IRLS); see formula ([10.26](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0076)) for the iteration scheme.

Next, we illustrate the effectiveness of logistic regression on the HSI example. **R** has a built‐in function `glm()` (standing for generalized linear model) for performing logistic regression, whose output format is similar to that of `lm()`. The last parameter `binomial` specifies the *link function* of logistic regression in `glm()`. In [Programme 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3007), the MLEs of the coefficients are generally large, this may be caused by the presence of many outliers.

In [Programme 10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3008), the `glm()` output is saved in `lreg`, which contains many items. An important one is `fitted.values`, which are the estimated success probabilities ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c10-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> from ([10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0033)) for these 680 stocks in 2002. The extremely large MLEs of the coefficients mean the fitted values are very close to 0 or 1. To obtain predicted labels, we can assign a value of `pr=True` if the fitted value is greater than or equal to 0.5; otherwise `pr=False` is placed. Finally, we generate a confusion matrix / cross tabulation table of `pr` versus `HSI` to see how well this logistic regression model predicts. We see there are ![634 plus 30 equals 664](images/c10-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>634</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>664</mn></math> correct classifications with ![14 plus 2 equals 16](images/c10-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math> misclassifications. There are 2 stocks with ![monospace HSI equals 1](images/c10-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> being misclassified as `pr=False`, while 14 stocks with ![monospace HSI equals 0](images/c10-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> are misclassified as `pr=True`. The correct classification rate is therefore ![664 slash 680 equals 97.65 percent-sign](images/c10-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>664</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>97.65</mn><mi>%</mi></math>.

As mentioned before, regarding [Programme 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3007), the large coefficients could be caused by outliers. To get a more robust model with smaller coefficients, we may use the Mahalanobis distance (defined in (3.3) in [Section 3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0005)) to detect outliers, remove them, then fit a more reasonable model. In [Programme 10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3009), we introduce a function `mdist()` in ![bold upper R](images/c10-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></mrow></math> to compute the Mahalanobis distance. For the dataset of `fin‐ratio.csv`, we separate the data into two groups, `d0` of those with ![monospace HSI equals 0](images/c10-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and `d1` of those with ![monospace HSI equals 1](images/c10-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, as shown in [Programme 10.10](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3010). We detect and throw away the outliers in `d0`, while leaving `d1` untouched as it contains too few cases.

![FIGURE 10.5 Scatter plot of the Mahalabonis distances, generated in Programme 10.10.](images/c10f005.png)

[**FIGURE 10.5**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0005) Scatter plot of the Mahalabonis distances, generated in [Programme 10.10](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3010).

In [Figure 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0005), points with a large distance are potential outliers which will be discarded. But what is an appropriate cut‐off value? the Mahalanobis distance ![upper D Subscript i](images/c10-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for each ![bold-italic x Subscript display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Moreover, these ![upper D Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c10-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>'s are also approximately independent of each other for large ![n](images/c10-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, based on this observation, we can remove the stocks in `d0` with Mahalanobis distances exceeding the top ![1 percent-sign](images/c10-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mi>%</mi></math> percentile of the chi‐square distribution with degrees of freedom ![p equals 6](images/c10-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>; and then combine this resulting family with the data of `d1` to obtain the cleansed dataset `d3`; see the implementation in [Programme 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3011).

Next, we fit a logistic regression to this cleansed dataset `d3`, and remove financial variables with coefficients having large ![p](images/c10-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐values by backward eliminations. A final model can eventually be obtained following [Programme 10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3012). From the corresponding confusion matrix, the correct classification rate has increased to ![653 slash 658 equals 99.24 percent-sign](images/c10-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>653</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>658</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>99.24</mn><mi>%</mi></math> on this reduced training dataset. In particular, throwing away the outliers actually gives a simpler model with smaller coefficients.

 

### 10.4.1 Logistic Regression (Threshold Type) with Dummy Variables

Like ordinary regression, there could be categorical variables as independent (feature) variables in a logistic regression. In [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml), by using a decision tree, we shall see that `ln_MV>9.4776` serves as an important indicator for classifying stocks with ![monospace HSI equals 0](images/c10-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> or 1. Taking this as given, we propose to use a dummy (categorical) variable ![g colon equals 1 plus double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace ln normal bar MV greater-than 9.4776 right-brace Baseline](images/c10-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mtext>MV</mtext><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>9.4776</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math>, and fit a logistic regression with this ![g](images/c10-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> in addition to the other five financial variables, apart from `MV`, together with their interaction terms. This primitive threshold logistic regression model is shown in [Programme 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3013).

The coefficient of `CFTP*g` has the largest ![p](images/c10-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐value (0.9721), and that of `CFTP` has the second largest (0.9607). We can then exclude `CFTP` and `CFTP*g` in the next regression fitting; see [Programme 10.14](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3014) for the revised model.

In [Programme 10.14](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3014), the coefficient `DTE*g` has the largest ![p](images/c10-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐value (0.7147) and that of `DTE` itself also has the second largest (0.6745), so we exclude `DTE` and `DTE*g` in the next trial. We keep on excluding variables with large ![p](images/c10-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐values, and after several rounds we finally obtain the ultimate model as shown in [Programme 10.15](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3015). This threshold model is simpler than that in [Programme 10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3012), yet its classification power remains as good as before, and it reads:

![ln left-parenthesis StartFraction ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Over 1 minus ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ EndFraction right-parenthesis equals negative 18.6304 plus 12.9236 normal g plus 1.4036 DY minus 1.2860 left-parenthesis g asterisk DY right-parenthesis comma](images/c10-math-0036.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>18.6304</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12.9236</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1.4036</mn><mtext>DY</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1.2860</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>g&#42;DY</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

or equivalently,

![ln left-parenthesis StartFraction ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Over 1 minus ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ EndFraction right-parenthesis equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column negative 5.6944 plus 0.1176 DY comma 3rd Column for ln normal bar MV less-than-or-equal-to 9.4776 semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column 7.2416 minus 1.1684 DY comma 3rd Column for ln normal bar MV greater-than 9.4776 semicolon EndLayout](images/c10-math-0037.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5.6944</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.1176</mn><mtext>DY</mtext><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mtext>MV</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>9.4776</mn><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>7.2416</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1.1684</mn><mtext>DY</mtext><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mtext>MV</mtext><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>9.4776</mn><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![pi](images/c10-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math> is the probability that ![monospace HSI equals 1](images/c10-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> given the features. When ![monospace ln bar MV greater-than 9.4776](images/c10-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>9.4776</mn></math>, the intercept is bigger than that if ![monospace ln bar MV less-than-or-equal-to 9.4776](images/c10-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>9.4776</mn></math>. Thus the probability that ![monospace HSI equals 1](images/c10-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> looks higher when `ln_MV` is large, as it should.

 

### 10.4.2 Decision Threshold for Binary Logistic Regression

In logistic regression, casual users may take an observation, with a feature vector ![bold-italic x](images/c10-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, and classify it to group ![c 1](images/c10-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> if the predicted probability satisfies ![ModifyingAbove double-struck upper P With Ì‚ left-parenthesis normal y equals c 1 vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0.5](images/c10-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math>. However, this decision threshold of 0.5 is not always appropriate. For instance, in a medical diagnosis of a rare disease, a considerable number of infected patients may receive a negative diagnosis result that delays treatments if the decision threshold is set too high. On the other hand, the diagnosis becomes meaningless if the threshold is set too low. It is crucial to select an appropriate deciding probability ![u](images/c10-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, so that a patient with a feature vector ![bold-italic x](images/c10-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is classified as positive when the predicted probability is greater than ![u](images/c10-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>; or negative otherwise. Another example, from finance, is the estimation of the probability of default of a client and the classification of his credit‐worthiness via binary logistic regression. For a loan application, the decision threshold ![u](images/c10-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> can be chosen suitably as follows: first, consider the following table of potential losses incurred for lending:

| Decision ![set-minus](images/c10-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8726;</mo></mrow></math> Borrower || Non‐default (actual ![y equals 0](images/c10-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) || Default (actual ![y equals 1](images/c10-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accept (predict ![y equals 0](images/c10-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) || correct || error (![cost equals dollar-sign u 2](images/c10-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>cost</mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>) |
| Reject (predict ![y equals 1](images/c10-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) || error (![cost equals dollar-sign u 1](images/c10-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>cost</mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>&#36;</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>) || correct |

There are two costs of misclassification errors ![u 1](images/c10-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![u 2](images/c10-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, and they need not be equal. Let ![p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis Default vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>Default</mtext><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![1 minus p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis Non hyphen default vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>Non&#8208;default</mtext><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The expected loss of rejecting a non‐default borrower is therefore given by ![u 1 left-parenthesis 1 minus p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; while the expected loss of accepting a default borrower is given by ![u 2 p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. On the average, it is sensible to reject an application if ![u 1 left-parenthesis 1 minus p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis less-than u 2 p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, or equivalently ![p left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis greater-than StartFraction u 1 Over u 1 plus u 2 EndFraction equals colon u](images/c10-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mi>u</mi></math>, which is a desired *decision threshold*. In the special case when ![dollar-sign u 1](images/c10-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> equals ![dollar-sign u 2](images/c10-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#36;</mi><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, ![u](images/c10-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> is simply ![one half](images/c10-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.

 

### 10.4.3 Multinomial Logistic Regression for Categorical Response

Binary logistic regressions can be easily extended to *Multinomial Logistic Regression* in which the response ![normal y](images/c10-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is categorical, with more than two categories. For instance, let ![normal y](images/c10-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> take ![k](images/c10-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> categories, namely ![c 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma c Subscript k Baseline](images/c10-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, and we model the corresponding probabilities by:

![double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace y Sub Subscript i Subscript equals c Sub Subscript j Subscript right-brace Baseline equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 0 comma 2nd Column if y Subscript i Baseline not-equals c Subscript j Baseline semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column 1 comma 2nd Column if y Subscript i Baseline equals c Subscript j Baseline period EndLayout](images/c10-math-0041.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

These ![bold-italic beta Subscript j](images/c10-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s can be estimated by maximum likelihood estimation, numerically via the Gauss–Newton algorithm similar to those in [Section 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0002) for binary responses. In particular, the IRLS in [Appendix \*10.A.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0019) can also be extended.

In **R**, there is a built‐in function `multinom()`, in the `nnet` (standing for neural network) library, which estimates the parameters in a multinomial logistic regression model. Referring to [Programme 10.16](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3016), this example uses Fisher's famous *Iris flower dataset* ![FIGURE 10.6 Photo of an Iris virginica flower; original picture from https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iris\_virginica.jpg.](images/c10f006.png)

[**FIGURE 10.6**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0006) Photo of an Iris virginica flower; original picture from [https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iris\_virginica.jpg](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iris_virginica.jpg).

For our last example of logistic regression, we revisit the classification problem for the MNIST dataset mentioned in Subsection 6.1.2. To this, we first apply the multinomial logistic regression in [Programme 10.17](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3017) via Python (resp. [Programme 10.18](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3018) via **R**). There are ![28 times 28 equals 784](images/c10-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>784</mn></math> feature variables with ![784 times left-parenthesis 10 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 7 comma 056](images/c10-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>784</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>056</mn></math> coefficient weights and ![10 minus 1 equals 9](images/c10-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>10</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math> biases.

From [Programme 10.17](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3017), the accuracy on the test dataset is 92.56%, which is much greater than the 67.84% achieved by the EM algorithm. However, one should notice that the EM algorithm is an unsupervised learner, and it is reasonable to expect a lower accuracy. The difference in accuracies obtained via different programming languages is due to difference in values of initial seeds taken and variation in the numerical computation schemes used.

 

## 10.5 POISSON REGRESSION

For insurance policies, a policyholder files claims to insurance companies once an insured contingent event occurs, so as to compensate his/her financial losses. It is essential for the insurance industry to model the random arrivals of claims within a specified period of time. Poisson regression is commonly used to model this type of count data by assuming the response variable ![normal y](images/c10-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> follows a Poisson distribution with a hazard rate, or mean arrival rate, of ![lamda](images/c10-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. As a representative example of GLMs, we note that a Poisson response ![normal y](images/c10-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is in the EDF; indeed, the pmf of ![normal y](images/c10-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> can be written as:

so that the natural parameter is ![theta equals ln lamda](images/c10-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>&#955;</mi></math>, the scale parameter is ![phi equals 1](images/c10-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and ![b left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals e Superscript theta](images/c10-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msup></math>. In general, there is no closed‐form solution to ![nabla Subscript bold-italic beta Baseline upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis equals bold 0](images/c10-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></msub><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math>, and we may find the numerical maximizer ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic beta With Ì‚ Subscript MLE](images/c10-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mtext>MLE</mtext></msub></math> via the usual Gauss–Newton algorithm.

Next, we give an application of Poisson regression on predicting counts. The *1976 Panel Study of Income Dynamics Dataset*

In [Programme 10.19](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3019), **R** reported that the relations between the number of children under 18 and most of the features are insignificant, so we first remove the insignificant features and then fit the model again. This backward elimination is repeated until all the remaining features are significant enough.

[Programme 10.20](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3020) presents the ultimate model with remaining features `hoursw`, `agew`, and `experience`. Firstly, the feature `hoursw` stands for a wife's hours of work in 1975. Its coefficient is negative (![negative 0.0001087](images/c10-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.0001087</mn></math>), which implies that if the wife would work for longer hours, her expected number of children decreases. Secondly, the feature `experience` is the actual number of years of a wife's previous working experience in the labour market. Its negative coefficient (![negative 0.0259452](images/c10-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.0259452</mn></math>) indicates a negative correlation between the wife's working experience and her own expected number of children. Finally, we also observe a similar negative correlation between the response variable and the feature `agew`.

A reasonable explanation for the negative correlations between the count variable and the features is as follows: if a woman spent more time on work, she would have less time available for her family, and so she tends to have fewer kids. Finally, the feature `agew` represents the wife's age with its coefficient being negative (![negative 0.0550786](images/c10-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.0550786</mn></math>). This negativity could be attributed to the fact that as the mother got older, her children would eventually become adults, resulting in a decline in the number of children under 18; in addition, as the wife ages, she tends to not bear more children.

 

## 10.6 MODEL EVALUATION AND CONSIDERATIONS IN PRACTICE

 

### 10.6.1 Model Selection: Backward Elimination and Information Criterion

In ordinary linear regression or logistic regression, selecting the most relevant feature variables is a critical issue. One common procedure is backward elimination, a stepwise approach mentioned earlier, which starts with all the variables and then eliminates variables with the largest ![p](images/c10-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐values one‐by‐one in each step. There are alternative methods for model selection. For instance, an *Information Criterion* (IC) can be applied to choose the suitable complexity and parameter estimation in one step of the regression model by minimizing the overall IC which is defined as ![minus 2 ln upper L plus k theta](images/c10-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></math>, where ![ln upper L](images/c10-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi></math> is the log‐likelihood function corresponding to the underlying statistical model, and ![theta](images/c10-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is the effective degrees of freedom which is the number of free parameters in the model. In particular, for ![k equals 2](images/c10-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, the corresponding IC is called the *Akaike Information Criterion* (AIC) (see [\[1\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001)). The motivation for AIC is that a decent model should have a good predictive power for the *out‐sample* by using the likelihood approach based on the in‐sample; and AIC serves as an asymptotic unbiased estimate for the expected predictive log‐likelihood. For ![k equals ln n](images/c10-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>n</mi></math>, it is called the *Bayesian Information Criterion* (BIC) (see [\[19\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020)). For a finite set ![script upper M equals StartSet upper M EndSet](images/c10-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> of models, by using a Laplace integral approximation and Taylor expansion up to order 2, one can show that given a sample ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c10-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, the posterior probability of a model ![upper M](images/c10-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper M vertical-bar bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is proportional to ![exp left-parenthesis minus BIC slash 2 right-parenthesis double-struck upper P left-parenthesis upper M right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>BIC</mtext><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, asymptotically for a large sample size ![n](images/c10-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, the smaller the BIC, the more preferable the model; readers may refer to Appendix 12.A.2 in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml) for a more detailed introduction to BIC. In general, with more parameters included in the model, the log‐likelihood function tends to increase in value and so ![minus 2 ln upper L](images/c10-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>L</mi></math> decreases, yet for a more complex model, it tends to overfit the in‐sample and result in a larger ![k theta](images/c10-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></math>. The IC penalizes an excessive inclusion of parameters, and the corresponding optimal model, with reasonable accuracy and model complexity, is indicated at the IC minimum.

Let us illustrate with the cleansed dataset of `fin‐ratio_cleansed.csv`, which has had outliers removed by [Programme 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3011), we choose the model with the smallest AIC. In [Programme 10.21](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3021), the `step()` function in **R** implements the stepwise regression. Note that the ultimate model (with smallest AIC) is ![monospace HSI equals negative 69.931 minus 3.038 monospace CFTP plus 7.256 monospace ln bar MV plus 1.322 monospace BTME](images/c10-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>69.931</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3.038</mn><mtext mathvariant="monospace">CFTP</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>7.256</mn><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>1.322</mn><mtext mathvariant="monospace">BTME</mtext></math>, which is the same as that determined by the backward elimination in [Programme 10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3012); and this agreement is generally the case.

 

### 10.6.2 Lift Chart for Assessing Performance

The fitted value (`lreg$fit`) in the logistic regression output gives the estimated probability of success of ![ModifyingAbove double-struck upper P With Ì‚ left-parenthesis normal y equals 1 vertical-bar bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Sorting variables ![y](images/c10-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>'s (`d3$HSI` in our example) according to the decreasing order of `lreg$fit` and assigning them with rankings, we expect most of the records with ![normal y equals 1](images/c10-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> to appear on the top of the list. However, due to the inaccuracy of the model, some with ![normal y equals 1](images/c10-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> may appear low in the list. We can then compute the cumulative percentage of ![normal y equals 1](images/c10-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and plot them against their rankings, which gives a plot called a *lift chart* that indicates how well this logistic regression model predicts.

More precisely, suppose that the sample data are randomly arranged according to indexing subscript ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c10-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. We then sort them in descending order of ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline equals monospace lreg dollar-sign fit](images/c10-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext mathvariant="monospace">lreg&#36;fit</mtext></math>, and label them with a new index (ranking) ![i prime equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c10-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. [Programme 10.22](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3022) gives the lift chart of ranking ![i prime](images/c10-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> versus ![f 1 left-parenthesis i Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction 1 Over i Superscript prime Baseline EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript i Superscript prime Baseline Endscripts HSI Subscript j Baseline](images/c10-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msubsup><msub><mtext>HSI</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></math>.

As a variant, instead of cumulative percentage, we can plot against the cumulative proportion, namely, ![i prime](images/c10-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> versus ![f 2 left-parenthesis i Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript i Superscript prime Baseline Endscripts HSI Subscript j Baseline Over sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts HSI Subscript j Baseline EndFraction](images/c10-i0334.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msubsup><msub><mtext>HSI</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mtext>HSI</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>; see [Programme 10.23](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3023).

For both resulting plots in [Figure 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0007), we also plot the ideal cases (dashed lines in red), where all ![normal y equals 1](images/c10-i0335.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> records are ranked higher than ![normal y equals 0](images/c10-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> records against the sorted index (ranking) ![i prime](images/c10-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math>. Deviations of the actual cases (solid lines in blue) from the ideal cases reflect the inaccuracy of the logistic regression model; the more the discrepancy, the less reliable the model is.

 

### 10.6.3 Confusion Matrices and ROC Curve

When assessing the performance of a classifier, its accuracy as shown in the classification table is not a very robust measure, and can be sometimes misleading. To remedy its shortcomings, we can introduce other measurements such as *precision*, *recall* (a.k.a. *True Positive Rate* (TPR)), *False Positive Rate* (FPR) and the ![upper F 1](images/c10-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> *score* ![FIGURE 10.7 Using the cleansed dataset d3 from Programme 10.11, lift charts of ranking versus cumulative percentage and proportion, respectively.](images/c10f007.png)

[**FIGURE 10.7**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0007) Using the cleansed dataset `d3` from [Programme 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3011), lift charts of ranking versus cumulative percentage and proportion, respectively.

![TABLE 10.1  Confusion matrix for a medical test.](images/c10-i0343.png)

[**TABLE 10.1**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-tbl-0001)  Confusion matrix for a medical test.

Based on [Table 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0001), the precision, recall (a.k.a. True Positive Rate, TPR), FPR (False Positive Rate), and ![upper F 1](images/c10-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score of the test are defined one‐by‐one as follows:

![Precision colon equals StartFraction TP Over TP plus FP EndFraction](images/c10-math-0047.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Precision</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>TP</mtext><mrow><mtext>TP</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>FP</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

is the proportion of correct test results among positive results;

![Recall left-parenthesis a period k period a period TPR right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction TP Over TP plus FN EndFraction](images/c10-math-0048.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Recall (a.k.a. TPR)</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>TP</mtext><mrow><mtext>TP</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>FN</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

is the proportion of observations correctly classified as positive among all observations which are actually positive;

![FPR colon equals StartFraction FP Over TN plus FP EndFraction](images/c10-math-0049.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>FP</mtext><mrow><mtext>TN</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>FP</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

is defined as the proportion of observations that are incorrectly classified as positive among all negative observations (also see [Figure 10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0008) for an illustration of the definitions of TPR and FPR);

![upper F 1 colon equals StartFraction 2 Over 1 slash Precision plus 1 slash Recall EndFraction equals StartFraction 2 times Precision times Recall Over Precision plus Recall EndFraction](images/c10-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mtext>Precision</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mtext>Recall</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mtext>Precision</mtext><mo>&#215;</mo><mtext>Recall</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext>Precision</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>Recall</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Its advantage can be seen by considering the test of a rare disease as in [Table 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0002).

![TABLE 10.2  A confusion matrix of a test of a rare disease.](images/c10-i0349.png)

[**TABLE 10.2**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-tbl-0002)  A confusion matrix of a test of a rare disease.

![FIGURE 10.8 Illustration of TPR and FPR.](images/c10f008.png)

[**FIGURE 10.8**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0008) Illustration of TPR and FPR.

The overall accuracy of the test is ![left-parenthesis 2 plus 195 right-parenthesis slash 200 equals 98.5 percent-sign](images/c10-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>195</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>98.5</mn><mi>%</mi></math>, which is high only due to the rareness of the disease. Indeed, most of the correct predictions come from the true negatives; yet the precision of the test is only ![2 slash 4 equals 50 percent-sign](images/c10-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mi>%</mi></math> while the recall (TPR) of the test is ![2 slash 3 equals 66.7 percent-sign](images/c10-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>66.7</mn><mi>%</mi></math>. Together, these make the ![upper F 1](images/c10-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score become ![4 slash 7 equals 57.14 percent-sign](images/c10-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>57.14</mn><mi>%</mi></math>; also, the FPR of the test is ![2 slash 197 equals 1.02 percent-sign](images/c10-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>197</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1.02</mn><mi>%</mi></math>.

Another use of TPR and FPR is to see whether a classification algorithm is effective enough. In particular, an efficient classifier should maximize the TPR as much as possible, while ideally at the same time it could reduce the FPR. This mutual relation can be better understood by using the *Receiver Operating Characteristic* (ROC) curve

Consider [Table 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0003), which shows a training dataset of 20 observations ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with their corresponding label ![y Subscript i](images/c10-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 20](images/c10-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn></math>. Ten of the observations have ![y Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c10-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (in positive class) while the rest are ![y Subscript i Baseline equals 0](images/c10-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> (in negative class). The last column shows the predicted probability ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline equals ModifyingAbove double-struck upper P With Ì‚ left-parenthesis normal y Subscript i Baseline equals 1 vertical-bar normal x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline equals x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma normal x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline equals x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given by a logistic regression in ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The observations are arranged in descending order of ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c10-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>.

Let the probability threshold ![u](images/c10-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> (Sub[section 10.4.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0007)) vary from positive infinity down to 0. We can observe the changes of TPR and FPR as functions of ![u](images/c10-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>. Note that a classification algorithm applied to a dataset gives one classifier for each value of the probability threshold ![u](images/c10-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>; in essence, it produces a collection of classifiers. For instance, for the extreme scenario of ![u greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c10-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, all observations in [Table 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0003) are simply classified as negative as clearly all ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline less-than-or-equal-to 1 less-than u](images/c10-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>u</mi></math>. No observation is classified as positive, making both ![TPR equals FPR equals 0](images/c10-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, which gives the following confusion matrix ([Table 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0004)).

![TABLE 10.3  The dataset of 20 labeled samples with the respective predicted probabilities using binary logistic regression.](images/c10-i0364.png)

[**TABLE 10.3**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-tbl-0003)  The dataset of 20 labeled samples with the respective predicted probabilities using binary logistic regression.

![TABLE 10.4  A confusion matrix of a test using the dataset in Table 10.3.](images/c10-i0375.png)

[**TABLE 10.4**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-tbl-0004)  A confusion matrix of a test using the dataset in [Table 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0003).

Next, for ![u equals 0.95](images/c10-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></math>, any observation is classified as positive whenever ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline greater-than 0.95](images/c10-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.95</mn></math>. Then, only one of the 10 positive observations (![i equals 1](images/c10-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) will be correctly classified, hence ![TPR equals 1 slash 10 equals 0.1](images/c10-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math> as ![TP equals 1](images/c10-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TP</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![FN equals 9](images/c10-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>FN</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>. On the other hand, there is no false positive, i.e. ![FP equals 0](images/c10-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>FP</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, so ![FPR equals 0](images/c10-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

From the above two particular values of ![u](images/c10-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, we can see that, as the probability threshold ![u](images/c10-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> decreases, both TPR and FPR generally increase. The ROC curve, depicted in [Figure 10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0009), illustrates the change of TPR (![y](images/c10-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>‐axis) and FPR (![x](images/c10-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>‐axis) as the probability threshold ![u](images/c10-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> varies from 1 down to 0. In general, the ROC curve tends to be smoother as the sample size ![n](images/c10-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> increases. In fact, given the observations ranked in descending order of ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c10-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, a general procedure to draw the ROC curve is as follows: we start from the origin ![left-parenthesis 0 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and refer to the labels of the observations in order. If ![ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c10-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (resp. 0), then we move up by ![StartFraction 1 Over n 1 EndFraction](images/c10-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> in size vertically (resp. by ![StartFraction 1 Over n 0 EndFraction](images/c10-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> in size to the right horizontally), where ![n 1](images/c10-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![n 0](images/c10-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> are the number of observations in the classes 1 and 0, respectively. We ultimately end up at ![left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> when we repeat this for all observations. This procedure also indicates the concave nature of the curve.

![FIGURE 10.9 ROC curve for the data extracted from Table 10.3, where each point represents a value u equals ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i of the threshold, for i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 20, along the curve.](images/c10f009.png)

[**FIGURE 10.9**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0009) ROC curve for the data extracted from [Table 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0003), where each point represents a value ![u equals ModifyingAbove pi With Ì‚ Subscript i](images/c10-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> of the threshold, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 20](images/c10-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, along the curve.

![FIGURE 10.10 ROC curves of two binary logistic regressions deployed to two different datasets.](images/c10f010.png)

[**FIGURE 10.10**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0010) ROC curves of two binary logistic regressions deployed to two different datasets.

[Figure 10.10](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0010) shows two different ROC curves examining the performance of two binary logistic regressions for two respective datasets. The dashed line in red shows the ROC curve of a dataset which is easier to be separated into two groups, so that a higher value of TPR matches with a smaller value of FPR. In contrast, the solid ROC curve in blue corresponds to a classification which is relatively harder to be separated cleanly. Generally, the ROC curve of an easily separable dataset or from a very reliable classification algorithm tends to lean towards the top left‐hand corner of the unit square. When all positive observations can be correctly classified (![TPR equals 1](images/c10-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) while no negative observation is misclassified as positive (![FPR equals 0](images/c10-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>), no matter what values of ![u](images/c10-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, then the corresponding ROC curve degenerates to the single point at the top left‐hand corner of the unit square.

Besides, ROC curves can be used to compare the performances of different classification algorithms applied to the same dataset. One possible way is to compare the *Area Under Curve* (AUC) of the ROC curves, so that the greater the AUC, the better the performance of the algorithm is.

Just as the top left‐hand corner of the unit square represents a perfect classifier, the other corners of the unit square also possess their own interpretations; see [Figure 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0011). For instance, at the bottom left‐hand corner, the classifier identifies all observations as negative; since no observation is classified as positive, we have ![TPR equals FPR equals 0](images/c10-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. On the other hand, the top right‐hand corner corresponds to another extreme scenario: the corresponding classifier identifies all observations as positive; now all positive observations are correctly classified while all negative observations are misclassified, and we have ![TPR equals FPR equals 1](images/c10-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>TPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>FPR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The diagonal line joining the origin and the top right‐hand corner has another important interpretation. Suppose that we randomly classify an observation as positive with a probability ![p](images/c10-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and as negative with a probability ![1 minus p](images/c10-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Let ![n 1](images/c10-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![n 2](images/c10-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> be the total number of observations having a disease and having no disease, respectively. Since no matter the observation is positive or negative it will be classified as positive with a probability ![p](images/c10-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, from [Table 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0005), both ratios TPR and FPR approach ![p](images/c10-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> as both ![n 1](images/c10-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![n 2](images/c10-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> tend to infinity. In other words, the point ![left-parenthesis p comma p right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> on the main diagonal is associated with the algorithm which randomly classifies any observation as positive with a probability ![p](images/c10-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, if the ROC curve of a classification algorithm lies below this main diagonal, we can interpret its performance even worse than unintentional random classification.

![FIGURE 10.11 Evaluation of the performance of a classification algorithm using its ROC curve.](images/c10f011.png)

One advantage of using PCR is to remove the multicollinearity in the set of input covariates, especially when two or more ![x Subscript j](images/c10-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s are close to collinear. Generally, rather than just the linear structure, there can be a functional relation between ![bold y](images/c10-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> and covariates ![bold x](images/c10-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> given by:
