Therefore ![normal epsilon overTilde Subscript i](images/c10-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is also uncorrelated with ![upper P Subscript j Baseline left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for those ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper N](images/c10-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math>, and the same theory as MANOVA (Multivariate Analysis of Variances, see [\[12\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012)) on the diagnostics of the significance of various coefficients can still be applied.

As an illustration of PCR, we again use the Boston housing dataset depicted in Sub[section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0003). We first split the housing dataset into training and test datasets with a ratio of 8 to 2, then PCA is applied to the correlation matrix of the training dataset. [Programme 10.24](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3024) shows the application of PCA in Python. As discussed in [Programme 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-3003), we standardize each feature variable first before feeding the training dataset into the `PCA()` class in Python, and we shall also use the same in‐sample sample means and sample standard deviations to standardize the corresponding feature variables in the test dataset.

![FIGURE 10.12 Scree plot of the Boston housing training dataset in Python, generated in Programme 10.24.](images/c10f012.png)

[**FIGURE 10.12**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0012) Scree plot of the Boston housing training dataset in Python, generated in [Programme 10.24](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3024).

From the output of [Programme 10.24](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3024), we observe that the first 9 principal components can explain over 95% of the total variance; [Figure 10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0012) further justifies this claim and shows that the total variance decreases only slightly after the first 9 principal components. Therefore, the first 9 principal components can be adopted to fit a multiple linear regression model.

In [Programme 10.26](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3026), we compare the PCR model with the multiple linear regression model for full dataset via Python, by computing the corresponding root‐mean‐squared errors (RMSEs, different from the residual mean squared error defined before) based on the test dataset:

![FIGURE 10.13 Scree plot of the Boston housing training dataset in R, generated in Programme 10.27.](images/c10f013.png)

[**FIGURE 10.13**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0013) Scree plot of the Boston housing training dataset in **R**, generated in [Programme 10.27](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3027).

As expected, the RMSE of PCR is slightly higher than that of the multiple linear regression model for full dataset, because in the end we did ignore some information in the original Boston housing dataset by selecting only 9 of the total of 13 PCs.

Analogously, the `pcr()` function in the `pls` (principal least square) package adopted in **R** can carry out PCR. From [Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013), we observe that the fifth principal component is the kink point of the scree plot, suggesting that the first 5 PCs can be used for PCR. Comparing the respective outputs in [Figures 10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0012) (Python) and [10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013) (**R**), despite the small difference in the shape of curves due to the random subsamples of training datasets being drawn, some of their key characteristics, such as the locations of kink points are indeed very similar. Besides, the difference in the numbers of PCs selected by the two programmes is due to the difference of selection criteria between Python and **R**; while Python chooses the PCs that explain over ![95 percent-sign](images/c10-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>95</mn><mi>%</mi></math> total variance, **R** simply sets the kink point as the maximum number of PCs chosen.

Recall that in the MNIST example in [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0005), fitted with a generic multinomial logistic regression model, there were ![28 times 28 equals 784](images/c10-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>784</mn></math> feature variables, leading to a huge ![7 comma 056](images/c10-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>056</mn></math> coefficient weights and 9 biases. Let us take a leap by extending the dimension reduction technique via PCA from linear regression to multinomial logistic regression. To this end, as before, we choose the number of principal components that explain 95% of the total variance. Since the pixel feature variables are of the same gray scale between 0 and 255, we only standardize each feature variable in the training feature data matrix by centering them with their respective feature mean; we do not rescale each feature variable with their respective standard deviations. This process is directly performed via `PCA()` in [Programme 10.28](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3028) via Python.

From the results obtained in Programme 10.28, 154 principal components are selected and the resulting accuracy for the test dataset is 92.33%, which is similar to [Programme 10.17](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3017) with the use of full set of feature variables, but the number of parameters is reduced to ![left-parenthesis 154 plus 1 right-parenthesis times left-parenthesis 10 minus 1 right-parenthesis equals 1 comma 395](images/c10-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>154</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>395</mn></math>. Moreover, for a common desktop computer, the time required for running the codes in Python is greatly reduced from 1 minute to 8 seconds.

For the **R** codes in [Programme 10.29](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3029), we plug the MNIST training data into the `princomp()` function with the two arguments `center=TRUE` and `scale=FALSE`, as we only perform the centering for each feature variable. Comparing the results obtained in [Programmes 10.18](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3018) (without PCA) and 10.29 (with PCA) in **R**, the accuracy for the test dataset slightly increases from 91.67% to 92.19% with the use of PCA. Moreover, **R** generally executes much slower than Python.

 

## \*10.A APPENDIX

  

### \*10.A.1 Derivation of Gauss–Newton Algorithm

The Gauss–Newton algorithm is a modification of Newton's method, used to numerically evaluate the (local) minimum point of a broad class of functions. It helps to solve many practical least square problems subject to regularization, commonly found in the context of semi‐parametric regressions. The algorithm makes use of a linear approximation for the residual function ![r Subscript j Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic beta right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (see below) so that it is not necessary to compute its second or higher‐order derivatives. The formalization of the algorithm first appeared in [\[8\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0008) written by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1809.

More precisely, consider the parameter vector ![bold-italic beta equals left-parenthesis beta 1 comma ellipsis comma beta Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript In general, the convergence rate of the algorithm is linear; recently, there has been work [\[13\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013) which claims that by rectifying and modifying the tail of the square loss function in almost linear growth, a quadratic convergence rate can still be attained.

\*10.A.2 Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) 

Let us adopt Newton's method, similar to ([10.23](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0068)), to the finding of MLEs for logistic regression. upper X Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper R Superscript left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis Baseline bold-italic upper X](images/c10-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></math> for some ![m much-less-than k](images/c10-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>, meaning that we only update the Hessian matrix once after quite a number of steps. Such a shortcut approach is a special case of the *quasi‐Newton method* (see [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017)). This method can be useful yet it can lead to some limitations, namely as the iteration proceeds, some of the ![pi Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0597.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>'s approach rapidly to 0 or 1, and their values may then be incorrectly recorded by the computer program as 0 or 1 due to a limited number of floating digits used. At that point, the Hessian ![bold-italic upper H left-parenthesis bold-italic beta Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c10-i0598.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> becomes singular and the iteration ([10.26](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0076)) turns to be ill‐conditioned; also see [Figure 10.14](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0014).

# CHAPTER 11  
Linear Classifiers

 

A linear classifier aims to find a ![left-parenthesis p minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>‐dimensional hyperplane to separate a given collection of data points into two categories. Mathematically, suppose that each data point is represented by a ![p](images/c11-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional feature vector ![bold-italic x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> together with a label ![y element-of StartSet negative 1 comma plus 1 EndSet](images/c11-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, representing to which category it belongs. A linear classifier is a hyperplane defined by the equation ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis colon equals bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b equals 0](images/c11-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, where ![bold-italic omega element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is the weight vector and ![b element-of double-struck upper R](images/c11-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> is the bias. A data point ![left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is classified as belonging to the category of “![plus 1](images/c11-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>” if ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c11-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; and is classified as belonging to the category of “![negative 1](images/c11-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>” if ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c11-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. The data point is correctly classified by this hyperplane if ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis dot y Subscript i Baseline greater-than 0](images/c11-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; but it is misclassified if ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis dot y Subscript i Baseline less-than 0](images/c11-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

[Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0001) illustrates a dataset ![left-brace left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma x Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c11-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> of two‐dimensional feature vectors, which is linearly separated by the line:

[(11.1)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0001)![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals b plus omega 1 x 1 plus omega 2 x 2 equals 0 period](images/c11-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Given its feature vector ![bold-italic x](images/c11-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, an observation is classified as the category ![plus 1](images/c11-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (resp. ![negative 1](images/c11-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>) if it lies above (resp. below) this separating line of ([11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0001)). In this chapter, we shall introduce two traditional binary linear classifiers, namely the *perceptron* and *support vector machine* (SVM).

![FIGURE 11.1 An example of a linear classifier for two‐dimensional feature vectors with blue dots (resp. orange crosses) having a label plus 1 (resp. negative 1).](images/c11f001.png)

[**FIGURE 11.1**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0001) An example of a linear classifier for two‐dimensional feature vectors with blue dots (resp. orange crosses) having a label ![plus 1](images/c11-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (resp. ![negative 1](images/c11-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>).

Both methods are processes of reducing the number of misclassified data. Intuitively, the algorithms improve the separating hyperplane by leaning it forward to the misclassified data in order to reduce their distances to the hyperplane. During the training, a *loss function* is chosen as a measure of misclassification. A greater value of the loss function indicates a lower accuracy in the prediction. Perceptron and SVM differ from the choice of the loss function. In addition, SVM can perform non‐linear classification while the perceptron is mostly restricted to linear classification.

 

## 11.1 PERCEPTRON

Rosenblatt [\[20\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0021), inspired by the mechanism of the neurons in our brain to process information, invented the very first version of the perceptron. It is one of the earliest linear binary classifiers, and is generally regarded as an ancestor of recently developed *Neural Networks* and *Deep Learning*. In layman terms, each layer of neuron is connected to other layer of neurons, where information is passed from one layer to the latter. For the connection of one neuron to another, variation in the strength of impulse sent from the first to the latter, as neuroscientists believe, is crucial for our brain to process information; more discussions can be found in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml). In the simplest case of an abstract perceptron model, the strength of connection can be modelled by assigning different coefficient weights. After the neuron sums up the information received from the few neurons attached, if the total sum reaches a certain threshold, the neuron fires to the next neuron with output value 1; or with output value 0 otherwise.

Rosenblatt also proposed that perceptrons could perform visual tasks such as facial and object recognition. For instance, in recognizing the handwritten digit (as introduced in [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml)), a perceptron model can be used to differentiate whether a given handwritten digit is a certain number.

Minsky and Papert (1969) [\[18\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0018) criticized the effectiveness of perceptrons by showing that it can only solve limited types of questions perfectly and gave their mathematical evidence in a book titled *Perceptrons: an introduction to computational geometry*. For instance, no perceptron can handle the XOR (eXclusive OR) logic function, which receives two binary inputs. In [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0002), the yellow dots represent the situation that exactly either one takes value 0 and the other one takes value 1; while the red crosses represent the situation that both take value 0 or both take value 1. In the same book, Minsky and Papert suggested that this matter can be addressed by adding an additional “layer” of neurons such that the resulting multilayer neural network can deal with an arbitrary Boolean function. However, tuning a suitable multilayer neural network model was not broadly studied during that time; now this can commonly be accomplished by using *backpropagation* as we shall discuss in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml).

This motivates us to define the loss function as

An equivalent expression can be given by:

and our goal now is to find the parameter ![bold-italic omega equals left-parenthesis omega 0 comma omega 1 comma ellipsis comma omega Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c11-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, that minimizes the loss function ![upper L](images/c11-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>. One of the difficulties involved in this optimization problem is the implicit dependence of ![upper L](images/c11-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> on the parameter ![bold-italic omega](images/c11-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></math> through the index set ![upper I Subscript n](images/c11-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>. We shall employ the *gradient descent* method, which can effectively refine the parameter values iteratively; also see Appendix \*11.A.1 for an overview of the gradient descent method.

To this end, we first initialize ![bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and then a sequence of estimates ![left-brace bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace Subscript t equals 1 Superscript infinity](images/c11-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> is constructed as follows. For ![t element-of double-struck upper N](images/c11-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>, we define ![upper I Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> to be the set of indexes of misclassified data given the current linear function ![f Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> based on ![bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and we also recursively define

![upper L Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic omega right-parenthesis colon equals sigma-summation Underscript i element-of upper I Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline Endscripts StartAbsoluteValue bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i element-of upper I Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline Endscripts y Subscript i Baseline bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma](images/c11-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></munder><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></munder><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

such that the new iterated estimate is given by

where, ![eta greater-than 0](images/c11-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> is a hyperparameter called the *learning rate*. The idea behind gradient descent is that the value of a function ![g](images/c11-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> decreases most rapidly in the direction ![minus nabla g](images/c11-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>. stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></math>. Geometrically, as seen in [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004), we update the separation line ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c11-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> by correcting its intercept and the normal vector ![bold-italic omega Subscript negative 0 Baseline colon equals left-parenthesis omega 1 comma omega 2 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c11-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> step by step.

The gradient descent method described above is not recommended when the sample size ![n](images/c11-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is large, as this results in a high demand of computational effort for the sum ![sigma-summation Underscript i element-of upper I Subscript n Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Endscripts y Subscript i Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c11-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msub><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in each iteration. As a popular alternative, the *stochastic gradient descent* (SGD) method can be used; also see Appendix \*11.A.1 for a brief introduction. In SGD, the parameter is updated by considering only one single datum in each iteration; and we repeat the procedures, aiming to obtain the ultimate estimate for ![bold-italic omega](images/c11-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></math>. If the data happen to be truly linearly separable, that is, there exists ![bold-italic omega Superscript asterisk Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p plus 1](images/c11-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> such that sgn![left-parenthesis left-parenthesis bold-italic omega Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals y Subscript i](images/c11-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for all ![i](images/c11-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, then the convergence to optimal weights of ![bold-italic omega](images/c11-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></math> via stochastic gradient descent method can be guaranteed. To this end, by comparing ![bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, the respective parameters before and after each update, the loss function dealing with SGD at the ![left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>‐th step is actually reduced. At each step, there are two scenarios to consider:

After a certain number of iterations, if there are no more misclassified points, the numerical scheme stops, and by definition, a perceptron classifier that correctly classifies all data is attained. Otherwise, if there are still misclassified points, modification of weights will still be carried out, and we now want to demonstrate that there is a ceiling for such a number of iterations, and so the optimal classifier should ultimately be obtained. The number of iterations we mean here is the effective number of attempts so that ![bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline not-equals bold-italic omega Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8800;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> for every step. which means that the effective number of updates required is at most ![t Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math>. In other words, there can be no more misclassified points beyond ![t Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> steps, which holds regardless of the value of the learning rate ![eta](images/c11-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>.

Logistic regression is another commonly used method for classification problems with binary responses, as we introduced in [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0005). A perceptron is essentially logistic regression by replacing the logit transform by the sign function (a step function) which can be considered as the derivative of the *Rectified Linear Unit* (ReLU) function. A generic numerical comparison between these two tools is given in [Figure 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0006). The two illustrations on the top show two datasets that are linearly separable and the other two illustrations at the bottom show inseparable situations ![FIGURE 11.6 Performance of logistic regression represented by solid lines, and perceptron represented by dashed lines.](images/c11f006.png)

[**FIGURE 11.6**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0006) Performance of logistic regression represented by solid lines, and perceptron represented by dashed lines.

Finally, we illustrate the implementation of perceptron in [Programme 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3001) via Python (resp. [Programme 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3002) via **R**).

Let us apply this `perceptron()` function in [Programme 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3001) (resp. [Programme 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3002)) to the HSI financial ratio dataset in [Programme 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3003) via Python (resp. [Programme 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3004) via **R**). From the output of [Programme 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3003) (resp. [Programme 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3004)), we see that the accuracy rate is ![left-parenthesis 646 plus 23 right-parenthesis slash 680 equals 98.38 percent-sign](images/c11-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>646</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>98.38</mn><mi>%</mi></math> (resp. ![left-parenthesis 646 plus 24 right-parenthesis slash 680 equals 98.53 percent-sign](images/c11-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>646</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>24</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>98.53</mn><mi>%</mi></math>).

 

## 11.2 SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE

*Support vector machines* (SVMs) choose a separating hyperplane which maximizes the margin between the two classes. In other words, the distance from the hyperplane to the nearest data point from each category is maximized. There are a number of monographs that discuss this tool in detail, such as [\[1](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001), [10](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0010), [11](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0011), [23\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0023).

![FIGURE 11.7 An example of an SVM model for two‐dimensional feature vectors.](images/c11f007.png)

[**FIGURE 11.7**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0007) An example of an SVM model for two‐dimensional feature vectors.

For choosing the hyperplane, SVM does not make use of all the available data. Instead, only the points, called *support vectors*, that are closest to the hyperplane are relevant; see [Figure 11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0007). Support vectors are used to define the hyperplane, and at the same time, they are the most difficult to be classified correctly; they carry the most important information for the classification problem.

Let ![bold-italic x 0](images/c11-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> be an arbitrary point lying on the plane. For any ![bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>, standard coordinate geometry tells us that the distance ![d left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> between ![bold-italic x](images/c11-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and the hyperplane ![bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b equals 0](images/c11-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>

The *geometric margin* is then defined by

![gamma colon equals min Underscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Endscripts gamma Subscript i Baseline period](images/c11-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

Suppose that the dataset is linearly separable, then there exists ![left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma b right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> such that all the data are correctly classified by the hyperplane ![bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b equals 0](images/c11-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Our goal is to look for ![left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma b right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> such that this separating hyperplane is as far as possible from the two groups of points. In other words, we aim to find the optimal hyperplane that solves the following optimization problem:

[(11.7)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0015)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column maximize Underscript bold-italic omega comma b Endscripts 3rd Column gamma comma 2nd Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column subject to 3rd Column y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0 comma for-all i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n period EndLayout](images/c11-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><munder><mtext>maximize</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></munder><mspace width="2em"/></mtd><mtd><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="2em"/></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

Note that for any feasible solution ![left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma b right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we can always find an alternative separating hyperplane that is parallel to the former with parameters ![left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma b prime right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and sits in the middle between the two groups. Simple geometry tells us that the corresponding geometric margin of the alternative separating hyperplane is greater than that of the original feasible hyperplane. Finally, as pointed out in the footnote, the definition of a separating hyperplane is invariant with rescaling of parameter vector, we can assume that ![y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c11-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> for all ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c11-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, so that the equality holds for the two points closest to the separating hyperplane, hence ![gamma equals 1 slash double-vertical-bar bold-italic omega double-vertical-bar Subscript 2](images/c11-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. Now, Problem [11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0015) can be converted as:

### 11.2.1 Primal and Dual Problems in SVM

One can observe that ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0018)) is indeed a *Quadratic Programming* (QP) problem. To solve this (primal) problem of finding the optimal parameters ![bold-italic omega Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> and ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> in ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0018)), we can adopt the duality approach for QP problems by maximizing the *dual Lagrangian* (the corresponding *dual problem*); see Appendix \*11.A.2.3 for more details. To this end, we first write down the Lagrangian:

More precisely, with strong duality [\[5](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005), [21](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0022), [24\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0025) in place, the minimum value attained by Problem ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0018)) and the maximum value attained by ([11.11](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0023)) coincide, and their respective solutions are related by the *complementary slackness condition*:

[(11.12)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0024)![lamda Subscript i Baseline left-brace y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b right-parenthesis minus 1 right-brace equals 0 comma for all i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n period](images/c11-math-0024.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for all </mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

To obtain the optimal parameters ![bold-italic omega Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> and ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> in ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0018)), one can first solve the dual problem ([11.11](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0023)) to obtain ![lamda Subscript i Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>'s. It turns out that in most cases, most of these ![lamda Subscript i Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>'s are equal to zero. A feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c11-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is called a *support vector* if the corresponding multiplier ![lamda Subscript i Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is strictly positive, then ![y Subscript i Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b equals 1](images/c11-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. After deriving the values of ![lamda Subscript i Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>'s from the dual problem, ![bold-italic omega Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> can then be obtained from ([11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0021)), which is a linear combination of support vectors. On the other hand, from the complementary slackness condition ([11.12](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0024)), the optimal ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c11-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> can be obtained from any support vector ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c11-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> (with ![lamda Subscript i Superscript asterisk Baseline greater-than 0](images/c11-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) as

### 11.2.2 Kernel Trick for Coping with Non‐Linearity

As mentioned before, some datasets are only non‐linearly separable in nature, such as the dataset shown in [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008)a. However, if we manage to transform the original space into a higher dimensional space, there is a chance that the data points might become linearly separable in the new transformed space. This transformation method is called the *kernel trick*.

[Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008) illustrates a dataset with a two‐dimensional feature vector ![bold-italic x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c11-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, labeled in blue dots and green crosses. The original data points as shown in [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008)a cannot by separated by any linear line. However, after adding one more dimension given by ![upper K left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis equals x 1 squared plus x 2 squared](images/c11-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> to the feature vector as shown in [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0008)b, a plane can now be used to separate the blue dots and green crosses perfectly.

![FIGURE 11.8 Kernel trick: 2D to 3D transformation.](images/c11f008.png)

[**FIGURE 11.8**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0008) Kernel trick: 2D to 3D transformation.

Alternatively, one can also think of the transformation ![bold-italic phi colon left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline right-arrow from bar left-parenthesis x 1 squared comma StartRoot 2 EndRoot x 1 x 2 comma x 2 squared right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c11-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>&#8614;</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>; also see [Figure 11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0009). which is computationally inefficient. It is more convenient to pick a *kernel* ![upper K](images/c11-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> such that, for any ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>,

(11.14)![upper K left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline right-parenthesis equals bold-italic phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c11-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is symmetric in its two arguments. One of the most widely used kernel functions is the *Radial Basis Function* (RBF) kernel: for any ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>,

![upper K Subscript RBF Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline right-parenthesis equals exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2 Baseline Over 2 sigma squared EndFraction right-parenthesis comma](images/c11-math-0031.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>K</mi><mtext>RBF</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![sigma](images/c11-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is a hyperparameter that determines the regularity and connectedness of the separating boundary hypersurface in the original space of ![bold-italic x](images/c11-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>. For instance, [Figure 11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0010) depicts the boundaries of the separating hypersurfaces obtained in SVM with the use of RBF kernels with different ![sigma](images/c11-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>'s. The original space is two‐dimensional and the data points are transformed into infinite‐dimensional ones via the RBF kernel. When ![sigma](images/c11-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is small, say ![sigma equals 0.3](images/c11-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></math> as in [Figure 11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0010)a, the zooming‐in effect of the corresponding kernel is strong, allowing the two classes to be separated easily. The resulting separation boundary in the original two‐dimensional space tends to be clear and sharp, yet it is more prone to overfitting. When ![sigma](images/c11-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is large, say ![sigma equals 1](images/c11-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> as in [Figure 11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0010)b, the zooming‐out effect of the resulting kernel comes into play and the separation boundary in the original two‐dimensional space tends to be smoother and more connected in one piece. Though it often makes some occasional misclassifications, the predictions tend to be more robust.

![FIGURE 11.10 SVM with RBF kernel resulting in different boundaries of the separating hypersurfaces shown in the original two‐dimensional space.](images/c11f010.png)

[**FIGURE 11.10**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0010) SVM with RBF kernel resulting in different boundaries of the separating hypersurfaces shown in the original two‐dimensional space.

For the RBF kernel, we can actually identify the corresponding transformation ![bold-italic phi](images/c11-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> as follows. This ![bold-italic phi](images/c11-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> actually lifts a finite‐dimensional datum from ![double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> to the infinite‐dimensional space of ![double-struck upper R Superscript infinity](images/c11-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msup></math>. To see this, we observe that:

movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>K</mi><mo Therefore, the equation of the separating hypersurface is given by:

### 11.2.3 Soft‐Margin SVM for Dealing with Noise

In the previous subsection, we focused on the case where the data points are not linearly separable in their original space, but they can be separated after a transformation, such as a higher‐degree polynomial. In this subsection, we focus on dataset with noise, as in [Figure 11.11](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0011).

When dealing with noise, we impose some penalties to data points lying on the wrong side of the separation boundary. To this end, we introduce a *hinge loss function* for SVM:

![max left-brace right-brace comma 0 comma minus minus 1 times times yi left-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus plus times times xi down-tack omega b period](images/c11-math-0037.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">&#125;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

In other words, if the ![i](images/c11-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th data point lies on the correct side of the separating hyperplane, i.e. ![y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c11-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, the individual hinge loss is zero. On the other hand, if the ![i](images/c11-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th data point lies on the wrong side of the separation boundary, ![y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega plus b right-parenthesis less-than 1](images/c11-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and the individual hinge loss is almost proportional to its distance from the separating hyperplane. The objective function for SVM with noise is the following cost function

(11.15)![upper C double-vertical-bar bold-italic omega double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2 Baseline plus StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts max left-brace right-brace comma 0 comma minus minus 1 times times yi left-parenthesis right-parenthesis plus plus times times xi down-tack omega b comma](images/c11-math-0038.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![upper C](images/c11-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is the hyperparameter that determines the tradeoff between increasing the geometric margin and ensuring that most of the ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c11-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s lie on the correct side of the separating hyperplane. For sufficiently large values of ![upper C](images/c11-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, the hinge loss function becomes negligible, so SVM tries to find the optimal solution with the greatest geometric margin by essentially ignoring misclassification. As we reduce the value of ![upper C](images/c11-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, making classification errors becomes more costly, so SVM tries to make fewer mistakes by sacrificing the geometric margin size. However, a larger margin is better for generalization. Therefore, ![upper C](images/c11-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> regulates the balance between classifying the training data well (minimizing empirical risk) and classifying future examples well (generalization) with better out‐sample fitting.

![FIGURE 11.11 Example of the existence of some outliers or noise in a dataset.](images/c11f011.png)

### 11.2.4 Application to Credit Scoring

Banks earn interest from loans, and it is crucial for banks to examine the credit scores of applicants for loans and approve applications accordingly. Let us use the credit scoring dataset [\[9\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0009)

For Python in [Programme 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3005), the SVM model is implemented via the `SVC` function provided in the `sklearn` library. In particular, two arguments are required in `SVC`, namely `gamma` defined as ![gamma equals 1 slash left-parenthesis 2 sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and `kernel="rbf"` for using the radial basis function defined by ![exp left-parenthesis minus gamma double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic x Subscript script l Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as the kernel function. Based on the results obtained, a small (resp. large) value of ![sigma](images/c11-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> yields a higher (resp. lower) training accuracy and a lower (resp. higher) testing accuracy. Indeed, the SVM model with a larger ![sigma](images/c11-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is less likely to result in overfitting, and is therefore better at generalizing. [Figure 11.12](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0012)a shows the training and testing accuracies of the SVM models against different values of ![sigma](images/c11-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> for the RBF kernel. Clearly, the training accuracy levels as ![sigma](images/c11-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> increases beyond 50, hence for this particular dataset, we may choose this kink point at the value for ![sigma](images/c11-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>. This choice can be further justified by the leveling‐out behavior of the test accuracy at ![sigma equals 50](images/c11-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></math>, as shown in [Figure 11.12](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0012)b.

![FIGURE 11.12 Plot of training and testing accuracies of the SVM models with different sigma's of the RBF kernel for the credit scoring dataset, based on Programme 11.5 via Python.](images/c11f012.png)

[**FIGURE 11.12**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0012) Plot of training and testing accuracies of the SVM models with different ![sigma](images/c11-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>'s of the RBF kernel for the credit scoring dataset, based on [Programme 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3005) via Python.

Similarly, in [Programme 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3006) via **R**, the SVM model is implemented via the `svm()` function provided in the library `e1071`. In particular, we adopt the RBF kernel via the argument `kernel="radial"` with `gamma`, ![gamma](images/c11-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> parameter defined equivalently as in `SVC` in Python. The outcomes in [Figure 11.13](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0013) agree with those in Python.

## \*11.A APPENDIX

  

### \*11.A.1 (Stochastic) Gradient Descent Methods

 

**\*11.A.1.1 Gradient Descent Method** In machine learning, one usually obtains a desired model by choosing optimal parameter values to minimize a certain loss function, which often takes the form of a sum or an average of a large number of individual losses. Gradient descent, and its stochastic version called stochastic gradient descent (SGD), are the two most frequently used iterative optimization algorithms for searching local minima. We shall briefly discuss these algorithms in this appendix, while we refer readers to our another treatise [\[8\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008), as well as other textbooks such as [\[14](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0014), [17](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0017), [22\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0024), for more detailed discussions. The general steps for the gradient descent algorithm are:

1.  start with a random seed; then
2.  modify the current parameter estimate by an amount proportional to the negative of the gradient of the loss function evaluated at the current point.

Very often, the loss function to be minimized may possess multiple local minima. This is especially the case when one is confronted with training various deep neural networks. The choice of initial guess is therefore crucial for seeking and locating the ultimate local minimum.

In Step 2 of the gradient descent algorithm, the negative of the gradient is pointing in the direction towards the next guess, while the step size for the modification will be determined by a hyperparameter ![eta](images/c11-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>, called the learning rate. With a learning rate ![eta](images/c11-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> and loss function ![upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis colon double-struck upper R Superscript q Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c11-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> in terms of the parameter ![bold-italic theta element-of bold upper Theta subset-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c11-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#920;</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math>, the gradient descent method updates the value of ![bold-italic theta](images/c11-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> as follows:

(11.16)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Step Size left-parenthesis Signed right-parenthesis 2nd Column equals eta dot nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis semicolon 2nd Row 1st Column Next Move 2nd Column equals Last Move minus Step Size period EndLayout](images/c11-math-0039.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtext>Step Size (Signed)</mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtext>Next Move</mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mtext>Last Move</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>Step Size</mtext><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

Mathematically, we have

[(11.17)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0040)![bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline minus eta dot nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis vertical-bar Subscript bold-italic theta equals bold-italic theta Sub Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Subscript Baseline period](images/c11-math-0040.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

If the learning rate ![eta](images/c11-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> is set too large, it is often not possible to reach the targeted nearby optimal point, as it may jump to one far away from the initial seed (see [Figure 11.14](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0014)a). On the other hand, if the learning rate is set too small, more iterations are needed to get to the optimal point (see [Figure 11.14](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0014)b). In practice, a learning rate of ![eta equals 0.001](images/c11-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></math> is often used. Generally, it is more desirable to adopt a sequence of learning rates ![left-brace eta Subscript t Baseline right-brace](images/c11-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#951;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> decreasing to zero. There are several techniques suggested in the literature on how these learning rates can be adjusted dynamically to achieve the best results. For the sake of simplicity, we adopt a constant learning rate in the rest of this discussion.

![FIGURE 11.14 The MSE plot against parameter bold-italic theta Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis of the first three iterations of gradient descent method.](images/c11f014.png)

The popularity of the gradient descent method stems from its easiness to implement and its nice convergence property. The convergence rate can be improven if one further assumes that ![upper K](images/c11-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> satisfies stronger regularity conditions, such as strong convexity.

\*11.A.1.2 Stochastic Gradient Descent Method 

Recall that in a perceptron, the loss function to be minimized is (as given in ([11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0004))):

in which ![n](images/c11-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is typically quite large. To minimize ![upper L](images/c11-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> using gradient descent, it is more reasonable to update the model parameters by using only a portion of the dataset ![script upper S](images/c11-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> (or training set), and the corresponding method is often referred to as *mini‐batch stochastic gradient descent* (mini‐batch sgd). To explain this, we consider a more general setting: given a training set ![script upper S equals left-brace left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c11-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, and a particular learning method parameterized by ![bold-italic theta element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c11-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math>, consider the loss function

By the Law of Large Numbers again, with a sufficiently large ![upper M much-less-than n](images/c11-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, the theoretical expectation ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline script l left-parenthesis bold-italic theta semicolon normal y comma bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be approximated instead by a small portion of size ![upper M](images/c11-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> of ![script upper S](images/c11-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>, that is,
