Therefore, with a very high probability, with both large ![upper M](images/c11-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and ![n](images/c11-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>,

![nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline upper L Subscript upper M Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis almost-equals StartFraction 1 Over upper M EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript m equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline script l left-parenthesis bold-italic theta semicolon y Subscript m Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript m Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c11-math-0046.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>M</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

and this is the main philosophy of mini‐batch SGD: replacing the gradient of the overall loss by only a portion average of gradient individual losses.

Instead of using the same batch of the first ![upper M](images/c11-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> data in ![script upper S](images/c11-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> to approximate the gradient of the loss function for every iteration, it is more common to shuffle the data first. This can help to prevent the learned model from overfitting to specific patterns of the first ![upper M](images/c11-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> data and therefore having poor generalization. The batches used have to be selected randomly from ![script upper S](images/c11-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>. One way to achieve this is by *random shuffle*. In this approach, we first shuffle the data randomly to obtain ![script upper S overTilde equals left-brace left-parenthesis bold-italic x overTilde Subscript i Baseline comma y overTilde Subscript i stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> to itself. We then split ![script upper S overTilde](images/c11-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></math> into ![upper B](images/c11-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> batches, each of equal size of ![upper M](images/c11-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, so that ![upper B equals left ceiling n slash upper M right ceiling](images/c11-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="&#8968;" close="&#8969;" separators=""><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>, and for ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper B](images/c11-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></math>, the ![j](images/c11-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th batch is given by ![left-brace left-parenthesis bold-italic x overTilde Subscript i Baseline comma y overTilde Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals left-parenthesis j minus 1 right-parenthesis upper M plus 1 Superscript j upper M](images/c11-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. These ![upper B](images/c11-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> batches will be used to approximate the gradient of the loss function as described above in the next ![upper B](images/c11-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> iteration steps. After all ![upper B](images/c11-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> batches have been used up, the whole process is then repeated.

In practice, a commonly used batch size is ![upper M equals 2 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 32 greater-than 30](images/c11-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>30</mn></math>, thirty being the rule‐of‐thumb number for the law of large numbers to yield good enough approximation results. There are two particular cases of mini‐batch SGD worth mentioning:

1.  the common stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a special case when ![upper M equals 1](images/c11-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, in which a randomly picked sample point is used in each iteration for an update of the parameter estimate;
2.  the (whole) batch gradient descent is also a special case of mini‐batch SGD but now the batch size ![upper M equals n](images/c11-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, so that all training data are used at a time.

A comparison of SGD, mini‐batch SGD, and whole batch SGD methods for parameter updates is illustrated in [Figure 11.15](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0015).

![FIGURE 11.15 Gradient descent for SGD (dotted trace in grey), mini‐batch SGD (dashed trace in green), and whole batch SGD (solid trace in blue).](images/c11f015.png)

[**FIGURE 11.15**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0015) Gradient descent for SGD (dotted trace in grey), mini‐batch SGD (dashed trace in green), and whole batch SGD (solid trace in blue).

The red spot in the middle represents the ultimate local minimum point we are looking for. The solid trace in blue represents the sequence of updates under the whole batch gradient descent. It seems to be the fastest possible geographical path, going directly to the minimum point, and it involves the least number of steps. However, the computational cost is much higher in each step than the other two methods. Even worse, in the computation of the overall average loss ![upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we might encounter numeric overflow or underflow due to a huge number of terms being dealt with at one time. The dotted trace in grey in [Figure 11.15](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0015) corresponds to the stochastic gradient descent when ![upper M equals 1](images/c11-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Though its path is of zigzag shape, the mean direction of the path is still pointing towards the ultimate minimum point. It requires more iterations in comparison with batch gradient descent to get sufficiently close to the ultimate minimum point. Interestingly, SGD only requires the computation of a single gradient ![nabla Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline script l](images/c11-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>&#8467;</mi></math> of an individual loss at a randomly selected point in each iteration, so that generally speaking, SGD requires far fewer computational steps (= number of zigzag steps ![tilde](images/c11-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo></mrow></math>

 

**\*11.A.1.3 Convergence of SGD** In this section, we briefly introduce the well‐known *Robbins–Monro theorem* [\[19\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0020) on the convergence of SGD; more discussions can be found in [\[8\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008). To this, we write the individual loss as ![script l left-parenthesis bold-italic theta semicolon bold x right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> where ![bold x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is a random variable, and ![bold-italic theta element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c11-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> is the model parameter that we want to tune so as to minimize the sum (or average) of the individual losses. We assume that

1.  **(A1)** (*Lipschitz continuity*) The individual loss function ![script l colon double-struck upper R Superscript q Baseline times double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline right-arrow ### \*11.A.2 Quadratic Programming

 

**\*11.A.2.1 Formulation** Since the work of Frank and Wolfe [\[12\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0012), *Quadratic Programming* (QP) has become an indispensable tool to solve a broad class of quadratic optimization problems. Conventionally, a QP problem is formulated as follows:

[(11.23)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0051)![min Underscript bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline Endscripts one half bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper P bold-italic x plus bold-italic q Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x plus r comma](images/c11-math-0051.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="2.1em"/><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo></math> [(11.24)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0052)![subject to bold-italic upper G bold-italic x less-than-or-equal-to bold-italic h and bold-italic upper A bold-italic x equals bold-italic b comma](images/c11-math-0052.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mtext> and </mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold-italic upper P element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times p](images/c11-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> is positive definite matrix, ![bold-italic upper G element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper K times p](images/c11-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>, ![bold-italic upper A element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper M times p](images/c11-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>, ![bold-italic q element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> and ![bold-italic b element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper M](images/c11-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></math>; and the symbol ![less-than-or-equal-to](images/c11-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo></mrow></math> here means that every entry of vector ![bold-italic upper G bold-italic x](images/c11-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></math> is less than or equal to the corresponding entry of the right‐hand side vector ![bold-italic h element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper K](images/c11-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></math>. Note that the objective function in ([11.23](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0051)) is convex in ![bold-italic x](images/c11-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, and ![bold-italic upper P colon equals left-parenthesis p Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis Subscript i comma j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p Baseline](images/c11-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> is usually, without loss of generality, assumed to be symmetric, since

Note that the constraints are equivalent to ![StartAbsoluteValue x 1 EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 1 comma StartAbsoluteValue x 2 EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c11-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, which is represented by the square shown in [Figure 11.16](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0016). Within the square, the optimal point indicated by the star symbol is the contact point touched by the purple elliptical contour. We can use the `solve_qp()` function in the `qpsolvers` library of Python ([Programme 11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3007)) or the `solve.QP()` function in the `quadprog` package of **R** ([Programme 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3008)) to solve and plot out the corresponding solution of this quadratic programming problem.

In [Programme 11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3007) via Python, the `np.meshgrid()` function returns a coordinated matrix for the two input arrays, and the `solve_qp()` function aims to solve a quadratic programming problem as formulated in ([11.23](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0051)) and ([11.24](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0052)).

In [Programme 11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3008) via **R**, the `outer()` function takes three main arguments: (i) the first input array (vector) ![bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper Q](images/c11-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>Q</mi></msup></math> as `X`; (ii) the second input array (vector) ![bold-italic y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper K](images/c11-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></math> as `Y`; and (iii) the function ![f colon double-struck upper R times double-struck upper R right-arrow double-struck upper R](images/c11-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math> to be adopted in `outer()` as `FUN`. The output of this function is a two‐dimensional grid matrix ![bold-italic upper O equals left-parenthesis o Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper Q times upper K](images/c11-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">O</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></math> with entries ![o Subscript i j Baseline equals f left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![i equals 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma upper Q](images/c11-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi></math> and ![j equals 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma upper K](images/c11-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>. On the other hand, also in **R**, the `solve.QP()` function aims to solve the QP problem in the following form:

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column min Underscript bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline Endscripts one half bold-italic x Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic upper P bold-italic x minus bold-italic q Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x subject to bold-italic upper G Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x greater-than-or-equal-to bold-italic h comma 2nd Column Blank EndLayout](images/c11-math-0056.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>subject to </mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where the first `meq` constraints are treated as equality constraints, i.e. ![bold-italic upper G 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x equals h 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic upper G Subscript monospace meq Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x equals h Subscript monospace meq Baseline](images/c11-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">meq</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext mathvariant="monospace">meq</mtext></msub></math>; while the rest are treated as inequality constraints, i.e. ![bold-italic upper G Subscript monospace meq plus 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x greater-than-or-equal-to h Subscript monospace meq plus 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic upper G Subscript upper K Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x greater-than-or-equal-to h Subscript upper K Baseline](images/c11-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">meq</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">meq</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></math>.

 

**\*11.A.2.2 Minimax Theorem and Duality** In this subsection, we first recall the celebrated *von Neumann's Minimax theorem*, from which we derive general results concerning the duality of constrained minimization problems. The results will then be applied to solve the special case of quadratic programming problems in the next subsection. Readers may also refer to textbooks on convex analysis for more discussions, such as [\[2](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0002), [4\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0004).

A set ![script upper X subset-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is said to be *convex* if for any two points ![bold-italic x 1 comma bold-italic x 2 element-of script upper X](images/c11-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>, the line segment joining them is still contained in ![script upper X](images/c11-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>, that is, ![alpha bold-italic x 1 plus left-parenthesis 1 minus alpha right-parenthesis bold-italic x 2 element-of script upper X](images/c11-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math> for any ![alpha element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. A set ![script upper X subset-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is said to be *compact* if ![script upper X](images/c11-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math> is closed and bounded.

![FIGURE 11.17 (a) A compact convex set; (b) A convex, but non‐compact, set; (c) A compact non‐convex set.](images/c11f017.png)

**FIGURE 11.17** (a) A compact convex set; (b) A convex, but non‐compact, set; (c) A compact non‐convex set.

In the proof below, we demonstrate that under the assumptions of [Theorem 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0002), a saddle point ![left-parenthesis bold-italic x 0 comma bold-italic y 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of ![f](images/c11-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> always exists, which by definition is a point that satisfies

![max Underscript bold-italic y element-of script upper Y Endscripts f left-parenthesis bold-italic x 0 comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis equals f left-parenthesis bold-italic x 0 comma bold-italic y 0 right-parenthesis equals min Underscript bold-italic x element-of script upper X Endscripts f left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y 0 right-parenthesis semicolon](images/c11-math-0058.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>;</mo></math> 

moreover, the existence of a saddle point in fact implies the validity of ([11.26](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0057)):

mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Here, the leftmost expression corresponds to the lower path in blue in [Figure 11.18](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0018), while the rightmost term corresponds to the upper path in red in the same figure. Both paths settle at the same point ![left-parenthesis bold-italic x 0 comma bold-italic y 0 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Nevertheless, in general, even if the saddle point of ![f](images/c11-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> does not exist, the minimax theorem still remains valid.

Notice that the max‐min inequality ([11.28](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0064)) holds for any function ![f](images/c11-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> regardless of whether ![f](images/c11-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> possesses any convexity or concavity property, and regardless of the topological structure of ![script upper X](images/c11-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math> and ![script upper Y](images/c11-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></math>.

As a side discussion, von Neumann's minimax theorem is actually closely related to the vitally important concept of the *Nash equilibrium* in Economics, which is central to *noncooperative game theory*. Define a joint satisfaction function when playing a game between two players by ![upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![bold-italic x element-of script upper X](images/c11-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math> and ![bold-italic y element-of script upper Y](images/c11-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></math> are the respective strategies independently adopted by Players 1 and 2. We say a pair of strategies ![left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript asterisk Baseline comma bold-italic y Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis element-of script upper X times script upper Y](images/c11-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></math> is a *Nash equilibrium* if

![max Underscript bold-italic x element-of script upper X Endscripts upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript asterisk Baseline comma bold-italic y Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis and max Underscript bold-italic y element-of script upper Y Endscripts upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript asterisk Baseline comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis equals upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript asterisk Baseline comma bold-italic y Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c11-math-0065.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="1em"/><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></munder><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

By definition, the Nash equilibrium represents a stable solution of the game in that if the players play in this way, either player has no incentive to unilaterally change to another strategy because each player's strategy is the best response to the strategy adopted by his opponent. A fundamental result in game theory states that Nash equilibrium always exists for every such game, under the following assumptions:

1.  **(A1)** both ![script upper X](images/c11-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math> and ![script upper Y](images/c11-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></math> are nonempty compact and convex subsets of finite dimensional spaces;
2.  **(A2)** ![upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is concave in ![bold-italic x](images/c11-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> for each ![bold-italic y element-of script upper Y](images/c11-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></math>, and is also concave in ![bold-italic y](images/c11-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> for each ![bold-italic x element-of script upper X](images/c11-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>;
3.  **(A3)** ![upper J left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is jointly continuous.

To establish its validity, the following argument is essentially the same as discussed above for von Neumann's minimax theorem. If we define the *dual Lagrangian*

![script upper D left-parenthesis bold-italic lamda right-parenthesis colon equals min Underscript bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline Endscripts left-parenthesis f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis plus bold-italic lamda Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic g left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma](images/c11-math-0073.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

then we arrive at the so‐called *weak duality*:

[(11.31)](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-disp-0074)![m equals min Underscript bold-italic x element-of script upper X Endscripts f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to max Underscript bold-italic lamda greater-than-or-equal-to bold 0 Endscripts script upper D left-parenthesis bold-italic lamda right-parenthesis period](images/c11-math-0074.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

The minimization on the left, our original problem, is called the *primal problem*, and the maximization on the right is called the *dual problem*. This result shows that the solution to the dual problem provides a lower bound to the solution of the primal problem. The difference between the optimal values of primal and dual is called the *duality gap*; see the illustration in [Figure 11.19](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0019). We conclude this subsection by closing the gap via the *Fenchel–Rockafellar duality* (see Theorem 1.9 in [\[24\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0025)) of convex optimization problems.

We say that *strong duality* for ([11.29](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0068)) holds if the duality gap is equal to zero:

When Problem ([11.29](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0068)) is convex, that is, the objective function ![f](images/c11-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> and all constraint functions ![g Subscript k](images/c11-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s are convex, a classical condition that guarantees the validity of strong duality is the *Slater condition*: there exists ![bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> such that ![g Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c11-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> for all ![k](images/c11-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>; see [\[5\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005) for a more comprehensive discussion. When strong duality holds, there is a close relationship between the optimal solutions of the primal problem and the dual problem. **\*11.A.2.4 Quadratic Programming in Markowitz Portfolio Selection** Consider a financial market with ![p](images/c11-i0526.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> financial assets, and let their daily logarithmic returns on day ![t](images/c11-i0527.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> be ![bold r Subscript t](images/c11-i0528.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. These returns are often assumed to be iid random vectors following a ![p](images/c11-i0529.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐variate Gaussian distribution with a mean vector ![bold-italic mu element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0530.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> and a covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times p](images/c11-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>:

![bold r Subscript t Baseline tilde Overscript i i d Endscripts script upper N Subscript p Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic mu comma bold upper Sigma right-parenthesis comma for t equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis period](images/c11-math-0106.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mover class="overset"><mo>&#8764;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mover><msub><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Let us assume short‐selling has been prohibited and investors are risk averse whenever two investments yield the same expected return, they prefer the less risky one. In these circumstances, a portfolio is simply a combination of the ![p](images/c11-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> assets with a non‐negative weight vector ![bold-italic omega element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript p](images/c11-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></math> that sums to 1 (no short‐selling allowed), and the investors have to pick their desired portfolio to have an expected portfolio return of at least ![mu Subscript upper P](images/c11-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></math>. Equivalently, the portfolio should satisfy ![mu Subscript upper P Baseline less-than-or-equal-to bold-italic mu Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega](images/c11-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></math> but with the lowest possible level of risk, as measured by the variance of the portfolio return. Markowitz [\[16\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0016) formulated the optimal portfolio selection problem as a QP problem:

(11.45)![minimize Underscript bold-italic omega element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript p Baseline Endscripts one half bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma bold-italic omega comma](images/c11-math-0107.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mtext>minimize</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></munder><mspace width="2em"/><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> (11.46)![equation](images/c11-math-0108.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mspace width="2.8em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width=".3em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mspace width="1.4em"/><mtext>i) </mtext><mspace width="0.8em"/><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="right"><mspace width="1.4em"/><mtext>ii)</mtext><mspace width="1em"/><msup><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mspace width="1.4em"/><mtext>iii)</mtext><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where ![bold 1 element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is a column vector of value 1 and ![bold 0 element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c11-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is a column vector of value 0. Readers can also refer to [\[7\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0007) for more discussions on portfolio selection.

For this problem, the Lagrangian ![script upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0538.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with Lagrange multipliers ![lamda 1 greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c11-i0539.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, ![lamda 2 element-of double-struck upper R](images/c11-i0540.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, and ![bold-italic lamda 3 greater-than-or-equal-to bold 0](images/c11-i0541.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></math> is given by

![script upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis equals one half bold-italic omega Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma bold-italic omega plus lamda 1 left-parenthesis mu Subscript upper P Baseline minus bold-italic mu Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega right-parenthesis plus lamda 2 left-parenthesis bold 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic omega minus 1 right-parenthesis plus bold-italic lamda 3 Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold 0 minus bold-italic omega right-parenthesis period](images/c11-math-0109.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Differentiating the Lagrangian with respect to ![bold-italic omega](images/c11-i0542.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></mrow></math> gives:

![nabla Subscript bold-italic omega Baseline script upper L left-parenthesis bold-italic omega comma lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis equals one half left-parenthesis bold upper Sigma plus bold upper Sigma Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis bold-italic omega minus lamda 1 bold-italic mu plus lamda 2 bold 1 minus bold-italic lamda 3 equals bold upper Sigma bold-italic omega minus lamda 1 bold-italic mu plus lamda 2 bold 1 minus bold-italic lamda 3 period](images/c11-math-0110.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

Provided that the covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma](images/c11-i0543.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math> is symmetric and invertible, setting this derivative to zero yields:

![bold-italic omega equals minus bold upper Sigma Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis minus lamda 1 bold-italic mu plus lamda 2 bold 1 minus bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis period](images/c11-math-0111.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Finally, substituting the solution back to the Lagrangian gives the dual Lagrangian:

![script upper D left-parenthesis lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis equals minus one half left-parenthesis minus lamda 1 bold-italic mu plus lamda 2 bold 1 minus bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper Sigma Superscript negative 1 Baseline left-parenthesis minus lamda 1 bold-italic mu plus lamda 2 bold 1 minus bold-italic lamda 3 right-parenthesis plus lamda 1 mu Subscript upper P Baseline minus lamda 2 period](images/c11-math-0112.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

Therefore, the dual optimization problem is written as the following:

Let us illustrate Markowitz Portfolio Selection with real data. The dataset `S&P500_Open_hourly_2021.csv` contains the (unadjusted) hourly *Opening Prices* of 375 securities

The hourly logarithmic returns are first computed in [Programme 11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3009) via Python. Those in the training set are used to compute the sample covariance matrix ![bold-italic upper P](images/c11-i0544.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> and estimate the mean vector ![bold-italic mu](images/c11-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow></math> via EWMA (as seen in [Section 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0003)) with the mean vector defined as ![bold-italic mu Subscript t Baseline equals lamda bold-italic r Subscript t Baseline plus left-parenthesis 1 minus lamda right-parenthesis bold-italic mu Subscript t minus 1](images/c11-i0546.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, for ![t equals 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c11-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, with ![lamda equals 0.94](images/c11-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.94</mn></math> and ![bold-italic mu 1 equals bold-italic r 1](images/c11-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> by convention. Suppose that the investor would like to achieve an annual return of at least ![mu Subscript upper P Baseline equals 15 percent-sign](images/c11-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mi>%</mi></math>

From the output of [Programme 11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3010) in Python, 27 stocks are selected to be included in the optimal portfolio. In contrast, the weights for the other ![375 minus 27 equals 348](images/c11-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>375</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>348</mn></math> securities are less than the threshold of ![1 0 Superscript negative 2](images/c11-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>, so that they are totally discarded.

Finally, as a comparison, we consider the buy‐and‐hold strategy on the S&P500 portfolio with the same initial investment amount of USD 100,000, see [Programme 11.11](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-3011).

From [Figure 11.20](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0020), the optimal portfolio performs better than the S&P500 portfolio. However, even without counting in transaction costs and market friction, the optimal portfolio only yields a marginally positive return of USD 106.567 at the end of the test period when the market closes on 7 Jan 2022. In general, the performance of portfolio selection via quadratic programming, though certainly not the worst, is mostly mediocre. That is why we do not expect a very promising return for those utilizing this approach in actual trading.

![FIGURE 11.20 Value of the optimal portfolio and the S&P500 index in the test dataset, generated by Programme 11.11.](images/c11f020.png)

# PART Three  
Nonlinear Models

 

 

# CHAPTER 12  
Bayesian Learning

 

In this chapter, we introduce another important class of semiparametric model‐based learning, called *Bayesian inference*, or *Bayesian learning* especially if we focus on the model calibrations. Whereas Bayesian inference follows many of the conventional steps of semiparametric modelling, including model specification, criterion selection for evaluation, and parameter estimation, it differs from other approaches in terms of the criterion adopted. Indeed, the criterion used for Bayesian inference is the probability of attaining various parameter values, which serves as an alternative to the previously mentioned criteria such as the minimization of loss functions and maximum likelihood estimations. We shall highlight a few useful Bayesian‐based tools for data analysis in *FinTech* and *InsurTech*.

 

## 12.1 SIMPLE CREDIBILITY THEORY

Credibility theory, as a linear Bayesian model, has long been a core topic in *actuarial science*. It involves the pricing of insurance products using the historical information from both the policyholder herself and the risk class she belongs to. Readers may refer to [\[2](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002), [11\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0011) for a detailed and extensive discussion, as well as [\[4\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0004) and references therein for more recent developments in the field. More precisely, let ![normal x Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c12-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math> be the loss amount of a policyholder at time ![i](images/c12-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, whose risky position is governed by an unknown parameter ![theta element-of chi](images/c12-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#967;</mi></math>; ![theta](images/c12-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is also known as the *risk profile* of the policyholder, and ![chi](images/c12-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#967;</mi></mrow></math> is the collection of all possible risk profiles in the community. From the Bayesian perspective, ![theta](images/c12-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is regarded as a realization of the random variable ![normal upper Theta](images/c12-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math>, which describes the uncertainty due to the limit of knowledge. As a primitive model, we also assume that ![normal x 1 comma normal x 2 comma ellipsis](images/c12-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math> are conditionally iid given ![normal upper Theta equals theta](images/c12-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></math>.

The key question in credibility theory is to determine the fair premium to be collected in the next time period, say ![n plus 1](images/c12-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, given the history of losses ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript n Baseline](images/c12-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> of the policyholder. This would be straightforward with the knowledge of her risk profile ![theta](images/c12-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> and the distribution of ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> given ![normal upper Theta equals theta](images/c12-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></math>; indeed, the fair premium should be ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline bar normal upper Theta equals theta right-parenthesis equals colon mu left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This quantity is also called the *hypothetical mean*, and we note it does not depend on ![n](images/c12-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> because of the conditional iid assumption. However, as neither ![theta](images/c12-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> nor the conditional distribution is known in reality, we may adopt the Bayesian approach to estimate this quantity by using the whole loss history of the policyholder.

To this end, let ![t left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be an estimator of ![mu left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, a statistic of the historical loss vector ![bold x equals left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma normal x 2 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>= </mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. For any given value of ![theta](images/c12-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, we define the *risk function* to be the expected squared loss of ![t left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> across all possible values of ![bold x](images/c12-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>:

![upper R Subscript t Baseline left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis colon equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis left-parenthesis mu left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis minus t left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis equals integral Underscript double-struck upper R Superscript n Baseline Endscripts left-parenthesis mu left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis minus t left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared f Subscript bold x bar normal upper Theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x bar theta right-parenthesis d bold-italic x period](images/c12-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mtext>.</mtext></math>

Naturally, we shall select the estimator that minimizes the Bayes risk, and it suffices to look for one that minimizes the inner integral in the last line of ([12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0002)). Due to the squared loss function, it can be shown by standard arguments that the resulting minimizer is given by the posterior mean:

Next we illustrate the calculation of the Bayesian premium via a simple example. Therefore, together with the fact that ![mu left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis bold x bar normal upper Theta equals theta right-parenthesis equals theta](images/c12-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></math>, the Bayesian premium is simply equal to:

[(12.3)](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-disp-0005)![ModifyingAbove t left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis With Ì‚ equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis mu left-parenthesis normal upper Theta right-parenthesis bar bold x right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal upper Theta bar bold x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction n tau squared normal x overbar plus sigma squared mu Over n tau squared plus sigma squared EndFraction equals z normal x overbar plus left-parenthesis 1 minus z right-parenthesis mu comma](images/c12-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![z colon equals StartFraction n tau squared Over n tau squared plus sigma squared EndFraction](images/c12-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8201;+&#8201;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> is called the *credibility factor* as it represents the extent to which, when determining the premium, we believe in the historical claims instead of our prior belief from the prior distribution. Moreover, this credibility factor tends to 1 as the sample size ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c12-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, indicating that we have a stronger belief in the policyholder's claim history over time.

The special linear form of the credibility estimator in ([12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0005)) is not a coincidence. In fact, if the likelihood function belongs to the *exponential dispersion family* (EDF) introduced in [Section 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0004) and the prior distribution is the conjugate prior with respect to the likelihood, the Bayesian estimator always takes the form of a convex combination of the sample mean and the theoretical expectation under the prior with weights that are the same as those in the example above. In this case the Bayesian credibility is said to be an *exact credibility*; its proof is given in [\[10\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0010).

 

## \*12.2 BAYESIAN ASYMPTOTIC INFERENCE

As we have seen in the previous section, though we illuminate the Bayesian nature of the credibility estimator, too many restrictions (including its simple linearity) limit its use in a broader scope. We want a more generalized *Bayesian decision theory* that can allow for (i) a larger family of loss functions, not just the squared loss; (ii) an explicit approximation of the corresponding Bayesian estimator, especially when the prior is not the conjugate prior of the likelihood; and (iii) an approximated posterior distribution for further statistical inference like hypothesis testing.

As before, we interpret the parameter ![theta element-of chi](images/c12-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#967;</mi></math> as an outcome of the random variable ![normal upper Theta](images/c12-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math> following the prior distribution ![pi](images/c12-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math>, and the data ![bold x](images/c12-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> follows a distribution with a joint density function ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic x semicolon theta right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given ![theta](images/c12-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, that is the likelihood. The objective of *average risk optimality* is sought for:

![delta Subscript pi Baseline colon equals arg min Underscript delta left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis Endscripts r left-parenthesis pi comma delta right-parenthesis colon equals arg min Underscript delta left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis Endscripts double-struck upper E left-bracket upper L left-parenthesis normal upper Theta comma delta left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-bracket equals arg min Underscript delta left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis Endscripts integral Underscript chi Endscripts upper R left-parenthesis theta comma delta right-parenthesis pi left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis d theta comma](images/c12-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>&#960;</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min&#8201;</mtext><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min</mtext><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mi>&#967;</mi></msub><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo></math>

overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as a function is the Bayesian estimator. The proof can be found in many standard textbooks on statistical estimation, such as [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) in [\[16\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0016). An example of this claim is that the posterior mean of ([12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0003)) is the Bayesian estimator when the loss function is the squared loss. When the loss function is an absolute difference, by a simple combinatorial argument, the corresponding Bayesian estimator is given by the posterior median. Generally speaking, for any differentiable loss function satisfying enough regularity conditions, its Bayesian estimator satisfies the first order condition:

The corresponding integrals (conditional expectations) are usually intractable, especially when the prior is not a conjugate of the likelihood, and so we lack the explicit expression of the Bayesian estimator. Nevertheless, if the sample is large, we can obtain an approximation by the *Laplace method*. Considering general likelihoods and priors, without loss of generality, we focus only on the one‐dimensional case here. Most often, the corresponding Bayesian estimator can be written in terms of several conditional expectations of the following form:

Using Laplace's approximation, we can also motivate the setting behind the *Bayesian Information Criterion* (the BIC as mentioned in [Section 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0010)) commonly used in practice. We discuss this topic as a supplement in [Appendix 12.A.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0018).

As a final remark, in the event of a relatively small finite sample, we usually use Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to evaluate the posterior distribution or the relevant posterior statistics; we refer readers to Section \*6.4 of [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml) for more detailed discussions.

 

## 12.3 REVISITING POLYNOMIAL REGRESSION

We briefly introduced polynomial regression in [Section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0003). Let us revisit this class of models from the Bayesian learning perspective. We take the simplest univariate polynomial model as an illustration:

Using ([12.9](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0018)) and ([12.10](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0019)), the posterior density of ![bold-italic beta](images/c12-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> is given by
