Instead of considering the posterior mean of ![bold-italic beta](images/c12-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, which is commonly used in Bayesian methods, we focus on the *maximum a posteriori probability* (MAP) estimate, which is defined as the maximizer of the posterior ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic beta vertical-bar bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, or equivalently, the minimizer of the following error function:

[(12.12)](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-disp-0021)![script upper E colon equals StartFraction lamda Over 2 EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis g left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis minus y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared plus StartFraction alpha Over 2 EndFraction bold-italic beta Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic beta period](images/c12-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Note that as ![alpha right-arrow 0](images/c12-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, ![script upper E right-arrow StartFraction lamda Over 2 EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis g left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis minus y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared](images/c12-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, hence the MAP estimate converges to the least square estimate. Furthermore, as ![alpha greater-than 0](images/c12-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, the second term of ![script upper E](images/c12-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi></mrow></math> in ([12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0021)) increases with the norm of ![bold-italic beta](images/c12-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, thus it can be regarded as a regularization term, meaning that MAP estimation can be regarded as a regularization on the least square estimation. The resulting ![bold-italic beta](images/c12-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> tends to ![bold 0](images/c12-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></math> for a larger value of ![alpha](images/c12-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>; while the prior distribution becomes closer to a uniform distribution as ![alpha](images/c12-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> decreases, echoing a weaker regularization in ![script upper E](images/c12-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi></mrow></math>. As a remark, the selection of the parameter ![alpha](images/c12-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> may vary according to the data structure. For instance, when all ![x Subscript i](images/c12-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s lie between 0 and 1 while the responses ![y](images/c12-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>'s have a larger magnitude, the estimate of ![bold-italic beta](images/c12-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> may inevitably be large. To this end we may choose a smaller ![alpha](images/c12-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> to strike a balance.

Apart from regularization, the penalty term in the expression of ![script upper E](images/c12-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi></mrow></math> in ([12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0021)) can also help to prevent overfitting, as a simpler model is sought. Models with a larger degree ![upper M](images/c12-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> are usually subject to a larger penalty, and by comparing the values of ![script upper E](images/c12-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi></mrow></math> across models with various values of ![upper M](images/c12-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, we can select an appropriate degree ![upper M](images/c12-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> of the estimated polynomial to avoid overfitting and to enhance out‐sample predictions. This can be considered as an alternative to the well‐known *Bayesian Information Criterion* (BIC), defined as ![BIC colon equals minus 2 ln ModifyingAbove upper L With caret plus k ln n](images/c12-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>BIC</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>n</mi></math>, where ![ModifyingAbove upper L With caret](images/c12-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> is the maximized likelihood, ![k](images/c12-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is the number of parameters to be estimated, and ![n](images/c12-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is the sample size; also see [Appendix 12.A.212.6.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0018) for a motivation of BIC via Laplace's approximation.

Straightforward calculations of ([12.11](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0020)) show that the posterior is indeed another multivariate normal distribution:

## 12.4 BAYESIAN CLASSIFIERS

So far, we have only mentioned linear Bayesian models. Now we turn to non‐linear Bayesian models. Bayesian methods play a vital role in many classification algorithms in supervised learning, and the classification threshold is the conditional probability of a certain label given a feature vector taking the observed values, calculated using the Bayes' theorem (1.10). It has found extensive applications in various fields, such as text document classification and spam filters.

Mathematically, suppose we are given the following training dataset with ![n](images/c12-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> samples:

![script upper S colon equals StartSet left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 comma c left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis bold-italic x 2 comma c left-parenthesis bold-italic x 2 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline comma c left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndSet comma](images/c12-math-0026.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where each datum is represented by its feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c12-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> and its actual label ![c left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Take the detection of a list of ![p](images/c12-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> keywords in a collection of ![n](images/c12-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> text documents as an example. We set ![x Subscript i j Baseline equals 1](images/c12-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> if the ![j](images/c12-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th keyword appears in the ![i](images/c12-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th document, or ![x Subscript i j Baseline equals 0](images/c12-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> otherwise. In addition, we use ![script upper Y colon equals StartSet c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript upper M Baseline EndSet](images/c12-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> to denote the set of all possible classification labels. In the case of spam filters, we usually have only two labels, ![script upper Y equals StartSet double-turned-comma-quotation-mark spam double-comma-quotation-mark comma double-turned-comma-quotation-mark not spam double-comma-quotation-mark EndSet](images/c12-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mtext>&#8220;spam&#8221;</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#8220;not spam&#8221;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>.

Given a new feature vector, the Bayesian classifier first assigns probabilities to the feature vector belonging to each class in ![script upper Y](images/c12-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></math> based on Bayes' Theorem. It then assigns the class with the largest probability as the final prediction. Mathematically, for a new observation with feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript asterisk Baseline colon equals left-parenthesis x Subscript asterisk 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript asterisk p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, Bayesian classifiers in general estimate the conditional probability ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis c left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals c Subscript k Baseline vertical-bar bold x equals bold-italic x Subscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the probability its classification label is ![c Subscript k](images/c12-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper M](images/c12-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math>, by the following conditional empirical probability based on the training dataset ![script upper S](images/c12-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>:

Note that these empirical (joint) probabilities would only be accurate enough when the sample size of ![script upper S](images/c12-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> is large for different labels and subsets with various features. Meanwhile, when a large number of new observations need to be classified, it is more efficient to calculate these probabilities in advance. However, they would take up an enormous amount of time and memory as ![2 Superscript p](images/c12-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></msup></math> number of probabilities have to be calculated and stored for every classification label. In order to be more efficient in the training process while attaining a similar performance with a smaller training dataset, we usually consider a *naïve* model, with the extra assumption that all ![p](images/c12-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> feature variables ![normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline](images/c12-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> are conditionally independent given any classification label. This special model is known as the *Naïve Bayes* classifier. Treating the new observation ![bold-italic x Subscript asterisk Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript asterisk 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript asterisk p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> as a realization of the random vector ![bold x equals left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, we have:

Upon putting this procedure into code, the issue of arithmetic underflow may emerge when the products in ([12.13](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0029)) are computed. We usually deal with this by calculating their logarithms. Besides, while the conditional independence assumption yields effective computations of the probabilities, it often deviates from reality when the feature variables are dependent. For instance, feature variables in real data rarely exhibit conditional independence. To illustrate this drawback, consider a classification problem involving ![p equals 2](images/c12-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> binary feature variables ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. A new observation ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is classified as class A when ![x 1 equals x 2](images/c12-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, or class B otherwise. Suppose that for a given training dataset, the number of samples taking every combination of values ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the same, so that each class has half of the observations, while the values of ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are also evenly distributed in each class. By simple calculations, the product to be maximized on the right‐hand side of ([12.14](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0031)) is ![one half times one half times one half equals one eighth](images/c12-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#215;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#215;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></math> for all combinations of ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, implying that the classifier is no better than flipping a coin. Due to this limitation and other ones like it, we propose in the next section how to enhance the Bayes classifiers by incorporating a well‐known notion from actuarial science, namely tail comonotonicity for dependence modelling.

 

## 12.5 COMONOTONE‐INDEPENDENCE BAYES CLASSIFIER (CIBER)

To remedy the drawbacks of the Naïve Bayes discussed in the previous section, we introduce a variant [\[5\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0005) that incorporates comonotonicity, as introduced briefly in [Section 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0015) of [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml). Our aim is to better recover and model the dependence structure among feature variables without complicating the calculations of conditional joint probabilities too much. This variant is called the *Comonotone‐Independence Bayes Classifier*, or *CIBer* for short. This new classifier can effectively deal with discrete feature variables with numerical values, also known as “discrete features”. However, in financial and insurance contexts, the presence of all three types of feature variable, namely discrete, continuous and categorical, is common. To that end, we introduce a unified feature engineering scheme: by binning continuous feature variables and employing the method of *Joint Encoding* for categorical ones, as we shall discuss in Sections [12.5.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0008) and [12.5.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0009), we convert all feature variables into discrete features, as the inputs of the new classifier.

Let us first clarify some terms and notation to be adopted in this section. As explained above, all feature variables are first transformed into discrete feature variables. We denote the sample space of each such discrete feature ![normal x Subscript j](images/c12-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, as an input of CIBer, by ![script upper X Subscript j Baseline colon equals StartSet s Subscript j Baseline 1 Baseline comma s Subscript j Baseline 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma s Subscript j comma upper M Sub Subscript j Subscript Baseline EndSet](images/c12-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, where ![s Subscript j Baseline 1 Baseline less-than s Subscript j Baseline 2 Baseline less-than midline-horizontal-ellipsis less-than s Subscript j comma upper M Sub Subscript j Subscript](images/c12-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper M Subscript j Baseline colon equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper X Subscript j Baseline EndAbsoluteValue element-of double-struck upper Z Superscript plus](images/c12-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>.

The notion of comonotonicity is central to CIBer. In addition to what we have introduced in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), let us discuss some further properties. As a concept widely used in actuarial science, finance, and economics, comonotonicity describes the strong possible positive dependence among several random variables: whenever the realization of one random variable changes, all the rest follow suit along the same direction. Mathematically, a random vector ![bold x equals left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> is said to be *comonotonic* if there is a *comonotonic subset* ![upper C](images/c12-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> of ![double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c12-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> such that ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis bold x element-of upper C right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c12-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Here, ![upper C](images/c12-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is comonotonic if it is totally ordered so that either ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline less-than-or-equal-to bold-italic y Subscript i](images/c12-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> or ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to bold-italic y Subscript i](images/c12-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for all ![i](images/c12-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, for any ![bold-italic x comma bold-italic y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c12-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>. One can prove that the following characterizations of comonotonicity are equivalent:

1.  the random vector ![bold x equals left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> is comonotonic;

The definition and properties of (unconditional) comonotonicity mentioned above could also be applied analogously to the conditional sense, resulting in the *conditional comonotonicity* that we shall find more useful in the context of Bayesian classification, as we are ultimately interested in computing the conditional probability. To this end, suppose that the *label function* ![c left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (indicating the actual label of ![bold x](images/c12-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>) only takes finitely many values, say ![c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c12-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></math>. ### 12.5.1 Clustered Comonotonicity

As in reality not all feature variables are necessarily comonotonic, a more appropriate and realistic approach in classification problems is to first partition the feature variables into several subgroups, and then treat the feature variables within each group as comonotonic while the totality of features in a group is independent of those in another group. However, the exhaustive searching time for the optimal partition grows rapidly with the number of features involved. We therefore have to deploy an efficient heuristic search to approximate this optimal partition without traversing all possibilities. The solution turns out to be a method of clustering. In principle, two features with a small value of some pre‐specified “distance” are regarded as comonotonic and should be clustered into the same group. Some popular distance metrics for the purpose of measuring comonotonic dependence include the *Normalized Mutual Information* ![upper U](images/c12-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>, *Pearson's* ![r](images/c12-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, *Kendall's* ![tau Subscript b](images/c12-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></math>, and *Spearman's* ![rho](images/c12-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>. We introduce another one based on Kendall's ![tau Subscript b](images/c12-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></math>, specifically built for CIBer. It should be noted that the selection of the distance metric varies case by case, and we always aim to choose the one leading to the best performance. Let us list out these metrics in their natural empirical form, where ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![normal x Subscript j](images/c12-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> are any two distinct features with observed pairs ![left-parenthesis x Subscript 1 i Baseline comma x Subscript 1 j Baseline right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma left-parenthesis x Subscript n i Baseline comma x Subscript n j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>:

5.  **Totally‐ordered Kendall's** ![ModifyingAbove tau With Ì‚ Subscript como](images/c12-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mtext>como</mtext></msub></math>: this metric is based on Kendall's ![ModifyingAbove tau With Ì‚ Subscript b](images/c12-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></math>, and is specifically built for CIBer to utilize the totally ordered set as much as possible. Instead of focusing on concordant and discordant pairs as in Kendall's ![ModifyingAbove tau With Ì‚ Subscript b](images/c12-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></math>, we combine concordant and tied pairs, and the number of the resulting *concordant‐tied* pairs ![upper C overbar](images/c12-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> is used in calculating the metric: [(12.17)](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-disp-0042)![ModifyingAbove tau With Ì‚ Subscript como Baseline colon equals StartFraction upper C overbar minus upper D Over StartBinomialOrMatrix n Choose 2 EndBinomialOrMatrix EndFraction comma](images/c12-math-0042.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mtext>como</mtext></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> where ![upper D equals StartBinomialOrMatrix n Choose 2 EndBinomialOrMatrix minus upper C overbar](images/c12-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> is the number of discordant pairs as defined before.

All metrics discussed above are measurements for statistical association or “similarity”, hence they are also called *association measures*. However, this is inconsistent with the notion of “dissimilarity” generally used in clustering. Therefore, we also introduce the following notion of a random distance matrix: given a ![p](images/c12-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional random vector ![bold x equals left-parenthesis normal x 1 comma ellipsis comma normal x Subscript p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, a random matrix ![bold upper A colon equals left-parenthesis normal a Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times p](images/c12-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> is said to be a distance matrix if its entries satisfy:

Its empirical counterpart is ![bold-italic upper A colon equals left-parenthesis a Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times p](images/c12-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math>, where

where ![ModifyingAbove asso With Ì‚ left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mtext>asso</mtext><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the corresponding sample association measure between ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![normal x Subscript j](images/c12-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, such as those mentioned above.

This distance matrix plays a vital role in the following hierarchical clustering algorithm, called *Agglomerative Nesting* (AGNES), first proposed in [\[12\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0012), which we shall employ to cluster the features. The implementation of this algorithm relies on an additional notion of a distance measure between two disjoint clusters of features, say with respective index sets

![d Subscript complete Baseline left-parenthesis script upper G 1 comma script upper G 2 right-parenthesis colon equals max Underscript i element-of script upper G 1 comma j element-of script upper G 2 Endscripts a Subscript i j Baseline period](images/c12-math-0045.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>complete</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8201;j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

As a bottom‐up approach for hierarchical clustering, the AGNES algorithm begins with all ![p](images/c12-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> features as singletons, so that the initialized clusters are ![StartSet 1 EndSet comma ellipsis comma StartSet p EndSet](images/c12-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. We then iteratively merge two clusters with the smallest complete linkage into one, which reduces the total number of clusters by one in each iteration, until the complete linkage between any two clusters becomes greater than a preset threshold ![delta element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c12-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, or only one cluster remains (which implies all features are regarded as comonotonic). The pseudocode of AGNES is shown in the following Algorithm 12.1.

After partitioning the feature variables into different comonotonic clusters using AGNES, we compute the conditional joint pmf given the class label by adopting the philosophy of clustered comonotonicity. ### 12.5.2 Binning Continuous Features

Intuitively, individuals in the same class ![c Subscript k](images/c12-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> should share similar characteristics, and the values of their respective continuous features are also expected to cluster in a certain range. It suffices to predict an individual's label based on whether her continuous features lie in a characterizing range, rather than on their exact values. To this point, it is natural to apply discretization to continuous variables for the purpose of classification. As an alternative to the commonly used approaches such as equal‐width binning, we consider another discretization method proposed in [\[3](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003), [9\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0009), based on the concept of entropy.

The goal of discretization with respect to a given continuous feature ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is to find the “optimal” partition of ![script upper X Subscript i](images/c12-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> into a number of disjoint subsets ![script upper X 1 Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma script upper X Subscript k Sub Subscript i Subscript Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> so that ![square-cup script upper X Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis Baseline equals script upper X Subscript i](images/c12-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8852;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, where ![k Subscript i](images/c12-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> can be arbitrarily chosen, such that the following *class information entropy* is minimized:

Nevertheless, the arbitrariness of the choice of ![k Subscript i](images/c12-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and the lack of restriction on the partition render this optimization problem *NP‐hard*. Hence, we resort to a binary search method to obtain the partitions instead.

### 12.5.3 Joint Encoding for Categorical Features

Categorical features are more difficult to cope with in general, in view of their pure distinguishable nature and lack of natural ordering. As a result, association measures cannot be directly applied to them, nor can the notion of comonotonicity be applied immediately. To overcome this issue, being inspired by *optimal transport* theory, we introduce a novel encoding scheme for them that can “boost up” the inherent dependence among categorical features by making use of the frequencies of various grouped feature values. This encoding scheme, capable of handling several categorical features in one go, is named *Joint Encoding*.

Let us illustrate the procedure and effectiveness of joint encoding via a simple example. Consider the contingency table of a sample dataset with each datum possessing two categorical variables ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. The corresponding contingency table is shown in [Table 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0001).

To determine the magnitude of dependence between ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, we plan to assign numerical values to the possible feature values they can take, and then calculate the association measures. By the nature of this dataset, namely a large number of repeated observations ![left-parenthesis s Subscript 1 i Baseline comma s Subscript 2 j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>'s, Pearson's ![ModifyingAbove r With caret](images/c12-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> is a more suitable measure than others. Besides, it is also a useful association measure being invariant with respect to any affine transformation of coding. We first consider an arbitrary encoding scheme for ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, namely, for the values of ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, we encode ![s Subscript 1 i](images/c12-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> as ![i](images/c12-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma 3](images/c12-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>; while for the values of ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, we encode ![s Subscript 2 j](images/c12-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> as ![j](images/c12-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> for ![j equals 1 comma 2](images/c12-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Under this encoding scheme, we have

![x overbar Subscript 1 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 times 240 plus 2 times 300 plus 3 times 180 Over 720 EndFraction equals 1.91667 and x overbar Subscript 2 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 times 320 plus 2 times 400 Over 720 EndFraction equals 1.55556 comma](images/c12-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>240</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>720</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1.91667</mn><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>320</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><mn>720</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1.55556</mn><mo>,</mo></math> ![TABLE 12.1  The contingency table of a sample dataset with two categorical feature variables normal x 1 and normal x 2.](images/c12-i0425.png)

We calculate the empirical Pearson's ![ModifyingAbove r With caret](images/c12-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> as follows:

![ModifyingAbove r With caret equals StartFraction negative 16.66667 Over StartRoot 415 times 177.77778 EndRoot EndFraction equals negative 0.06136 comma](images/c12-math-0052.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16.66667</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>415</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>177.77778</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.06136</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is fairly close to 0, and thus gives no hint of a possible (linear) relation between ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>.

Nevertheless, we can indeed observe from [Table 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0001) that the cells ![left-parenthesis s 11 comma s 22 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>22</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![left-parenthesis s 12 comma s 21 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>21</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![left-parenthesis s 13 comma s 22 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>22</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> have higher frequencies than the others. Such non‐uniform distribution of data points indicates some hidden association between ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, which could not be accurately reflected by the arbitrary encoding scheme as proposed above. This suggests that a more systematic encoding approach has to be adopted to reveal the hidden connection between ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> as much as possible. To this end, we propose the following heuristic scheme:

1.  Find the combination of values of ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> with the highest frequency, and encode the corresponding feature values as 1;
2.  Find the combination with the highest frequency within those of un‐encoded values of ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, and encode the corresponding values by the next unassigned integer;
3.  Repeat Step 2 until a feature variable has precisely one value left that is not encoded, then automatically assign to it the next unassigned integer. If this is the case for both feature variables, then we assign the same integer to the values of both feature variables. Otherwise, if the remaining feature variable has two or more values that are not encoded, then we encode its remaining values sequentially in descending order of their corresponding marginal frequencies.

Following this scheme, we shall first encode ![s 12](images/c12-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></math> and ![s 21](images/c12-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>21</mn></msub></math> as 1 by noting that ![left-parenthesis s 12 comma s 21 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>21</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> has the largest frequency of 250. As ![s 22](images/c12-i0462.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>22</mn></msub></math> now becomes the only value of ![normal x 2](images/c12-i0463.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> that is not yet encoded, we encode it as 2. As ![normal x 1](images/c12-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> now still has two un‐encoded values, namely ![s 11](images/c12-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></math> and ![s 13](images/c12-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>13</mn></msub></math>, we encode them in descending order according to their marginal frequencies listed at the bottom row of [Table 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0001), so that ![s 11](images/c12-i0467.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></math> is encoded as 2 and ![s 13](images/c12-i0468.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>13</mn></msub></math> as 3, respectively. Under this encoding scheme, we can compute that:

![x overbar Subscript 1 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 times 300 plus 2 times 240 plus 3 times 180 Over 720 EndFraction equals 1.83333 and x overbar Subscript 2 Baseline equals StartFraction 1 times 320 plus 2 times 400 Over 720 EndFraction equals 1.55556 comma](images/c12-math-0053.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>240</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>720</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1.83333</mn><mspace width="0.8em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.8em"/><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>320</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><mn>720</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1.55556</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

which together yield

The pseudocode of joint encoding for this high‐dimensional setting is shown in Algorithm 12.2.

 

### 12.5.4 Computation of Empirical Probabilities in CIBer

Let us see how CIBer compares with a Naïve Bayes classifier via a numerical example. Suppose that there are six features, five of them continuous and one discrete, taking values 1, 2, or 3. We train a Naïve Bayes classifier and CIBer after discretization, respectively, for classifying the dummy label ![y](images/c12-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> with 2,614 of them taking value 0 and 1,386 of them taking value 1 in a training dataset. For the sake of illustration, we adopt the naïve equal‐width binning approach for discretization, so that each continuous feature is discretized into 10 bins. The resulting empirical proportions for ![y equals 0](images/c12-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![y equals 1](images/c12-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> are shown in [Tables 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0002) and [12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0003), respectively. Notice that some rows may not sum up exactly to 1 due to rounding. The frequencies of the sixth categorial variable are listed in [Table 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0004).



Let us elaborate on the formation of comonotonic clusters by applying AGNES Algorithm 12.1 with ![delta equals 0.1](images/c12-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math>. First, we consider the case of label 0, while the case for label 1 is similar. The algorithm begins with a collection of singletons as individual clusters ![script upper Y 0 equals StartSet StartSet 1 EndSet comma ellipsis comma StartSet 6 EndSet EndSet](images/c12-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Since the pair of Features 1 and 3 has the smallest complete linkage among all cluster pairs, with ![d Subscript complete Baseline left-parenthesis StartSet 1 EndSet comma StartSet 3 EndSet right-parenthesis equals 0.0028 less-than delta](images/c12-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>complete</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0028</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi></math>, they are merged first leading to the revised ![script upper Y 0 equals StartSet StartSet 1 comma 3 EndSet comma StartSet 2 EndSet comma StartSet 4 EndSet comma StartSet 5 EndSet comma StartSet 6 EndSet EndSet](images/c12-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. In the next step, the pair of Features 4 and 5 has the smallest complete linkage of ![d Subscript complete Baseline left-parenthesis StartSet 4 EndSet comma StartSet 5 EndSet right-parenthesis equals 0.0061 less-than delta](images/c12-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>complete</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0061</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi></math>, hence they are merged, resulting in the second revised ![script upper Y 0 equals StartSet StartSet 1 comma 3 EndSet comma StartSet 2 EndSet comma StartSet 4 comma 5 EndSet comma StartSet 6 EndSet EndSet](images/c12-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Among these clusters, the pair of ![StartSet 1 comma 3 EndSet](images/c12-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> and Feature 2 has the smallest complete linkage of ![d Subscript complete Baseline left-parenthesis StartSet 1 comma 3 EndSet comma StartSet 2 EndSet right-parenthesis equals max left-brace right-brace comma 0.0317 comma 0.0416 equals 0.0416 less-than delta](images/c12-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>complete</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0.0317</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.0416</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0416</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi></math>; they are then merged, and then the third revised ![script upper Y 0](images/c12-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> becomes ![StartSet StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 EndSet comma StartSet 4 comma 5 EndSet comma StartSet 6 EndSet EndSet](images/c12-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. As the complete linkage of any pair of clusters is greater than ![delta equals 0.1](images/c12-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math>, the AGNES algorithm stops. By the same procedure, the set of comonotonic clusters ![script upper Y 1](images/c12-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> with the label ![y equals 1](images/c12-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> can be shown the same as ![script upper Y 0](images/c12-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> under ![delta equals 0.1](images/c12-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math>. ### 12.5.5 Robustness of Comonotonic Copula

As discussed in [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), copulae can be used to model the general dependence structure of underlying feature variables. While many copulae are readily available for use, CIBer focuses on utilizing the comonotonic copula. A natural question for readers to raise at this point would be: why choose comonotonic copula over other alternatives? To address this, let us provide a comprehensive simulation study to justify the use of comonotonic copula as first choice.

We investigate the robustness of comonotonicity as a modelling copula in CIBer, by comparing CIBer against three other Archimedean copula‐based classifiers, namely Gumbel, Frank, and Clayton copulae. To mimic the variety of real‐world datasets, for each feature variable ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> we randomly pick a distribution from a pre‐selected list of common distributions. For simplicity, on the one hand we consider only one cluster where all five feature variables in the class label ![c 1](images/c12-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> have a strong dependence. On the other hand, those feature variables in the class label ![c 2](images/c12-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> have a weak dependence, but the same type of copulae govern both dependence structures. Although this setting favors the three Archimedean copula‐based classifiers, we shall demonstrate that CIBer performs comparatively well against them. The simulation procedure is depicted in Algorithm 12.3.

By construction, CIBer with ![delta Subscript max Baseline equals 0.1](images/c12-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></math> captures only one comonotone cluster for the class label ![c 1](images/c12-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, i.e. ![script upper G Subscript 1 comma 0 Baseline equals StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet](images/c12-i0538.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, and five singleton clusters for the class label ![c 2](images/c12-i0539.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, i.e. ![script upper G Subscript i comma 1 Baseline equals StartSet i EndSet](images/c12-i0540.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 5](images/c12-i0541.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. From [Figure 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0002), boxplots of ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0542.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores show that both `CIBer (normal)` and `CIBer (auto)` generally perform better than all other copula‐based classifiers, including ones that were originally used to simulate the data. In particular, `CIBer (normal)` discretizes each continuous feature variable ![normal x Subscript i](images/c12-i0543.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of the corresponding fitted normal distribution with a cdf ![ModifyingAbove upper F With caret Subscript normal x Sub Subscript i](images/c12-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>F</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math>. Likewise, instead of only considering the normal distribution, `CIBer (auto)` chooses the best distribution (within a list of candidate distributions) by using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (introduced in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml)), in which the fitted distribution from the list having the smallest value of KS statistic is selected. Similar findings regarding the accuracies are shown in [Figure 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0003).

While copulae have been widely used in recent years for modelling dependence structures, using a copula requires parameter estimation and is usually suitable only for scenarios where all feature variables are of the same type. If only continuous feature variables are present, those three Archimedean copula‐based classifiers naturally perform better than CIBer. With the presence of ![normal x 5](images/c12-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></math>, a randomly discretized feature variable, which happens normally in practice (perhaps due to censoring and personal privacy, for example), CIBer steadily performs better than those three copula‐based classifiers. Instead of merely focusing on datasets with all feature variables of the same type, CIBer is designed to handle datasets with multiple feature variable types at the same time. In the real world, discrete, continuous, and categorical feature variables do appear in a dataset. Moreover, independence and comonotonicity are two extreme and universal dependence structures that are entirely non‐parametric. By making use of only these two dependence structures, CIBer can avoid complex computations, in contrast to classifiers based on specific parametric copulae, which also risk overfitting on the training dataset. CIBer is not prone to this error, and it demonstrates a promising performance on the test dataset. To echo the end of [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), CIBer can be regarded as a special case of the highly versatile vine copula, with an all‐or‐nothing treatment of the dependence among feature variables which does not lose much generality.

 

### 12.5.6 CIBer in Action in Finance and Insurance

A Python package has been created and is available for download on PyPI *(The Python Package Index*). It can be installed by the command `pip install CIBer`. As discussed in [Section 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0004), we shall first open a command terminal such as Anaconda Prompt, and then type the command in. The package will be downloaded automatically, as seen in [Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0004), and an installation guide is available through the QR code in [Figure 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0005).

In this subsection, we demonstrate the effectiveness of CIBer versus some representative machine learners through the evaluation of several model assessment methods by analyzing two real datasets from finance and insurance:

1.  **Bank Churners** [\[20\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0020): An important source of income for banks is the annual fees and charges paid by credit card holders. As a result, customer attrition is one of the major issues of concern. It is crucial for banks to predict whether a cardholder is likely to withdraw their credit card services because this can better facilitate their analysis on the attributing factors, helping them to improve their services in a timely manner.
