2.  **Default Premium Payment** [\[18\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0018): The on‐time collection of insurance premiums is crucial to insurance companies as this is a major component of their cash flow. However, policyholders may defer or even terminate premium payments due to various reasons. Therefore, it is important for insurance companies to be able to predict the emergence of such unfavourable events and alert their company agents to take timely action in advance.

Both datasets are highly imbalanced in nature. For example, a balanced dataset with roughly half of their customers in default would obviously bankrupt the company. We also note that there are some missing entries in both datasets. For simplicity, we assume the missing mechanism of *missing completely at random* and remove observations containing any missing entry. [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006) shows the distribution of the labels in the bank churners (left) and default premium payment (right) datasets after missing entries are removed.

![FIGURE 12.6 Class label distributions of bank churners (left) and default premium payment (right) datasets after removing missing entries.](images/c12f006.png)

[**FIGURE 12.6**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0006) Class label distributions of bank churners (left) and default premium payment (right) datasets after removing missing entries.

Next, we describe the experimental procedure for each of the two datasets. Since each dataset contains thousands of records, it suffices for us to (under‐)sample a small, yet representative enough, portion of the original dataset as our training dataset. We denote the training sample size by ![n Subscript train](images/c12-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></math>. Next, we shall randomly pick ![n Subscript test](images/c12-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub></math> data points from each label of the remaining dataset as our test dataset, resulting in a testing size of ![2 n Subscript test](images/c12-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub></math>. The actual values of ![n Subscript train](images/c12-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></math> and ![n Subscript test](images/c12-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub></math> for each dataset are subject to their original sizes of each binary label and hence their corresponding degrees of imbalance, which we shall state explicitly in the course of the following discussion. Algorithm 12.4 presents a summary of the experimental procedure.

As before, in implementing CIBer, we shall first discretize the continuous features by binning (referring to [Section 12.5.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0008)), and then perform a joint encoding scheme for categorical features. Comonotonic clusters are then identified using the AGNES algorithm with the totally‐ordered Kendall's ![ModifyingAbove tau With Ì‚ Subscript c o m o](images/c12-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> ([12.17](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0042)) as the underlying association measure. The value of the maximum cluster‐wise distance ![delta](images/c12-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math> is determined by grid search at the values of ![0 comma 0.05 comma 0.1 comma 0.15 comma ellipsis comma 1](images/c12-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.15</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, with the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score as the assessment metric.

We shall compare the results of CIBer with those from other commonly used alternatives, namely *Composite Naïve Bayes* (CNB), *Gaussian Naïve Bayes* (GNB), Support Vector Machine (SVM) with RBF kernel, Logistic regression (LR), *Multi‐layer Perceptron* (MLP), *Linear Discriminant Analysis* (LDA), *Decision Tree* (DT), and ![upper K](images/c12-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐Nearest Neighbour* (![upper K](images/c12-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN). Note that we choose only the primitive machine learners but not their boosted versions which involve various ensembling tools, and compare CIBer only with the primitive models (we could as well apply the same ensembling tools to CIBer and compare it with the ensembled variants of the others). In particular, CNB builds from two Naïve Bayes classifiers, namely GNB for modelling continuous and discrete features and the Categorical Naïve Bayes for categorical ones. Moreover, we also consider a variant of LDA, in which we first adopt PCA (see [Section 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0002)) to transform all features into continuously and uncorrelatedly distributed ones, and then perform the usual LDA. Last but not least, an additional CIBer with ![delta equals 0](images/c12-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> is adopted as a base comparison without incorporating comonotonicity, similar to an empirical Naïve Bayes classifiers.

 

#### 12.5.6.1 Bank Churners in Finance

The Bank Churners dataset

CIBer shares similar capabilities and functions for fitting

Before fitting the model, the dataset needs to be prepared. In Programm 12.2 via Python, `pd.factorize` is a `pandas` function for jointly encoding categorical features' values into discrete ones.

Then in [Programme 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-3003) via Python, we split the dataset into the training and testing sets. Since this dataset is highly imbalanced, we sample 7,000 data points as the training dataset and then pick 200 data points in each class as the test dataset.

In Programm 12.4 in Python, `cont_col` is a list of indices for the continuous feature variables and `min_asso` is the minimum threshold adopted in measuring the linear association for all pairs of feature variables, which can be found by a grid search. To fit a CIBer, we create a CIBer object called `CIBer_clf`, then fit the model using the training dataset `X_train` and its label set `y_train`. Finally, we get the predictions and its corresponding probabilities from CIBer by calling the functions `predict()` and `predict_porba()`, respectively.

[Figure 12.7](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0007) shows the boxplot of the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores for each classifier. We immediately observe that the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score of CIBer with ![delta equals 0.05](images/c12-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>, denoted by `CIBer (Normal)`, is slightly higher than that of CIBer with ![delta equals 0](images/c12-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, denoted by `CIBer (No CM)`, which does not involve any comonotonic structures. Besides, the ranges of both boxplots of CIBer are smaller than those of composite Naïve Bayes and Gaussian Naïve Bayes classifiers, and their positions are also higher than those of the latter two, indicating that the feature engineering techniques applied in CIBer improve both the robustness and effectiveness of the Naïve Bayes classifier.

![FIGURE 12.7 Boxplot of upper F 1‐score for each classifier in the bank churners dataset.](images/c12f007.png)

[**FIGURE 12.7**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0007) Boxplot of ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score for each classifier in the bank churners dataset.

The results show that both versions of CIBer are second only to the multilayer perceptron (MLP) and classification (decision) tree (DT). As a remark, we note that the results obtained by both MLP and classification tree are often unexplainable, whereas in the case of CIBer, we are able to justify the rationale behind the comonotonic clusters obtained. Taking this dataset as an example, we obtain one comonotonic cluster in the majority class with the actual label `0`, namely `Card_Category` and `Credit_Limit`. In particular, `Card_Category` is a categorical feature with four categories, including `Blue`, `Silver`, `Gold`, and `Platinum`, representing the status level of a credit card holder in an ascending order. For an existing cardholder with actual label 0, it is natural that the higher status level of a credit card comes with a higher credit limit, which explains why the two features are comonotonic. On the other hand, we also reveal a comonotonic cluster with actual label 1, namely (`Card_Category`, `Avg_Open_To_Buy`). Attrited cardholders in the minority class with actual label 1 tend to use their credit cards less often, resulting in a larger value of average open‐to‐buy. As a higher credit card level is subject to higher fees and charges, cardholders with a large average open‐to‐buy are expected to be more likely to terminate the services. Identifying these comonotonic structures does bring some improvement to the performance of CIBer, as shown in the slight increase in the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0568.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores from `CIBer (No CM)` to `CIBer (Normal)`. The ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0569.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores of the other classifiers are roughly the same, while ![upper K](images/c12-i0570.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN performs the worst. Similar observations are made in the boxplots of the corresponding accuracies for all classifiers as illustrated in [Figure 12.8](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0008).

The recall rate is important when examining the model performance on an imbalanced dataset, especially when one places more emphasis on the minority class than the majority. In this dataset, banks aim to solve the problem of customer attrition, hence they focus on making correct predictions for clients from the minority class. [Figure 12.9](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0009) shows the boxplots of recall rates for all classifiers. It is observed that the recall rates of the two versions of CIBer, as well as those of MLP and classification tree, are roughly 0.8, which are significantly higher than those of all other competitors, indicating that these classifiers perform well in detecting customer attrition.

![FIGURE 12.8 Boxplots of accuracies for all classifiers in the bank churners dataset.](images/c12f008.png)

[**FIGURE 12.8**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0008) Boxplots of accuracies for all classifiers in the bank churners dataset.

![FIGURE 12.9 Boxplots of recall rates for all classifiers in the bank churners dataset.](images/c12f009.png)

[**FIGURE 12.9**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0009) Boxplots of recall rates for all classifiers in the bank churners dataset.

 

#### 12.5.6.2 Default Insurance Premium Payment

This insurance dataset

[Figure 12.10](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0010) shows the boxplot of the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score for each classifier. Similar to the bank churners dataset, the incorporation of comonotonicity is beneficial, as the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score of CIBer with ![delta equals 0.05](images/c12-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math> (denoted as `CIBer (Normal)`) is significantly higher than that of CIBer with ![delta equals 0](images/c12-i0578.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> (denoted as `CIBer (No CM)`). Unexpectedly, the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0579.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores for the Gaussian Naïve Bayes are 0 in most trials, indicating that it predicts all policyholders in the test dataset to not default. By using the composite Naïve Bayes classifier, the ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0580.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores shoot up and even exceed those of CIBer with ![delta equals 0](images/c12-i0581.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, but its performance still a bit inferior to CIBer with ![delta equals 0.05](images/c12-i0582.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>. This again indicates that the feature engineering techniques applied in CIBer improve both the robustness and effectiveness of a Naïve Bayes classifier.

![FIGURE 12.10 Boxplots of upper F 1‐scores for all classifiers in the default premium payment dataset.](images/c12f010.png)

[**FIGURE 12.10**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0010) Boxplots of ![upper F 1](images/c12-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐scores for all classifiers in the default premium payment dataset.

![FIGURE 12.11 Boxplots of accuracies for all classifiers in the default premium payment dataset.](images/c12f011.png)

[**FIGURE 12.11**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0011) Boxplots of accuracies for all classifiers in the default premium payment dataset.

Let us provide some economic justifications for the comonotonic clusters obtained in CIBer with ![delta equals 0.05](images/c12-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>. For actual label 0 (policyholders do not default on premium payments), one comonotonic cluster is obtained, namely (`Count 3‐6`, `Count 6‐12`, `Count over 12`). Here, `Count xx` refers to the count of premium payments late by `xx` months. The strong dependence among these three variables is obvious: a client with a good record without a default on premium payments is also more likely to not delay future premium payments. This is also the reason why we do not observe such a cluster in the minority class with actual label 1 (policyholders default on premium payments), since those customers are more likely to defer premium payments by whatever number of months. This comonotonic relationship helps `CIBer (Normal)` perform significantly better than `CIBer (No CM)`. Similar observations can be made in comparison study on the accuracies and recall rates of all classifiers as shown in [Figures 12.11](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0011) and [12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0012).

In conclusion, CIBer has demonstrated its superiority and robustness over most traditional machine learners and is seen to be one of the best methods in the two real‐data applications discussed above. Additionally, CIBer can be extended into a regression context, by using similar arguments to those related to regression trees (to be introduced in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml)). Due to space limitations, details regarding this extension will not be discussed in this book; we invite interested readers to view our ongoing and future research works.

![FIGURE 12.12 Boxplots of recall rates for all classifiers in the default premium payment dataset.](images/c12f012.png)

## 12.A APPENDIX

  

### 12.A.1 Laplace's Approximation for Integrals

To avoid unnecessary technical details, we mainly focus on the one‐dimensional setting here. Results for higher dimensional framework follow analogously, and we leave these for readers. Laplace's approximation, or Laplace's method, is a commonly used approach for evaluating integrals of the following form:

[(12.19)](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-disp-0066)![upper G Subscript n Baseline colon equals integral Subscript a Superscript b Baseline e Superscript n g left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis Baseline d y period](images/c12-math-0066.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

It is motivated by the observation that the integrand decays exponentially as ![y](images/c12-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> deviates away from ![modifying above y with caret](images/c12-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi></mrow></math>, the global maximum of ![g](images/c12-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>, hence the major contributions to the integral mainly come from the values of ![y](images/c12-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in a close neighborhood of ![modifying above y with caret](images/c12-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi></mrow></math>.

Mathematically, assuming twice differentiablity of ![g](images/c12-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>, we consider the Taylor series expansion of ![g](images/c12-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> at ![modifying above y with caret](images/c12-i0592.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi></mrow></math> by recalling that ![g prime left-parenthesis modifying above y with caret right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c12-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![g double-prime left-parenthesis modifying above y with caret right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c12-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8243;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>:

### 12.A.2 Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)

Next, let us see how Laplace's approximation can motivate BIC. Consider a model ![script upper M](images/c12-i0607.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">M</mi></mrow></math> involving ![k](images/c12-i0608.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> parameters to be estimated, which are represented by a vector ![bold-italic theta element-of chi subset-of-or-equal-to double-struck upper R Superscript k](images/c12-i0609.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#967;</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math>. Then for the observations ![bold-italic x colon equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c12-i0610.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, we can compute their marginal likelihood under the model as follows:

This explains why ![BIC colon equals minus 2 ln ModifyingAbove upper L With caret plus k ln n](images/c12-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>BIC</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>n</mi></math> is used as a criterion for model selection under the Bayesian framework; indeed, the model with the smallest BIC has the largest log‐marginal likelihood, and so should be favourably selected. For a more detailed discussion, we refer to [\[14\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0014) and references therein.

# CHAPTER 13  
Classification and Regression Trees, and Random Forests

 

## 13.1 CLASSIFICATION (DECISION) TREES

The binary logistic regression and the multinomial logit model introduced in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) aim to classify observations based on linear combinations of feature variables. To common practitioners, especially for regulatory purposes, these models may be difficult to interpret, and it is desirable to have more transparent yet simple classification rules. *Classification (Decision) Tree* is a greedy algorithmic method to generate a set of simple rules that mechanically classify observations into different categories. It is extremely useful in data mining and has many potential financial applications. For example, it can be used to derive simple rules for credit approval decisions and determining financial stresses. Being one of the most popular methods in supervised learning, classification trees were first developed by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, and Stone in their celebrated book [\[1\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0001); from 1980 onwards, it has been an active research area, and some resulting developments can be found in [\[8\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0008). It has been even more widely applied to various disciplines since the beginning of the 21st century, including but not limited to financial and insurance contexts; see [\[6](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0006), [7](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0007), [12](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0013), [15](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0017), [18\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0020) for example.

[(13.1)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0001)![script upper S Subscript k Baseline colon equals StartSet left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma y right-parenthesis element-of script upper S colon bold-italic x element-of script upper D Subscript k Baseline EndSet period](images/c13-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

A classification tree is an acyclic graph, in which each internal node represents an attribute, which is characterized by certain quantitative relations specified by some feature components of ![bold x](images/c13-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, and the branches coming out from a node indicate the decision rule outcomes. Specifically, for simplicity, with a binary classification tree, each branching node of the tree examines a specific feature component of ![bold x](images/c13-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, say ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>: if the value of ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> falls below a certain threshold ![t Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, then the left branch route is taken; otherwise, the right branch is taken. Going down the tree, as this procedure continues, the dataset is partitioned into smaller and smaller subsets. The model stops building any new branch, that is, it stops at a certain leaf node, if all the labels ![y Subscript i](images/c13-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s in that leaf are essentially in the same category. Such a leaf (terminal) node is then identified as giving a “pure” class label ![c Subscript k](images/c13-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> in ![script upper Y](images/c13-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></math>. The route from the root to the leaf node indicates a classification rule. The depth of a tree is the maximum length of a path, that is, the maximum number of branches, from the root node to one leaf node. Naturally, one might ask the questions:

1.  Which feature should be examined at each node, and based on what criterion should we choose that feature?
2.  For a binary classification tree, what is the selection threshold value ![t Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> of each step? In general, if an attribute can take more than two values, or even a continuum, how many branches should we build?

These two issues will be addressed in this chapter; some of the discussions here are also extracted to our article [\[2\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002) as a separate user guide.

[Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001) shows a binary classification tree for a lady choosing her *Prince Charming*. The labels “Yes!” and “No” respectively indicate whether the lady would or would not consider that gentleman. The deciding attributes include the man's age, appearance, income and occupation. For instance, the lady would consider a man who is younger than 35, good looking and with high income.

![FIGURE 13.1 A classification tree showing criteria for choosing a Prince Charming.](images/c13f001.png)

[**FIGURE 13.1**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0001) A classification tree showing criteria for choosing a Prince Charming.

 

## \*13.2 CONCEPTS OF ENTROPIES

To find classification rules that are highly accurate and have strong predictive power, we need to specify an appropriate measure for impurity, with which we select the suitable features for splitting at each node of the tree. In particular, we want to maximize the information gain after each splitting. So how to quantify information gain? Guided by the greedy algorithm, one approach is to maximize the reduction of entropy of the data after each splitting. The smaller the entropy value (on the average) after each splitting, the more the information gain is. Before diving into the details, we first introduce some commonly used information‐theoretic quantities.

**(I) Shannon and Differential Entropies**

In 1948, Claude Shannon (see [\[13](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0015), [14\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0016)) introduced the concept of entropy from *thermodynamics* into *information theory*. In honour of him, the usual entropy used in the context of information is often called the *Shannon entropy* and is a common choice of measuring the concentration biasedness of a distribution other than a uniform distribution. In information theory, Shannon entropy is essential in defining the capacity of a communication channel, which measures the efficiency of the channel in information transmission.

Let ![normal x](images/c13-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> be a discrete random variable taking values in ![script upper X](images/c13-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math> with probability masses ![p left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x equals x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for finitely many ![i](images/c13-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. Its (unconditional) Shannon entropy, denoted by ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is defined as:

[(13.2)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0002)![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis colon equals minus í”¼ left-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis comma](images/c13-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where we adopt the convention of ![0 log Subscript 2 Baseline 0 equals 0](images/c13-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0&#8201;</mn><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. While the Shannon entropy is defined for random variables, it only depends on them through their distributions. Therefore, with a slight abuse of notation, we also talk about the entropy of a distribution. Empirically, given a dataset ![script upper S](images/c13-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>, ![p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be estimated by the empirical frequency

![p Subscript script upper S Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction number of data points in script upper S that are equal to x Over total number of data points in script upper S EndFraction comma](images/c13-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>number of data points in</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mtext>that are equal to</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>total number of data points in</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

with which we can empirically estimate the entropy by ![minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts p Subscript script upper S Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p Subscript script upper S Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Clearly, if ![normal x](images/c13-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is Bernoulli with ![p equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x equals 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, its entropy is given by

[(13.3)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0004)![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals minus p log Subscript 2 Baseline p minus left-parenthesis 1 minus p right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus p right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

Consider a sample ![script upper S](images/c13-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> with 20 observations in which 16 of them belong to the first class (![normal x equals 0](images/c13-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>) and the remaining 4 belong to the second class (![normal x equals 1](images/c13-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>). With the empirical probability masses ![p Subscript script upper S Baseline left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis equals 16 slash 20](images/c13-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>20</mn></math> and ![p Subscript script upper S Baseline left-parenthesis 4 right-parenthesis equals 4 slash 20](images/c13-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, the empirical entropy of ![normal x](images/c13-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is given by:

![minus StartFraction 16 Over 20 EndFraction log Subscript 2 Baseline left-parenthesis StartFraction 16 Over 20 EndFraction right-parenthesis minus four twentieths log Subscript 2 Baseline left-parenthesis four twentieths right-parenthesis equals 0.7219 period](images/c13-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7219</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

The unit of entropy taken here is a *bit*, i.e. 0 or 1. As entropy increases, the amount of useful distinguishable information reduces

As a remark, the concept of Shannon entropy has an intimate connection with Fisherian statistical inference. Given a random sample ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline](images/c13-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> of size ![n](images/c13-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> from a discrete random variable ![normal x](images/c13-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, the likelihood is ![product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts p left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, hence the average negative of log‐likelihood of the sample is ![minus StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts ln p left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. By the weak law of large numbers, as the sample size ![n](images/c13-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> goes to infinity, the limit of this average is stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is exactly ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math>. In addition, in information theory there is a strong motivation to use entropy for data compression. To compress the information stored in an ![n](images/c13-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional random sample ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis element-of script upper X Superscript n](images/c13-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></math> of a common random variable x by using binary codes, on average with ![n](images/c13-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> large enough, it suffices to use ![n upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> bits. See [Appendix 13.A.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0015) for more details.

From the definition, it is always clear that ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c13-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. If ![normal x](images/c13-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is degenerate, then ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c13-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and there is no ambiguity in ![normal x](images/c13-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>. If ![normal x](images/c13-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is Bernoulli taking values 0 or 1, we have ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c13-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, and ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c13-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> if and only if it is equally likely for ![normal x](images/c13-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> to take 0 and 1. In general, if ![normal x](images/c13-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is a discrete random variable taking ![n](images/c13-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> different values, with the corresponding probabilities ![p Subscript i](images/c13-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for ![i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c13-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, the Shannon entropy is maximized when ![p Subscript i Baseline identical-to StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction](images/c13-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math> for all ![i](images/c13-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, and the corresponding entropy ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is ![log Subscript 2 Baseline n](images/c13-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>n</mi></math>. This claim follows by an application of Jensen's inequality

Next, if ![normal x element-of script upper X](images/c13-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math> is a continuous random variable with a continuous density function ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the corresponding Shannon entropy is refined as the so‐called *differential entropy*

[(13.4)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0006)![h left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis colon equals minus í”¼ left-parenthesis ln f left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals minus integral Underscript script upper X Endscripts f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis ln f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis d x period](images/c13-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>&#54588;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln&#8201;</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></msub><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

However, differential entropy lacks a number of properties that Shannon entropy possesses, such as non‐negativity and scale invariance, hence differential entropy is not a direct generalization of Shannon entropy. which is clearly negative if ![sigma squared less-than StartFraction 1 Over 2 pi e EndFraction](images/c13-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>. Besides, when ![sigma squared right-arrow 0](images/c13-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, ![normal x](images/c13-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> becomes degenerate at ![mu](images/c13-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, while ![h left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> goes to ![negative infinity](images/c13-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> but not 0 as in the case of Shannon entropy. For some distributions, differential entropy may even not exist: for example, for ![k greater-than 1](images/c13-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, consider the density function ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals ln left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis slash left-parenthesis x left-parenthesis ln x right-parenthesis squared right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![x greater-than k](images/c13-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>, or 0 otherwise. The differential entropy for this density is not finite at all:

To illustrate the power of making educated guesses via entropy, in [Appendix 13.A.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0016) we apply the concept to solving a *Wordle* puzzle.

**(II) Conditional Entropy**

While unconditional entropy can be of use when there is no additional knowledge of ![normal x](images/c13-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, it is actually more common in practice that we often possess some more knowledge beforehand from other source variables. Intuitively, we expect that the level of randomness reduces with this extra knowledge, and so does the entropy. For instance, in a linguistic model to “predict” the appearance of the next text passages, the possible range of next words is much shrunk once the current words are known. This concept can be made formal as follows. Let us consider the simplest case with only a pair of discrete random variables ![left-parenthesis normal x comma normal y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a joint probability mass function ![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal x equals x comma normal y equals y right-parenthesis equals colon p left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![x element-of script upper X](images/c13-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math> and ![y element-of script upper Y](images/c13-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></math>. We want to examine how knowing a piece of knowledge of ![normal x](images/c13-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> affects the randomness of ![normal y](images/c13-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>, which in turn changes the entropy of y. Using the notion of conditional probability of ![p left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal y equals y vertical-bar normal x equals x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we define the *conditional entropy* of ![normal y](images/c13-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> given ![normal x](images/c13-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> as:

![upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis colon equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript y element-of script upper Y Endscripts p left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></munder><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

For the special case when ![normal y](images/c13-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is completely determined by ![normal x](images/c13-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, that is, ![normal y equals f left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for some known function ![f](images/c13-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, ![p left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> takes the value 1 when ![y equals f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; or 0 otherwise. As a result, ![upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript y equals f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Endscripts p left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts 0 equals 0](images/c13-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>&#8201;p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. On the other hand, from the definition of ![upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we can express ![p left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in terms of the conditional probability ![p left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and then interchange the order of summations to obtain:

stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

which echoes our intuition that any extra information will reduce the randomness or entropy of the original random variable.

Similar to the manner above, if ![normal y](images/c13-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is a continuous variable while ![normal x](images/c13-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is another one of any type with a distribution function ![upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we can use the conditional density ![f left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of y given x to define the *conditional differential entropy* of ![normal y](images/c13-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> given ![normal x](images/c13-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> as:

![h left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis colon equals minus integral Underscript script upper X Endscripts integral Underscript script upper Y Endscripts f left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis ln f left-parenthesis y vertical-bar x right-parenthesis d y d upper F Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period Superscript 4 Baseline](images/c13-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">Y</mi></mrow></msub><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;ln&#8201;</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mo>.</mo><mn>4</mn></msup></math>. 

For example, consider the bivariate normal pair ![normal x comma normal y](images/c13-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></math> so that each has the common marginal distribution ![script upper N left-parenthesis mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and they also have a correlation coefficient ![rho element-of left-parenthesis negative 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; clearly, ![normal y vertical-bar normal x equals x tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu left-parenthesis 1 minus rho right-parenthesis plus rho x comma sigma squared left-parenthesis 1 minus rho squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then the conditional differential entropy ![h left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be obtained from ([13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0007)) as:

![h left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis equals one half left-bracket 1 plus ln left-parenthesis 2 pi sigma squared left-parenthesis 1 minus rho squared right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-bracket comma](images/c13-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln&#8201;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

which is less than ![h left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis equals one half left-bracket 1 plus ln left-parenthesis 2 pi sigma squared right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c13-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln&#8201;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>. Again, this demonstrates a reduction in entropy.

To further motivate the concept of conditional entropy, we consider two examples that relate to mixed distributions. Firstly, consider ![normal x vertical-bar normal mu tilde script upper N left-parenthesis normal mu comma sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> and ![normal mu tilde script upper N left-parenthesis mu 0 comma sigma 0 squared right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>, then the conditional distribution (posterior) of ![normal mu vertical-bar normal x equals x](images/c13-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math> is given by

so ![normal lamda vertical-bar normal upper N equals n](images/c13-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math> follows a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter ![alpha equals n plus 1](images/c13-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and a rate ![beta equals 1 plus theta](images/c13-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></math>. **(III) Mutual Information**

Mutual information has a standalone position in information theory as it measures the mutual dependence between two distributions represented by two random variables of ![normal x](images/c13-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal y](images/c13-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>. It is defined as ![upper I left-parenthesis normal x comma normal y right-parenthesis colon equals upper H left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis minus upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, yet it is symmetric, i.e. ![upper I Based on the properties of entropy and conditional entropy, we can obtain the upper and lower bounds for mutual information, namely ![0 less-than-or-equal-to upper I left-parenthesis normal x comma normal y right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to upper H left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> since ![upper H left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c13-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> as shown in ([13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0011)). In particular, the upper bound of ![upper I left-parenthesis normal x comma normal y right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be achieved when ![normal y](images/c13-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> is completely determined by ![normal x](images/c13-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math>, by then ![upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c13-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>; while the lower bound of ![upper I left-parenthesis normal x comma normal y right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c13-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> is achieved when ![normal x](images/c13-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal y](images/c13-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math> are independent, giving ![upper H left-parenthesis normal y vertical-bar normal x right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis normal y right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

**(IV) Relative Entropy and Cross Entropy**

*Relative entropy* and *cross entropy* are common measures of difference between two probability distributions; however, they are not metric, though they still preserve some of the metric properties, for example nonnegativity

**i) Relative entropy:**

Let ![upper P](images/c13-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper Q](images/c13-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> be two discrete distributions (also identify them as their own probability mass functions) defined on a common discrete support ![script upper X](images/c13-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>,

From these examples, we clearly see that the definition of relative entropy is generally asymmetric, violating the usual commutative property of a metric. Nevertheless, when ![alpha equals 1 minus beta](images/c13-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></math> in the Binomial case, ![double-struck upper D left-parenthesis upper P double-vertical-bar upper Q right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper D left-parenthesis upper Q double-vertical-bar upper P right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can hold.

**ii) Cross Entropy:**

The *cross entropy* between two discrete distributions ![upper P](images/c13-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper Q](images/c13-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is defined as

where ![upper H left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis colon equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts upper P left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis ln upper P left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></msub><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the rescaled entropy of ![upper P](images/c13-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. By simplifying ([13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0029)), an equivalent definition is:

![upper H left-parenthesis upper P comma upper Q right-parenthesis equals minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts upper P left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis ln upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

As long as ![upper P](images/c13-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is fixed, ![upper H left-parenthesis upper P right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a constant independent of ![upper Q](images/c13-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>, so there is an equivalence between relative entropy and cross entropy. A similar notion of entropy can be defined for continuous distributions by replacing summation by integration. In real applications, cross entropy is often served as an objective function in deep learning to measure the similarities between the sample distribution of labels and the predicted distribution.

 

## 13.3 INFORMATION GAIN

*Information gain* plays a crucial role in selecting suitable attributes for a classification tree whenever it branches out. The entropy of the empirical distribution of observation is calculated at each decision node, and one decides whether the node should be split further by considering whether its information gain is sufficiently large enough, i.e., if the reduction of randomness (measured by entropy) after splitting is significant or not. At each node, among the ![p](images/c13-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> features, one ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> will be selected if the splitting causes the biggest possible information gain, which is actually the mutual information between the label y of the subsample at the node and this testing attribute ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. More precisely, let ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j Super Subscript i Superscript right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> be the chosen attribute at a node ![i](images/c13-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> with a subsample ![script upper S Superscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> attaching there.
