Since ![IG left-parenthesis script upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma normal upper R right-parenthesis greater-than IG left-parenthesis script upper S Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline comma normal upper S right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>IG</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mtext>IG</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, we conclude that “Risk level” is a better attribute for classifying the data into Class N or Y at this node. Interestingly, if we compare the entropies of the corresponding child nodes individually, we can see that ![upper H left-parenthesis script upper S Subscript normal upper H Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than upper H left-parenthesis script upper S Subscript normal upper F Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper H left-parenthesis script upper S Subscript normal upper L Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis script upper S Subscript normal upper M Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Based on these comparisons at child nodes, one might be tempted to conclude that the resulting entropy for the “Sex” attribute is lower than that of the “Risk level” attribute, suggesting the former can bring a higher information gain, which should be used for splitting. However, since a larger weight of ![nine fifteenths equals 0.6](images/c13-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>9</mn><mn>15</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></math> is assigned to ![script upper S Subscript normal upper L](images/c13-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></math> (with a relatively lower entropy) for the “Risk level” attribute, while the same larger weight is also assigned to ![script upper S Subscript normal upper F](images/c13-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></msub></math> (with a relatively higher entropy) for the “Sex” attribute, it turns out that the actual average entropy for “Risk level” is lower than that of “Sex”, and so “Risk level” is eventually selected due to a higher information gain. We now observe larger individual entropy values of two child nodes induced from “Risk level” than those of the corresponding ones induced from “Sex”, yet after taking into account the proportion contribution of each child node, the combined effect (here the average entropy) for the “Risk level” becomes smaller than that of “Sex”. That is a typical example of *Simpson's Paradox*, in which a trend appears in several different groups of data, but disappears or reverses when these groups are combined; also see [\[19\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0021).

 

## 13.4 OTHER IMPURITY MEASURES FOR INFORMATION

In addition to the various entropies and mutual information introduced before, here we introduce two additional commonly used measures of impurity.

1.  *Gini‐Index*
    
    Let ![normal x](images/c13-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> be a discrete random variable with a probability mass function ![p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for ![x element-of script upper X](images/c13-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>, the Gini‐index ![upper G](images/c13-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> of ![normal x](images/c13-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is defined as:
    
    [(13.11)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0035)![upper G left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis colon equals 1 minus sigma-summation Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts p squared left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0035.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 
2.  *Misclassification Error*
    
    The misclassification error of a discrete random variable ![normal x](images/c13-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is defined as:
    
    (13.12)![Misclassification Error left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis colon equals 1 minus max Underscript x element-of script upper X Endscripts p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0036.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Misclassification Error</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></munder><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

[Figure 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0004) illustrates the respective behavior of entropy, Gini‐index and misclassification error when ![normal x](images/c13-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> is a Bernoulli random variable with a success probability ![p](images/c13-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Simple calculus tells us that for all these impurity measures, the maxima are attained at ![p equals 1 minus p equals one half](images/c13-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, when both outcomes are equally likely. At that point the corresponding node of a binary tree is at the “most impure” state.

As in the case for entropy, for a discrete random variable ![normal x](images/c13-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> now taking ![n](images/c13-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> possible values, all impurity measures attain their respective maximum when all the probability masses ![p left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis identical-to StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction](images/c13-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8801;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>, meaning that all outcomes are equally likely; the corresponding maximum values for various impurity measures are: (1) for entropy, it is ![upper H left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals log Subscript 2 Baseline n](images/c13-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>n</mi></math>; (2) for the Gini‐index, it is ![upper G left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction](images/c13-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>;

As with maximizing information gain, to choose the best attribute for splitting a node, we generally compare the impurity of the parent node (before splitting) with the average of those of the child nodes (after splitting). where the function Im![left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a pre‐assigned impurity measure, such as one of the three introduced above. Again, each impurity measure is defined on the probability distributions of the labels, and the probability distribution in question here is the conditional one quoted in ([13.10](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0032)). Without causing much ambiguity, we slightly abuse the notation of Im![left-parenthesis script upper S Superscript left-parenthesis i comma v right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to stand for the impurity measure of this conditional probability distribution of the labels from the subsample ![script upper S Superscript left-parenthesis i comma v right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Furthermore, for the sake of convenience, we just identify the name of a node with the name of the subsample at the same node.

Once the impurity measure is chosen, it is consistently used throughout the construction of the whole tree (or even the whole random forest, see [Section 13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0011)). We aim to choose an attribute ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j Super Subscript i Superscript right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> such that ![normal upper Delta Im left-parenthesis normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j Super Subscript i Superscript right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mtext>Im</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the largest at each parent node, or equivalently the attribute that reduces the impurity measure the most after splitting.

We now consider a simple example to illustrate the calculations involving these alternative impurity measures. We are given a dataset of size 12, in which 6 of them belong to the Group 1 and the remaining 6 belong to Group 2. We choose between two binary attributes A and B to split the root note into two child nodes based on the information in [Table 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0002).

We first use Gini‐index as the impurity measure. At the parent node,

![upper G left-parenthesis parent right-parenthesis equals 1 minus left-parenthesis six twelfths right-parenthesis squared minus left-parenthesis six twelfths right-parenthesis squared equals 0.5 period](images/c13-math-0038.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>parent</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

At the child nodes, using the attribute A, we get:

As a result, the attribute B is preferred to A since ![normal upper Delta upper G left-parenthesis normal upper B right-parenthesis equals 0.1285 greater-than 0.014 equals normal upper Delta upper G left-parenthesis normal upper A right-parenthesis period](images/c13-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1285</mn><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.014</mn><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> If we repeat the calculation using entropy as the impurity measure, we get ![normal upper Delta upper G left-parenthesis normal upper A right-parenthesis equals 0.0207](images/c13-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0207</mn></math> and ![normal upper Delta upper G left-parenthesis normal upper B right-parenthesis equals 0.1957](images/c13-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1957</mn></math>; again, the attribute B is preferable. The same conclusion can also be obtained by using misclassification error as the impurity measure.

 

## 13.5 SPLITTING AGAINST CONTINUOUS ATTRIBUTES

The calculation of ![normal upper Delta left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> through a specific choice of impurity measure ![Im left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Im</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be easily extended to find the best splitting condition for a continuous attribute ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, where we basically divide the feature space of ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, its range of values, into a number of disjoint and consecutive intervals. Then, based on the distribution (now still probability mass) on all these intervals, every impurity measure at each of the different child nodes can be calibrated. As an example, consider [Table 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0003), where values of taxable income are sorted, and by setting a fictitious initial value of 50 and terminal value of 240, the mid‐points between two consecutive values are used as the splitting boundary points, and we denote them by ![m Subscript k](images/c13-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> in order. Then we try to compute the goodness for each attribute of ![double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace Taxable income less-than m Sub Subscript k Subscript right-brace](images/c13-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mtext>Taxable income</mtext><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math> for every boundary mid‐point ![m Subscript k](images/c13-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>; particularly, one can check that the splitting condition of Taxable Income ![less-than-or-equal-to](images/c13-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo></mrow></math> 97 provides the smallest impurity measure. Hence the best attribute for this parent node can be chosen by comparing the magnitudes of impurity measures evaluated at other discrete and categorical attributes, and those of other indicators in the same form as above but now based on alternative continuous attributes. The attribute with the smallest impurity measure among all will be selected.

From [Table 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0003), the detailed calculations concerning the splitting condition of Taxable Income ![less-than-or-equal-to 97](images/c13-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>97</mn></math> are shown below.

We observe that the average Gini‐index and the average entropy are the smallest among all those of the other indicator attributes of “Taxable Income ![less-than-or-equal-to m Subscript k](images/c13-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>”. All these values of average impurity measures can be calculated in the same manner, and they are listed at the bottom rows of [Table 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0003). Other similar discussions can be found in various standard textbooks such as [\[16\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0018).

 

## 13.6 OVERFITTING IN CLASSIFICATION TREE

Recall that a classification tree corresponds to a partition of the space of feature vectors ![script upper D](images/c13-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow></math> into ![script upper D 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper D Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c13-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub></math>, corresponding to the predicted labels ![c 1 comma ellipsis comma c Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c13-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></math>. This then induces the partition of the dataset ![script upper S](images/c13-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> into ![script upper S 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper S Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c13-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub></math>, where ![script upper S Subscript k Baseline equals StartSet left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma y right-parenthesis element-of script upper S colon bold-italic x element-of script upper D Subscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c13-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Generally speaking, for a given sample ![script upper S equals left-brace left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c13-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, we aim to construct a classification tree ![script upper T](images/c13-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math>, whose number of terminal leaf nodes is denoted by ![upper T](images/c13-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> (see [Figure 13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0005) for an illustration), that minimizes the classification error:

While the classification tree is often an effective classifier, it sometimes results in overfitting, especially when its depth is too large. We need to strive for a balance between its complexity and its training classification error ![upper R left-parenthesis script upper T right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> given in ([13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0046)). For a more detailed discussion in this regard, for instance, using the chi‐square test to determine whether the splitting should be performed one step further, we refer the readers to our user guide [\[2\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002).

The first approach to reduce the complexity of a tree is *pre‐pruning*. It is intuitive at the first glance: if the value of the chosen impurity measure exceeds a certain threshold level, one expects that subsequent splittings cannot reduce the training error much, while the resulting tree becomes more complex as the tree size grows, so it is better to stop at the current node. Nevertheless, pre‐pruning is greedy in nature: the tree growing may stop at a seemingly bad splitting, even though a subsequent partition might be extremely valuable.

Another approach is called *post‐pruning*, in which we first construct the classification tree ![script upper T](images/c13-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math>, and then remove any unnecessary intermediate nodes, which prevents us from being misguided by seemingly worthless splittings. Intuitively, a post‐pruning procedure purposely removes branches which give little reduction in the training error. There are two major types of approach that depend on where the procedure is kicked off:

![FIGURE 13.5 An illustration of trees with different numbers of terminal nodes.](images/c13f005.png)

[**FIGURE 13.5**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0005) An illustration of trees with different numbers of terminal nodes.

1.  *bottom‐up pruning* starts at any one of the terminal nodes, and one recursively traces upwards along the chosen path to determine whether the splitting at each corresponding parent node along this backward traversing path is “valuable” under a pre‐determined measure; if a node is not “valuable”, for instance, the reduction in the training error is below a pre‐specified level, the splitting at this parent node is removed, which consequently becomes the immediate terminal node.
2.  *top‐down pruning* starts at the root of the tree. It checks the “value” of the splitting at each node, and removes the sub‐tree under a node whose “contributed reduction” is below a certain threshold. This approach is seemingly similar to the pre‐pruning, yet a significant difference between them is that pre‐pruning stops building classification trees in the training stage, while top‐down pruning starts to work only after building the whole tree.

A representative bottom‐up post‐pruning approach is called *(Minimal) Cost Complexity Pruning*. Let ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline equals script upper T](images/c13-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></math> be the original tree and ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> be the tree which consists only of the root. For ![k equals 0 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c13-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, we aim to construct a sequence of trees ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline superset-of midline-horizontal-ellipsis superset-of script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8835;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8835;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, where ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> is formed by removing a subtree from ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. For example, consider the classification tree in [Figure 13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0006).

There are four possible trees that can be formed from the tree in [Figure 13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0006). [Figure 13.7](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0007) shows three of them, and the last tree ![script upper T Superscript left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> is formed by removing ![script upper T Subscript upper N 1](images/c13-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math> from ![script upper T](images/c13-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math>, denoted by ![script upper T minus script upper T Subscript upper N 1](images/c13-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi><mo>&#8726;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math>, leading to a single node ![normal upper A](images/c13-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></math>, the root.

For more discussions on pre‐pruning and post‐pruning, readers can refer to various articles such as [\[4](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0004), [5](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0005), [11\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0012).

 

## 13.7 CLASSIFICATION TREES IN PYTHON AND R

In general, for both Python and **R**, a classification tree is built based on the binary splitting of feature variables ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, one at a time, for some ![j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c13-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Since this method will search for all possible splittings caused by all feature variables, building a tree is computationally intensive and time‐consuming. Usually, once the classification tree is built, given a carefully chosen hyperparameter ![alpha](images/c13-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> (for pruning), the subtree that minimizes ([13.16](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0048)) is chosen to be the final tree, and a set of simple classification rules can then be easily read off.

In Python, classification trees are implemented by `DecisionTreeClassifier` in the well‐known `sklearn` package under the Python class `tree`; see [Programme 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3001).

Here the `plot_tree()` is a function that helps to plot the resulting tree obtained by `DecisionTreeClassifier`, and `export_text()` is another function that returns a text report about its classification rules. Although the Python class `DecisionTreeClassifier` is quite easy to use, there are many options hidden in this class. In particular, `ccp_alpha` is the hyperparameter ![alpha](images/c13-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> used for cost complexity pruning, which is defaulted to be `0`; `criterion` picks the impurity measure function used and it is defaulted as `gini` for the Gini‐index in ([13.11](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0035)), other choices include `entropy` for the Shannon entropy in ([13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0002)), and `log_loss` for the differential entropy in ([13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0006)).

In **R**, classification trees are implemented by `rpart()` function inside the built‐in library `rpart`

Again, the `rpart()` function contains several options: for example, differential entropy can be adopted by plugging in the argument `parms=list(split="information")`, while `"gini"` for the Gini‐index is used as the default mode. Moreover, while the default value ![alpha equals 0.01](images/c13-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math> is used for the corresponding cost complexity pruning parameter, users can pick any non‐negative value of ![alpha](images/c13-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, say ![alpha equals 0.05](images/c13-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>, by taking the argument: `control=rpart.control(cp=0.05)`. There is one further important option which needs mentioning: the method option in `rpart` can be one of “`class`”, “`anova`”, “`poisson`”, or “`exp`”. For a classification problem, the target variable is a categorical one, therefore `method="class"` is used; meanwhile for a regular regression tree, we use `method="anova"` which attempts to minimize the mean squared errors summed at all terminal nodes. It is also worth mentioning that the “`poisson`” method is adopted for a Poisson regression. Last but not least, the “`exp`” method is adopted for building regression trees with exponential scaling, for example when the ![y Subscript i](images/c13-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s are data in survival analysis. Such trees are more commonly known as *survival trees*, which are a nonparametric alternative to the celebrated semiparametric *Cox proportional hazards model*.

**I. HSI dataset:**

Let us first illustrate using our `fin‐ratio.csv` file, which contains the stock data in 2002 and has not gone through outlier detection, for HSI classification. See [Programme 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3003) for the Python version and [Programme 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3004) for the **R** version.

The classification in [Figure 13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0008) is very simple. The dataset is split into two classes of `0` and `1` according to the value of the variable `ln_MV`. The classification rules and the corresponding quality measures are shown as below:

1.  R1: If ![monospace ln bar MV less-than 9.478](images/c13-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>9.478</mn></math>, then return as class = `0` (not HSI) (644/3).
2.  R2: If ![monospace ln bar MV greater-than-or-equal-to 9.478](images/c13-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>9.478</mn></math>, then return as class = `1` (HSI) (4/29).

![FIGURE 13.8 Classification trees for the 2002 data without removing outliers.](images/c13f008.png)

[**FIGURE 13.8**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0008) Classification trees for the 2002 data without removing outliers.

The numbers in the terminal nodes represent the number of cases. For example, in the group with `ln_MV9.478`, there are 644 “zeroes” and 3 “ones”; while in the group `ln_MV9.478`, there are 4 “zeroes” and 29 “ones”. The outputs in Programmes 13.3 and 13.4 show the details at each node:

1.  At node 1 (root), there are altogether ![n equals 680](images/c13-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>680</mn></math> cases. Among them, 32 belong to group 1 (regarded as a loss). Since the majority is from group 0, the group label is classified as `yval=0` and the percentages of groups 0 and 1 are given in parentheses: they are ![0.952941176 equals 648 slash 680](images/c13-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.952941176</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>648</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn></math> and ![0.047058824 equals 32 slash 680](images/c13-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.047058824</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn></math>, respectively.
2.  At node 2 (the left branch), the split condition is `d$ln_MV9.478`. There are ![n equals 647](images/c13-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>647</mn></math> cases, 3 originating from group 1 of the root (node 1), and the group label is `yval=0`; again, the respective percentages are ![0.995363215 equals 644 slash 647](images/c13-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.995363215</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>644</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>647</mn></math> and ![0.004636785 equals 3 slash 647](images/c13-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.004636785</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>647</mn></math>.
3.  At node 3 (the right branch), ![n equals 33](images/c13-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>33</mn></math>. There are 4 cases originating from the group 0 of the root, and the group label is `yval=1`; here, the percentages of the respective groups are ![0.121212121 equals 4 slash 33](images/c13-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.121212121</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>33</mn></math> and ![0.878787879 equals 29 slash 33](images/c13-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.878787879</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>29</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>33</mn></math>.

This output actually implies that we can predict or classify whether a stock is a Blue Chip based on only one simple condition of ![monospace ln bar MV less-than 9.478](images/c13-i0425.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>9.478</mn></math>. Since the classification tree in this example is very simple, we can actually plot the observations: see the full plot in [Figure 13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0009).

![FIGURE 13.9 Plot of ln\_MV versus HSI, with the horizontal line monospace ln bar MV equals 9.478 representing the classification rule.](images/c13f009.png)

[**FIGURE 13.9**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0009) Plot of `ln_MV` versus `HSI`, with the horizontal line ![monospace ln bar MV equals 9.478](images/c13-i0426.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">ln\_MV</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>9.478</mn></math> representing the classification rule.

A cross tabulation table for this classification tree can easily be found; see [Programme 13.7](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3007) (Python) and [Programme 13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3008) (**R**). From the output, 3 Blue Chips are misclassified as non‐Blue Chips while 4 non‐Blue Chips are misclassified as Blue Chips.

**II. Iris flower dataset:**

Recall the Iris flower dataset from [Section 10.4.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0008). On this occasion, we build classification trees to categorize species of the Iris flowers; see [Programme 13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3009) (Python) and in [Programme 13.10](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3010) (**R**).

![FIGURE 13.10 Classification tree for the iris flower dataset.](images/c13f010.png)

[**FIGURE 13.10**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0010) Classification tree for the iris flower dataset.

From the outputs shown in [Figure 13.10](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0010), the classification rules and their corresponding quality measures are:

1.  R1: If ![monospace Petal period Length less-than 2.45](images/c13-i0427.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.Length</mtext><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>2.45</mn></math>, then species = `setosa` (50/0/0).
2.  R2: If ![monospace Petal period Length greater-than-or-equal-to 2.45](images/c13-i0428.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.Length</mtext><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2.45</mn></math> and ![monospace Petal period width less-than 1.75](images/c13-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.width</mtext><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1.75</mn></math>, then species = `versicolor` (0/49/5);
3.  R3: If ![monospace Petal period Length greater-than-or-equal-to 2.45](images/c13-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.Length</mtext><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2.45</mn></math> and ![monospace Petal period width greater-than-or-equal-to 1.75](images/c13-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.width</mtext><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1.75</mn></math>, then species = `virginica` (0/1/45).

Although the two classification trees produced by Python and **R** look similar, Python constructed a much larger tree. In fact, there are other hyperparameters involved in building a classification tree, including `minsplit`, which specifies the minimum number of observations that must exist in a node in order for a split to be attempted, and `maxdepth`, which sets the maximum depth of the final tree with the root node counted as at depth 0.

Since both classification trees are relatively simple and the rules also depend mainly on two variables, we can again plot the observations for illustration. See [Programme 13.11](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3011) (Python) and [Programme 13.12](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3012) (**R**).

From [Figure 13.11](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0011), we can clearly see how these classification rules work. Finally, we can produce cross tabulation via Python ([Programme 13.13](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3013)) and **R** ([Programme 13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3014)).

![FIGURE 13.11 Plot of Petal.Length versus Petal.width, with the horizontal lines monospace Petal period width equals 1.65 and 1.75, and the vertical lines monospace Petal period Length equals 2.45 and 4.95 representing the classification rules.](images/c13f011.png)

[**FIGURE 13.11**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0011) Plot of `Petal.Length` versus `Petal.width`, with the horizontal lines ![monospace Petal period width equals 1.65](images/c13-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.width</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1.65</mn></math> and ![1.75](images/c13-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1.75</mn></mrow></math>, and the vertical lines ![monospace Petal period Length equals 2.45](images/c13-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">Petal.Length</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>2.45</mn></math> and ![4.95](images/c13-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>4.95</mn></mrow></math> representing the classification rules.

From the table produced by [Programme 13.13](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3013) via Python, there are 3 versicolor species being misclassified as virginica species, and the error rate is 3/150 = 2%. On the other hand, the table produced by [Programme 13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3014) via **R** shows an error rate of (1+5)/150 = 4%, with 5 virginica species being misclassified as versicolor species and 1 versicolor species being misclassified as virginica species. The difference in error rates between the uses of Python and **R** is due to the depth of their corresponding trees.

 

## 13.8 REGRESSION TREES

A *regression tree* is similar to a classification tree, except that while the label variable ![y](images/c13-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> must be categorical for a classification tree, for a regression tree it takes a continuum of values. Recall that the main inspiration behind classification trees is segmenting the space of feature vectors ![script upper D](images/c13-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow></math> into ![upper M](images/c13-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> simpler regions, namely ![script upper D 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper D Subscript upper M Baseline](images/c13-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub></math>. The predictor function ![ModifyingAbove f With caret](images/c13-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></math> (to predict the label in this case) is written as:

[(13.18)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0050)![ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript upper M Endscripts c Subscript k Baseline double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace bold-italic x element-of script upper D Sub Subscript k Subscript right-brace Baseline period](images/c13-math-0050.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

Building a classification tree ![script upper T](images/c13-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math> is essentially finding a set of terminal leaf nodes ![StartSet script upper T 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper T Subscript upper T Baseline EndSet](images/c13-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> that minimizes the misclassification error ![upper R left-parenthesis script upper T right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in ([13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0046)) (or ([13.16](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0048)) if cost complexity pruning is adopted). For building a regression tree, we shall replace the 0‐1 loss of ![double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace y Sub Subscript i Subscript not-equals modifying above y with caret Sub Subscript script upper T Sub Sub Subscript script l Sub Subscript Subscript right-brace](images/c13-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math> by the squared loss function:

and the resulting tree built from minimizing ([13.19](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0051)) is commonly called a regression tree with ![upper M equals upper T](images/c13-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi></math> being the total number of partitions. where the predictor function ![ModifyingAbove f With caret left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> takes the same form as ([13.18](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0050)) where ![c Subscript script l](images/c13-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></math> can now take any continuous value. With this in mind, a regression tree is just a special case of the threshold regression model, whose predictor function takes the more generic form:

where ![ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript script l](images/c13-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></math> is a regression function with a domain of ![script upper D Subscript script l](images/c13-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></math>, for ![script l equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper T](images/c13-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></math>.

Similar to classification trees, we build a regression tree by searching greedily via a top‐down approach. Starting from the root node, we determine the best splitting attribute that minimizes the squared loss function, and we iterate the search followed by a child node. In the following, we only focus on the most common scenario of binary splitting, yet this is not necessary for regression trees, and the treatment below can easily be adapted for the general case when a parent node is split into three or more child nodes.

We try to determine the optimal pair of attribute variable ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and its threshold value ![t Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> that makes ([13.21](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0057)) as small as possible. To achieve this, for each attribute ![normal x Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, we first determine the optimal threshold ![t Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> by minimizing ([13.21](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0057)), using the boundary points obtained from a certain discretization method to serve as the set of all possible thresholds ![t Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>; also see [Section 13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0006). Next, we compare the obtained minimum values of mean squared errors arising from all finitely many attributes, and pick the one with the smallest value. The same process continues until a stopping criterion is attained at a terminal node ![script upper T Subscript script l](images/c13-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></math>; by then no more splitting will be carried out. Typical stopping criteria include the following:

1.  the number of samples in the present node falls below a pre‐specified threshold ![n 0](images/c13-i0462.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>: ![StartAbsoluteValue script upper T Subscript script l Baseline EndAbsoluteValue less-than n 0 semicolon or](images/c13-math-0058.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>or</mtext></math> 
2.  the sum of squared errors at the present node falls below a pre‐determined threshold ![epsilon](images/c13-i0463.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>: ![sigma-summation Underscript left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis element-of script upper T Subscript script l Baseline Endscripts left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus modifying above y with caret Subscript script upper T Sub Subscript script l Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis squared less-than epsilon semicolon or](images/c13-math-0059.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>;</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mtext>or</mtext></math> 
3.  the reduction in the mean squared error ([13.21](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0057)) by making an extra splitting of the present node ![script upper S](images/c13-i0464.png)<math display="inline" After building the regression tree, the prediction for a given test observation is the mean of the training observations in the region ![script upper D Subscript script l](images/c13-i0469.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></math> to which that test observation belongs.

As an example, [Figure 13.13](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0013) shows a dataset containing four categories, with only one feature variable ![normal x](images/c13-i0470.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> and one label variable ![normal y](images/c13-i0471.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow></math>, both real‐valued. At the root node, the dataset is split into two groups according to whether ![normal x less-than t 1](images/c13-i0472.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> or ![normal x greater-than-or-equal-to t 1](images/c13-i0473.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>. The averages ![modifying above c with caret 1](images/c13-i0474.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#265;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![modifying above c with caret 2](images/c13-i0475.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#265;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> for the two groups are then calculated. Each subgroup is further divided into two smaller groups with respect to the splitting thresholds ![t 2](images/c13-i0476.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![t 3](images/c13-i0477.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>, respectively, so that we finally have that each cluster corresponds to its own label.

While regression trees are commonly used, one should be award of their pitfalls. Specifically, the tree‐building process is a top‐down, greedy binary search with the following characteristics:

1.  Each splitting is the best given the past splittings in the previous nodes; it is only valid locally, but not necessarily the best one from the global viewpoint.
2.  Some partitions of the space ![script upper D](images/c13-i0478.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow></math> cannot be obtained in a regression tree. For example, suppose that there are only two feature variables, then a regression tree can possibly partition ![script upper D](images/c13-i0479.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow></math> in the way of [Figure 13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0014)(a), but the space ![script upper D](images/c13-i0480.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi></mrow></math> cannot be partitioned as in [Figure 13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0014)(b). It is because there is no splitting in (b) that can serve as an initial one, while the leftmost vertical line at ![x Superscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis Baseline equals s 11](images/c13-i0481.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></math> inside the big square in (a) can, since it splits this into two smaller rectangles. Therefore, the configuration depicted in [Figure 13.14](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0014)(b) cannot arise from a regression tree.
    
    ![FIGURE 13.13 Regression tree splitting algorithm for one attribute.](images/c13f013.png)
    
    [**FIGURE 13.13**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0013) Regression tree splitting algorithm for one attribute.
    
    ![FIGURE 13.14 Illustrations of a feasible partition of a space of feature vectors caused by a regression tree, and an impossible one.](images/c13f014.png)
    
    [**FIGURE 13.14**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0014) Illustrations of a feasible partition of a space of feature vectors caused by a regression tree, and an impossible one.
    
3.  Sometimes, this tree‐building process may overfit the training dataset, leading to poor test performance. This could be remedied by constructing a smaller tree with fewer splits that may lead to higher variance but a better interpretation.

 

### 13.8.1 A Medical Insurance Example

We now consider another example, where the goal is to predict the `Premium Price` charged by a medical insurance company with two feature variables of customers, namely their `Age` and `Weight`.

![FIGURE 13.15 A regression tree for the medical premium data via Python, generated in Programme 13.15.](images/c13f015.png)

[**FIGURE 13.15**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0015) A regression tree for the medical premium data via Python, generated in [Programme 13.15](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3015).

![FIGURE 13.16 A regression tree for the medical premium data via R, generated in Programme 13.16.](images/c13f016.png)

[**FIGURE 13.16**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0016) A regression tree for the medical premium data via **R**, generated in [Programme 13.16](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3016).

Comparing the results in [Figures 13.15](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0015) and [13.16](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0016), respectively from Programmes 13.15 via Python and 13.16 via **R**, the decision rules found by `sklearn` in Python and `rpart` in **R** are slightly different because of their choice of the splitting criterion, in which `sklearn` chooses the split that minimizes the squared error while `rpart` chooses the split that maximizes the between‐groups sum of squares in ANOVA. Based on these two regression tree models, we obtain the following interpretations:

1.  `Age` is the most relevant factor in determining the `Premium Price` of a customer. Customers under the age of 29.5 would be generally charged a lower amount of premium. Customers aged between 29.5 and 46.5 would be charged a medium amount of premium, and those customers above age 46.5 would be charged a higher amount of premium.
2.  Given that a customer is either below the age of 29.5 or of age between 29.5 and 46.5, his or her `Weight` barely plays a role in the premium charged.
3.  Given that a customer is of age above 46.5, his or her weight would affect his `Premium Price`. Customers heavier than 94.5 kg would be charged a higher amount of premium.

 

## 13.9 RANDOM FOREST

Random forests are based on the idea of *bagging*. Given a training set ![script upper S](images/c13-i0482.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>, we create ![upper B](images/c13-i0483.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> (a hyperparameter) random samples ![script upper S 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper S Subscript upper B Baseline](images/c13-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>B</mi></msub></math> of ![script upper S](images/c13-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>, on which we build ![upper B](images/c13-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> classification and regression tree models with respective labels ![ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript upper B Baseline](images/c13-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>B</mi></msub></math>. To sample each ![script upper S Subscript b](images/c13-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></math> for some ![b equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper B](images/c13-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></math>, we perform sampling with replacement from ![script upper S](images/c13-i0490.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> until ![StartAbsoluteValue script upper S Subscript b Baseline EndAbsoluteValue equals n equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper S EndAbsoluteValue](images/c13-i0491.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>. Besides these bootstrapping, to reduce the computational complexity especially when the number of features ![p](images/c13-i0492.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is large, one may confine the candidate features to ![m left-parenthesis much-less-than p right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0493.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> randomly selected from the ![p](images/c13-i0494.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> originals when a specific tree is built. Alternatively, the random selection of ![m](images/c13-i0495.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> features can be carried out at every node, and the splitting attribute for the node is the most effective one out of the ![m](images/c13-i0496.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> selected features. After training, we obtain ![upper B](images/c13-i0497.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> different trees. In the regression tree case, the prediction for a new input ![bold-italic x](images/c13-i0498.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is obtained from the average of the ![upper B](images/c13-i0499.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> predictions:

![ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript r f Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over upper B EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript b equals 1 Overscript upper B Endscripts ModifyingAbove f With caret Subscript b Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis comma](images/c13-math-0061.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

while in the classification case the prediction is the majority vote.

As an illustration, we apply the random forest algorithm to the 2002 financial dataset using Python and **R**, and we compare the results to those obtained from the (single) classification tree.

The misclassification rate is ![0 percent-sign](images/c13-i0500.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mi>%</mi></math>, which is much better than that of the classification tree in [Programme 13.7](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3007) via Python (resp. [Programme 13.8](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3008) via **R**).

![FIGURE 13.17 A graphical illustration of the random forest method.](images/c13f017.png)

**FIGURE 13.17** A graphical illustration of the random forest method.

One can observe from this example that at each splitting in the tree building process, only a random selection of ![m equals 2](images/c13-i0501.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> (`max_features=2` in Python and `mtry=2` in **R**) features from the original ![p equals 6](images/c13-i0502.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> features are inspected; this is the only difference between random forest and the vanilla bagging when ![m equals p](images/c13-i0503.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>; as now ![2 equals m less-than p equals 6](images/c13-i0504.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, this allows the possibility that a random forest can perform less favourably than an ordinary classification tree. The above value of ![m](images/c13-i0505.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> (hyperparameter) agrees with the common rules of thumb: choose ![m equals left floor StartRoot p EndRoot right floor](images/c13-i0506.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8970;</mo><msqrt><mi>p</mi></msqrt><mo>&#8971;</mo></math> for classification and ![m equals left floor StartFraction p Over 3 EndFraction right floor](images/c13-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8970;</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>&#8971;</mo></math> for regression.

The reason for the random selection of subsets of features is to de‐correlate different trees that are built. This reduces the variance of the final model further from bagging. If one or a few features are very strong predictors for the label, these features will be selected to split the samples in many trees. This would result in many correlated trees in our “forest”. Correlated predictors cannot help in improving the accuracy of prediction by reducing the variance. The main reason behind a better performance of model ensembling is that good models will likely agree on the same prediction, while bad models will likely disagree on different ones, so combining them can diversify the error and hence reduce the variance. Correlation makes bad models more likely to agree, possibly hampering the majority vote or the average.

 

### 13.9.1 Credit Card Default Prediction

In a credit card rating system, data are collected from potential customers to predict whether future customers will default or not. As an illustration, we consider a dataset which contains information on default payments, demographics, credit data, payment history, and bill statements of credit card clients in Taiwan from April 2005 to September 2005 [\[10\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0011). Each feature vector contains 26 features, such as “Amount of credit”, “Gender”, “Education Level”, “Marital status”, and “Age”. The label takes a value of 1 if the client defaults next month, or 0 otherwise. In Programmes 13.19 (Python) and 13.20 (**R**), classification trees and random forests are built for prediction.

![FIGURE 13.18 Classification trees for the Taiwan credit default dataset.](images/c13f018.png)

[**FIGURE 13.18**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0018) Classification trees for the Taiwan credit default dataset.

From the output of [Programme 13.19](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-3019), various measures of the classification tree built in Python such as precision, recall, ![upper F 1](images/c13-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>‐score, and accuracy are:

From [Figure 13.18](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0018)a, Python splits the dataset according to only 2 out of 26 feature variables, namely `PAY_0` and `PAY_2`, which represent the repayment status in September of 2005 and August of 2005, respectively. They record the number of months that the client delayed his/her payments, with `‐1` indicating no delay and a maximum value of nine months. It is true that a customer will likely default if his/her payments have already been delayed for several months, and the magic number found by Python is 2 (the smallest integer that is larger than 1.5) found by Python. Similarly, from [Figure 13.18](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0018)b, **R** splits the dataset according to `PAY_0` with the same magic number of 2. We here adopt the `confusionMatrix()` function from the `caret` library to compute various performance metrics in **R**. Readers can also refer to our user guide [\[2\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002) for more discussions.

### 13.A.1 Entropy in Information Theory

We here motivate the definition of entropy introduced in [Section \*13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0003) with its information‐theoretic importance. Readers can refer to [\[3\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0003) for more details. ### 13.A.2 Solving Wordle with Entropy

*Wordle* is a web‐based word game developed by *Josh Wardle*, released regularly by the *New York Times* as a word puzzle for its readers. Players have six attempts to guess a five‐letter word, with feedback given for each guess: each guessed letter is marked as either green, yellow or gray. Green indicates that the corresponding letter appears in the correct position of the target word; yellow color indicates that the corresponding letter is in the target word but not positioned correctly; while gray color means that the corresponding letter is not in the target word. As a special rule, in the event of multiple copies of a specific letter in the guess, let say ![m](images/c13-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> of them, appear in a guess, such as the A's and R's in RADAR (where ![m](images/c13-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> = 2 for both letters) or the M's in MUMMY (where ![m](images/c13-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> = 3), those in the correct positions, let say ![m 0](images/c13-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> of them, will first be colored as green, then the leftmost ![left-parenthesis m minus m 0 right-parenthesis Subscript plus](images/c13-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msub></math> among the remaining copies will be colored yellow, while the rest of them are displayed as gray; see [Figure 13.19](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0019) for an illustration, where readers can try to recover the color of each position in every attempt based on the aforementioned rules

To illustrate the idea, suppose that the word bank contains the totality of ![n](images/c13-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> five‐letter words, and that each word in the bank is equally probable to be selected as the target word. Furthermore, we represent the 26 letters from A to Z by numerals 1 to 26 in order, respectively. There are at most ![3 Superscript 5 Baseline equals 243](images/c13-i0574.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>243</mn></math> possible realizations of ![bold-italic c](images/c13-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow></math>. When a guess is made, the color vector is revealed, based on which one can narrow down the range of possible five‐letter words. The key iteration step in the algorithm is to find the “best” guess in the sense that it can narrow down the range of candidate words for the next step as much as possible on average.

To explain the algorithm, we denote by ![script upper W Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline colon equals script upper W](images/c13-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></math> the initial word bank, and ![script upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline comma k equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis](images/c13-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>, the shortlisted collection of words after the ![k](images/c13-i0578.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th guess and the color information revealed so far, also denote ![n Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline colon equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c13-i0579.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>.
