At the stage before making the ![k](images/c13-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th guess, for each specific guess, we can calculate the proportion of five‐letter words in the word bank that lead to each possible realization of the color vector assuming that they are the correct word. More rigorously, we consider the random color vector ![bold-italic c left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that clearly depends on the guess ![bold-italic omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#969;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and randomness comes from the unknown target word. The probability mass function of ![bold-italic c left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is then the proportion of the words in the word bank ![script upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c13-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> that, were they to be target words, would lead to a certain realization of the color vector. For example, the color vector (Green, Green, Green, Green, Green)^⊤ can only appear when the target word happens to be the same as the guess, therefore we have

![double-struck upper P left-parenthesis bold-italic c left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis Green comma Green comma Green comma Green comma Green right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over n Superscript left-parenthesis k minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline EndFraction equals colon p 1 left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c13-math-0071.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>Green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>Green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>Green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>Green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>Green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where we systematically assign an index from 1 to 243 for each realization of the color vector for the sake of convenience. The entropy of this random variable can then be calculated as:

![upper H left-parenthesis bold-italic c left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis colon equals minus sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript 243 Endscripts p Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis log Subscript 2 Baseline p Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold omega overTilde Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c13-math-0072.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>243</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8201;log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#969;</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math> 

In order to find a multipurpose word that can provide as much information for subsequent guesses as possible via the color signals, the best word for the ![k](images/c13-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th guess is the one that maximizes the entropy, as opposed to maximizing “information gain” in the classification tree algorithm

## NOTES

1.  [1](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-note-0001) In fields such as communication and signal processing, the term “information” quantifies the level of uncertainty, and the (chaotic) information increases with the entropy. For instance, by simple calculus, ([13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0004)) attains its maximum value of 1 when ![p equals one half](images/c13-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>. Nevertheless, in the financial context, it is more natural to define the term otherwise, i.e., the (useful) information increases as the level of randomness becomes lower; indeed, it is least accurate to predict the outcome from tossing a fair coin, yet the more biased the coin is, the more certain one can predict, i.e. the more useful information in predicting the outcome.

[8](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-note-0008) In fact, ([13.13](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0037)) is a version of a *Laplacian operator* ![normal upper Delta](images/c13-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> acting over the function of impurity measure ![Im](images/c13-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>Im</mtext></mrow></math>. The Laplacian also plays a key role in the fundamental equation (for *Riemannian metric*) modeling the flow (*Ricci flow*) of hot lava. Analogous to the lava flow that stops and solidifies when the change of its temperature becomes too small, for a classification tree, the branching procedure stops when the change in impurity measure induced by the subsequent splitting falls below a pre‐determined tolerance level.

# CHAPTER 14  
Cluster Analysis

 

Most of the methods mentioned in this book, such as logistic regression in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml), classification and regression trees and random forest in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml), as well as *neural networks* (to be discussed in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml)), require the presence of a response variable or a classification label for each observation. This allows us to monitor or “supervise” how well the methods perform by comparing their predicted results with the actual labels; as such, we say they are examples of *supervised learning*. For instance, for the 2002 HSI dataset of `fin‐ratio.csv`, all stocks have the labels of ![monospace HSI equals 0](images/c14-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="monospace">HSI</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> or 1. Other examples are: customer transaction records with bad debt or not; patient health records with a certain disease or not. However, real‐life datasets that do not contain label information are prevalent. As a result, we may not know how many groups or labels actually exist in the dataset. Take marketing research for example. We want to classify the customers into several subgroups so that we can adopt different marketing strategies to promote tailor‐made products to each of them, while the actual number of subgroups is mostly unknown to us with limited data. The methods used in such scenarios have no objective reference points for us to monitor their performance, and are thus named *unsupervised learning*. The problems in unsupervised learning are generally much more difficult to cope with than those in supervised learning. For instance, in the previous marketing example, selecting an appropriate number of subgroups is already a challenge; too few subgroups may yield too general strategies to address specific needs of customers, and hence cannot fulfill the taste of and so retain customers; while too many subgroups would add to the cost of promotion, which is undesirable for the companies.

 

## 14.1 ![upper K](images/c14-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐MEANS CLUSTERING

As another example of an intrinsic difficulty in unsupervised learning, namely the absence of a unique objective criterion for grouping data, consider a deck of 52 playing cards. While normally we can group the cards according to their color (red or black), suits (spades, heart, club and diamond); or face values (J, Q, K, A or 1 to 10), we do not have clear objectives in unsupervised learning for picking an obvious choice of *measure of similarity* or *dissimilarity*. Nevertheless, as long as a measure of similarity (or dissimilarity) is fixed, we can classify the data into clusters such that observations within each cluster are as homogeneous as possible, meanwhile observations belonging to different clusters are as heterogeneous as possible. This approach is often referred to as *Cluster Analysis*, which is a branch of unsupervised learning. There are two major types of methods in cluster analysis, namely *hierarchical* and *non‐hierarchical* clustering. Hierarchical clustering methods merge (resp. split) observations based on the outcomes of the previous step in an iterative manner, which corresponds to the branch of *agglomerative* (resp. *divisive*) methods. One typical example is the AGNES algorithm used in CIBer in [Section 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0006). In general, this procedure formulates a tree‐hierarchy structure with lines joining all the observations. However, it may not be feasible when the number of observations is large. To overcome the hurdle of handling very large datasets, a very popular non‐hierarchical clustering method can be employed: ![upper K](images/c14-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐means clustering*.

**(I) Lloyd's Algorithm**

![upper K](images/c14-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is fast, efficient and suitable for *data mining* very large datasets. While the term “![upper K](images/c14-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means” was first coined by *James MacQueen* in [\[17\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0017), the standard algorithm for the clustering was in fact first proposed by *Stuart Lloyd* earlier in 1957 as a technique for *pulse‐code modulation* (PCM)

![upper K](images/c14-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is an approach based on partitioning. Let ![script upper S equals left-brace bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c14-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> be the dataset of observations, where ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. Suppose that they are partitioned into ![upper K](images/c14-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> regions (clusters), ![script upper S 1 comma ellipsis comma script upper S Subscript upper K Baseline](images/c14-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>K</mi></msub></math>, such that each region ![script upper S Subscript k](images/c14-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is represented generically by a vector ![bold-italic c Subscript k](images/c14-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, which is usually the *geometric centroid* of ![script upper S Subscript k](images/c14-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math>. In ![upper K](images/c14-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, the centroids ![bold-italic c 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic c Subscript upper K Baseline](images/c14-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></math>, and the map ![q](images/c14-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are constructed in such a way that the mean‐squared error between the observations and their assigned or associated centroids is minimized. Furthermore, by the quadratic nature of the mean squared error, ![bold-italic c Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is the unique minimum of ![sigma-summation Underscript bold-italic x element-of script upper S Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Endscripts double-vertical-bar bold-italic x minus bold-italic c Subscript k Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2](images/c14-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mspace width="-.2em"/><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>. By the arbitrariness of ![k](images/c14-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, this result holds for all clusters, which then yields ![upper L Subscript t comma 2 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper L Subscript t comma 1](images/c14-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> by summing up across clusters.

Now, since ![upper L Subscript t comma 2 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper L Subscript t comma 1 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper L Subscript t minus 1 comma 2](images/c14-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> for all ![t](images/c14-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, and ![upper L Subscript t comma 2 Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c14-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> by definition, we can conclude by the *monotone convergence theorem* that the objective function converges. Since there are only finitely many sample points, ![script upper S](images/c14-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> is therefore bounded, and the *Heine–Borel theorem* ensures the limiting point exists and it is a local minimizer. Furthermore, using the fact that the sample size is finite again, then so is the total number of possible clustering scenarios. Recall that by the nature of Lloyd's algorithm, each update of clusters and centroids results in an objective function not greater in value than that in the previous step, hence we can usually achieve the optimal clustering after a finite number of steps and remain there. How many steps are needed to attain the optimal clustering depends on the choice of initial seeds.

**(II) Illustrations for** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>**‐means clustering**

The ![upper K](images/c14-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering method is implemented in Python using the `KMeans()` function provided in the `sklearn` library, and in **R** using the built‐in function `kmeans()`. We first illustrate its use by using Fisher's Iris data in [Programme 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3001) via Python and [Programme 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002) via **R**.

For the Iris data, both outputs from [Programme 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3001) via Python and [Programme 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002) via **R** give 3 clusters of sizes 38, 50, and 62. Other items given in `km_iris` include:

1.  `cluster_centers_` in Python and `centers` in **R**: the mean vectors for all 4 measurements of these 3 groups;
2.  `labels_` in Python and `cluster` in **R**: the assigned cluster label for each datum based on the ![upper K](images/c14-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering; note that the numbering of these group labels is arbitrary, e.g., the label 1 may represent any one of these 3 groups;
3.  `inertia_` in Python and `tot.withinss` in **R**: the total within‐cluster sum of squares; see more details and discussions in the next item (III) and [Appendix \*14.A.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010).

Finally, we can produce the classification table of the labels from ![upper K](images/c14-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering with the underlying “true” species in [Programme 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3003) via Python and [Programme 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3004) via **R**.

![FIGURE 14.2 Scatter plots of pairwise components of observations for each group in the Iris flower dataset.](images/c14f002.png)

**FIGURE 14.2** Scatter plots of pairwise components of observations for each group in the Iris flower dataset.

[**TABLE 14.1**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-tbl-0001)  The correspondence between the original groups and the labels assigned for the Iris dataset.

| Label assigned  || Original group |
| --- | --- |
| Python || R || `setosa` || `virginica` || `versicolor` |
| 1 || 1 || 50 || 0 || 0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 || 2 || 0 || 48 || 14 |
| 0 || 3 || 0 || 2 || 36 |

Again, the numbering of the label is arbitrary: in Python, the labels 0, 1, and 2 correspond to the original species of `versicolor`, `setosa`, and `virginica`, respectively; whereas in **R**, the labels 1, 2, and 3 correspond to the original species of `setosa`, `virginica`, and `versicolor` groups respectively; see [Table 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0001). Therefore, the actual misclassification rates in Python and **R** are only ![left-parenthesis 14 plus 2 right-parenthesis slash 150 equals 10.67 percent-sign](images/c14-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10.67</mn><mi>%</mi></math>.

Next, we apply the ![upper K](images/c14-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering to the 2002 HSI example, via Python in [Programme 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3005) and via **R** in [Programme 14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3006).

From [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0003), `ln_MV` is visually the most important and useful decision variable in the ![upper K](images/c14-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering. In the third column, with `ln_MV` as the variable for the horizontal axis, the boundary between constituent and non‐constituent stocks (the red triangles and black circles, respectively) seems the most clear compared to those using other variables for the horizontal axis in other columns. However, upon closer inspection, we can see that the two types of stock are not as separated as the different species of Iris flowers in the previous example, as quite a few red triangles are actually hidden in the cloud of black circles. This explains the relatively poor classification performance of ![upper K](images/c14-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering in this case, with the misclassification rate as high as ![left-parenthesis 159 plus 21 right-parenthesis slash 680 equals 26.47 percent-sign](images/c14-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>159</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>21</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>26.47</mn><mi>%</mi></math> for Python and ![left-parenthesis 152 plus 24 right-parenthesis slash 680 equals 25.88 percent-sign](images/c14-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>152</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>24</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>680</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>25.88</mn><mi>%</mi></math> for **R**. Nevertheless, this result is not surprising; indeed, as an unsupervised learning approach, ![upper K](images/c14-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is more likely to give inferior results when the data with different class labels overlap.

**(III) On the suitable choice of** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>

An immediate question is the choice of an appropriate number ![upper K](images/c14-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> of clusters in the ![upper K](images/c14-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering. Fortunately, there is a useful statistic available to help us choosing a suitable ![upper K](images/c14-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. Recall that our objective is to find clearly separable groups in the dataset, such that the records within the same group should be as homogeneous as possible while those between different groups are as different as possible.

The within‐group and between‐group variations can be obtained in Python via the `inertia_` component and the `get_bcss()` function of the model trained by `KMeans()` respectively. They are available in **R** as the respective components `tot.withinss` and `betweenss` of the model trained by `kmeans()`. Intuitively though, recalling the objective of clustering, these two variations can be combined to give a useful statistic. First, we revisit the Iris dataset and illustrate how these two statistics are computed; [Programme 14.7](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3007) in Python (resp. [Programme 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3008) in **R**) demonstrates how to reconcile the corresponding numerical results in [Programme 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3001) (resp. [Programme 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002)).

![FIGURE 14.3 Scatter plot matrix colored corresponding to the output from upper K‐means clustering for the 2002 HSI data.](images/c14f003.png)

Summing them up over all the predicted labels ![k](images/c14-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> gives the total *within‐cluster sum of squares* (![WCSS](images/c14-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>WCSS</mtext></mrow></math>), that is ![WCSS colon equals sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript upper K Endscripts trace left-parenthesis SSCP Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>WCSS</mtext><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></msubsup><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mtext>SSCP</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This value is stored in `km_iris$inertia_` in Python ([Programme 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3001)) and `km_iris$tot.withinss` in **R** ([Programme 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002)). In Python ([Programme 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3001)); this sum of squares can be called out by the function `bcss`; while in **R** ([Programme 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002)), this value is stored in `km_iris$betweenss`.

With all these quantities in mind, we introduce the following *Calinski–Harabasz index* [\[4\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004):

![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction n minus upper K Over upper K minus 1 EndFraction StartFraction BCSS Over WCSS EndFraction comma](images/c14-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mtext>BCSS</mtext><mtext mathvariant="normal">WCSS</mtext></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

where both ![BCSS](images/c14-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>BCSS</mtext></mrow></math> and ![WCSS](images/c14-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>WCSS</mtext></mrow></math> are regarded as functions in ![upper K](images/c14-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. Clearly, ![BCSS](images/c14-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>BCSS</mtext></mrow></math> describes the dispersion of different clusters while ![WCSS](images/c14-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>WCSS</mtext></mrow></math> describes the dispersion of points within each cluster. A good clustering should be one for which the former is large but the latter is small. Notice that as a ratio of the between‐group and within‐group sums of squares, divided by their respective degrees of freedom, the index is analogous to the ![upper F](images/c14-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐test statistic in univariate analysis. We aim to seek for a value of ![upper K](images/c14-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> that simultaneously makes ![WCSS](images/c14-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>WCSS</mtext></mrow></math> small and ![BCSS](images/c14-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>BCSS</mtext></mrow></math> large as much as possible, and so make ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as large as possible. In [Appendix \*14.A.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010), we shall motivate why ![upper R left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> will indeed attain its maximum at its true cluster number, i.e., when ![upper L equals upper K](images/c14-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, in most practical scenarios, and also discuss about pitfalls of using it under some special cases.

In [Programme 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3009) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.10](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3010) via **R**), we illustrate how to compute ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> using the self‐defined function `kmstat()` in both Python and **R**. This function is designed to return the optimal choice of ![upper K](images/c14-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, with the corresponding maximized ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> statistic, and the corresponding cluster model. We also introduce another function `best_km()` in both Python and **R** that performs ![upper K](images/c14-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering several times for different values of ![upper K](images/c14-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, and generates the same two outputs, namely the best possible trial with the largest ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> statistic. See Programmes 14.9 via Python and 14.10 via **R**, respectively.

Furthermore, using the Iris dataset once again, we shall try several values of ![upper K](images/c14-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> in [Programme 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3011) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3012) via **R**) and determine the specific value of ![upper K](images/c14-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> at which the function ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is maximized.

In [Programme 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3011) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3012) via **R**), we enter a few values of ![upper K](images/c14-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> in the `best_km()` function, and see that ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> gives the maximum value of 561.6278 for ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, so ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> could be a suitable choice. The cluster label is also saved in `km_iris3`, and the cross‐tabulation table is exactly the one shown by [Programme 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3003) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3004) via **R**).

As another illustration, we also apply `best_km()` to the cleansed 2002 HSI dataset `fin‐ratio_cleansed.csv` (produced in [Programme 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-3011) via **R**), with the output as shown in [Programme 14.13](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3013) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.14](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3014) via **R**).

As expected, ![upper K equals 2](images/c14-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> gives the maximum value of ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> at 330.7535, which seems consistent with the number of possible actual labels of the dataset. Despite the same number of categories, the classification results may not be in accordance with the stock categories in HSI. To find out the characteristics of these clusters, we use [Programme 14.15](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3015) via Python (resp. [Programme 14.16](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3016) via **R**). The resulting boxplots in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004) are an effective graphical illustration of the characteristics of each cluster.

![FIGURE 14.4 Boxplots for each feature variable in the cleansed 2002 HSI dataset.](images/c14f004.png)

[**FIGURE 14.4**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0004) Boxplots for each feature variable in the cleansed 2002 HSI dataset.

From the boxplots in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004), the one for `DY` shows that the second cluster of points lies higher than those of the first one, while no significant difference is present in the plots of the other five variables. Based on this, we can simply describe these two clusters as the collection of stocks with lower values of `DY` as the first cluster and higher values of `DY` as the second.

 

### 14.1.1 Variants of ![upper K](images/c14-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐Means Clustering

**(I) Different Distance / Dis‐similarity Metrics**

![upper K](images/c14-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering as well as other clustering methods is based on the metric of distance (or *dis‐similarity*) between observations. It is thus important to properly define the metric between any two observations. In view of the different types of variables in our dataset, these metrics should also be defined in a tailor‐made manner. In the following, for the sake of convenience, first suppose that we have ![p](images/c14-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> variables of the same type in our dataset with size ![n](images/c14-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and the ![i](images/c14-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th observation ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c14-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>, ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>. In the case of mixed variable types, we just combine different metrics for the various types.

**Continuous variables**

If all the variables are continuous, it is common to use the following ![q](images/c14-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>‐norm as the distance measure:

![d Subscript q Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript q Baseline equals left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript p Endscripts left-parenthesis x Subscript i k Baseline minus x Subscript j k Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript q Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript 1 slash q Baseline period](images/c14-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math> 

This includes the well‐known *Euclidean distance* (![q equals 2](images/c14-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>), *Manhattan distance* (![q equals 1](images/c14-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>), and *Minkowski distance* (![1 less-than-or-equal-to q less-than-or-equal-to infinity](images/c14-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>) as special cases

**Ordinal variables**

If all the variables are ordinal, we can rank the ![n](images/c14-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> observations of each variable, respectively, and then rescale the observations to ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> as follows:

(14.4)![z Subscript i k Baseline equals StartFraction r Subscript i k Baseline minus 1 Over upper M Subscript k Baseline minus 1 EndFraction comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p comma](images/c14-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![r Subscript i k](images/c14-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the ranking of the ![k](images/c14-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th component variable for the ![i](images/c14-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th observation, and ![upper M Subscript k](images/c14-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is the number of possible values the ![k](images/c14-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th variable can take, and the additional term of ![negative 1](images/c14-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in the numerator is included to ensure that the observations with the lowest rank of 1 can be rescaled to 0. After the rescaling transformation, we can then treat the component variables as if they were continuous variables, and measure their distance using the ![p](images/c14-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐norm mentioned above.

**Binary variables**

If all the component variables are binary, then for each pair of observations ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic x Subscript j](images/c14-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, we can count the number of variables under each possible combination. In particular, we let ![m Subscript l 1 l 2 Superscript i j Baseline colon equals StartAbsoluteValue left-brace k element-of StartSet 1 comma ellipsis comma p EndSet colon x Subscript i k Baseline equals l 1 comma x Subscript j k Baseline equals l 2 right-brace EndAbsoluteValue](images/c14-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> denote the number of component variables that have a value of ![l 1](images/c14-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> in ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![l 2](images/c14-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> in ![bold-italic x Subscript j](images/c14-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, respectively, for ![l 1 comma l 2 equals 0 comma 1](images/c14-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Clearly ![m 00 Superscript i j Baseline plus m 01 Superscript i j Baseline plus m 10 Superscript i j Baseline plus m 11 Superscript i j Baseline equals p](images/c14-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>00</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>01</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Now we can use either of the following measures (for simplicity we omit the superscripts of ![i](images/c14-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and ![j](images/c14-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>):

*   Simple matching coefficient: ![d left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction m 00 plus m 11 Over m 00 plus m 01 plus m 10 plus m 11 EndFraction equals StartFraction m 00 plus m 11 Over p EndFraction semicolon](images/c14-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>00</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>00</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>01</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>00</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo>;</mo></math> 
*   *Jaccard coefficient*: ![d left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction m 10 plus m 01 Over m 00 plus m 01 plus m 10 EndFraction period](images/c14-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>01</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>00</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>01</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>10</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 

**Nominal or categorical variables**

If all the component variables are nominal, then we can use the dis‐similarity measure ![d left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction p minus m Over p EndFraction](images/c14-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi></mfrac></math>, where ![m colon equals StartAbsoluteValue StartSet k element-of StartSet 1 comma ellipsis comma p EndSet colon x Subscript i k Baseline equals x Subscript j k Baseline EndSet EndAbsoluteValue](images/c14-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> is the number of matches among these ![p](images/c14-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> component variables.

**Mixed types, missing values and scaling of data**

In practice, datasets usually contain missing values and variables of mixed types. The easiest way to handle the missing data is to delete all incomplete observations. The Python function `dropna()` and **R** function `complete.cases()` can be utilized to select all the complete observations and leave out the others. However, using only complete observations will potentially give up lots of hidden information and, more seriously, lead to the biased sampling of sub‐samples, especially when the missing mechanism is *missing not at random*. A better but more complicated way of handling them is to proceed with the calculation of the distance, but only using the variables available in both observations, or we can impute the missing observations.

Another issue is that the ranges of the variables may differ a lot, and using the original scale inevitably assigns more weight to those with a large magnitude. Therefore, we should rescale variables to the ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> interval before performing cluster analysis.

Altogether, combining discussions above, we are led to the following distance metric:

**(II) Enhancing Lloyd's Algorithm**

Let us discuss further the computational nature and some drawbacks of Lloyd's algorithm [\[7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007), [28\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0028), and then incorporate certain ways to improve the overall performance of the algorithm.

From (14.3), the computational complexity of Step 2 in Algorithm 14.1 of Lloyd's algorithm is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper K n p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; to see this, note that for each of the ![n](images/c14-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> observations, its distances to all ![upper K](images/c14-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> centroids need to be calculated, and calculating a distance requires ![upper O left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> units of time to complete since ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>. When we update the centroids in Step 3, the computational complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis n p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> since each addition of ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> consumes ![upper O left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> units of time, and there are essentially ![upper O left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> additions to be done in total. If the number of iterations is ![upper T](images/c14-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, then the total complexity of the algorithm becomes ![upper O left-parenthesis upper K n p upper T right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; therefore, Lloyd's algorithm for ![upper K](images/c14-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is a linear‐in‐time algorithm.

As we hinted earlier, Lloyd's algorithm is rather sensitive to initialization, as different initial seeds might result in a quite substantially different clustering result, since the algorithm only yields a local minimum to ([14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0002)) instead of the global one. To warrant a more robust performance, we can adopt a Monte Carlo‐like approach, namely repeating the clustering procedure using random initial seeds for a number of times. We then compare the results obtained from different initial seeds, and then select the set of seeds with the smallest sum of squares. As a tradeoff, this approach certainly requires a much longer computational time.

In [\[3\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0003), *David Arthur* and *Sergei Vassilvitskii* introduced a simple yet effective alternative numerical approach, called ![upper K](images/c14-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐means++*, by enhancing the original Lloyd's algorithm with an additional “initialization algorithm”. The algorithm guarantees the solution found is ![upper O left-parenthesis ln upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>*‐competitive* to the optimal solution: let ![StartSet script upper S 1 Superscript plus plus
