The “initialization algorithm” is summarized in Algorithm 14.2. ![upper K](images/c14-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means++ has an extra computational complexity of order ![upper O left-parenthesis upper K squared n p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> induced by Algorithm 14.2; indeed, when there are ![k](images/c14-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> centroids in ![script upper C](images/c14-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></math> in Algorithm 14.2, a total of ![k](images/c14-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> calculations will be needed at its Step 2 for each of the ![n](images/c14-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> observations, while every such calculation takes ![upper O left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> units of time. Therefore, the time needed in this iteration step is of the order ![upper O left-parenthesis k n p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and summing up for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c14-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> leads to a total complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis upper K squared n p right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Clearly, this newly revised algorithm still results in a polynomial (quadratic) computational time, yet on average it can guarantee the eventual clusters produced are effectively close to the ultimate optimal solution as indicated by the error bound ([14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0016)).

**Asymmetric Samples**

Recall that the classical ![upper K](images/c14-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm makes use of the square of Euclidean distance as the measure of dis‐similarity, which is symmetric in all component variables by assigning equal weights. It is therefore not surprising that the performance of ![upper K](images/c14-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm is relatively poor when handling samples that do not follow symmetric distributions. For instance, [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005) shows the performance of ![upper K](images/c14-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering when the two samples actually follow asymmetric distributions. To eliminate the restrictive distribution assumptions, variants of the ![upper K](images/c14-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm for more general metric spaces are also available, including the *Kernel* ![upper K](images/c14-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐means clustering* and *Spectral Clustering*.

![FIGURE 14.5 An example of a two‐dimensional asymmetric sample.](images/c14f005.png)

[**FIGURE 14.5**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0005) An example of a two‐dimensional asymmetric sample.

The Kernel ![upper K](images/c14-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm maps each observation ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> to a high‐dimensional space ![bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript m](images/c14-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></math> with ![m greater-than p](images/c14-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, via the *transformation* ![bold-italic x right-arrow from bar bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8614;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; see more details in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0003) on radial basis functions for SVM.

On the other hand, for spectral clustering, the collection of sample points in ![double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is viewed as a *complete graph*, where each sample feature vector represents a vertex, and an edge between any two vertices is represented by a weight. The weights computed, based on a chosen similarity measure, form a similarity matrix, which is certainly symmetric due to the symmetry of the similarity measure. In addition, this similarity matrix is mostly positive semi‐definite [\[20\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0020); for example, if the similarity measure (signed) between two observed feature vectors ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic x Subscript j](images/c14-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> is given by the cosine of their inscribed angle, i.e. ![StartFraction left pointing angle bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right pointing angle Over double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Baseline dot double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Baseline EndFraction](images/c14-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>, then the corresponding similarity matrix is clearly positive semi‐definite. By spectral decomposition (recall [Section 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007) for an introduction), we can obtain the first ![m](images/c14-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ![left-parenthesis m much-greater-than upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> eigenvectors corresponding to the ![m](images/c14-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> largest eigenvalues (all eigenvalues are positive) of this similarity matrix

**Bisecting** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>**‐means**

We introduce one more variant of ![upper K](images/c14-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means, but in the realm of hierarchical clustering, called *bisecting* ![upper K](images/c14-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐means*, where the desired number of clusters ![upper K](images/c14-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is pre‐determined as usual. The whole sample is first considered as a single cluster, which is then divided into two clusters by using the classical ![upper K](images/c14-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means method with ![upper K equals 2](images/c14-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. In each subsequent iterative step, the same method of bisection is carried out to the cluster with the largest sum of squared error (SSE) from its corresponding centroid, hence the number of clusters increases by 1 after every new step. The procedure continues until the apparent stopping criterion that there are already ![upper K](images/c14-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> clusters.

**(III) Applications of** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>**‐means Clustering**

![upper K](images/c14-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, especially Lloyd's algorithm, is very easily applicable to large datasets. Besides its immediate use in customer classification in marketing research as mentioned in the beginning of this chapter, we shall also discuss some of its interesting applications in other fields, such as *image processing* in computer science and *dictionary learning* in feature learning.

Here, we first illustrate the use of ![upper K](images/c14-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering in customer credential classification using the dataset `Credit Card Customer Data.csv`

From the output result of [Programme 14.17](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3017) via Python, the ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> statistic reaches its largest value of 747.539 at ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, indicating that `km_cCred3` is the most appropriate ![upper K](images/c14-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering scheme. [Figures 14.6a](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0006) and [14.6b](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0006) shows the resulting scatter plot for the total number of credit cards against the average credit card limit, and boxplots for each feature variable generated by [Programme 14.18](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3018) via Python. In particular, for the scatter plot, each orange star represents the centroids of the corresponding clusters. For the boxplots, one extra feature variable `Total_interactions` for the total number of times the customer made interactions with the bank is added.

![FIGURE 14.6 Scatter plot for two variables (left), and boxplots for each feature variable (right), for the credit card customer dataset via Python, generated by Programme 14.18.](images/c14f006.png)

[**FIGURE 14.6**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0006) Scatter plot for two variables (left), and boxplots for each feature variable (right), for the credit card customer dataset via Python, generated by [Programme 14.18](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3018).

From [Figure 14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0006)b, the three clusters can be interpreted as follows:

1.  Cluster 1: Customers who interact with the bank the least, and make their interactions mostly through in‐person visits. They have a moderate average credit limit and they hold a moderate number of credit cards;
2.  Cluster 2: Customers who interact with the bank the most, and make their interactions mostly online. They have the highest average credit limit and they hold the greatest number of credit cards;
3.  Cluster 3: Customers who interact with the bank slightly less often than the customers in Cluster 2, and make their interactions mostly by calling. They have the lowest average credit limit and they hold the least number of credit cards.

Based on the analysis above, many suggestions can be formulated for the banking industry. For example, as high‐net worth individuals tend to cherish the value of time more than others, they would rather save time by contacting the bank online directly, rather than queue up in the branch or make lengthy phone calls. It is then suggested that banks should promote and improve their online credit card services to attract more prestigious credit card users.

**Image Segmentation**

A typical example of image processing is *image segmentation*, which means partitioning an image into ![upper K](images/c14-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> different segments to make subsequent data processing easier, like using photo‐editing software such as *Photoshop*. To implement ![upper K](images/c14-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means in this context, we usually adopt the *CIE 1976 Lab color space* (a.k.a. ![normal upper L Superscript asterisk Baseline normal a Superscript asterisk Baseline normal b Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> channel) instead of the usual RGB channel. This color space also expresses a pixel in a 3‐tuple, namely the lightness ![upper L Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math>, the green‐red component ![a Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> and the blue‐yellow component ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math>. Compared with RGB setting, a numerical change in these three coordinates can better reflect the magnitude of color change perceived by a human.

To perform the segmentation according to colors, we can neglect the lightness component ![upper L Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math>, while the remaining ones ![a Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> and ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> are extracted from each pixel, forming a sample of two‐dimensional points, with a size equal to the total number of pixels in the picture. This sample is then clustered using the ![upper K](images/c14-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm or its variants as mentioned before, and pixels ending up in the same cluster are assigned the same values of ![a Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> and ![b Superscript asterisk](images/c14-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></math> of the corresponding centroid. [Figure 14.7](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0007) shows an illustration of image segmentation using ![upper K](images/c14-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering with ![upper K equals 5](images/c14-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. ![FIGURE 14.7 Image segmentation using upper K‐means clustering.](images/c14f007.png)

[**FIGURE 14.7**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0007) Image segmentation using ![upper K](images/c14-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering.

**Photo Denoising and Dictionary Learning**

Another example that we may already benefit from is *photo denoising*, a mechanism that helps photos get rid of random noises on brightness or color caused by electrons, and so make the photo more aesthetically pleasant. It is so prevalent nowadays that we barely perceive its existence, thanks to the technique of *dictionary learning* that speeds up the procedure.

Dictionary learning is similar to PCA: given a dataset we wish to extract a number of basic elements called *atoms* such that almost all feature vectors can be represented in terms of these fundamental building blocks. The collection of such atoms is called a *dictionary*. It is at this stage that ![upper K](images/c14-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering or its extension, ![upper K](images/c14-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐Singular Value Decomposition* (![upper K](images/c14-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐SVD) [\[2\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0002), is implemented.

Here, we briefly summarize ![upper K](images/c14-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐SVD: let ![bold-italic upper Y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times n](images/c14-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math> be the matrix of ![n](images/c14-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> observed image signals so that each has ![p](images/c14-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional features, and ![bold-italic upper D element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times upper K](images/c14-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></math> be the *dictionary* in which the ![k](images/c14-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th column ![bold-italic d Subscript k](images/c14-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is the ![k](images/c14-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th atom to be learnt, for ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c14-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>.

![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column min Underscript bold-italic upper D comma bold-italic upper X Endscripts double-vertical-bar bold-italic upper Y minus bold-italic upper D bold-italic upper X double-vertical-bar Subscript upper F Superscript 2 Baseline comma 2nd Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column subject to double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 0 Baseline less-than-or-equal-to upper T for all i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n comma EndLayout](images/c14-math-0017.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></munder><mspace width="2.4em"/><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.1em"/><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width=".1em"/><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>for all</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where ![bold-italic upper X equals left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a ![upper K times n](images/c14-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> matrix of coefficient columns with respect to dictionary ![bold-italic upper D](images/c14-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi></mrow></math> for each datum ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, while ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 0](images/c14-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width=".2em"/><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub></math> counts the number of non‐zero components. Therefore, we aim to describe the key message contained in ![bold-italic y Subscript i](images/c14-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> by not more than ![upper T](images/c14-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> key terms from the dictionary of ![bold-italic d 1 comma bold-italic d 2 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic d Subscript upper K Baseline](images/c14-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></math>. ![upper K](images/c14-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐SVD can be regarded as a generalized ![upper K](images/c14-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering problem because the problem degenerates to the latter if ![upper T equals 1](images/c14-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, or more precisely, ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 0 Baseline equals 1](images/c14-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>; indeed, in ![upper K](images/c14-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, (i) the observed matrix ![bold-italic upper Y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times n](images/c14-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math> is the transpose of the data matrix (with features); (ii) the dictionary matrix ![bold-italic upper D equals left-parenthesis bold-italic c 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic c Subscript upper K Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times upper K](images/c14-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></math>, where ![bold-italic c Subscript k Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is the ![k](images/c14-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th centroid; and (iii) the sparse coefficient matrix ![bold-italic upper X equals left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper K times n](images/c14-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math>, where ![x Subscript i j](images/c14-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> takes the value of 1 if the predicted label of ![bold-italic y Subscript i](images/c14-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is Class ![j](images/c14-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> or is equal to zero otherwise, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> and ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c14-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, such that ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 0 Baseline equals 1](images/c14-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

Just like ![upper K](images/c14-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, it is in general not convenient to find the explicit solution in a direct manner, hence we adopt the following numerical method instead; particularly, we first solve for the sparse coefficient matrix ![bold-italic upper X](images/c14-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> to locate its non‐zero elements given a dictionary matrix ![bold-italic upper D](images/c14-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi></mrow></math>, and this step is called *sparse coding*. Noting that ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic upper Y minus bold-italic upper D bold-italic upper X double-vertical-bar Subscript upper F Superscript 2 Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts double-vertical-bar bold-italic y Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic upper D bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2](images/c14-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, this leads to solving ![n](images/c14-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> sub‐problems: for each ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>,

Problem ([14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0018)) can be solved through a chosen *matching pursuit algorithm*; see more discussions in [\[11](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0011), [18\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0018). In the next step known as the *codebook update*, we update the ![k](images/c14-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th atom ![bold-italic d Subscript k](images/c14-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> and the ![k](images/c14-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th row of ![bold-italic upper X](images/c14-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> denoted by ![bold-italic x Superscript k](images/c14-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> while fixing the rest of the others ![bold-italic d Subscript j 1](images/c14-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold-italic x Superscript j 2](images/c14-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msup></math>:

To fulfill the sparsity constraint, we define an ordered set ![omega Subscript k Baseline colon equals StartSet i colon left-parenthesis bold-italic x Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis Subscript i Baseline not-equals 0 EndSet](images/c14-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfenced></math>, and denote ![omega Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as the ![i](images/c14-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th element ordered in magnitude in ![omega Subscript k](images/c14-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>. Therefore the solution ![bold-italic d Subscript k](images/c14-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> can be taken as the first column of ![bold-italic upper U](images/c14-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi></mrow></math>, and ![bold-italic x Superscript k Baseline bold upper Omega Subscript k Superscript down-tack](images/c14-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is the scalar product of ![sigma 1](images/c14-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> (the largest singular value in ![bold upper Sigma](images/c14-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow></math>) and the first column of ![bold-italic upper V](images/c14-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow></math>, where ![bold-italic upper E Subscript k Baseline bold upper Omega Subscript k Superscript down-tack Baseline equals bold-italic upper U bold upper Sigma bold-italic upper V Superscript down-tack](images/c14-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math>. The steps above are then implemented iteratively for ![k](images/c14-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> from 1 to ![upper K](images/c14-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> in this codebook update stage. Then we move to the next epoch of the sparse coding step and then the codebook update step again and again until convergence. Notice that convergence is guaranteed by the fact that MSE is monotonically non‐increasing at each iteration.

Unlike PCA where the basic elements have to be mutually orthogonal, this is not a must for atoms; in fact, dictionary matrices are usually of a larger size than the data matrix we want to represent. To examine a new image, it suffices for us to only call up the dictionary along with the so‐called *representation*, in the form of a linear combination of the atoms, which allows a fast and robust processing of the photos. As a simple example, consider a collection of ![script l](images/c14-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math> grayscale (training) pictures where each picture is of size ![h times w](images/c14-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>w</mi></math>. It is suggested in [\[2\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0002) that partitioning each picture into ![m](images/c14-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> non‐overlapping blocks of smaller images, each of which has ![p](images/c14-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> number of pixels such that ![h times w equals m times p](images/c14-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>. Each of these blocks is then flattened into a one‐dimensional vector ![bold-italic y Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>(train)</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n equals script l times m](images/c14-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi></math>, then the observed training matrix is given by ![bold-italic upper Y Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline equals left-parenthesis bold-italic y 1 Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic y Subscript script l times m Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mtext>(train)</mtext></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext>(train)</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>(train)</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; with this in mind, suppose that ![bold-italic upper D Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times upper K](images/c14-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mtext>(train)</mtext></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></math>, where ![upper K greater-than p](images/c14-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>p</mi></math> for an over‐complete dictionary, is the trained dictionary of ![upper K](images/c14-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐SVD. A new grayscale test image partitioned into ![m](images/c14-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> blocks in the same manner as in the training stage yields the observed test matrix ![bold-italic upper Y Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline equals left-parenthesis bold-italic y 1 Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic y Subscript m Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times m](images/c14-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext>(test)</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>(test)</mtext></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></math>. We aim to find a low‐rank approximation ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper Y With Ì‚ element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p times m](images/c14-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></math> of the matrix ![bold-italic upper Y Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0334.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup></math> of observed test image signals through ![upper K](images/c14-i0335.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐SVD. We then adopt a chosen matching pursuit algorithm in the sparse coding step to find the sparse coefficient matrix ![bold-italic upper X Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup></math> given the trained dictionary ![bold-italic upper D Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>train</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The low‐rank approximation is then ![ModifyingAbove bold-italic upper Y With Ì‚ equals bold-italic upper D Superscript left-parenthesis train right-parenthesis Baseline bold-italic upper X Superscript left-parenthesis test right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>train</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mtext>(test)</mtext></msup></math>, from which the reconstructed image can be built by reversing the block‐partitioning steps in the training stage. This approach bears a high resemblance to the prediction of movie ratings for recommender systems discussed in Section \*9.11, and is particularly useful for filling in missing pixels in images.

 

### 14.1.2 Application of PCA in ![upper K](images/c14-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means Clustering

In Subsection 10.4.3, we fitted a multinomial logistic regression model using the MNIST dataset before and after the dimension reduction via PCA. Here we shall illustrate the application of PCA in the context of ![upper K](images/c14-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering using the same dataset. As a benchmark, we first perform a standard and direct ![upper K](images/c14-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering on the dataset, with a training size of ![60 comma 000](images/c14-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> and testing size of ![10 comma 000](images/c14-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math>; see the Python codes in [Programme 14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3019) and **R** codes in [Programme 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3020). Note that we set ![upper K equals 10](images/c14-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> in this illustration in view of the 10 different digits from 0 to 9 in the dataset. In fact, readers can verify by themselves that under the reasonable constraint of ![upper K greater-than-or-equal-to 10](images/c14-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>10</mn></math> inspired by the nature of the dataset, ![upper R left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> indeed reaches its maximum at ![upper K equals 10](images/c14-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. Furthermore, since ![upper K](images/c14-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is supposed to be an unsupervised learning algorithm, the predicted clusters obtained should not be connected with the digits. However, for the sake of performance assessment in the present example, we still make such a connection via the majority vote approach, namely the digit with the highest frequency among the training data points in a cluster is selected as the label of the cluster. The labels assigned to the trained clusters are exhibited in `pos_dict`; for example, `4: 6` in the output means that the predicted label of the ![left-parenthesis 4 plus 1 equals right-parenthesis 5](images/c14-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>5</mn></math>th cluster is the digit 6.

In the outputs obtained in [Programme 14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3019) via Python, the ![i](images/c14-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th row of the first “confusion matrix” obtained is actually the distribution of actual digits among the testing pictures falling into the corresponding ![i](images/c14-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th trained cluster, and for each testing picture, its predicted digit is set to be the label assigned to the cluster it belongs. In the resulting second and final confusion matrix, the entries in the sixth and tenth rows are all zero, indicating that no clusters are assigned with a predicted label of 5 or 9, hence no testing images are identified as either of these two digits. An explanation is that the digit 5 looks similar to digits 3 and 8, while digit 9 may be easily mistaken as either 4 or 7, hence the large entries in the sixth and tenth columns of the confusion matrix, respectively. The testing accuracy of ![upper K](images/c14-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering with ![upper K equals 10](images/c14-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> is 0.5943, lower than the 0.6784 obtained by the EM algorithm in [Programme 6.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3009) via Python.

In **R**, since the built‐in function `kmeans()` for ![upper K](images/c14-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering does not support the `predict()` function for computing the predicted labels given the new feature matrix, we need to define an additional function `predict.kmeans()` for this purpose. This self‐defined function, as well as the codes and outputs for the standard ![upper K](images/c14-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, are shown in [Programme 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3020). We also remark that the actual digits as columns in the confusion matrix are arranged in the order of ![1 comma ellipsis comma 9 comma 0](images/c14-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, which is different from the order in Python (as ![0 comma 1 comma ellipsis comma 9](images/c14-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></math>). Lastly, the zero rows in the matrix are omitted in **R**. The prediction accuracy of 0.5848 is close to that obtained in Python.

Next, we perform PCA on the training dataset and choose the number of PCs that explain 95% of the total variance, that is, the first 154 PCs (referring to [Programme 10.28](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3028) via Python and [Programme 10.29](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3029) via **R**), then compute the corresponding PCs for the testing data points, which serve as the feature variables for ![upper K](images/c14-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering. From the outputs from Python in [Programme 14.21](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3021) and from **R** in [Programme 14.22](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3022), we observe that the resulting prediction accuracy remains at the same level of around 0.585. Furthermore, the implementation of this hybrid method takes less time than the standard ![upper K](images/c14-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering on Python, while on **R**, it is more time‐consuming.

In fact, if all the PCs are used in the example above, then the prediction accuracies of ![upper K](images/c14-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering with and without PCA should be exactly the same under an appropriate choice of initial seeds. This result can be verified using Python and **R** by slightly modifying the respective codes, which is left as a programming exercise for readers. To see this mathematically, suppose that the initial seeds in the direct ![upper K](images/c14-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering (with input data points ![bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline](images/c14-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>) are ![bold-italic c 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic c Subscript upper K Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>. Then for the PCA‐incorporated version of ![upper K](images/c14-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, using ![bold-italic y Subscript i Baseline equals bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0366.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math> as the input data, where ![bold-italic upper H](images/c14-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow></math> is a ![p times p](images/c14-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></math> orthogonal matrix of loading vectors for PCs (also see [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml)), we set ![bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic c 1 Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic c Subscript upper K Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> as the initial seeds. The distance metric ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic c Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2](images/c14-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> involved in the updating step (14.3) of Lloyd's algorithm becomes ![double-vertical-bar bold-italic y Subscript i Baseline minus bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack Baseline bold-italic c Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Superscript 2](images/c14-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>; ## 14.2 ![upper K](images/c14-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NEAREST NEIGHBOUR

Having obtained clustering results, the next stage is the cluster prediction of new observations. One of the most popular approaches is the ![upper K](images/c14-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐Nearest Neighbour algorithm* (![upper K](images/c14-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN), an example of *lazy‐learning*

**(I)** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>**‐NN classification**

In the ![upper K](images/c14-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm, the distance metric (or dis‐similarity) between the unlabelled observation and each existing one in the dataset is computed. The labels of the nearest (or most similar) ![upper K](images/c14-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> data points are then collected and counted, and the resulting class with the highest frequency is used to label the observation in question; see [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008) for an illustration.

In particular, in view of the majority voting nature of ![upper K](images/c14-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN classification, the parameter ![upper K](images/c14-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is usually chosen as an odd number to avoid ties, yet the classification result may differ with ![upper K](images/c14-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. Take [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008) as an example, namely classifying the unlabelled observation (the green spot at the center) as either a blue square or red diamond. When ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, the closest three observations involve two blue squares and one red diamond, hence the observation will be classified as a blue square. However, when ![upper K equals 9](images/c14-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, the classification result becomes red diamond instead as there are 4 blue squares and 5 red diamonds among the 9 closest observations.

Notationally, we assume a dataset with ![n](images/c14-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> data points partitioned into ![c](images/c14-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> classes, ![left-brace bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-brace](images/c14-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>, ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma c](images/c14-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></math> and ![i equals 1 comma 2 ellipsis comma n Subscript k Baseline](images/c14-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, where ![n Subscript k](images/c14-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is the number of data points in the ![k](images/c14-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th class. For general values of ![upper K](images/c14-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, we classify ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> by the most frequently occurring class label among the ![upper K](images/c14-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest data points. For ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma c](images/c14-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></math> and ![i equals 1 comma 2 ellipsis comma n Subscript k Baseline](images/c14-i0406.png)<math display="inline"
