mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, in ascending order. Then among the ![upper K](images/c14-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest data points, the number of observations in class ![k](images/c14-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is ![upper K Subscript k Baseline colon equals StartAbsoluteValue script upper K Subscript k Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c14-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>, where ![script upper K Subscript k Baseline colon equals StartSet i colon r Subscript bold-italic x Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to upper K EndSet](images/c14-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> represents the collection of these points. The classification result ![m Subscript bold-italic x](images/c14-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub></math> for ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is then the majority class:

![m Subscript bold-italic x Baseline colon equals arg max Underscript k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma c Endscripts upper K Subscript k Baseline period](images/c14-math-0023.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;max </mtext><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

In the special simple case of ![upper K equals 1](images/c14-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0418.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is classified using the nearest data point and we have:

![m Subscript bold-italic x Baseline equals arg min Underscript k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma c Endscripts left-parenthesis min Underscript i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n Subscript k Baseline Endscripts double-vertical-bar bold-italic x minus bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 2 Baseline right-parenthesis period](images/c14-math-0024.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;min</mtext><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> ![FIGURE 14.8 Illustration of upper K‐NN classification, the newly added point is identified as blue square if upper K equals 3, but red diamond if upper K equals 9.](images/c14f008.png)

[**FIGURE 14.8**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0008) Illustration of ![upper K](images/c14-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN classification, the newly added point is identified as blue square if ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, but red diamond if ![upper K equals 9](images/c14-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>.

When the sample size is small, the performance of ![upper K](images/c14-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN is very sensitive to the choice of ![upper K](images/c14-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and the distance metric. In comparison with ![upper K](images/c14-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering, which identifies the regions of different classes in the feature space, ![upper K](images/c14-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN relies on the labels of the neighbouring data points of a new observation. This explains its suitability for handling out‐samples with overlapping class regions. On the other hand, the straightforward design of ![upper K](images/c14-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN also leads to several drawbacks. For one thing, the ranking of distance metric from each ![bold-italic x Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> to ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0425.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> may be computationally expensive when the sample size is large. We can mitigate this issue by taking data points less significant to classification out of consideration at the preprocessing step. Another issue is that in the event of an imbalanced sample, a new observation from the minority class is more likely to be misclassified. Motivated by the intuition that minority observations often stay close to one another, we may tackle this issue by assigning weights to each of the ![upper K](images/c14-i0426.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest points which are disproportional to their actual distance to the data point in question.

**(II)** ![bold-italic upper K](images/c14-i0427.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi></mrow></math>**‐NN Regression**

Besides classification, ![upper K](images/c14-i0428.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN can also be applied in a regression context, like the approach via CART; for example, see [\[14\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0014). Recall that we can assign a larger weight to data points closer to a new observation ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> so as to reduce the misclassification rate for one from the minority class due to an imbalanced sample.

To predict the label of a new observation, we again focus on its ![upper K](images/c14-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest data points, and the predicted label is then the average label of these ![upper K](images/c14-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> data points:

![ModifyingAbove m With caret equals StartFraction 1 Over upper K EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript r Subscript bold-italic x Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to upper K Endscripts t Subscript i Baseline comma](images/c14-math-0025.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![t Subscript i](images/c14-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the label of the ![i](images/c14-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th data point ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in the dataset. Despite the simplicity of the prediction formula, the performance of the fitted ![upper K](images/c14-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN model may be severely affected by the choice of the hyperparameter ![upper K](images/c14-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, which is fairly arbitrary in practice. Furthermore, an equal weight is assigned to each of the ![upper K](images/c14-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest data points, while those observations close to the new one should be more important in the prediction task. It is more reasonable for them to receive higher weights compared with others farther away from the new observation. Besides the possible modifications on the ![upper K](images/c14-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm to be introduced below, another common resolution to address these drawbacks is simply taking all data points into consideration, corresponding to the case of ![upper K equals infinity](images/c14-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, and introducing an appropriate weight function, also known as a *kernel function* ![Kernel left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Kernel</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, that decreases with the distance metric between ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic y](images/c14-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math>. The resulting prediction formula for the label of the new observation then becomes:

![ModifyingAbove m With caret equals sigma-summation Underscript i Endscripts StartFraction Kernel left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript j Endscripts Kernel left-parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction t Subscript i Baseline period](images/c14-math-0026.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Kernel</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>j</mi></msub><mtext> Kernel</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

In the context of a more generic tool of *Kernel Regression* (to be introduced in the next section), we shall see that this formula has the same form as the renowned *Nadaraya–Watson estimator* for a special scenario in kernel regression. To this end, while kernel regression does not include ![upper K](images/c14-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression as a special case, it does try to tackle the aforementioned drawbacks of the latter.

**(III) Enhancing the Algorithm**

Another characteristic of ![upper K](images/c14-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN is its sensitivity to noise. Isolated points in the sample may cause a drastic impact on the result of classification and regression. These outliers can be eliminated by an *a priori* filtering and selection procedure. Meanwhile, the choice of ![upper K](images/c14-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> may also significantly affect the outcome, as illustrated in [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008). To remedy these shortcomings, let us introduce some modifications to the plain ![upper K](images/c14-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm.

**Ensemble (Learning) Methods**

In general, ensemble methods aim to improve the performance of a learning model by considering several independent models. The output is usually inferred from the results of voting from these collections of models. Depending on the weights assigned to each model, the voting is called *uniform voting* if all models share the same weight, or *weighted voting* otherwise. This general concept can also be applied to ![upper K](images/c14-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN for either classification or regression. We first randomly select multiple subsets of features and fit ![upper K](images/c14-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN models against the newly added observation accordingly. The predicted label of the classification (resp. regression) is then determined by voting (resp. taking a weighted average) among the outputs from these models. This is also known as *Random Subspace Ensemble* ![upper K](images/c14-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>*‐NN*; also see [\[12\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0012) for details.

**Kernel Methods**

The kernel methods here (see [\[25\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0025)) refer to the kernel trick of radial basis functions discussed in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0003), and should be distinguished from the kernel functions in ![upper K](images/c14-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression or kernel regression. Recall that under the kernel trick, each sample ![bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> is mapped to a higher dimensional feature space, say ![double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c14-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> with ![q greater-than p](images/c14-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, to untangle the overlapping clusters in the hope of achieving linear separability of the samples in ![double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c14-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math>.

Here, we briefly describe the implementation of kernel methods in ![upper K](images/c14-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN. Let the transformation be ![bold upper Phi colon double-struck upper R Superscript p Baseline right-arrow double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c14-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math>, so that the sample ![StartSet bold-italic x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline EndSet](images/c14-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is mapped to ![StartSet bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x 1 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c14-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Let ![upper K left-parenthesis dot comma dot right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> be the kernel function, then for any ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic x Subscript j](images/c14-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, it is defined in such a way that

![d left-parenthesis bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma bold upper Phi left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals upper K left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c14-math-0027.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![d left-parenthesis dot comma dot right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0462.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a distance function defined on ![double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c14-i0463.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math>. As we introduced in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0003), the kernel ![upper K left-parenthesis dot comma dot right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is usually proposed directly rather than the transformation ![bold upper Phi](images/c14-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi></mrow></math>. The implementation of ![upper K](images/c14-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN under this framework can be shown to greatly improve the performance, especially in a low‐dimensional setting in which the features are not linearly separable.

**Prior Clustering**

A sample can be clustered first (e.g., by ![upper K](images/c14-i0467.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means) before implementing the ![upper K](images/c14-i0468.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm; see [\[26\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0026). Roughly speaking, given a clustered sample and a new observation ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0469.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, we first calculate its distance to the centroid of each cluster, and accordingly denote ![script upper S Subscript left-parenthesis i right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0470.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>, as the ![i](images/c14-i0471.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th nearest cluster. Taking these clusters into account, the ![upper K](images/c14-i0472.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest neighbors can then be selected as follows: calculate the distance between the newly added observation ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0473.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and each of the points in ![script upper S Subscript left-parenthesis 1 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0474.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>, and one‐by‐one include those points, each of which has a distance from ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0475.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> smaller than a pre‐set threshold, into the set of neighbouring points of ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0476.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>, in ascending order of the distances. The procedure is repeated for ![i equals 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis](images/c14-i0477.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math> until there are ![upper K](images/c14-i0478.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> points in the set of neighboring points of ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0479.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>. Then ![bold-italic x](images/c14-i0480.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> attains its predicted label ![i 0](images/c14-i0481.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> such that ![script upper S Subscript left-parenthesis i 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0482.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> has the largest number of elements in this ![upper K](images/c14-i0483.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐point list.

**(IV) Application of** ![upper K](images/c14-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>**‐NN Algorithm**

While ![upper K](images/c14-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN can be used for general classification or regression tasks, it is widely applied in facial recognition. Typically, given an observation of a human face, we aim to infer certain characteristics of the person, such as age and ethnicity, using the information of the ![upper K](images/c14-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> most similar faces in the training dataset. A general procedure is described as follows, assuming that there are ![upper M](images/c14-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> possible class labels in total:

1.  For the ![i](images/c14-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th human face in the training dataset of size ![n](images/c14-i0489.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, extract its values of pre‐specified list of ![p](images/c14-i0490.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> features, possibly determined by principal components or more generally dictionary learning as discussed in [Section 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0002), and store them as the feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i p Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c14-i0491.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> for this face, for ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma n](images/c14-i0492.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></math>.
2.  Identify the feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1](images/c14-i0493.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> of the newly added human face.
3.  Identify the ![upper K](images/c14-i0494.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> nearest faces in the training set using the following (signed) similarity measure of cosine as the criterion: ![Sim left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals StartFraction sigma-summation Underscript Subscript i j](images/c14-i0495.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, where ![theta Subscript i j](images/c14-i0496.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the angle between ![bold-italic x Subscript i](images/c14-i0497.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold-italic x Subscript j](images/c14-i0498.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. In other words, we determine the ![upper K](images/c14-i0499.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> feature vectors that are closest in direction to ![bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1](images/c14-i0500.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and store them in a set ![script upper P Subscript upper K](images/c14-i0501.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi></mrow><mi>K</mi></msub></math>.
4.  For each class label ![c Subscript k](images/c14-i0502.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper M](images/c14-i0503.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math>, we calculate the following weight for the new photo with the feature vector ![bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1](images/c14-i0504.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>: [(14.9)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0029)![w Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis colon equals sigma-summation Underscript bold-italic x element-of script upper P Subscript upper K Baseline comma c left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals c Subscript k Baseline Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over 1 minus Sim left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline comma bold-italic x right-parenthesis EndFraction period](images/c14-math-0029.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi></mrow><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>Sim</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></math> 
5.  The new photo is then classified as the label that maximizes the weight ([14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0029)), i.e., ![ModifyingAbove k With caret equals arg max Underscript k Endscripts w Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic x Subscript n plus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0505.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>arg&#8201;max </mtext><mi>k</mi></munder><mspace width="-.1em"/><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Let us illustrate the idea in [Programme 14.23](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3023) via Python using the same dataset for facial recognition as used in [Programme 9.23](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3023). Note that the Python function `KNeighborsClassifier()` from the `sklearn.neighbors` library is used to perform ![upper K](images/c14-i0506.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN, and the function requires three input arguments, namely `n_neighbors=K` for the value of the hyperparameter ![upper K](images/c14-i0507.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, the number of nearest neighbours considered; `metric="cosine"` for using the cosine similarity metric described in Item 3 above; and `weight="distance"` for weighting the points by the inverse of their distance as described in ([14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0029)). Recall that the photos in [Programme 9.23](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3023) are not shuffled, and are arranged such that each individual has 9 faces and they are sorted in sequence, and stored in `y_train`. [Programme 14.23](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3023) demonstrates the implementation of ![upper K](images/c14-i0508.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN with a generally adopted choice of hyperparameter ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0509.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, using the 107 PCs obtained in [Section 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0009) as the features. It achieves a high accuracy of ![StartFraction 39 Over 40 EndFraction equals 97.5 percent-sign](images/c14-i0510.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>39</mn><mn>40</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>97.5</mn><mi>%</mi></math> and there is only one wrong recognition for the 34th individual. Indeed, the output weight vector for this individual contains only two positive weights, namely 0.3079 and 0.6921 on the 34th and 39th position, respectively, and the predicted label is determined to be 39 as it has the greater weight.

We also revisit the MNIST dataset, this time using the ![upper K](images/c14-i0511.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm. For simplicity, we select ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0512.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> as in the previous example. As before, we first execute a standard direct ![upper K](images/c14-i0513.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm as a benchmark. From the outputs obtained in [Programme 14.24](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3024) via Python, the prediction accuracy of the ![upper K](images/c14-i0514.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm with ![upper K equals 3](images/c14-i0515.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> on the test dataset is 0.9705, which is higher than the 0.9256 obtained in the logistic regression model coded in [Programme 10.17](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3017) via Python. Furthermore, due to the fact that ![upper K](images/c14-i0516.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN is a lazy algorithm, namely it does not process the training dataset until a prediction needs to be made, the running time for the Python programme is just about 6 seconds, much faster than the logistic regression (1 minute) in [Programme 10.17](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3017) and the ![upper K](images/c14-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering (15 seconds) in [Programme 14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3019). While the implementation via **R** in [Programme 14.25](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3025), with the `knn()` function in the `class` library, yields a similar testing accuracy of 0.9716, it is much more time‐consuming with the running time of over an hour

As in [Section 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0002), we also investigate the effect of PCA on the ![upper K](images/c14-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm, by reusing the PCs selected in the example of ![upper K](images/c14-i0519.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering as the feature variable inputs for ![upper K](images/c14-i0520.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN. From the outputs obtained in [Programme 14.26](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3026) via Python and [Programme 14.27](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3027) via **R**, the testing accuracy of ![upper K](images/c14-i0521.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN still remains at around 0.97 without notable improvements, yet the running time for **R** on a common desktop computer greatly reduces from over an hour to just roughly 2.5 minutes thanks to the dimension reduction. The unimproven accuracy comes as no surprise; once again, if all PCs are involved, then the Euclidean distances will not change upon applying the linear transform ![bold-italic upper H Superscript down-tack](images/c14-i0522.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> to the original data points, as shown in ([14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0020)), and the resulting ![upper K](images/c14-i0523.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN with PCA is then equivalent to the original version of ![upper K](images/c14-i0524.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN, with exactly the same prediction accuracy.

We conclude this example by remarking that, although the testing accuracy of around 97% is already satisfactory, we can improve on this with various new tools from Deep Learning, e.g. the *Multilayer Perceptron* (an accuracy of 97.83%) or a *Convolutional Neural Network* (an accuracy of 99.02%). We shall introduce the former in [Chapter 15](#c15.xhtml), while the latter is beyond the scope of this book, and it will be discussed in detail in [\[6\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0006).

 

## \*14.3 KERNEL REGRESSION

While ![upper K](images/c14-i0525.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering mainly focuses on separating out distinguishable clusters, there is still the puzzle of a prediction for the label of a new datum, which is the ultimate goal of clustering analysis. This is what ![upper K](images/c14-i0526.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression does in the previous section. One apparent drawback of ![upper K](images/c14-i0527.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression is the lack of clear guidelines for choosing ![upper K](images/c14-i0528.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. A commonly adopted alternative approach is to take all data points into consideration, corresponding to the case of ![upper K equals infinity](images/c14-i0529.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>. In light of this, we shall revisit a versatile tool of kernel regression in functional regression analysis, where we investigate a special case of a particular regressor called the *Nadaraya–Watson estimator* (see \[19, 27\]), which resembles the formula for ![upper K](images/c14-i0530.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression with ![upper K equals infinity](images/c14-i0531.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>. This greatly enriches the content of ![upper K](images/c14-i0532.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN and its use in practice.

Recall that the fundamental task in regression analysis is the prediction of the response vector ![bold y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c14-i0533.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> using the feature vector ![bold-italic x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c14-i0534.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>. A key quantity of interest in this scenario is the conditional mean ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis bold y bar bold x equals bold-italic x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0535.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. For the sake of simplicity, in this section we discuss the asymptotic theory for the simplest case of ![p equals q equals 1](images/c14-i0536.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> only, while the argument for the general case is essentially the same but involves more tedious notations. The general regression framework takes the following form:

![normal y equals m left-parenthesis normal x right-parenthesis plus normal epsilon comma](images/c14-math-0030.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0537.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is an unknown function of ![x](images/c14-i0538.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, ![normal epsilon](images/c14-i0539.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> and ![normal x](images/c14-i0540.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow></math> are uncorrelated, and ![double-struck upper E left-parenthesis normal epsilon bar normal x equals x right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c14-i0541.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. We define ![sigma squared left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis colon equals upper V a r left-parenthesis normal epsilon bar normal x equals x right-parenthesis equals upper V a r left-parenthesis normal y bar normal x equals x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0542.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. We often assume that ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0543.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is piecewise smooth, such that it is of class ![upper C Superscript k](images/c14-i0544.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> for the interior points and ![upper C Superscript k minus 1](images/c14-i0545.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> at the knots (boundary‐splitting points); here ![upper C Superscript k](images/c14-i0546.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> indicates that the derivatives up to the ![k](images/c14-i0547.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th order exist and are continuous. Then for a given point ![x 0 element-of double-struck upper R](images/c14-i0548.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, we expect that ![m left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0549.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> should be close to ![m left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0550.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for any observed value ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0551.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in the proximity of ![x 0](images/c14-i0552.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>. Therefore, a reasonable estimate for ![m left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0553.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> would be an average of the observed responses ![y Subscript i](images/c14-i0554.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s corresponding to those ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0555.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s.

By Taylor expansion of ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0556.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> up to order ![k](images/c14-i0557.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> at ![x 0](images/c14-i0558.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, in the proximity of ![x 0](images/c14-i0559.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, we have:

stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mo columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

which resembles a parametric model, with parameters ![left-brace beta Subscript j Baseline colon equals m Superscript left-parenthesis j right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis slash j factorial right-brace Subscript j equals 0 Superscript k](images/c14-i0560.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>!</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. While these can be estimated by parametric regression techniques using the observed data ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0561.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s scattered around ![x 0](images/c14-i0562.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, the results of this apparently local approach may deviate significantly if different datasets in closer or farther neighborhoods of ![x 0](images/c14-i0563.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> are used. Worse still, in the event of a sparse dataset, the limited number of observations near ![x 0](images/c14-i0564.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> further reduces the accuracy of estimates.

To remedy this shortcoming, we instead adopt a weighted least square approach by considering the following optimization problem which involves the full dataset ![left-brace left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c14-i0565.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>:

![min Underscript beta 0 comma ellipsis comma beta Subscript k Baseline Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus beta 0 minus beta 1 left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline minus x 0 right-parenthesis minus midline-horizontal-ellipsis minus beta Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline minus x 0 right-parenthesis Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis squared upper K Subscript h Sub Subscript n Subscript Baseline left-parenthesis x 0 minus x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c14-math-0032.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the weighting function ![upper K Subscript h Sub Subscript n](images/c14-i0566.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> is called a *kernel function*, and ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0567.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is its bandwidth, the subscript of which indicates that its choice usually depends on the sample size ![n](images/c14-i0568.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. This method is hence named *Kernel Regression*. The role of ![upper K Subscript h Sub Subscript n](images/c14-i0569.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> is to control the amount of effect brought by each sample point ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0570.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> so that its contribution to the estimation of ![beta Subscript j](images/c14-i0571.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>'s depends on the distance between ![x 0](images/c14-i0572.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and its own feature value ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0573.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Naturally, we expect a non‐increasing contribution as the distance increases; indeed, the following common choice of ![upper K Subscript h Sub Subscript n](images/c14-i0574.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> reflects this desired trend: ![upper K Subscript h Sub Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis x 0 minus x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction x 0 minus x Subscript i Baseline Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0575.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>, where ![upper K](images/c14-i0576.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is independent of ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0577.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, satisfying the following technical requirements:

1.  ![upper K left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0578.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a positive function, and ![integral Underscript double-struck upper R Endscripts upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis d u equals 1](images/c14-i0579.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></msub><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>;
2.  ![upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis equals upper K left-parenthesis negative u right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0580.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, i.e., ![upper K](images/c14-i0581.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is symmetric about the origin; and
3.  ![upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0582.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> attains its global maximum at ![u equals 0](images/c14-i0583.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, indicating that the weights are larger for the observations ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0584.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s that are close to ![x 0](images/c14-i0585.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>.

Several commonly adopted choices of kernel functions are the following:

1.  Uniform kernel (a.k.a. Box kernel): ![upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis equals one half double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace StartAbsoluteValue u EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 1 right-brace](images/c14-i0586.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math>;
2.  Gaussian kernel: ![upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over StartRoot 2 pi EndRoot EndFraction exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction u squared Over 2 EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0587.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>;
3.  *Epanechnikov* kernel: ![upper K left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis equals three fourths left-parenthesis 1 minus u squared right-parenthesis double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace StartAbsoluteValue u EndAbsoluteValue less-than-or-equal-to 1 right-brace Baseline period](images/c14-i0588.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="double-struck">1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math>

See [Figure 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0009) for the illustrations of the plots of these functions. We notice that despite the discrepancy in numerical results using different kernels, in practice they yield comparable estimates with carefully selected bandwidths ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0589.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>'s.

![FIGURE 14.9 Illustrations of three commonly adopted kernel functions.](images/c14f009.png)

[**FIGURE 14.9**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0009) Illustrations of three commonly adopted kernel functions.

Next, we illustrate the construction of an estimate ![ModifyingAbove m With caret left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0590.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for the simplest case of ![k equals 1](images/c14-i0591.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, when ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0592.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is approximated by a constant ![beta 0 equals m left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0593.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for a pre‐specified ![x 0 element-of double-struck upper R](images/c14-i0594.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>. As we shall show in the following, the estimate is a weighted average of the responses mainly contributed by those observations whose feature variables ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0595.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s lie in a close proximity of ![x 0](images/c14-i0596.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>. This resulting optimization problem is also known as *local constant regression* (also see [\[16\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0016)), with the following problem specification:

[(14.10)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0033)![min Underscript beta 0 Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction x 0 minus x Subscript i Baseline Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus beta 0 right-parenthesis squared comma x 0 element-of double-struck upper R period](images/c14-math-0033.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></munder><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Differentiating the objective function in ([14.10](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0033)) with respect to ![beta 0](images/c14-i0597.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and equating it with 0, we arrive at the following first order condition:

![minus StartFraction 2 Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction x 0 minus x Subscript i Baseline Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus beta 0 right-parenthesis equals 0 comma](images/c14-math-0034.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></math> 

resulting in the following estimate:

Its estimator version, with ![left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0598.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> replaced by ![left-parenthesis normal x Subscript i Baseline comma normal y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0599.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is called the *Nadaraya–Watson estimator* ![ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0600.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (see [\[19](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0019), [27\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0027)) for ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0601.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with ![x equals x 0](images/c14-i0602.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>:

where ![double-vertical-bar dot double-vertical-bar Subscript 2](images/c14-i0605.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></math> denotes the Euclidean norm. Again, echoing [Section 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0005), the ![upper K](images/c14-i0606.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐NN regression where ![upper K equals infinity](images/c14-i0607.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> resembles the Nadaraya–Watson estimator.

Under some regularity conditions (to be introduced later in this section), the bias and variance of ![ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0608.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> possess the following boundedness properties, where ![upper C 1 comma upper C 2 greater-than 0](images/c14-i0609.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> are some constants:

*   ![Bias left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals double-struck upper E left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis minus m left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0610.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Bias</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> has a magnitude less than ![upper C 1 h Subscript n Superscript 2](images/c14-i0611.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>;
*   ![upper V a r left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to StartFraction upper C 2 Over n h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c14-i0612.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">Var</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>.

Clearly, as the bandwidth ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0613.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> decreases, the estimator ![ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0614.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> tends to be less biased but more volatile. Thus, a larger ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0615.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> is more likely to result in a smoother estimate ![ModifyingAbove m With caret left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0616.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, while a smaller ![h Subscript n](images/c14-i0617.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> may lead to a more oscillatory ![ModifyingAbove m With caret left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0618.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Altogether, this phenomenon is sometimes called the *bias‐variance tradeoff* in the context of statistical machine learning. The optimal bandwidth that minimizes the sum of ![left-parenthesis bias right-parenthesis squared plus](images/c14-i0619.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>bias</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo></math> variance is then of the order of ![n Superscript negative 1 slash 5](images/c14-i0620.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></math>.

Alternatively, the Nadaraya–Watson estimator can also be motivated using the kernel density estimator of an unknown density function ![f Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0621.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, also known as the *Rosenblatt–Parzen kernel density estimator* (see [\[21](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0021), [24\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0024)):

[(14.12)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0038)![ModifyingAbove normal f With Ì‚ Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over n h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction x minus normal x Subscript i Baseline Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis period](images/c14-math-0038.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

The construction of the Rosenblatt–Parzen kernel density estimator is motivated by the original empirical distribution. To see why, we recall that the empirical cdf of an iid sample ![left-brace normal x Subscript i Baseline right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript n](images/c14-i0622.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, is defined by ![ModifyingAbove normal upper F With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace normal x Sub Subscript i Subscript less-than-or-equal-to x right-brace](images/c14-i0623.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">1</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math>. Because ![double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace normal x Sub Subscript i Subscript less-than-or-equal-to x right-brace](images/c14-i0624.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">1</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></math> can be thought of as changing infinitely rapidly from 0 to 1 at ![x](images/c14-i0625.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> while staying unchanged everywhere else, we can interpret its formal derivative as a Dirac delta function (formally, as a generalized function, Dirac delta ![delta Subscript z Baseline left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis equals plus infinity](images/c14-i0626.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> at ![u equals z](images/c14-i0627.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></math> and equals 0 elsewhere, such that ![integral Underscript double-struck upper R Endscripts delta Subscript z Baseline left-parenthesis u right-parenthesis d u equals 1](images/c14-i0628.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>). Therefore, as a formal “derivative”, the empirical density function can be taken to be ![StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts delta Subscript normal x Sub Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0629.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. As a kernel, ![StartFraction 1 Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction x minus normal x Subscript i Baseline Over h Subscript n Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0630.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> mimics the behaviour of ![delta Subscript normal x Sub Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0631.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> asymptotically, and so it is reasonable to estimate the density by using ([14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0038)). Indeed, ![ModifyingAbove normal f With Ì‚ Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0632.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a valid density as ![integral Underscript double-struck upper R Endscripts ModifyingAbove normal f With Ì‚ Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis d x equals 1](images/c14-i0633.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8747;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> by the properties of ![upper K left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0634.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Furthermore, for each ![x](images/c14-i0635.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, the estimator converges to the true density ![f Subscript normal x Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0636.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in probability under some regularity conditions. Meanwhile, recall the case for a general value of order ![k](images/c14-i0664.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0665.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is approximated by a ![k](images/c14-i0666.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐th order polynomial in ![x minus x 0](images/c14-i0667.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> for a fixed ![x 0 element-of double-struck upper R](images/c14-i0668.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>, and the resulting estimator is called the *local polynomial kernel regression estimator*; see [\[9\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0009) for a detailed discussion. The solution to this problem is the following weighted least squares estimate:
