Let us illustrate the use of kernel regression through the following simulation. In [Programme 14.28](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3028) via Python and [Programme 14.29](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3029) via **R**, we generate a random sample of size ![n equals 500](images/c14-i0673.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></math> from ![normal x tilde script upper N left-parenthesis 2 comma 16 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0674.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Then for each observed ![x Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma 500](images/c14-i0675.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>500</mn></math>, we generate the corresponding response ![y Subscript i](images/c14-i0676.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> by the following model:

![normal y Subscript i Baseline equals m left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis plus normal epsilon Subscript i Baseline comma](images/c14-math-0048.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis colon equals x squared cosine x](images/c14-i0677.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi><mi>x</mi></math> and ![normal epsilon Subscript i Baseline tilde Overscript i i d Endscripts script upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma 4 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0678.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mover class="overset"><mo>&#8764;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mover><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The Nadaraya–Watson estimates ![ModifyingAbove m With caret left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0679.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for values of ![x](images/c14-i0680.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from ![negative 15](images/c14-i0681.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>15</mn></math> to 15 with an increment of 0.3 are then calculated with the bandwidth ![h Subscript n Baseline equals 0.5](images/c14-i0682.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math>, and they are plotted together with the true underlying function ![m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0683.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as defined above; see [Figure 14.10](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0010). It can be observed from the plots that the estimates are fairly close to (resp. deviate from) the true values for those ![x](images/c14-i0684.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>'s close to (resp. far from) 0, which can be justified by the sample generation for ![x Subscript i](images/c14-i0685.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>'s. Indeed, most of the observed values lie within two standard deviations from the mean, that is, in the interval ![left-bracket negative 6 comma 10 right-bracket](images/c14-i0686.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, hence the estimates tend to be more accurate when ![x](images/c14-i0687.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> also falls within this interval.

![FIGURE 14.10 Comparison of Nadaraya–Watson estimates and the true underlying function m left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x squared cosine x.](images/c14f010.png)

**Bias and Variance of** ![ModifyingAbove bold m With Ì‚](images/c14-i0689.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>

Next, we present a rigorous analysis regarding the bias and variance of the Nadaraya–Watson estimator ![ModifyingAbove normal m With Ì‚ left-parenthesis x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0690.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> at any pre‐specified point ![x 0 element-of double-struck upper R](images/c14-i0691.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>. To this end, we lay down the following regularity conditions:

We shall claim that asymptotically the CH index attains its maximum value at ![upper L equals upper K](images/c14-i0751.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, the true cluster number. According to the classical reference [\[4\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004), “*there is no satisfactory probabilistic foundation to support the use of CH index*”, and there have not been any further significant breakthroughs along this direction in the literature until now, as echoed in the *Wikipedia* entry for CH index

Let us state our assumptions and notations. Although the CH index as a clustering metric to evaluate the appropriateness of the hyperparameter ![upper K](images/c14-i0794.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> shows good performances in many practical examples such as those in this chapter, it still fails in an obvious manner in some cases; this issue is also briefly mentioned in [\[4\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004), while we shall provide a mathematical discussion as follows. For instance, consider the data points generated by uniform distribution with the support ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0795.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, and we assume that the true clusters are ![left-bracket 0 comma StartFraction 1 Over upper K EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0796.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></math>, ![left-bracket StartFraction 1 Over upper K EndFraction comma StartFraction 2 Over upper K EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0797.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></math>, ![midline-horizontal-ellipsis](images/c14-i0798.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8943;</mi></mrow></math>, ![left-bracket StartFraction upper K minus 1 Over upper K EndFraction comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0799.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo></math> with points generated uniformly from each bucket for some positive integer ![upper K](images/c14-i0800.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. In the limiting case of ![n right-arrow infinity](images/c14-i0801.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, suppose that an ![upper L](images/c14-i0802.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>‐means clustering is applied to the dataset, then by symmetry, the resulting ![upper L](images/c14-i0803.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> clusters are the ![upper L](images/c14-i0804.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> equal‐length subintervals of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0805.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, namely ![left-bracket 0 comma StartFraction 1 Over upper L EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0806.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></math>, ![left-bracket StartFraction 1 Over upper L EndFraction comma StartFraction 2 Over upper L EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0807.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></math>, ![midline-horizontal-ellipsis](images/c14-i0808.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8943;</mi></mrow></math>, ![left-bracket StartFraction upper L minus 1 Over upper L EndFraction comma 1 right-bracket](images/c14-i0809.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo></math>. 

based on which we have

![r Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis long right-arrow Overscript p Endscripts StartFraction 1 Over upper L minus 1 EndFraction StartStartFraction one twelfth minus StartFraction 1 Over 12 upper L squared EndFraction OverOver StartFraction 1 Over 12 upper L squared EndFraction EndEndFraction equals upper L plus 1 as n right-arrow infinity comma](images/c14-math-0069.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover class="overset"><mo>&#x027F6;</mo><mi>p</mi></mover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>12</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;&#160;as&#160;</mtext><mspace width="0.25em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

so ![r Subscript n Baseline left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0819.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is asymptotically affinely increasing with ![upper L](images/c14-i0820.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>. In this case, the CH index loses its power as an evaluating metric for clustering; indeed, without the presence of natural clusters, no point can be more representative of its neighborhood than the others, hence as argued in [\[4\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004), “*no reasonably better partition of the points exists than that into individuals*”. Instead, when a *concentration effect* emerges so that natural clusters are clearly observed (for example, if the data points in each true cluster are normally distributed), and the distances among true cluster means are significantly greater than the standard deviation within any true cluster, the CH index can reach a maximum at the true value of ![upper K](images/c14-i0821.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. In the following, we shall make an attempt to provide a set of sufficient conditions that warrant the optimality of ![r Subscript infinity Baseline left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0822.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> at ![upper L equals upper K](images/c14-i0823.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi></math>.

To this end, we first introduce different possible groupings to the collection of all artificial clusters: let us denote ![upper B Subscript k Baseline colon equals upper B Subscript a delta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic mu Subscript vertical-bar k dot Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0824.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![upper F Subscript l Baseline equals StartSet bold x Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar upper F left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals l EndSet](images/c14-i0825.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Using these, we define

1.  ![script upper A 1](images/c14-i0826.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>: for every ![l element-of script upper A 1](images/c14-i0827.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, the artificial cluster ![upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0828.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> contains all the points in one ball but no more points from any other ball, i.e., there is exactly one ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c14-i0829.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> such that ![upper B Subscript k Baseline subset-of-or-equal-to upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0830.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8838;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> but ![upper B Subscript k prime Baseline intersection upper F Subscript l Baseline equals empty-set](images/c14-i0831.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo>&#8745;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math> for any ![k prime not-equals k](images/c14-i0832.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>. 
2.  ![script upper A 2](images/c14-i0833.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>: for every ![l element-of script upper A 2](images/c14-i0834.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, the artificial cluster ![upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0835.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> contains the points from one ball but not exactly all its points, and it contains no points from any other ball, i.e. there is exactly one ![k equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper K](images/c14-i0836.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> such that ![upper B Subscript k Baseline intersection upper F Subscript l Baseline equals empty-set](images/c14-i0837.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8745;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math> but ![upper B Subscript k Baseline neither-a-subset-of-nor-equal-to upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0838.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8840;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math>, while ![upper B Subscript k prime Baseline intersection upper F Subscript l Baseline equals empty-set](images/c14-i0839.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo>&#8745;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math> for all ![k prime not-equals k](images/c14-i0840.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>. 
3.  ![script upper A 3](images/c14-i0841.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math>: for every ![l element-of script upper A 3](images/c14-i0842.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math>, the artificial cluster ![upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0843.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> contains points from more than one ball ![upper B Subscript k](images/c14-i0844.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>. 
4.  ![script upper A 4](images/c14-i0845.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></msub></math>: for every ![l element-of script upper A 4](images/c14-i0846.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></msub></math>, the artificial cluster ![upper F Subscript l](images/c14-i0847.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> is disjoint from all balls ![upper B Subscript k](images/c14-i0848.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>'s. 
    
    [Figure 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0011) illustrates two possible scenarios. On the left, ![upper K equals 4](images/c14-i0853.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and ![upper L equals 3](images/c14-i0854.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, ![script upper A 1 equals StartSet 1 comma 2 EndSet](images/c14-i0855.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, ![script upper A 2 equals empty-set](images/c14-i0856.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math> and ![script upper A 3 equals StartSet 3 EndSet](images/c14-i0857.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. On the right, there are four true clusters and five artificial clusters such that ![script upper A 1 equals StartSet 3 comma 4 EndSet](images/c14-i0858.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, ![script upper A 2 equals StartSet 1 comma 2 EndSet](images/c14-i0859.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> and ![script upper A 3 equals StartSet 5 EndSet](images/c14-i0860.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Next, we state the assumption that confines the sizes of variances and the distances between true cluster means. Combined, these hint at why the optimality of CH index is attained at the true cluster number ![upper K](images/c14-i0861.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>.

    then we have ![r Subscript infinity Baseline left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis less-than r Subscript infinity Baseline left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0884.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.
    
    Let us show by contradiction that ![script upper A 3](images/c14-i0885.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> contains at least one artificial cluster when ![upper L less-than upper K](images/c14-i0886.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>K</mi></math>. If ![script upper A 3 equals empty-set](images/c14-i0887.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math>, we clearly have ![StartAbsoluteValue script upper A 2 EndAbsoluteValue greater-than-or-equal-to upper K minus StartAbsoluteValue script upper A 1 EndAbsoluteValue](images/c14-i0888.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> by the definition of ![script upper A 2](images/c14-i0889.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. This, together with the fact that ![script upper A 4](images/c14-i0890.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></msub></math> contains no true clusters at all, shows that the number of artificial clusters is more than ![upper K](images/c14-i0891.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. This is absurd if ![upper L less-than upper K](images/c14-i0892.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>K</mi></math>. When ![upper L greater-than upper K](images/c14-i0893.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, we can sometimes see an artificial cluster containing points from at least two true clusters. In that case, ![script upper A 3 not-equals empty-set](images/c14-i0894.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math> still holds, and [Condition 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fea-0006) and the validity of ([14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0069)) essentially demand that the cluster variances be small and the distances between the true clusters be large, and the following argument works well particularly when ![script upper A 3 not-equals empty-set](images/c14-i0895.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math>. If ![script upper A 3 equals empty-set](images/c14-i0896.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8709;</mo></math>, especially when ![upper L greater-than upper K](images/c14-i0897.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>K</mi></math>, the clustering algorithm tends to carry out further splittings within true clusters; by combining [Condition 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fea-0006) with an additional condition regarding upper and lower bounds for all the variances of different components of ![bold x Subscript i](images/c14-i0898.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, we can still establish that ![r Subscript infinity Baseline left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis less-than r Subscript infinity Baseline left-parenthesis upper K right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0899.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> holds for any ![upper L greater-than upper K](images/c14-i0900.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>K</mi></math> too. For details of the overall result, we refer to our article [\[5\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0005).
    
    Next, we take a closer look at the respective bounds for the numerator and denominator of ([14.18](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0066)) under [Condition 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fea-0006) and the validity of ([14.19](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0069)). To this end, we first establish an upper bound for the expectation of the conditional variance given the true clusters:

## NOTES

1.  [1](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-note-0001) PCM is a method in signal processing used to digitally represent analog signals, where an analog signal is first sampled, and then each sample is discretized by a predefined set of bins. Finally, the discretized samples are encoded into binary codes.
2.  [2](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-note-0002) In *computational complexity theory*, an NP‐hard (non‐deterministic polynomial‐time hard) problem is characterized as follows: should an algorithm in polynomial time be developed for an NP‐hard problem, for all other problems where we can check the solution in polynomial time, we could also develop algorithms in polynomial time to solve the problem. A typical example of an NP‐hard problem is the *Travelling Salesman problem*.

# CHAPTER 15  
Applications of Deep Learning in Finance

 

Binary logistic regression, multinomial logits and classification trees as introduced in previous chapters are common statistical classifiers. A completely different approach is based on Neural Networks (NNs) which aim to mimic the functioning mechanism of human brains. Although how a human brain memorizes, recognizes patterns and generalizes concepts is still not thoroughly understood, some of its aspects are well‐known to neuroscientists, which helps to build a workable model for our brains as a NN.

In 1943, McCulloch and Pits [\[18\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0018) postulated a simple mathematical model to explain how biological neurons work. From then there was not much progress until 1970 when the modern computer was first invented. In the 1970s, *Linnainmaa Seppo* invented the *backpropagation* algorithm to train neural networks so as to match as much as possible the fitted output with the observed response [\[13](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0013), [14\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0014). There followed many successful examples and applications in the laboratories. In the 1980s, research moved from the labs to the commercial world, with typical applications being the detection of fraudulent credit card transactions, real estate appraisal, and data mining. Before we dive into NNs, we introduce some typical structures of our brains.

 

## 15.1 HUMAN BRAINS AND ARTIFICIAL NEURONS

Our brains consist of approximately 86 billion special cells known as neurons. Each of these neurons is typically connected with thousands of other neurons. Most importantly, unlike other cells, these neurons will not regenerate. It is widely accepted that these neurons are responsible for our ability for memorizing, learning, generalizing concepts and thinking. Within each neuron, there are four basic components: *dendrites*, the *cell body*, the *axon* and *synapses*; see [Figure 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0001). These neurons are connected to form a huge network. Though the exact function of these neurons is still a mystery, a simple mathematical model that mimics these neurons provides a surprisingly good performance in pattern recognition, classification and prediction problems in image processing and text mining.

![FIGURE 15.1 An illustration of the analogy between actual neurons and abstract ones. (Source: https://stock.adobe.com/in/images/cerebral-cortex-pyramidal-neuron/653658834)](images/c15f001.png)

[**FIGURE 15.1**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0001) An illustration of the analogy between actual neurons and abstract ones. (Source: [https://stock.adobe.com/in/images/cerebral-cortex-pyramidal-neuron/653658834](https://stock.adobe.com/in/images/cerebral-cortex-pyramidal-neuron/653658834))

![FIGURE 15.2 An artificial neuron.](images/c15f002.png)

[**FIGURE 15.2**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0002) An artificial neuron.

Dendrites are responsible for receiving information from other neurons; a cell body is for processing information collected; an axon amplifies the signal carried by the processed information to other neurons; and a synapse is the junction between axon end and those dendrites of other neurons. To mimic the functioning of a neuron, we refer to the artificial neuron as illustrated in [Figure 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002).

Here ![x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript p Baseline](images/c15-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> are the inputs received from other neurons or the outside environment. The total input ![h](images/c15-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> is formed from a linear combination of these inputs with weights ![w 1 comma ellipsis comma w Subscript p Baseline](images/c15-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> together with ![w 0](images/c15-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> serving as a *bias* term. The *transfer function* (or *activation function*) converts the input ![h](images/c15-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> of ![bold-italic x](images/c15-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> to the output ![h prime equals f left-parenthesis h right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In turn, this output ![h prime](images/c15-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> may go to other neurons as input. Some commonly used transfer functions for the axon are shown in [Figure 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0003).

![FIGURE 15.3 Commonly used activation functions for an axon.](images/c15f003.png)

[**FIGURE 15.3**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0003) Commonly used activation functions for an axon.

Very often, a logistic transfer function is used; that is why artificial neural network is considered as a significant extension of logistic regression.

 

## 15.2 FEEDFORWARD NETWORK

These artificial neurons are connected from one layer to another to form a network.

![FIGURE 15.4 Illustration of a 4‐3‐2 ANN.](images/c15f004.png)

[**FIGURE 15.4**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0004) Illustration of a 4‐3‐2 ANN.

Referring to [Figure 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0004), there are three layers: input, hidden and output layers. The numbers of neurons in the input, hidden and output layers are 4, 3 and 2 respectively; and so it is known as a 4‐3‐2 Artificial Neural Network (ANN).

1.  For a standard ANN, there is only one hidden layer. With more than one hidden layer, it is called a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP); see [Section 15.7](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0008) for a more detailed discussion on the latter.
2.  The numbers of neurons in the input and output layers are determined by the nature of the problem, while the number of neurons in the hidden layer is user‐defined.
3.  Within each layer, neurons are not connected with each other. Neurons in one layer are connected only with neurons in the next layer in the forward direction; this mechanism is called *feeding forward*.
4.  Each line joining two neurons, from the ![i](images/c15-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th neuron to the ![j](images/c15-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th neuron in the next layer, is associated with a weight ![w Subscript j i](images/c15-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>. These weights are unknown parameters to be estimated from a training dataset.

 

## 15.3 ANN WITH LINEAR OUTPUTS

Given the input ![bold-italic x](images/c15-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and the output ![bold-italic y](images/c15-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> in a training dataset, we aim to find the weights ![w Subscript j i](images/c15-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s such that the sum of squared error:

![upper E colon equals one half left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o prime right-parenthesis](images/c15-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

is minimized, where ![bold-italic o prime](images/c15-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> is the predicted label from the ANN; in particular, ![bold-italic o prime equals bold-italic o](images/c15-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi></math>, the directed output without an additional activation, if a linear output is generated. In general, the objective function ![upper E](images/c15-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> has many local minima, and usually the backpropagation algorithm, an iterative form of the usual stochastic gradient descent method, is used to find the “almost global” minimum. In Python, the `MLPRegressor()` (*Multiple Layer Perceptron Regressor*) function in the `sklearn` library can implement single‐layer or even multi‐layer ANN, as specified by the parameter `hidden_layer_sizes`. In particular, the logistic activation function is used in the hidden layer with the argument `activation` `="logistic"`, and 2 hidden neurons are used in the hidden layer with the parameter `hidden_layer_sizes=2` (If a 4‐3‐2‐1 model is used, we can set `hidden_layer_sizes=(3,2)`, however, the activation function used is uniformly the same across all hidden layers). In **R**, ANN can be implemented using the built‐in function `nnet()` inside the library `nnet`. We next illustrate the construction of an ANN with the Iris flower dataset in Programmes 15.1 and 15.2 via Python and **R**, respectively.

The above ANN is represented as the following [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005):

![FIGURE 15.5 Illustration of a 4‐2‐1 ANN.](images/c15f005.png)

[**FIGURE 15.5**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0005) Illustration of a 4‐2‐1 ANN.

As a remark, the coefficients of model trained by Python usually possess a much smaller magnitude than their counterparts trained by **R**; this is due to the presence of various underlying training mechanisms in Python, including but not limited to *batch normalization* (see [\[24\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0024)) and *dropout* (see [\[9\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009)) procedures, which helps to improve the robustness of the trained model. Nevertheless, in this particular example, the coefficients in the two models exhibit similar orders of magnitude, and hence we illustrate only the calculation for the model trained in **R** due to the page limit.

In Python, ![bold-italic o prime](images/c15-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> can be obtained via the `predict()` function, and we can produce the confusion matrix as shown in [Programme 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3003).

In **R**, ![bold-italic o prime](images/c15-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> is stored in `iris.nn$fitted.values`, and we can produce the confusion matrix as in [Programme 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3004).

We next try the HSI example in [Programme 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3005) via Python and [Programme 15.6](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3006) via **R**.

![FIGURE 15.6 The three solutions of four different initial seeds in the parameter space.](images/c15f006.png)

[**FIGURE 15.6**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0006) The three solutions of four different initial seeds in the parameter space.

A major problem of ANNs is that the solution of weights depends on the initial seeds. When we run `nnet()` each time, we may obtain different results. This is illustrated in [Figure 15.6](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0006), where the solid curve represents the loss function.

The error function ![upper E](images/c15-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>, while depending on the weights ![left-parenthesis w Subscript j i Baseline right-parenthesis Subscript i comma j](images/c15-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> of the ANN, contains a lot of local minima in the multi‐dimensional spaces in ![w Subscript j i](images/c15-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s. As `nnet()` randomly assigns an initial set of parameters ![w Subscript j i](images/c15-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> (*Xavier initialization* [\[5\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0005)) and uses backpropagation for minimizing the error function, the estimated ![w Subscript j i](images/c15-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>'s may only be a local minimum of the error function. Therefore, we usually run `MLPRegressor()` in Python (resp. `nnet()` in **R**) several times with different sets of initial seeds to attempt to obtain the “globally optimal” weights. See [Programme 15.7](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3007) via Python (resp. [Programme 15.8](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3008) via **R**) for an improven version of the function `MLPRegressor()` in Python (resp. `nnet()` in **R**).

This newly built function can specify the number of trials and save the best result; see [Programme 15.9](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3009) via Python (resp. [Programme 15.10](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3010) via **R**) for example.

 

## 15.4 ANN WITH LOGISTIC OUTPUTS

In the last section, the output is a linear function of the values from the neurons in the hidden layer, and it is a real number. When using this in a classification problem, like the Iris flower and HSI examples, we have to round the output to its nearest integer. However, we may use the default option `linout=False` in Python (resp. `linout=FALSE` in **R**) (but not `linout=True` now), then ![r](images/c15-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> different logistic functions are used to connect the neurons of the output layers and the final output. This can be interpreted as the probability of an observation with certain features belonging to a particular one out of ![r](images/c15-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> groups. Let us look at how to use this logistic output option in [Programme 15.11](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3011) via Python (resp. in [Programme 15.12](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3012) via **R**).

Note that the fitted values in the output have ![r](images/c15-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> columns, and the probability (final output) of the ![i](images/c15-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th observation, of a sample of size ![n](images/c15-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, belonging to the ![j](images/c15-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th group is

![o prime Subscript i j Baseline equals StartFraction exp left-parenthesis o Subscript i j Baseline right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript r Endscripts exp left-parenthesis o Subscript i k Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma n comma j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma r period](images/c15-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>r</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

Instead of looking for the least squares estimates for the weights and biases as in the linear output case in [Section 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0004), we here aim to minimize the so‐called *categorical cross‐entropy loss function*:

![upper E colon equals minus StartFraction 1 Over n EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript r Endscripts double-struck 1 Subscript left-brace y Sub Subscript i Subscript equals c Sub Subscript j Subscript right-brace Baseline ln o Subscript i j Superscript prime Baseline period](images/c15-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">1</mi><mrow><mo>&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#125;</mo></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

Normally speaking, we predict that the ![i](images/c15-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th observation belongs to group ![j](images/c15-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> if ![o prime Subscript i j](images/c15-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is maximum in the ![i](images/c15-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th row of (![o prime Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma o prime Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma o prime Subscript i r](images/c15-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>). It is clear that ![o prime Subscript i j](images/c15-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is the maximum if and only if ![o Subscript i j](images/c15-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the maximum. For **R** in particular, we assign the label to the `pred` column according to the maximum ![o prime Subscript i j](images/c15-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> among all ![j equals 1 comma ellipsis comma r](images/c15-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></math> in each row of `iris.nn$fit`, and notably, the resulting model yields no error out of 150 cases and the error rate is 0%!

Since in the Iris flower example, the output has three levels, the diagram for this ANN with logistic output is shown in [Figure 15.7](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0007):

Note that for logistic output, the output of the ![i](images/c15-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th record is

![o prime Subscript i j Baseline equals StartFraction e Superscript o Super Subscript i j Superscript Baseline Over 1 plus e Superscript o Super Subscript i j Superscript Baseline EndFraction equals double-struck upper P left-parenthesis normal y Subscript i Baseline equals c Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis comma j equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma r period](images/c15-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

We next illustrate with the HSI example. For this example, the output variable is binary (![r equals 2](images/c15-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>). The fitted value in the output can only have one column, say the probability of belonging to Group 1, then the probability of belonging to Group 2 is the one minus the former.

We assign the label to the `pred` column according to the probability given in `fin.nn$fit`. Note that there are only 2 error cases out of a total of 680 cases and the error rate is only ![0.29 percent-sign](images/c15-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0.29</mn><mi>%</mi></math>!

 

## 15.5 ADAPTIVE LEARNING RATE

In the old‐fashioned stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, the learning rate is fixed and uniform for the updates of all parameters. This is far from perfect, especially since the updates of less frequently occurring parameters are relatively slow. A better approach therefore is to take the current values of parameters into account and tune the learning rate accordingly. Roughly speaking, the learning rate for infrequently encountered parameters should be greater than that of frequently occurring ones. With this in mind, we introduce three commonly used variants of SGD in this section.

We first suppose that ![upper E left-parenthesis bold-italic w Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a loss function with respect to the parameter ![bold-italic w Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline equals left-parenthesis w 1 Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma w Subscript p Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c15-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> after ![t](images/c15-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> updates. For ![i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma p](images/c15-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></math>, also denote by ![g Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline colon equals StartFraction partial-differential upper E Over partial-differential w Subscript i Baseline EndFraction left-parenthesis bold-italic w Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and let ![eta](images/c15-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> be the starting learning rate.

**I. AdaGrad**

The *adaptive gradient method* (*AdaGrad*) adjusts the learning rate by dividing its starting value ![eta](images/c15-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> by the root of the sum of squares of the gradients. Mathematically, the update from ![w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> to ![w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is given by

[(15.3)](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-disp-0008)![w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline equals w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline minus StartFraction eta Over StartRoot sigma-summation Underscript s less-than-or-equal-to t Endscripts left-parenthesis g Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis s right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis squared plus epsilon EndRoot EndFraction g Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma p comma](images/c15-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#951;</mi><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![epsilon](images/c15-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is a small number to avoid division by zero.

This method is particularly suitable for handling sparse datasets in which the rates of update for both frequently and infrequently encountered parameters become comparable; indeed, as the gradient terms accumulate, the learning rate diminishes and by then the parameters cease to be updated.

**II. RMSprop**

To avoid the possibility of a vanishing learning rate (caused by truncation), *Geoffrey Hinton* suggested replacing the sum of square of historical gradients in ([15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0008)) by a moving average [\[8\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0008). This revised method is called the *root mean square propagation* (*RMSprop*); it starts with defining the second moment of gradient at time ![t](images/c15-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>:

![v Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline colon equals gamma v Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline plus left-parenthesis 1 minus gamma right-parenthesis left-parenthesis g Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis squared comma](images/c15-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![gamma element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c15-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. Then, the update of the parameter is given by

(15.4)![w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline equals w Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline minus StartFraction eta Over StartRoot v Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline plus epsilon EndRoot EndFraction g Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis Baseline period](images/c15-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#951;</mi><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>.</mo></math> 

Moreover, Hinton suggested that ![gamma equals 0.9](images/c15-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></math> and ![eta equals 0.001](images/c15-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></math> could be good candidates for an efficient algorithm.

**III. Adam**

The *adaptive moment estimation* (*Adam*) is another variant of SGD first introduced by *Diederik Kingma* and *Jimmy Ba* in 2015 [\[12\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012). It incorporates both the first and second moments of the gradients for parameter updates. Let ![m Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![v Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> respectively be the average of historical gradients and their squares of the ![i](images/c15-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th weight parameter with respective decay rates ![beta 1 comma beta 2 element-of left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; more precisely,

## 15.6 TRAINING NEURAL NETWORKS VIA BACKPROPAGATION

As seen in [Section 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0004), training a neural network is equivalent to finding the appropriate weight parameter ![bold-italic w](images/c15-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math> such that the loss function ![upper E equals one half left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o prime right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o prime right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is minimized, and this is achieved by using a backpropagation algorithm. Let us illustrate this approach by a simple 2‐2‐1 ANN with a linear output; also see [Figure 15.8](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0008) for an illustration.

Suppose the four sample input vectors, the target vector of the labels and the initial weights are as follows:

First, we compute the output from the ANN using the initial weights in [Programme 15.14](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3014) via Python (resp. [Programme 15.15](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3015) via **R**) as follows.

Next, we update the output layer weights `W2` and hidden layer weights `W1` in [Programme 15.16](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3016) via Python (resp. [Programme 15.17](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3017) via **R**) as follows.

Note that the new weights `new_W1` and `new_W2` are computed and the mean SSE decreases from 0.232 to 0.203. We can update the weights `W1` by `new_W1` and `W2` by `new_W2` based on the above programmes, and iterate them until the SSE is small enough or the maximum number of iteration is exceeded. Note that we can scale up the learning rate (`lr = 1.1*lr`) in the next iteration if the mean SSE decreases, or we can scale it down (`lr = 0.5*lr`) if the mean SSE increases.

Let us justify the above two programmes by providing the mathematical details of the backpropagation algorithm. Consider a general ![p](images/c15-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>‐![q](images/c15-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>‐![r](images/c15-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ANN with logistic transfer function ![f Subscript h](images/c15-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></math> (so ![f prime Subscript h Baseline equals f Subscript h Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus f Subscript h Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>) and linear output ![f Subscript o](images/c15-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></math>. The outputs of the hidden layer from the input variables are:

and from the hidden layer to the final linear output, they are:

The backpropagation algorithm is the typical gradient descent method applied to the network by working from the final output backward in time to the layer of input variables for minimizing the error function:

![upper E equals one half left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic y minus bold-italic o Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis equals one half sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript r Endscripts left-parenthesis y Subscript k Baseline minus o prime Subscript k right-parenthesis squared period](images/c15-math-0018.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">o</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>o</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>.</mo></math> 

Based on the law of total derivative, we first have, by viewing the matrix ![bold-italic upper W 1](images/c15-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> (resp. ![bold-italic upper W 2](images/c15-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>) as a vector after standard vectorization in machine learning,

![normal upper Delta upper E equals left-parenthesis StartFraction partial-differential upper E Over partial-differential bold-italic upper W 1 EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline normal upper Delta bold-italic upper W 1 plus left-parenthesis StartFraction partial-differential upper E Over partial-differential bold-italic upper W 2 EndFraction right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack Baseline normal upper Delta bold-italic upper W 2 period](images/c15-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math> 

The direction of ![left-parenthesis normal upper Delta bold-italic upper W 1 comma normal upper Delta bold-italic upper W 2 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> which can maximize the reduction of ![normal upper Delta upper E](images/c15-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>E</mi></math> by a unit change is along the negative direction of ![StartBinomialOrMatrix StartFraction partial-differential upper E Over partial-differential bold-italic upper W 1 EndFraction Choose StartFraction partial-differential upper E Over partial-differential bold-italic upper W 2 EndFraction EndBinomialOrMatrix](images/c15-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd class="array"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math>. The gradient descent algorithm for updating ![bold-italic upper W](images/c15-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></mrow></math> reads as:

## 15.7 MULTILAYER PERCEPTRON

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) (see [Figure 15.9](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0009)) is essentially a deep

We next illustrate the application of a MLP to stock price prediction. Unlike traditional time series models such as ARIMA and GARCH ones, some restrictive and unrealistic assumptions such as stationarity of the stock movements are not necessary for MLPs.

![FIGURE 15.9 Illustration of a multilayer perceptron. Each node is connected with the preceding (hidden) layer, over which a non‐linear activation function is applied. A linear transformation is carried within each node, with a (common) bias stored in a node disconnected from the preceding layers.](images/c15f009.png)

[**FIGURE 15.9**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0009) Illustration of a multilayer perceptron. Each node is connected with the preceding (hidden) layer, over which a non‐linear activation function is applied. A linear transformation is carried within each node, with a (common) bias stored in a node disconnected from the preceding layers.

**(I) Data source**

Stock price data are readily available at *Yahoo Finance* ([https://finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com)) or *Bloomberg* ([https://www.bloomberg.com/markets/stocks](https://www.bloomberg.com/markets/stocks)). Note that the prices quoted at Yahoo Finance are adjusted for share splits and dividend payments.

**(II) Data pre‐processing**

We use the past 900 price quotes, starting from 15 March 2016 to 9 October 2019, as the training dataset, and the remaining 358 price quotes, starting from 10 October 2019 to 12 March 2021, as the test dataset. For each security, every set of consecutive ten trading days of price quotes is used as the observation input ![bold-italic x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma x 10 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![x Subscript i](images/c15-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> stands for the price quote on the first ![i](images/c15-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th day of these ten consecutive days, and the immediate following 11th‐day price quote is considered as the label, i.e. ![y equals x 11](images/c15-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></math>. By then, the size of the training dataset is ![900 minus 10 plus 1 minus 1 equals 890](images/c15-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>900</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>890</mn></math>, and the size of the test dataset is ![358 minus 10 plus 1 minus 1 equals 348](images/c15-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>358</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>348</mn></math>, where the last observation only serves as the label. The training dataset is first shuffled and then fed into the MLP model to be specified below.

**(III) Model implementation**

For each stock, we use the prices over a period, now 10 consecutive days, as the input features to predict the next day's price, as a label, after the censored period, i.e. the 11th‐day price. We apply an MLP with 2 hidden layers each with 100 neurons. The activation function for each neuron is chosen to be the ReLU function, i.e. ![left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis Subscript plus](images/c15-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo></msub></math>. [Figures 15.10](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0010) and [15.11](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0011) illustrate the proposed MLP model.

**(IV) Backpropagation for parameter training**

As before, we consider the mean squared error as the individual loss function:
