**(V) Programming code in Python**

We here enclose the detailed programming code in Python for the present MLP model of stock price prediction; see [Programme 15.18](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3018).

Before we finish this section, we make some remarks on some relevant syntax and coding practice.

The `tensorflow` library has been widely used for deep learning in Python and **R**. It was first developed by the *Google Brain* team for their own internal use [\[1\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0001), and then it was released for public use in 2015. However, `tensorflow` itself is built from Python, C++, and CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture)

The `generate_dataset()` function receives two parameters, the `price` parameter takes in the training dataset as well as the test dataset, while the `seq_len` accepts an integer indicating the moving window width of input features, which is 10 in our stock price prediction example. This function returns two `numpy` arrays, the observations ![bold-italic x](images/c15-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and the label ![y](images/c15-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> for the dataset.

Next, the `MLP_stock` class object builds our MLP model. Under `tf.keras.models`, the `Sequential()` function builds a sequential/hierarchical model, which is composed of a plain stack of layers, where each layer has exactly one input tensor and one output tensor. For instance, our 10‐100‐100‐1 model is a sequential model, where all layers are stacked transversely along a horizontal axis. The `Dense()` function under `tensorflow.keras.layers` builds a *densely* or fully‐connected layer with the number of neurons being the first argument; the activation function is specified by the second argument `activation`, and here we adopted ReLU as the activation function, which can be imported by using `tf.nn.relu`, where `nn` stands for Neural Network, as expected. Finally, we configure our MLP model with `compile function`, where the Adam algorithm is chosen as the optimizer with a learning rate ![eta equals 0.01](images/c15-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></math> being specified by the command `lr=0.01` and MSE is used as the loss function with a specification through the command `loss="mse"`. We feed in the `train()` function with four parameters, namely (i) the observation of the training set `X_train`; (ii) the label of the training set `y_train`; (iii) minibatch size ![upper M](images/c15-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, by default set as `bs=32`; and (iv) the total number of models built, defaulted to be `ntry=5`. The purpose of this `train()` function is the same as the `ANNet()` function in [Programme 15.8](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3008) in **R**. Different initial seeds lead to different set of optimal weights and biases, and we need to try several times in order to obtain the best possible model. Since the most recent stock prices are more relevant to our next‐day prediction, the past ![50 plus 10 equals 60](images/c15-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></math> days are enough for evaluating the loss of our model. Finally, the `predict()` function accepts only one parameter, the observation of the test dataset as `X_test`. Lastly, we plot both the test label and the predicted label for each stock. The resulting plots for the prediction performance for different companies are shown in [Figure 15.12](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0012), from which the effectiveness of MLP is reasonably convincing.

![FIGURE 15.12 Predicting the day‐11 price for Anglo American (AAL), Goldman Sachs (GS), Meta (FB), and Morgan Stanley (MS) by using Programme 15.18 in Python.](images/c15f012.png)

[**FIGURE 15.12**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0012) Predicting the day‐11 price for *Anglo American* (AAL), *Goldman Sachs* (GS), *Meta* (FB), and *Morgan Stanley* (MS) by using [Programme 15.18](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3018) in Python.

 

## 15.8 UNIVERSAL APPROXIMATION THEOREM

As the previous discussions have shown, the input to each neuron not in the input layer is a weighted average of the output from the neurons in the preceding layer, which is in turn fed into a non‐linear activation function as its corresponding output. One common example of an activation function is a *sigmoid function*, which is an S‐shaped increasing function defined on all real numbers, such as the logistic function ![s left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis colon equals 1 slash left-parenthesis 1 plus e Superscript negative x Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a range of ![left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, or the hyperbolic tangent function ![hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis colon equals left-parenthesis e Superscript x Baseline minus e Superscript negative x Baseline right-parenthesis slash left-parenthesis e Superscript x Baseline plus e Superscript negative x Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">tanh</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a range of ![left-parenthesis negative 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>; see [Figure 15.13](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0013).

In practice, we often have to cope with different sophisticated functional relations between feature variables and response variables. An ANN can approximate these complex functions by using simple building blocks, namely the sigmoid neurons. Likewise, a deep neural network with a certain number of hidden layers can also achieve the same goal while also allowing for more flexibility for self‐adjustments. All of these are guaranteed by the celebrated *Universal Approximation Theorem*.

![FIGURE 15.13 Examples of sigmoid functions.](images/c15f013.png)

[**FIGURE 15.13**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0013) Examples of sigmoid functions.

The precise formulation of the theorem and its proof requires more advanced knowledge in *real analysis*, which we shall not discuss here. Nevertheless, we still illustrate the main idea behind its proof.

Consider the simple case when both input ![x](images/c15-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and output ![y](images/c15-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are in ![double-struck upper R](images/c15-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>, and the functional relation between ![x](images/c15-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and ![y](images/c15-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is ![y equals f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, such as in [Figure 15.14](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0014)a, for example. We approximate this function by a step function (see [Figure 15.14](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0014)b), such that each “step” can be considered as a simple function of the form ![double-struck 1 Subscript left-bracket x Sub Subscript i Subscript comma x Sub Subscript i plus 1 Subscript right-bracket](images/c15-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">1</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msub></math>, for some ![x Subscript i Baseline less-than x Subscript i plus 1](images/c15-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. The linear combination of these simple functions clearly can approximate ![f](images/c15-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> arbitrarily well by reducing the mesh size of the underlying partition of the real line.

![FIGURE 15.14 Illustration of approximating a function by simple functions.](images/c15f014.png)

[**FIGURE 15.14**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0014) Illustration of approximating a function by simple functions.

Consider two sigmoid functions ![h 1](images/c15-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![h 2](images/c15-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> with very steep slopes such that for a small ![delta greater-than 0](images/c15-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, ![h 1](images/c15-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> stays at 0 for any ![x less-than-or-equal-to negative delta](images/c15-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi></math>, but reaches 1 linearly at ![x equals negative delta slash 2](images/c15-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, and it remains constant thereafter. Similarly, ![h 2](images/c15-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> stays at 0 for any ![x less-than-or-equal-to delta slash 2](images/c15-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, but reaches 1 at ![x equals delta](images/c15-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#948;</mi></math> and remains constant thereafter, as seen in [Figures 15.15](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0015)a and [15.15](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0015)b. Then the function ![h colon equals h 1 minus h 2](images/c15-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> can approximately give us any one of the simple functions in [Figure 15.14](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0014)b as desired, as [Figure 15.15](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0015)c shows.

![FIGURE 15.15 Construction of a simple function.](images/c15f015.png)

[**FIGURE 15.15**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0015) Construction of a simple function.

Hence, for an input ![x](images/c15-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> being passed into two sigmoid neurons with respective activation functions ![h 1](images/c15-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![h 2](images/c15-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, if we apply the weights ![plus 1](images/c15-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![negative 1](images/c15-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> to them in the neuron in the next layer, we can obtain the desired approximation for one simple function. By combining several similar components, as in [Figure 15.16](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0016), we can approximate an arbitrary function ![f](images/c15-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>. Finally, note that by properly scaling the domain for the logistic or hyperbolic tangent function, either one can also well approximate ![h 1](images/c15-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> or ![h 2](images/c15-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. Therefore, the claim of the theorem follows, and this in some sense justifies the effective *representational power of deep neural networks* in general.

![FIGURE 15.16 A component in an ANN used to construct a rectangular partition.](images/c15f016.png)

[**FIGURE 15.16**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0016) A component in an ANN used to construct a rectangular partition.

 

## 15.9 LONG SHORT‐TERM MEMORY (LSTM)

*Long Short‐Term Memory* (LSTM) model is a kind of *recurrent neural network* (RNN). This DNN was designed to learn and store long‐term dependencies in temporal sequences. It was first introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber [\[10\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010). Since then, LSTM has been widely used in various sequence‐to‐sequence tasks, such as natural language processing, speech recognition, and time series prediction; also see [\[6](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006), [11](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0011), [15](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0015), [22\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0022).

The key ingredient in LSTM is the use of memory cells which enable the network to learn and remember long‐term dependencies. Each memory cell consists of three main components: an input gate, a forget gate, and an output gate; see [Figure 15.17](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0017) and more information in [\[10\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010). These gates control the flow of information within the cell, allowing the cell to selectively store, update, and retrieve information from its internal state. This gating mechanism helps to mitigate the *vanishing gradient problem*, which is a common issue in traditional RNNs [\[2\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0002). The input gate determines the extent to which new input data is stored in the cell state. The forget gate decides which parts of the cell state should be forgotten or retained, allowing the network to learn when to discard irrelevant information. Finally, the output gate controls the output of the cell based on its current state; more discussions can be found in [\[7](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0007), [10](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010), [23\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0023).

![FIGURE 15.17 A standard LSTM memory cell; also see \[20\].](images/c15f017.png)

[**FIGURE 15.17**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0017) A standard LSTM memory cell; also see [\[20\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0020).

1.  for this memory cell, ![bold-italic x Subscript t Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript p](images/c15-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> stands for the input feature vector at the present timestep ![t](images/c15-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>;
2.  matrices ![bold-italic upper W Subscript f Baseline comma bold-italic upper W Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic upper W Subscript c overTilde Baseline comma bold-italic upper W Subscript o Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q times p](images/c15-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> correspond to the weights of inputs ![bold-italic x Subscript t](images/c15-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> used for the forget gate, input gate, cell input and output gate, respectively;
3.  matrices ![bold-italic upper V Subscript f Baseline comma bold-italic upper V Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic upper V Subscript c overTilde Baseline comma bold-italic upper V Subscript o Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q times p](images/c15-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></math> correspond to the weights of the cell output activated value ![bold-italic h Subscript t minus 1](images/c15-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, fed from the one‐step delay of itself for the forget gate, input gate, cell input and output gate, respectively;
4.  vectors ![bold-italic b Subscript f Baseline comma bold-italic b Subscript i Baseline comma bold-italic b Subscript c overTilde Baseline comma bold-italic b Subscript o Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c15-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> correspond to the biases of the forget gate, input gate, cell input, and output gate, respectively;
5.  activation functions ![bold-italic g 1 comma bold-italic g 2 comma bold-italic sigma element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c15-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> are used for the cell input, cell output and all other gates, respectively. Typically, hyperbolic tangent function *tanh* is chosen for ![bold-italic g 1](images/c15-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold-italic g 2](images/c15-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>; while the logistic function can be adopted for ![bold-italic sigma](images/c15-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi></mrow></math>.

In an LSTM model, the cells are connected in a sequential manner, forming a recurrent neural network. A single cell receives the output of the cell state ![bold-italic c Subscript t minus 1 Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c15-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> and cell output ![bold-italic h Subscript t minus 1 Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript q](images/c15-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></math> from the previous time step as input, together with the input vector ![bold-italic x Subscript t](images/c15-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> from the current time. This connection allows information to flow from one cell to the next, enabling the model to capture long‐term dependencies in sequential data. To initialize the LSTM model, the cell state ![bold-italic c 0](images/c15-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and the cell output ![bold-italic h 0](images/c15-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> are often initialized with independent standard normals as a common practice of Xavier initialization. [Figure 15.18](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0018) illustrates this architecture.

LSTM has been further improven upon by the introduction of different variants, such as the *Gated Recurrent Unit* (GRU) [\[4\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0004) which simplifies the LSTM architecture by merging the input and forget gates. Another notable variant is the *Bidirectional LSTM* (BiLSTM) [\[21\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0021) which processes input sequences in both forward (from the beginning) and backward (from the end) directions, capturing information from both top‐down and bottom‐up contexts.

Lastly, we shall use [Figure 15.19](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0019) to motivate the idea of backpropagation in a multilayer LSTM model. For simplicity, consider the two‐layer LSTM model with the first layer containing ![q](images/c15-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> LSTM memory cells (each depicted by a square with a round arrow inside, standing for their recurrent nature), each outputting a real value, as shown in the left diagram of [Figure 15.19](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0019) in a compressed form; the input is a sequence of ![upper T equals 5](images/c15-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> temporal data each containing ![p equals 4](images/c15-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> features (these memory cells altogether form a ![q](images/c15-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> tensor of outputs). For the second layer, we just take one single memory cell with the input of (again) a sequence of ![upper T equals 5](images/c15-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> temporal data each containing ![q](images/c15-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> features from the first layer output with one real output by itself.

![FIGURE 15.18 Connections of cells in a LSTM model.](images/c15f018.png)

[**FIGURE 15.18**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0018) Connections of cells in a LSTM model.

![FIGURE 15.19 A two‐layer LSTM model with an equivalent unfolded representation for backpropagation.](images/c15f019.png)

[**FIGURE 15.19**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0019) A two‐layer LSTM model with an equivalent *unfolded representation* for backpropagation.

To consider the error propagation for this model, it is equivalent to consider the right diagram of [Figure 15.19](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0019) an *unfolded form*, so that the cells are connected in a more elaborated manner than those in [Figure 15.18](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0018). Therefore, schematically, training the right model of [Figure 15.19](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0019) is equivalent to coping with the error flows in [Figure 15.20](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0020). Particularly, to train an LSTM model, unlike a traditional DNN introduced before, the errors of the LSTM model can be backpropagated through both time (along horizontal direction) and layers (along vertical direction as for a DNN), where ![upper E Subscript t](images/c15-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is the individual loss function for each cell output ![bold-italic h Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis 2 right-parenthesis](images/c15-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>. Indeed, the dashed arrows represent the backpropagation process through layers, while the dash‐dotted arrows correspond to the backpropagation process through time. This means that during parameter training, the errors can flow through the LSTM model in both the layer and temporal directions. As the intricate calculus chain rules and formulas involved in the backpropagation process are beyond the scope of this book, we omit the details here but the underlying philosophy is actually the same as that of DNNs, the only difference is that there are two dimensions of error backpropagation for training LSTM compared to only one for DNN. We shall provide the details in our future book [\[3\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0003).

![FIGURE 15.20 LSTM backpropagation for the two‐layer model.](images/c15f020.png)

[**FIGURE 15.20**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0020) LSTM backpropagation for the two‐layer model.

 

### 15.9.1 Bitcoin Price Prediction

In [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0004), we fitted an ARIMA model for predicting the price of Bitcoin for the last quarter of the year 2018, except for the very last day 31 December 2018. We now illustrate an application of LSTM in using intraday minute data with `Open`, `High`, `Low`, `Close`, and `Volume`. In fitting a deep learning model, especially for RNN, the range of each feature will first be limited to a narrow space, so as to prevent the issue of the gradient exploding or vanishing in the implementation of the mini‐batch stochastic gradient descent method. Regarding this, we apply 1‐lag differencing to the prices of `Open`, `High`, `Low` and `Close`, and apply a natural logarithmic transformation to (![1 plus](images/c15-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></math>`Volume BTC`). Since the price process may exhibit rather different behaviours in the higher and lower price regions, an application of the 1‐lag differencing “stabilizes all price level components”. Then we shall add one additional feature variable of the *relative ratio of* the closing price in the current minute to that in the first minute of the training period at 00:00:00 on 01 Oct 2018. Note that while one usually uses the initial time points of the moving windows as the denominator of the aforementioned relative ratio, a simplified treatment by setting it to the starting point of the entire period will not cause much extra trouble thanks to the stability around a certain threshold of the price process. In fact it actually yields even better prediction results in this example. In our model, we propose using six feature variables (![p equals 6](images/c15-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>) to predict the closing prices per minute on the last day of 2018. We first lay down the codes for data cleansing in the following [Programme 15.19](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3019) via Python:

In the data cleansing process, we first remove all redundant feature variables, such as `unix` referring to the unit timestamp, `symbol` representing the cryptocurrency Bitcoin (BTC), and the underlying currency USD with entries `BTC/USD`, and `Volume USD` standing for the total trading volume in USD, which is simply the product of `close` (closing price) and `Volume BTC` (volume of transactions). Secondly, the intraday data are arranged in backward order in time, which means that the very last minute of 2018 intraday data serves as the first observation; we perform this step by using the command `::‐1`. As mentioned before, the price variables are large in magnitude, so we perform 1‐lag differencing that subtracts the previously observed price from the current observed one, while we also put ![ln left-parenthesis 1 plus](images/c15-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></math>`Volume BTC`) in place. Lastly, the parameter `seq_len` in the `generate_dataset()` function denotes the length of each input sequence block, i.e., ![upper T](images/c15-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> minutes of intraday data are used to predict the closing price in the next minute ![upper T plus 1](images/c15-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

*Dropout*, first proposed in [\[9\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009), is a regularization technique, which results in essentially the same effect as regularization for regression, as mentioned in [Chapter 11](#c11.xhtml). It is commonly used in deep neural networks to prevent overfitting and improve generalization to out‐samples. During the training phase, a fraction of the units are randomly selected to halt their functioning by setting their corresponding outputs to zero; in other words, they are temporarily “dropped out” from the processing procedure. This introduces stochastics into the system yet reduces the interdependencies among the LSTM units, henceforth forcing the network to learn more robust and generalized representations. By randomly dropping units, dropout prevents individual units from relying too heavily on specific input patterns or co‐adapting with other units. This encourages the network to learn more diverse and independent features, enhancing its ability to generalize unseen data. Loosely speaking, to understand the concept of dropout heuristically, one can imagine a factory with many workers. They work collaboratively on a given “massive” production procedure, so that each of the small duties for each worker is relatively simple while each worker needs not just work on one single service but could work on few; nevertheless, each worker is still responsible for one single simple duty. This massive production therefore is composed of a huge number of small tasks, and a few workers are responsible for each portion of the whole production. Certainly, different workers have different strengths and weaknesses, and they will affect the overall quality of the final output. For instance, a careless worker may make mistakes at an early stage of the production, and other workers in the subsequent stages may worsen the situation and fail to rescue the overall quality of the final output. Therefore, as a rule of thumb, in order to raise the quality of production, a successful factory should have workers that are able to collaborate with any others despite their relative weakness at the time, and the latter can be trained up by learning from the other capable workers. Similarly, in LSTM, if one LSTM unit outputs a “wrong” value, due to the highly connected network structure, all subsequent LSTM units cannot avoid making poorer predictions. That means different units have different prediction powers; as in the factory analogy above, a model can become more stable if most of its weaker units can learn from those more capable ones by a smaller grouped training. With the dropout layer mechanism, each unit has a chance to learn to work closely with a portion, around ![1 minus d](images/c15-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi></math> where ![d](images/c15-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the dropout ratio, of other units in different layers. This normally increases the overall performance of each unit, and breaks the co‐adaptation issue so that the units can now be less dependent on each other, and therefore reduce any possible redundancy of each unit by encouraging them to exercise in full power.

We shall build a two‐layer LSTM model with the first and second layers containing ![p](images/c15-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c15-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> one‐tensor LSTM memory cells, respectively, for the predictions of Bitcoin price. In particular, the number of one‐tensor memory cells ![p](images/c15-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![q](images/c15-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> in the two layers are known as hyperparameters. There are a large number of hyperparameters to be determined for the LSTM model. Other hyperparameters include, for example, the length of the input sequence ![upper T](images/c15-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, and the dropout ratio ![d](images/c15-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> for each LSTM layer. In order to pick the correct set of hyperparameters, the only option available is to try them one by one. However, this approach can be extremely time‐consuming and inefficient. In practice, we can limit the set of possible candidates and obtain a sub‐optimal set among them by comparing the corresponding loss computed from a validation dataset. The validation dataset should be independent of the training dataset, and must not be used in training. In this example, we consider the following choices of hyperparameters: (i) ![upper T equals 5 comma 10 comma 15](images/c15-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn></math>; (ii) ![p comma q equals 8 comma 16 comma 32](images/c15-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></math>, corresponding to the number of memory cells for each LSTM layer; and (iii) ![d 1 comma d 2 equals 0 comma 0.2 comma 0.4](images/c15-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn></math>, corresponding to the dropout ratio in the first and second LSTM layer, respectively. We shall randomly draw 10% of the training data as validation data (In Python, this is done by stating `validation_split=0.1` when calling `fit()`), the candidate (![upper T equals 10](images/c15-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, ![q equals 16](images/c15-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math>, ![r equals 32](images/c15-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></math>, ![d 1 equals 0](images/c15-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and ![d 2 equals 0.4](images/c15-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></math>) achieves the lowest MSE on the validation dataset. Therefore, we shall employ this set of hyperparameters for our LSTM model based on the MSE of the validation data. Finally, we shall train our LSTM model with the full training dataset using `tensorflow`.

If we naïvely use the average of Bitcoin prices from the training dataset to predict prices in the test dataset, the mean squared error (MSE) of the out‐sample predictions is 19.722. In contrast, when we employ a 6‐8‐8‐1 LSTM model with the architecture as shown in [Figure 15.21](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0021), the MSE decreases to 19.171, indicating that the LSTM model can achieve better prediction performance compared to a simple constant value, and even slightly outperform the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 3](images/c15-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></math>) model with an MSE of 19.249 using Python and the fitted ARIMA(![2 comma 1 comma 2](images/c15-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) model with an MSE of 19.261 using **R**. On the other hand, the MSE of the in‐sample predictions based on the average of Bitcoin prices from the training dataset is 25.927. When we evaluate the in‐sample predictions of the LSTM model, the MSE is reduced to 25.491, which has a similar reduction compared to the corresponding out‐sample prediction. Therefore, the representation power of this network can be improven by applying dropouts in the second LSTM layer. To visualize the price predictions over time for the test dataset, the following [Programme 15.21](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3021) (via Python) plots the predictions in [Figure 15.22](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0022) obtained from fitting the LSTM model in [Programme 15.20](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-3020) (via Python).

![FIGURE 15.21 A 6‐8‐8‐1 LSTM model for Bitcoin price predictions.](images/c15f021.png)

[**FIGURE 15.21**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0021) A 6‐8‐8‐1 LSTM model for Bitcoin price predictions.

![FIGURE 15.22 Plot of Bitcoin price predictions via LSTM.](images/c15f022.png)

[**FIGURE 15.22**](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0022) Plot of Bitcoin price predictions via LSTM.

As a concluding remark, the example shows the best performance occurs in the presence of dropout, and LSTM models without a dropout layer may not always be optimal for prediction tasks due to the potential for overfitting. Nevertheless, they are still effective in detecting *market anomalies* or capturing exceptional patterns within financial numerical data by involving more convoluted information contained in a long temporal series from the present back to the past. This possible success relies typically on employing an effective and robust feature extraction procedure, such as signature methods in the *theory of rough paths*; see [\[16](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0016), [17](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0017), [19\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0019) for more discussion, and we may explore more in our future book [\[3\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0003).

# Postlude

 

We have introduced different useful tools in financial data analytics in a rather independent way throughout different chapters. In reality, there is no single “silver bullet” that works best for every aspect of any single question, and all methods have their own pros and cons. To this end, it is important to understand the similarities and differences among them, and choose the approach best tailor‐made for a specific context. Take the estimation of the drift ![mu](images/both-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> in the calibration of the Kelly fraction as discussed in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml): while the trading strategy with the aid of Bollinger bands does lead to a decent performance that remedies the less accurate real‐life estimation of ![mu](images/both-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, it can still be further improven by using the regressor version of CIBer in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml). In particular, as CIBer can handle the categorical data in financial reports in addition to the numerical information from various security prices and control indices, it can yield an even better estimate of ![mu](images/both-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, which in turn allows the formulation of more profit‐making trading strategies even without the assistance of Bollinger bands.

We have reached the end of this book, but certainly not the end of our journey of exploration into financial data analytics. We hope that this book can nurture you, our readers, with the mindset to establish connections among all the approaches, and analyze each problem in a multifaceted manner via the use of a wide spectrum of methods, which will undoubtedly involve more advanced techniques to be formulated by future generations. Nevertheless, the core ingredients inside this rapid evolution, including the importance of mathematics, statistics, and metaprogramming, will stay unchanged over time.
